    Act

    IL HB5552 — School Code omnibus rewriting educator licensure, testing exemptions and the Preparation & Licensure Board, signed as Public Act 104-0803

    The statutory machinery governing Relay's Illinois program is now rewritten and in force, not pending. The section-by-section read of the enrolled text (see

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionIllinois
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationAct · impact 88
    Latest actionGovernor Approved 2026-08-07; Effective Date August 7, 2026; Public Act 104-0803. Verified from the ilga.gov bill-status action list this run. This supersedes last run's reading that the bill would become law by constitutional default on 2026-08-24 — it was signed on August 7, seventeen days ahead of that date, and is already in force. · 2026-08-07
    SourceIllinois General Assembly (ilga.gov bill status, action list, and synopsis) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    The statutory machinery governing Relay's Illinois program is now rewritten and in force, not pending. The section-by-section read of the enrolled text (see text_analysis) stands: the direction is predominantly loosening — a new provisional educator endorsement for out-of-state and out-of-country trained applicants, content-test reciprocity, coursework exemptions, and assessment exemption windows extended a year. The State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board's appointments move from the State Board of Education to the State Superintendent, which is governance rather than standards. Because the Act is effective immediately, the provisional-endorsement and reciprocity pathways are available to candidates now, and the open question moves entirely to ISBE's implementing rules.

    What it does

    Omnibus School Code rewrite signed by Governor Pritzker on 2026-08-07 as Public Act 104-0803, effective the same day. It amends the departments and functions of the Illinois State Board of Education, the teacher supply and demand report, the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board, the qualifications of educators, provisional educator endorsements on Educator Licenses with Stipulations, educator testing exemptions, the Teacher Performance Assessment Advisory Committee, and teacher and principal model evaluation templates. It also touches evidence-based funding, charter school renewals, waivers and modifications of mandates and administrative rules, school district audits and statements of affairs, the Illinois Purchased Care Review Board, and provisions for students who are parents, expectant parents, or victims of domestic or sexual violence. It renames the Teacher Certificate Fee Revolving Fund the Teacher Licensure Fee Revolving Fund, replaces 'foreign language' with 'world language' and 'ethnic school' with 'community-based heritage language school', repeals the Community Service Education Act, and makes conforming changes to the Postsecondary and Workforce Readiness Act, the State Finance Act, and various public-university governance Acts. Roll calls as printed in the ILGA action list: House Third Reading 071-034-000 (2026-04-09), Senate Third Reading 043-014-000 (2026-05-20), House concurrence in Senate Committee Amendment No. 1, 074-037-000 (2026-05-27).

    Implications

    • Program. The new provisional educator endorsement (105 ILCS 5/21B-20(2)(P)) and the 21B-35 reciprocity exemptions are live as of 2026-08-07 — no waiting period. Fold both into Illinois admissions and candidate advising now; the recruiting window for out-of-state-trained teachers opened this month, not in September.

    • Compliance. Relay's Illinois program approval now sits under a board whose members and secretary are appointed by the State Superintendent rather than the State Board of Education. Update the relationship map; the approval standards themselves are unchanged in the sections read.

    • Advocacy. The veto question is closed. Remaining advocacy surface is downstream ISBE rulemaking — the rules implementing the provisional endorsement, the content-test reciprocity exemption, and the coursework-checklist exemption. Watch the Illinois Register for those proposals.

    • Risk. Districts may now seek waivers from the mandate that student-performance data be a significant factor in teacher and principal evaluations (the 2-3.25g deletion). If uptake spreads, evaluation practice in partner districts could drift away from Relay's training content.

    Leader brief

    Illinois: the teacher-licensing rewrite is now law, and it eases entry routes (IL HB5552)

    The sweeping Illinois education bill we have been tracking was signed by the Governor on August 7 and took effect the same day, as Public Act 104-0803. It is now law seventeen days earlier than our last briefing projected, which assumed it would pass into law automatically on August 24 without a signature. Our section-by-section read of the final text holds: the changes mostly make it easier, not harder, to become a teacher in Illinois. There is a new two-year provisional credential for teachers trained in other states or countries, recognition of licensing tests already passed elsewhere, and fewer duplicate coursework requirements. Oversight of the board that approves teacher-preparation programs like Relay's moves from the State Board of Education to the State Superintendent.

    • Nothing in the law raises barriers for Relay's Illinois program, and several changes work in our favor — especially the new on-ramp for teachers trained out of state, a pool a national program reaches better than most in-state ones. Because the law is already in effect, this is operational work with no runway: Illinois admissions and candidate advising should reflect the new credential and test-recognition rules for the cohort being recruited now.

    Questions to ask

    • The law is in force today rather than on August 24 — does that pull anything forward for the current Illinois recruiting cycle, and who owns updating admissions and advising materials?

    • Should Illinois relationship-building shift toward the State Superintendent's office, which now appoints the board that approves our program?

    • The practical details now sit in state agency rules that have not been written yet. Do we want to be a voice in that rulemaking, and if so, who carries it?

    Act

    TN Public Chapter 1133 — private child care programs become eligible educator-preparation clinical sites, but only for EPPs running an approved registered apprenticeship

    Tennessee is one of the five states where Relay has deep partnerships, and this act sets a condition on who may host clinical practice for a birth-to-K

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionTennessee
    ClassBill
    StagePassed · Enacted; rulemaking authority live since 2026-05-22, substantive provisions since 2026-07-01. Next expected event: State Board of Education rules under the Uniform Administrative Procedures Act — no filed rule observed this run (tn.gov SBE meetings page returned 404 to a plain client; not confirmed either way). Task force report due 2026-12-31.
    RecommendationAct · impact 81
    Latest actionComp. became Pub. Ch. 1133; effective 2026-05-22 and 2026-07-01 · 2026-05-27
    Sourcelegiscan_tn · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Tennessee is one of the five states where Relay has deep partnerships, and this act sets a condition on who may host clinical practice for a birth-to-K endorsement: only an educator preparation program operating a Department-approved registered apprenticeship unlocks the new private child care site pool. That is a direct program-design lever — the apprenticeship is the key, not the endorsement. The task force's December 31 report is the second surface: it is explicitly permitted to draw on nonprofit organizations, and it will name the gaps that later funding follows.

    What it does

    HB2426 / SB2404, passed 2026-04-21 and approved by the Governor in May 2026 as Public Chapter 1133. Section 2 adds a new section to Tenn. Code Ann. Title 49, Chapter 5, Part 56 directing the State Board of Education to promulgate rules creating a pathway for privately operated child care programs (as defined in 49-1-1102) and licensed child care agencies (as defined in 71-3-501) serving children from birth to kindergarten enrollment to be approved as CLINICAL PRACTICE SITES for an educator preparation program offering a birth-to-kindergarten endorsement on the initial license. The pathway is conditional: the educator preparation program must operate a registered apprenticeship program approved by the Department of Education, and the site must be either a DHS-licensed child care agency or a child care program certified, approved or otherwise authorized by the Department of Education, and must meet the State Board's clinical-experience requirements and standards. Rules are to be promulgated under the Uniform Administrative Procedures Act. Section 1 creates an early educator workforce development resource task force chaired by the Commissioner of Labor and Workforce Development, which must catalog existing state-supported routes into early education (Tennessee Promise, Tennessee Reconnect, career and technical education and dual enrollment, registered apprenticeships for aspiring early educators, federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act funds, and Workforce Pell), assess gaps including those left by discontinued programs, and report findings and recommendations to the Governor and legislative committees by 2026-12-31, at which point the task force ceases to exist. Members serve without compensation and the task force may draw on nonprofit or community-based organizations for stakeholder engagement and data collection. Section 3 makes Section 1 and the rulemaking authority in Section 2 effective on becoming law (2026-05-22); Section 2 takes effect for all other purposes on 2026-07-01.

    Implications

    • Program. A Department-approved registered apprenticeship program is the entry condition for the new clinical-site pool. If Relay Tennessee wants birth-to-K clinical placements in private child care settings, the apprenticeship is the prerequisite to build, not an optional add-on.

    • Partnership. Private child care providers and licensed child care agencies become a viable placement network for the first time, which is a different partner set from the LEA and charter relationships Relay already holds in Tennessee.

    • Advocacy. The State Board rules are unwritten. What counts as a qualifying registered apprenticeship, and what clinical-experience standards a child care site must meet, are both open.

    • Funding. The task force must report by 2026-12-31 on gaps in early-educator training and credentialing, naming Workforce Pell and Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act dollars among the resources to be better leveraged. Gap findings in that report are where the next Tennessee early-educator funding is most likely to attach.

    Leader brief

    Tennessee opened private child care centers as training sites for early-childhood teacher candidates — but only for programs that run an apprenticeship

    Tennessee enacted a law in May that does two things. It ordered the State Board of Education to write rules letting private child care centers and licensed child care agencies serve as approved clinical practice sites — the settings where teacher candidates do their supervised student teaching — for programs that prepare teachers for a birth-through-kindergarten credential. There is a condition: only a preparation program that runs a registered apprenticeship approved by the state Department of Education can use those sites. It also created a temporary state task force that must report by December 31, 2026 on what is missing in Tennessee's pipeline for early educators. The State Board has not yet written the rules.

    • If we want to prepare birth-through-kindergarten teachers in Tennessee using private child care placements, the registered apprenticeship is the gate we have to pass through first. Separately, the task force report is the document that will shape where Tennessee's next early-educator dollars go, and it is due in four and a half months.

    Questions to ask

    • Is a birth-through-kindergarten pathway in Tennessee something we want, given the apprenticeship infrastructure it now requires?

    • Do we have a route to the State Board of Education while the clinical-site rules are still being drafted?

    • Should we be a named contributor to the task force's stakeholder engagement, which the law expressly allows nonprofits to support?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Stipend-for-student-teaching would change residency economics in a deep Relay state; the enacted licensure act needs a text read for cert-requirement changes.

    What it does

    Illinois passed SB1947 (educator licensure, Public Act, 2025-08-01) and HB1375 (student-teaching stipend) is engrossed; Grow-Your-Own and licensure bills pending (per LegiScan).

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Illinois has an enacted educator-licensure law we still have not read, and a student-teaching stipend bill part-way through

    This item sits in the ACT lane because the mechanical scorer promoted it there this run; the underlying facts have not changed since it was last reviewed. Brief written on promotion. Illinois enacted SB1947, a law amending educator licensure, in August 2025. A separate bill, HB1375, which would pay stipends to student teachers, has passed one chamber. Other Grow-Your-Own and licensure bills are pending. Our record of SB1947 comes from a legislative database summary; nobody has read the statute text to establish what it actually changed about certification requirements.

    • Illinois is one of Relay's deepest jurisdictions, so an unread licensure statute is a real gap rather than a housekeeping note. A student-teaching stipend, if it becomes law, changes the economics of residency in that state — candidates in unpaid placements are the constraint on who can afford to enter the profession.

    Questions to ask

    • Should someone read SB1947 in full to establish whether any Relay Illinois program requirement changed?

    • If HB1375 passes, does it change how Relay recruits or finances Illinois residents?

    CommentComment

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is a direct rewrite of what Relay's registered New York programs in childhood education, students with disabilities and any ESOL/bilingual-extension offerings must teach and how their clinical placements must be structured, with a September 1, 2028 compliance date and a residency-specific clause: the entire student teaching or residency experience must include teaching and assessing reading and writing. The comment window is the first and only formal input point before the Regents adopt in October. Never on the board: the rule was published July 29 while the NYSED newsroom source was down and the State Register is not a wired source; found by the cross-engine sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 29 issue.

    What it does

    Proposed rulemaking EDU-30-26-00007-P, published in the July 29, 2026 State Register (no hearing; 60-day comment period, so comments are due September 27, 2026; the Register text and the NYSED full-text index both list the rule and neither prints a calendar deadline, so the date is computed from publication). Amends §52.21 program-registration requirements for teacher preparation programs in bilingual education, early childhood (birth-grade 2), childhood (grades 1-6), ESOL, literacy, and special education (blind/visually impaired, deaf/hard-of-hearing, speech and language disabilities, students with disabilities at every level). Requires the study of literacy skills or methods of teaching reading in those programs to align with the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including theories of literacy development, evidence-based instruction, assessment and intervention through a multi-tier framework, and dyslexia, dysgraphia and other language-based learning disabilities (definitions, detection, screener administration, evidence-based instruction, accommodations for ELLs); removes the 'methods of reading enrichment and remediation' language. Clinical requirements for candidates first enrolling Fall 2028 or later: at least 15 of the 100 field-experience clock hours must include evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with one or more students with reading difficulties, and candidates must teach reading and writing throughout the student teaching or residency experience (70 days or longer), assessing learning in whole-group and small-group settings; literacy programs must spend at least 25 of 50 practicum hours the same way. Programs must comply by September 1, 2028 or at new-program registration, whichever is first. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs must add three semester hours in language acquisition and literacy development (six to nine total) for candidates first enrolling Fall 2029 or later; §80-3.7 makes the same 6 → 9 change for the individual-evaluation certification pathway from September 1, 2033. The notice states SWD programs in childhood and adolescence will no longer be registered on or after September 1, 2029. Cost statement names $1,335 CUNY tuition per three-credit course and $7,100 per adjunct literacy course as illustrative private-party costs. Permanent adoption anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Grounded in the Hunt Institute Path Forward initiative (NY joined Fall 2023) and the December 2024 NYS Dyslexia and Dysgraphia Task Force report.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Every affected Relay New York program (childhood, students with disabilities, and ESOL or bilingual extension if registered) must show literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including dyslexia and dysgraphia content, by September 1, 2028 or at the next new-program registration, whichever comes first.

    • Program. For candidates enrolling Fall 2028 or later, 15 of the 100 pre-student-teaching field hours must involve evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with a struggling reader, and the residency itself must include teaching and assessing reading and writing throughout, in whole-group and small-group settings; Relay's residency design and partner-school placements will need to guarantee that exposure for secondary-leaning placements too.

    • Program. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs gain a three-credit language-acquisition-and-literacy course for Fall 2029 entrants (six to nine credits total); the notice also says SWD childhood and adolescence programs stop being registered after September 1, 2029, which bears on how Relay's special-education offerings are structured in New York.

    • Advocacy. Comments are open through September 27 to the Office of Higher Education; a program-level comment from Relay could address the residency-wide literacy clause for adolescence and secondary placements, the clock-hour accounting, and the 2028/2029 phase-in.

    • Funding. The cost statement anticipates new coursework and literacy-expert instructors for registered programs; Relay would bear curriculum-development and faculty cost for the affected New York programs.

    Leader brief

    New York wants every teacher preparation program that touches reading to teach the science of reading, and the comment period closes September 27

    Update September 21: four business days remain. Comments are formally due Sunday, September 27, which in practice means filing by Friday, September 25. The New York State Education Department has proposed a rule that would rewrite the literacy requirements for teacher preparation programs in childhood education, early childhood, special education, English as a second language, bilingual education and literacy. Coursework on teaching reading would have to follow the state's Science of Reading Framework, including specific content on dyslexia and related disabilities. Starting with students who enroll in fall 2028, a set share of pre-service field hours would have to be spent teaching a struggling reader, and the student-teaching or residency year would have to include teaching and assessing reading and writing throughout. Special-education programs would add a three-credit literacy course for students who enroll in fall 2029. Programs would have until September 1, 2028 to comply. The Board of Regents is expected to adopt the rule in October; public comments are being accepted until September 27.

    • Relay's New York programs in childhood education and special education fall squarely within the rule, and any ESOL or bilingual offering does too. The residency clause matters most: Relay's residency model would need to guarantee that every affected resident teaches and assesses reading and writing across the year, which is straightforward for elementary placements and harder for some secondary and special-education placements. Curriculum revisions and literacy-qualified instructors would be needed before the 2028 deadline, and the comment window is the only formal chance to shape the phase-in and the residency language.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay submit a comment by September 27, and if so on which points: the residency-wide literacy requirement, the clock-hour accounting, or the 2028 and 2029 phase-in dates?

    • How far is Relay's current New York literacy coursework from the state's Science of Reading Framework, and who owns the gap analysis?

    • Do any of Relay's New York special-education programs sit in the childhood or adolescence categories that the state says it will stop registering after September 2029?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Worth one line as a correction, not as movement: the licensure content Relay would care about is no longer in this bill. Anyone tracking Illinois early-childhood alternative endorsement should know the vehicle was hollowed out and the House refused to go along. The bill sits mid-concurrence with the 104th General Assembly still in session, so the shell could in principle be revived, but nothing has moved since 2026-05-30.

    What it does

    As introduced and as passed the House 101-000-000 on 2026-04-17, HB4795 would have amended the Educator Licensure Article of the School Code to let the State Board issue a National Board certification–early childhood generalist endorsement on an Educator License with Stipulations to any holder of a valid NBPTS Early Childhood Generalist certificate, deeming that holder qualified to teach pre-kindergarten and to meet or exceed the State Board's early childhood instructional competency requirements, with the endorsement valid to 2029-06-30 and an ISBE report to the General Assembly due 2029-01-01. Senate Floor Amendment No. 1 (Lightford), adopted 2026-05-30, replaced everything after the enacting clause with an unrelated provision repealing the requirement that students entering 9th grade complete two years of foreign language courses as a high school graduation prerequisite beginning in 2028-29. The Senate passed the gutted bill 055-000-000 the same day; Rep. Ammons filed a motion to non-concur in the House on 2026-05-30, which is the last recorded action.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    An Illinois early-childhood licensure route was removed from its own bill; this is a correction, not movement

    This item sits in the ACT lane because the mechanical scorer promoted it there this run; the underlying facts have not changed since it was last reviewed. Brief written on promotion. HB4795 originally would have let Illinois issue an early-childhood endorsement to anyone holding a National Board Early Childhood Generalist certificate, treating that as meeting the state's early-childhood competency requirements through mid-2029. The House passed it unanimously in April. In May a Senate floor amendment replaced the entire bill with an unrelated provision repealing a high-school foreign-language graduation requirement. The House refused to agree. The licensure content Relay would care about is no longer in this bill.

    • Anyone tracking an Illinois early-childhood alternative endorsement should know the vehicle was emptied out. The General Assembly is still in session and the shell could in principle be revived, but nothing suggests it will be.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay have an interest in an Illinois early-childhood alternative endorsement worth pursuing through a different vehicle?

    CO SB26-126 — out-of-state teacher licensure opened: 7-year recency limit repealed, 30-day Compact licensing with no added coursework, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 67)

    This cuts both ways for Relay and the honest read holds both. Subsection (6)(b) forbids Colorado from requiring additional program completions of Compact-state

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionColorado
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationAct · impact 75
    Latest actionGovernor signed 2026-04-20 (signed act document dated 2026-04-21); Session Laws Chapter 67; effective 12:01 a.m. 2026-08-12 (ninety days after sine die adjournment on 2026-05-13), subject to referendum petition. Verified this run from leg.colorado.gov: bill page status 'Became Law', session-law effective-date table, and the Final Act text. · 2026-08-12
    SourceColorado General Assembly (leg.colorado.gov bill page SB26-126; Final Act text, bill_files/114203; Session Laws Ch. 67) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This cuts both ways for Relay and the honest read holds both. Subsection (6)(b) forbids Colorado from requiring additional program completions of Compact-state licensees at initial issuance, which is a straightforward reduction in demand for Colorado-specific preparation among already-licensed teachers. At the same time, a national, multi-state, primarily-online provider benefits more than an in-state one from a regime where a license earned in one state travels cleanly: Relay completers licensed elsewhere gain a fast, thirty-day path into Colorado classrooms, and the removal of the seven-year recency limit helps career-changers and returners, a population Relay's model already serves. The annual endorsement-crosswalk table is a concrete artifact worth obtaining as soon as CDE first publishes it — it will state, officially, how licenses Relay's completers hold map onto Colorado endorsements.

    What it does

    Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 67 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act amends C.R.S. 22-60.5-201 to widen two routes into a Colorado teacher license for people licensed elsewhere. First, it removes the requirement that the three years of successful, evaluated out-of-state teaching experience supporting a professional teacher license have occurred within the previous seven years, so older experience now counts. Second, it adds a new subsection (6) requiring the Department of Education to issue an INITIAL teacher license within thirty days of receiving a complete application from a person licensed by a state participating in the Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact, where the applicant holds an unencumbered eligible license equivalent to a Colorado eligible license, is not subject to current disciplinary action, suspension, investigation or restriction, and has cleared a Colorado criminal history record check. Critically, subsection (6)(b) bars the department from requiring any additional coursework, examinations or program completions beyond those three conditions as a condition of INITIAL license issuance, while expressly preserving its authority to require them for license RENEWAL. The department must determine which Colorado endorsement areas most closely correspond to the applicant's out-of-state license, and must publish an annual table mapping licenses from each reciprocal-agreement state to Colorado endorsement areas. Subsection (6) self-repeals once the department begins issuing licenses under the Compact itself.

    Implications

    • Risk. Subsection (6)(b) prohibits Colorado from requiring additional coursework, examinations or program completions of Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact licensees at initial issuance. For already-licensed teachers moving into Colorado, that removes a route by which preparation providers pick up incremental enrollment.

    • Program. Relay completers licensed in a Compact state now have a statutory thirty-day path to a Colorado initial license. A multi-state footprint becomes a recruiting argument in Colorado in a way it was not before.

    • Program. Repeal of the seven-year recency limit on the three-years-experience route reopens the professional-license path for career-changers and re-entrants whose classroom experience is older — a population that maps onto Relay's candidate profile.

    • Compliance. The department may still require additional coursework, examinations or program completions as a condition of license RENEWAL. Advising should distinguish the initial-issuance bar from renewal requirements rather than treating Compact entry as a permanent exemption.

    • Advocacy. CDE must publish an annual table mapping each reciprocal state's licenses to Colorado endorsement areas. Obtaining the first published table establishes how Relay completers' credentials are officially classified, and the table's construction is a reasonable point of engagement.

    Leader brief

    Colorado: licensed teachers from other states can now enter Colorado classrooms faster, and without extra coursework (CO SB26-126)

    A Colorado law in force since August 12 makes it substantially easier for a teacher already licensed in another state to get a Colorado license. If the teacher is licensed in a state belonging to the Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact — an agreement among states to recognise each other's teaching licences — Colorado must issue an initial license within thirty days, and may not require any additional coursework, exams, or completion of another preparation program as a condition of that first license. It may still require those things later, when the license comes up for renewal. Separately, the law drops an old rule that out-of-state teaching experience had to be recent (within seven years) to count toward a Colorado professional license.

    • This runs in two directions at once and we should hold both. For teachers already licensed elsewhere, Colorado has just removed a requirement to complete additional preparation at entry — that is a reduction in demand for what we sell, in that specific segment. But we are a national program operating in thirteen states, and a world where a license travels cleanly across state lines favours us over providers rooted in a single state: our completers now have a fast, guaranteed route into Colorado, and dropping the seven-year recency rule helps career-changers, who are a core part of who we serve. Colorado's education department must publish an annual table showing how out-of-state licenses map onto Colorado endorsement areas; that document will tell us exactly how our graduates' credentials get classified.

    Questions to ask

    • Does easier license portability into Colorado read, on balance, as a threat to preparation demand or as an advantage for a thirteen-state provider — and does that answer change how we talk about our multi-state footprint in recruiting?

    • Is it worth engaging Colorado's education department as it builds the first endorsement-crosswalk table, given that the table will define how our completers' credentials are recognised?

    • The thirty-day route disappears automatically once Colorado starts issuing licenses under the Compact itself. Do we want visibility into when that switch happens, since it changes the entry rules again without any new legislation?

    Act

    TN Public Chapter 1056 — every grade 6-12 teacher must complete a state-approved asynchronous AI course, carrying licensure professional development points

    This is a licensure-attached professional development mandate in a Relay deep-partnership state, and it creates a state-approved course market: the Department

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionTennessee
    ClassBill
    StagePassed · Enacted and effective 2026-05-22. Teacher deadline 2028-08-01 or two years post-licensure, whichever is later. No formal comment window; the actionable surface is the Department of Education's course-approval process, whose criteria were not located from a primary source this run.
    RecommendationAct · impact 74

    Sourcelegiscan_tn · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is a licensure-attached professional development mandate in a Relay deep-partnership state, and it creates a state-approved course market: the Department of Education must approve the courses, and the statute says content is to come from an entity with subject-matter experience. Relay's Teacher Professional Education line sells into exactly this. It also sets an expectation Relay's Tennessee completers will carry — new licensees get two years from licensure, so graduates entering 6-12 classrooms from 2026 onward are inside the requirement.

    What it does

    HB0545 / SB0677, approved 2026-05-26 as Public Chapter 1056, effective 2026-05-22. It adds a new section to Tenn. Code Ann. Title 49, Chapter 1, Part 2. Subsection (a) requires the Department of Education to provide at least one professional development course giving asynchronous instruction on the use of artificial intelligence in the classroom, made available at no cost to teachers in grades six through twelve, usable to earn professional development points; the course CONTENT must be created by an entity with experience in a related subject area, such as computer science or another science, technology, engineering and mathematics field. Subsection (b) makes it a requirement rather than an offer: by 2028-08-01, or within two years of becoming licensed as a teacher in Tennessee, whichever is later, teachers in grades 6-12 MUST complete at least one department-approved professional development course providing asynchronous instruction on classroom use of artificial intelligence. Every LEA and public charter school must approve professional development points for a teacher's completion of at least one department-approved artificial intelligence training, under the State Board of Education's educator licensure policies and rules.

    Implications

    • Program. An asynchronous AI-in-the-classroom module is now a statutory requirement for every Tennessee secondary teacher. Building one that meets the Department's approval criteria is a defined product with a defined statewide market and a 2028-08-01 backstop.

    • Partnership. The statute's content-creator qualification (an entity with computer science or STEM experience) points toward a co-development partnership rather than a solo build.

    • Compliance. Relay's Tennessee 6-12 completers inherit the obligation two years after licensure. Whether Relay's own preparation coursework can satisfy it, or whether a separate department-approved course is required, is unresolved and worth confirming with the Department.

    Leader brief

    Tennessee now requires every middle and high school teacher to take an approved AI course

    A Tennessee law effective since May 22, 2026 requires the state Department of Education to offer a free online, self-paced course on using artificial intelligence in the classroom for teachers in grades six through twelve. It also makes the training mandatory: by August 1, 2028, or within two years of getting licensed if that is later, every 6-12 teacher in the state must finish at least one course the Department has approved. School districts and charter schools must credit it toward the continuing-education points teachers need to keep their licenses. The law says course content has to be built by an organization with real subject-matter experience, such as in computer science.

    • This is a statewide, statutory demand for a specific professional development product, with a state approval process attached and a firm deadline. Our teacher professional education work sells into exactly this space. It also lands on our own Tennessee graduates, who pick up the obligation two years after they are licensed.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want to pursue Tennessee Department of Education approval as a provider of this course, and what would that take?

    • The law wants content built by an entity with computer science or STEM experience — is that a partnership we should be sourcing now rather than a capability we build?

    • Should our Tennessee preparation coursework be designed so graduates satisfy this requirement on the way through, and would the Department accept that?

    TX SBEC opens two more certification rule actions Sept 18 — a four-year review of Chapter 233, the categories of classroom teaching certificates, with comments open Oct 16 to Nov 16 and adoption due in December, and a proposed amendment to the personnel-assignment rule 19 TAC 231.1

    Chapter 233 is the map of what Texas certificates exist and what each one authorizes its holder to teach, which is the structure every Relay Texas completer is

    Why it matters to Relay

    Chapter 233 is the map of what Texas certificates exist and what each one authorizes its holder to teach, which is the structure every Relay Texas completer is certified into; Chapter 231 governs how districts may assign the people holding them. A review that anticipates no revisions is still the one scheduled opening to argue for a change, and the comment window is a month long.

    What it does

    Two discussion-and-action items on today's State Board for Educator Certification agenda, both read raw from the posted item packets. Item 4 is the proposed four-year review of 19 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 233, Categories of Classroom Teaching Certificates, required by Texas Government Code 2001.039. Those rules establish the separate certificate categories within the classroom-teacher certificate class, identifying the content areas or special populations a holder may teach, the grade levels, and the earliest dates each certificate may be issued. The packet states 'ANTICIPATED REVISIONS TO RULES: None.' The Texas Education Agency will file the notice of proposed review with the Texas Register after the September meeting; the public comment period runs 2026-10-16 to 2026-11-16, and the review is scheduled for adoption at the December 2026 meeting, where registered oral and written comment will be taken. Item 5 proposes an amendment to 19 TAC 231.1, Criteria for Assignment of Public School Personnel, to clarify the requirements for districts making personnel assignments against the corresponding certification requirements. If approved for filing as proposed and later adopted, subject to State Board of Education review, the proposed effective date is 2027-03-08.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Chapter 233 defines the certificate categories, grade bands and content fields Relay's Texas programs prepare candidates for; any change made through this review changes what Relay's completers are authorized to teach.

    • Advocacy. The Chapter 233 comment period, 2026-10-16 to 2026-11-16, is the scheduled opening to argue that a certificate category should be added, narrowed or kept, and oral comment is taken at the December meeting.

    • Partnership. The 19 TAC 231.1 amendment governs how districts match certified staff to assignments, which affects where Relay's Texas partner districts can place newly certified teachers.

    Leader brief

    Texas is reopening the rulebook that defines its teaching certificates

    At today's meeting the Texas board that governs educator certification takes up two items beyond the accountability rules already on our board. The first is the routine four-year review of the rules that define the categories of classroom teaching certificates: which subjects and student populations each certificate covers, which grade levels, and when each may be issued. Agency staff say they anticipate no revisions, but the review still opens a formal public comment period from October 16 to November 16, with adoption scheduled for December. The second item proposes to clarify the rule that tells districts how to match staff assignments to the certificate a person holds; if it moves forward it would take effect in March 2027.

    • Texas certificate categories define what Relay's Texas graduates are licensed to teach, so this review is the scheduled opportunity to seek or resist changes. The assignment rule shapes how our partner districts can deploy newly certified teachers.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we have a position worth filing during the October-November comment window on any certificate category our Texas programs depend on?

    • Who owns monitoring the Texas Register notice so we see the actual proposed text when it publishes?

    IN Public Law 150 (SB204) — a STEM bachelor's plus nine credits now earns a grades 5-12 initial teaching license, treated by statute as equal to finishing a preparation program

    Indiana is an authorized Relay jurisdiction, and this is a nine-credit statutory substitute for the thing Relay sells. A candidate with a STEM bachelor's and a

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionIndiana
    ClassBill
    StagePassed · Enacted and in force. Signed into law as Public Law 150 on 2026-03-12; the amended IC 20-28-5-16.5 is effective July 1, 2026, so the route is live now. Next expected event is Department of Education implementation — the statute leaves the Department to determine the grade range and which of the four experience options applies, and no Indiana rulemaking notice was located this run.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Indiana is an authorized Relay jurisdiction, and this is a nine-credit statutory substitute for the thing Relay sells. A candidate with a STEM bachelor's and a 2.5 GPA can reach a grades 5-12 Indiana license without enrolling in a preparation program at all, and the statute forbids treating that licensee differently from a program completer. That is a direct competitive threat to a graduate teacher-preparation pathway in exactly the shortage fields where alternative certification demand concentrates. It is also an opening: the nine credits have to be taught by someone, the coursework list reads like a syllabus Relay already teaches, and Indiana law does not say who may offer it. One caveat on our own side of the ledger — Relay's Indiana operating footprint is an open verification item in the org profile, so the size of the exposure is not yet established.

    What it does

    Senate Bill 204, enacted as Public Law 150, amends Indiana Code 20-28-5-16.5 effective July 1, 2026. As amended, the Department of Education SHALL grant an initial practitioner license to an individual who: holds a bachelor's degree with a grade point average of at least 2.5 on a 4.0 scale from an accredited postsecondary institution with a major in any combination of science, technology, engineering or mathematics; completes at least nine academic credits covering high-impact practices in lesson planning, instructional design, instructional activities, learning modalities and (where applicable) laboratory experiments, use of digital media, learning management software and technology, teaching inductive and deductive reasoning, metacognition, problem framing, interpreting results and data-based decision making, diagnostic, direct, indirect, formative and summative assessment, feedback loops, engagement and peer-to-peer and small-group strategies, constructive feedback and preventing disruptive behavior, early intervention strategies and professional standards, and teaching students with disabilities; demonstrates subject-matter proficiency by written examination under IC 20-28-5-12(b)(2); completes the training in IC 20-28-5-12.3; and participates in one or more of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives, or full-term student teaching, as determined by the Department. A licensee under this section may teach only in grades 5 through 12 as determined by the Department, may not be granted the license to teach special education, and — by express statutory command — 'shall be treated in the same manner as an individual who receives an initial practitioner license after completing a traditional teacher preparation program,' including during the transition from an initial practitioner to a practitioner license. The section was originally added by P.L.194-2025; this act amends it.

    Implications

    • Risk. A nine-credit, no-program route to a grades 5-12 Indiana license, statutorily equal to a preparation-program completion, undercuts the value proposition of a graduate teacher-prep pathway for STEM candidates in Indiana.

    • Program. The nine required credits map closely onto content Relay already delivers. Indiana law does not name an approved provider for them, which makes a for-credit nine-hour sequence for STEM degree holders a concrete product question rather than a speculative one.

    • Compliance. The license may not be issued for special education and is capped at grades 5-12, so Relay's special-education advanced certificate line and any K-4 pathway are outside the substitution.

    • Advocacy. The Department of Education decides which of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives or full-term student teaching satisfies the clinical requirement. That determination is where preparation quality is either preserved or hollowed out, and it is made administratively, not legislatively.

    Leader brief

    Indiana now licenses STEM graduates to teach after nine credits, and the law says they count the same as our graduates

    A new Indiana law in force since July 1 lets someone with a science, technology, engineering or math bachelor's degree and a 2.5 grade point average get an initial teaching license for grades 5 through 12 after completing nine college credits of teaching coursework, passing a subject-matter test, and doing some form of classroom experience that the state education department chooses — which can be as light as job shadowing. The law explicitly requires that these teachers be treated exactly the same as people who completed a full teacher preparation program. The license cannot be used to teach special education. Indiana is one of the states where Relay is authorized to operate.

    • This is the cheapest competing route to a teaching license we have seen enacted in one of our states, and it targets the STEM candidates who are the hardest for districts to hire and the most expensive for us to recruit. The same law is also an opportunity, because someone has to teach those nine credits and Indiana has not said who. The honest caveat is that we do not yet have a confirmed picture of Relay's current Indiana footprint, so we cannot size the revenue at risk until that is settled.

    Questions to ask

    • What is Relay's actual Indiana enrollment and revenue today? Our own profile flags this as unverified, and the answer determines whether this is a live threat or a market we have not entered.

    • Do we want to compete with this route or supply it — is a nine-credit for-credit sequence for STEM degree holders a product we would build?

    • Is this pattern worth watching as a template? Georgia legislators filed a comparable experience-based route this year that did not pass, which suggests Indiana's version will be cited elsewhere.

    Why it matters to Relay

    California is a watch state, so this caps at SCAN. The bill writes the registered-apprenticeship model of teacher preparation into state law with a paid-hours floor and a mentoring floor, the architecture Relay's residency already runs. If signed, it becomes the reference design other states cite when they legislate apprenticeship routes.

    What it does

    Assembly Bill 1904 (Gipson and Muratsuchi), an act to amend Education Code section 44225.6, add Article 10.5 (commencing with section 44375) to Chapter 2 of Part 25 of Division 3 of Title 2, and add Labor Code sections 3075.4 and 3075.45, was enrolled 2026-09-02 after a final amendment on 2026-08-13 and awaits the Governor's action. Per the sweep's read of the bill text (not re-read this run), it establishes credentialed educator apprenticeship programs that give student teachers at least 300 hours of paid on-the-job training and at least 200 hours per school year of mentoring, support and supervision. Status, authors, code sections and the enrollment date were verified this run from the leginfo status page.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    California would write paid teacher apprenticeships into statute, with floors for paid hours and mentoring

    This item sits in the ACT lane because the mechanical scorer promoted it there this run; the underlying facts have not changed since it was last reviewed. Brief written on promotion. Assembly Bill 1904 would create credentialed educator apprenticeship programs in California law, requiring at least 300 hours of paid on-the-job training for student teachers and at least 200 hours per school year of mentoring, support and supervision. It was enrolled on September 2 and awaits the Governor's signature or veto. California is a watch-only jurisdiction for Relay, so this is context rather than an operating concern.

    • The bill writes into statute the architecture Relay's residency model already uses: paid clinical hours with a mentoring floor. If California signs it, it becomes the reference design other states cite when they legislate apprenticeship routes to certification — including states where Relay does operate.

    Questions to ask

    • If California's floors become a template, do Relay's residency designs meet or exceed 300 paid hours and 200 mentoring hours per year?

    CO HB26-1090 — teacher, EPP-student and charter-hire criminal-disclosure certifications rewritten into four categories, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 68)

    Section 2 amends the record check that Relay's own Colorado educator-preparation students execute, so this is a Relay compliance surface rather than an

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionColorado
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationAct · impact 72
    Latest actionGovernor signed 2026-04-20 (signed act document dated 2026-04-21); Session Laws Chapter 68; effective 12:01 a.m. 2026-08-12 (ninety days after sine die adjournment on 2026-05-13), subject to referendum petition. Verified this run from leg.colorado.gov: bill page status 'Became Law', session-law effective-date table, and the Final Act text. · 2026-08-12
    SourceColorado General Assembly (leg.colorado.gov bill page HB26-1090; Final Act text, bill_files/114467; Session Laws Ch. 68) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Section 2 amends the record check that Relay's own Colorado educator-preparation students execute, so this is a Relay compliance surface rather than an ecosystem observation: the certification language and the itemized-listing requirement changed, and the act has been in force since yesterday. Section 3 does the same for charter-school hiring, which is the placement channel for much of Relay's network. The stripped private-school waiver is the quieter finding: had it survived, Colorado would have let two years of private-school experience substitute for completing a preparation program, a direct substitution for what Relay sells. It did not survive, and that is worth recording as a live legislative appetite rather than a settled question.

    What it does

    Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 68 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act rewrites the criminal-conviction certification that three different populations must sign under penalty of perjury, and it makes the same change in all three places: teacher-license applicants (C.R.S. 22-60.5-103(2)(a)), students in educator preparation programs (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3(2)(a)), and applicants offered employment by a charter school (C.R.S. 22-30.5-110.7(2)). The prior form required disclosure of every misdemeanor regardless of date, excluding only traffic offenses. The act replaces that with four categories: (A) any felony, regardless of date; (B) any misdemeanor for which an element of the offense was that the victim was an at-risk person as defined in section 18-6.5-102 or a child under eighteen, regardless of date; (C) any other misdemeanor where the application is submitted within seven years after the disposition of the conviction, still excluding traffic offenses and infractions; and (D) any misdemeanor enumerated as grounds for denial, annulment, suspension, or revocation of a license, certificate, endorsement, or authorization under 22-60.5-107(2)(b), regardless of date. New language requires that each conviction in these four categories be listed individually, with the offense, the date of conviction, and the court entering judgment. Each of the three statutes also gains a savings clause stating the change does not alter the department's obligation to evaluate criminal convictions under C.R.S. 24-5-101. A provision in the introduced bill that would have required the department to waive the program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for applicants with two or more years of Colorado private school teaching experience does NOT appear in the final act — it was removed before enactment.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Relay's Colorado educator-preparation record-check certification (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3) must match the new four-category language and the requirement that each conviction be listed individually with offense, date and court. The act is already in force, so any form still using the old 'all misdemeanors regardless of date' text is out of date now, not at some future compliance date.

    • Program. Candidates previously deterred by having to disclose decades-old minor misdemeanors now disclose non-traffic misdemeanors only within a seven-year window, which modestly widens the admissible Colorado applicant pool. Offenses against at-risk persons or children, and licensure-disqualifying misdemeanors, remain lifetime-disclosable.

    • Risk. The introduced version would have waived program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for two years of Colorado private-school experience. It was removed before enactment, but the proposal establishes that an experience-for-preparation substitution has sponsors in Colorado and may return in a later session.

    • Partnership. Section 3 changes the same certification for charter-school employment offers, so Relay's Colorado charter partners are updating the identical form on the identical timeline — a low-cost, concrete reason to compare notes with placement partners.

    Leader brief

    Colorado: the background-disclosure form our teacher candidates sign changed on August 12 (CO HB26-1090)

    Colorado enacted a law, in force since August 12, that rewrites the criminal-history disclosure form signed by three groups: people applying for a teacher license, students enrolled in teacher-preparation programs like ours, and people being hired by charter schools. Instead of disclosing every past misdemeanor no matter how old, an applicant now discloses any felony ever, any misdemeanor against a child or an at-risk person ever, any other non-traffic misdemeanor from the last seven years, and any misdemeanor that can itself cost someone a teaching license. Every disclosed conviction must now be listed individually with the offense, the date, and the court. We surfaced this only now because a defect in our own bill-search code left these Colorado bills without their bill numbers until it was fixed on August 12.

    • Our Colorado teacher-preparation program uses the exact form this law rewrites, so the practical task is updating that certification and the guidance our admissions and advising staff give candidates about it. The law is already in effect, so this is catch-up rather than preparation. There is a second thing worth knowing: an earlier version of this bill would have let two years of private-school teaching experience substitute for completing a preparation program altogether. That language was removed before the bill passed, but the idea has backers in Colorado and could return.

    Questions to ask

    • Who owns updating the Colorado educator-preparation record-check certification, and how quickly can it be corrected given the law is already in force?

    • Do we need to say anything to candidates who signed the old form during this admissions cycle, or does the change apply only going forward?

    • Is an experience-for-preparation substitution — the provision stripped from this bill — something we want to be positioned on before it returns in a future Colorado session?

    Act

    IL HB5321 — only accredited graduate credit with an instructor of record may count for teacher salary advancement (Public Act 104-0795)

    This regulates the market for Relay's Illinois products directly, and it cuts both ways. Relay is a Middle States-accredited, master's-degree-granting

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionIllinois
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationAct · impact 72
    Latest actionGovernor Approved 2026-08-07; Effective Date August 7, 2026; Public Act 104-0795. The coursework-completion trigger in the Act's own text is July 1, 2026, so it reaches coursework already completed this summer. Verified from the ilga.gov bill-status action list and the enrolled full text this run. · 2026-08-07
    SourceIllinois General Assembly (ilga.gov bill status + enrolled full text) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This regulates the market for Relay's Illinois products directly, and it cuts both ways. Relay is a Middle States-accredited, master's-degree-granting institution, so its MAT and advanced-certificate coursework is exactly the transcripted graduate credit the Act preserves as salary-bearing — competitors selling ungraded, self-paced, non-transcripted seat-hour PD are now barred from Illinois salary lanes. The same clause is a risk to Relay's other Illinois line: Teacher Professional Education, the job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD product, does not carry transcripted graduate credit and so cannot support a lane change under the new Section unless it is delivered through the degree-granting side with an instructor of record.

    What it does

    Adds a new Section 24-8.2 to the Employment of Teachers Article of the Illinois School Code, signed 2026-08-07 as Public Act 104-0795 and effective the same day. For continuing education coursework completed on or after July 1, 2026, a school district, special education cooperative, or other public educational employer may recognize that coursework for salary advancement ONLY IF it (1) is graduate-level, degree-eligible credit offered through a regionally accredited institution of higher education and documented on an official academic transcript, and (2) includes an instructor of record. The Act defines 'graduate-level, degree-eligible credit' as transcripted credit applicable toward a master's, education specialist, or doctoral degree, and defines 'instructor of record' as a credentialed educator holding at least a master's degree, academically qualified in the content area, who provides substantive instructional support throughout the course and returns individualized written feedback aligned to course objectives. It applies only to licensed classroom teachers holding a Professional Educator License under Section 21B-20 who are covered by a collective bargaining agreement, and expressly excludes administrators. Carve-outs: nothing requires an employer to create a salary schedule or advancement pathway that does not already exist, nothing precludes bargaining over other compensation-related advancement, and implementation — documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, compliance monitoring — is left to each employer rather than to State Board rulemaking. Passed unanimously at every recorded vote: House 105-0-0 (2026-04-16), Senate 57-0-0 (2026-05-21), House concurrence 112-0-0 (2026-05-28).

    Implications

    • Risk. Relay's Teacher Professional Education line (job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD) is not graduate-level, degree-eligible transcripted credit. Where Illinois district contracts were sold partly on teachers earning salary-lane movement, that value proposition no longer holds for coursework completed on or after 2026-07-01. Audit the Illinois PD contracts and any marketing language that implies lane credit.

    • Program. The clean response is a credit-bearing delivery path: route Illinois PD sequences through the degree-granting side so participants receive transcripted graduate credit with a named instructor of record who grades and gives written feedback. The Act's instructor-of-record definition (master's degree, content-qualified, substantive support throughout, individualized written feedback) is a design spec, not a formality.

    • Partnership. Section 24-8.2(f) leaves documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, and compliance monitoring to each district and special education cooperative individually. Illinois partners now need a per-district answer on what evidence they will accept — an opening to supply that documentation package rather than wait to be asked for it.

    • Funding. For the MAT and advanced-certificate lines this is favorable demand policy: Illinois teachers seeking lane movement are pushed toward accredited graduate credit, which is what Relay sells. Worth testing in Illinois enrollment messaging for the coming cycles.

    • Compliance. The Act imposes no direct obligation on Relay as an institution — the duty runs to the employer recognizing the credit. Relay's exposure is entirely commercial and reputational: being able to evidence regional accreditation, transcripting, and instructor of record on demand.

    Leader brief

    Illinois now requires accredited graduate credit for teacher pay-lane raises (IL HB5321)

    Illinois enacted a new law on August 7 governing which coursework a school district may count when a teacher moves up a salary lane. Starting with coursework finished on or after July 1 of this year, districts may only count courses that carry graduate-level credit from a regionally accredited college or university, appear on an official transcript, and have a real instructor who grades the work and gives written feedback. It passed unanimously in both chambers. Each district decides for itself how to verify all of this; the state is not writing rules for it.

    • Two opposite effects for us in Illinois. Our degree programs are precisely what the law protects — accredited, transcripted graduate credit — so teachers seeking a pay raise are steered toward the kind of coursework we grant, and low-cost providers who sell ungraded professional development hours are pushed out of that market. But our own coaching and microcredential professional-development line does not carry transcripted graduate credit, so where an Illinois district bought it partly because teachers could use it for a raise, that reason is gone unless we deliver it for credit through our degree-granting side.

    Questions to ask

    • How much Illinois professional-development revenue was sold on the promise of salary-lane credit, and who confirms what we have actually told districts?

    • Do we want to convert Illinois professional-development sequences into credit-bearing courses with a named instructor of record, and what would that cost in faculty time and margin?

    • Do we lead with this in Illinois enrollment messaging for our degree programs, given that the law now steers teachers toward accredited graduate credit?

    Act

    IL ISBE awards FY2027 Teacher Vacancy Grants: $15M to 100 high-need districts covering 77% of statewide vacancies; participating districts' vacancies down 28% since FY23

    Illinois is one of Relay's deepest jurisdictions and this is the state's main district-level shortage program, now in its fourth cycle with an evaluation behind

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionIllinois
    ClassAgency
    Stageawarded · FY2027 awards announced; the program is in its fourth year and is being evaluated by IWERC. Next expected event: FY2028 appropriation and cohort selection.
    RecommendationAct · impact 72
    Second opinionModel scorer: Act · impact 72; reviewer: Track · impact 67
    Latest actionAwards announced 2026-09-01 for FY2027 (100 districts, $15M). Verified this run from the ISBE press release. · 2026-09-01
    SourceIllinois State Board of Education newsroom (press release 2026-09-01) — cross-engine sweep (Codex; verified by Opus and this session) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Illinois is one of Relay's deepest jurisdictions and this is the state's main district-level shortage program, now in its fourth cycle with an evaluation behind it. The grants fund exactly the district-side activities Relay partners on — residency partnerships, endorsement pathways, grow-your-own, professional learning — so the list of 100 districts is a partnership map with fresh money attached. No window; the actionable step is matching the district list against Relay's Illinois partners and prospects. Found by the cross-engine sweep; the ISBE newsroom is not a wired source.

    What it does

    Illinois State Board of Education press release, September 1, 2026: 100 school districts selected for Fiscal Year 2027 Teacher Vacancy Grant funding, with $15 million allocated. The cohort was identified from ISBE's annual Unfilled Positions Report, limited to eligible districts in Evidence-Based Funding Tiers 1-3 with the highest numbers of unfilled teaching positions; the selected districts account for about 77% of reported vacancies statewide while making up 12% of Illinois local education agencies. Since the pilot's creation in 2023, $120 million has gone to districts for recruitment, retention and professional-learning strategies and partnerships; in the first two years 15,988 educators received grant-funded support and 1,135 certified staff were helped to earn endorsements in high-need subjects. Among participating districts, vacancies fell from 2,858 in FY23 to 2,060 in FY26 (28%) and the vacancy rate from 4.6% to 3.2%, consistent with the Illinois Workforce and Education Research Collaborative's preliminary evaluation. The cohort includes returning and newly identified districts.

    Implications

    • Partnership. One hundred Illinois districts, chosen because they hold 77% of the state's unfilled teaching positions, now have FY2027 funds designated for recruitment, retention, endorsement pathways and partnerships. Cross-referencing the award list against Relay's Illinois district partners and prospects is the concrete next step.

    • Funding. The $15M is district money, not provider money; Relay's route to it is as a partner or vendor on a district's grant-funded strategy, which the program explicitly contemplates.

    Leader brief

    Illinois has given $15 million in teacher-vacancy grants to 100 districts that hold most of the state's unfilled teaching jobs

    The Illinois State Board of Education announced on September 1 which districts will receive this year's Teacher Vacancy Grants: 100 districts, chosen because they report the highest numbers of unfilled teaching positions, sharing $15 million. Together they account for about three-quarters of the state's teacher vacancies. The program began in 2023, has distributed $120 million so far, and the state reports that vacancies in participating districts have fallen by 28 percent. Districts use the money for recruiting, keeping teachers, helping staff earn credentials in shortage subjects, and partnerships.

    • This is district money, not money Relay can apply for, but it pays for the kinds of work Relay does with districts: residencies, credential pathways, and professional learning. The list of 100 districts is effectively a map of where Illinois has just put money behind solving teacher shortages. Comparing that list with Relay's current and prospective Illinois partners is a low-cost step.

    Questions to ask

    • Which of the 100 awarded districts are current Relay partners, and which are prospects worth a conversation now that they have funding in hand?

    • Is there a case for a standard Relay offer designed around what these grants allow districts to buy?

    Act

    CT Public Act 26-149 — aspiring educators scholarship redefined and opened statewide (up to $10k/yr), teacher-shortage areas now include underrepresented subgroups

    Two Relay-relevant asymmetries. The scholarship — the money in this act — is restricted to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionConnecticut
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationAct · impact 71
    Second opinionModel scorer: Act · impact 71; reviewer: Track · impact 69
    Latest actionSigned by the Governor 2026-06-04 as Public Act 26-149. Sections 2, 3 and 6 effective 2026-07-01; Section 4 effective 2027-01-01. Verified this run from the Connecticut General Assembly's published public act text. · 2026-06-04
    SourceConnecticut General Assembly (cga.ct.gov, Public Act 26-149 full text) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Two Relay-relevant asymmetries. The scholarship — the money in this act — is restricted to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education, which excludes a graduate school of education, so Relay's Connecticut candidates cannot reach these dollars. But Section 3's distribution duty runs to every institution offering a teacher preparatory program, which does include Relay Connecticut, and the newly required identification of underrepresented population subgroups as formal shortage areas is a designation Relay's recruitment work is well positioned to speak to. Section 4's charge to advise educator preparation programs on alternative-route and bridge programs for native ASL users is the clearest programme-design opening in the act, though it does not begin until January 2027.

    What it does

    Substitute Senate Bill 220, signed 2026-06-04 as Public Act 26-149. Section 2 rewrites C.R.S.-equivalent Conn. Gen. Stat. 10-156ii, renaming the 'aspiring educators diversity scholarship' the 'aspiring educators scholarship' and changing who qualifies: the geographic restriction to graduates of alliance-district high schools is replaced with graduation from any public high school in the state, while the beneficiary definition narrows from 'diverse students' to 'aspiring educators', meaning individuals in a population subgroup that is underrepresented in the teaching profession AND identified as a teacher shortage area by the Commissioner of Education under section 10-8b. The award remains up to $10,000 per year while the recipient is enrolled and in good standing in a teacher preparation program at any FOUR-YEAR institution of higher education. The department must develop an administration policy by 2027-01-01 and award annually from the fiscal year ending 2027-06-30 onward; the Commissioner must develop repayment criteria for recipients who do not go on to teach as certified teachers in Connecticut. Section 3 rewrites section 10-8b so the Commissioner must annually by December 1 identify teacher shortage areas in three categories — subject, geographic, and population subgroups underrepresented in the profession — certify them to the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, and by March 1 distribute shortage-area information covering at least the prior five years to the president of every institution of higher education in the state offering a teacher preparatory program. Section 4 (effective 2027-01-01) establishes an American Sign Language education working group charged with recommending curriculum guidance, ASL teacher certification standards including a proficiency benchmark, an alternative certification pathway for native ASL users and interpreters, and reciprocity with other states' ASL certifications, plus guidance to educator preparation programs on expanding ASL programs, creating incentives such as tuition support and credit enhancement, and establishing bridge, endorsement or alternative programs. Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in a public school rather than only those employed by a local or regional board of education, reaching charter school paraeducators, with up to $300,000 of unexpended FY2026 funds transferred by 2026-07-15.

    Implications

    • Risk. The up-to-$10,000 aspiring educators scholarship is limited to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education. Relay's Connecticut candidates are structurally outside it, and the same exclusion appears in Delaware's new Teacher Academy scholarship — a pattern worth naming rather than treating as two coincidences.

    • Advocacy. From December 1 each year the Commissioner must formally identify population subgroups underrepresented in teaching as shortage areas. That designation drives scholarship eligibility, and it is a decision Relay's recruitment and completer data speak to directly.

    • Program. Section 4's working group must advise educator preparation programs on bridge, endorsement and alternative-route programs for native ASL users and certified interpreters seeking teacher certification — an alternative-certification design space matching what Relay already operates. It convenes from 2027-01-01.

    • Compliance. By March 1 annually the department must send five years of shortage-area data to every Connecticut institution offering a teacher preparatory program. Relay Connecticut should be on that distribution list and should confirm it is.

    • Partnership. Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in public schools including charter schools, strengthening a paraeducator-to-teacher pipeline population that alternative-route providers recruit from.

    Leader brief

    Connecticut: a redesigned teacher scholarship our candidates cannot use, and a shortage-area process they can (CT Public Act 26-149)

    Connecticut signed a law on June 4 that reworks its scholarship for people training to become teachers. It is now open to graduates of any public high school in the state rather than only those in designated high-need districts, and it pays up to $10,000 a year. Eligibility now turns on belonging to a group that is underrepresented in teaching and that the state's Commissioner of Education has formally designated as a shortage area. The scholarship is restricted to teacher-preparation programs at four-year colleges, so our Connecticut candidates cannot receive it. A separate part of the law requires the state to send teacher-shortage data every March to every institution that runs a teacher-preparation programme, which does include us. A third part sets up a working group in January 2027 to design alternative routes into teaching for fluent American Sign Language users.

    • The notable thing is the exclusion, and it is the second one this run: Connecticut's scholarship and Delaware's new Teacher Academy scholarship both route money exclusively to undergraduate, four-year teacher-preparation pathways. As states put more dollars into growing their own teachers, a graduate-level provider is structurally outside that funding even where it is fully authorised to operate. Where we do have standing is the shortage-area designation process, which now formally includes underrepresented groups and which determines who the money follows, and the 2027 ASL working group, which is explicitly chartered to advise on alternative certification routes of the kind we already run.

    Questions to ask

    • Two states in one week have funded teacher pipelines in a way that structurally excludes graduate-level providers. Is that a pattern we want to contest, design around, or simply track?

    • Should we seek a role in Connecticut's annual shortage-area determination, given it now decides which underrepresented groups scholarship money follows?

    • Is the January 2027 ASL working group worth pursuing a seat on, or is it too narrow to justify the effort?
