    Why it matters to Relay

    Incidental teaching is the state's alternative to certifying more teachers in shortage subjects: every hour a district covers this way is an hour it does not need a teacher with an additional certificate or extension, which is the coursework and pathway business of a New York educator-preparation provider. Seven straight renewals make the 'temporary' flexibility a fixture; the January 2027 permanent-adoption step and the 60-day comment window from September 30 are the places to say whether Relay wants a sunset or a certification-linked condition.

    What it does

    Higher Education Committee item HE (A) 1 (memo dated 2026-09-03 from William P. Murphy, read this run from the Regents agenda). The Committee is asked to recommend, and the Full Board to adopt as an emergency rule effective September 15, 2026, an amendment to section 80-5.3 extending through the 2026-27 school year the flexibility that lets a certified teacher teach up to 10 classroom hours a week (the permanent rule allows five) in a subject not covered by their certificate, after the district determines through documented recruitment that no certified or qualified teacher is available. The same one-year extension was adopted in December 2020, October 2021, September 2022, September 2023, November 2024 and November 2025; the memo's stated rationale is 'ongoing staffing challenges'. A Notice of Emergency Adoption and Proposed Rule Making is to be published in the State Register on September 30, 2026 for a 60-day comment period (through about November 29); permanent adoption is anticipated at the January 2027 Regents meeting, with a further emergency re-adoption expected before then because the emergency action lapses first.

    Implications

    • Program. Districts can keep covering shortage-subject sections with out-of-field certified teachers for another year, which reduces near-term demand for additional-certificate and extension coursework in those subjects.

    • Advocacy. The 60-day comment window from September 30 and the January 2027 permanent-adoption step are the opportunities to ask for a sunset, a reporting requirement, or a link between incidental assignments and enrollment in a certification pathway.

    • Partnership. Districts using incidental teaching heavily are the districts with the deepest shortage-subject needs; that is the target list for residency and additional-certification partnerships.

    Leader brief

    New York is renewing, for a seventh year, a rule that lets certified teachers cover classes outside their license area for up to 10 hours a week

    Since 2020 New York has let a certified teacher teach up to ten hours a week in a subject their certificate does not cover, when the district shows it could not find a properly certified teacher. On September 15 the Regents' Higher Education Committee recommended that the full Board renew that flexibility for the 2026-27 school year as an emergency rule; the Board met the same morning, though it publishes no separate vote record. A public comment period opens September 30, and permanent adoption is expected in January 2027.

    • This is the state's pressure valve for teacher shortages, and it competes with the route Relay sells: getting a teacher fully certified in the subject. Each renewal lowers the urgency for districts to send teachers into additional-certificate coursework. It also marks the districts with the most acute shortages, which are the natural partners for residency and certification programs.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay want to file a comment in the September 30 window, for example asking that incidental assignments be paired with enrollment in a certification pathway?

    • Which partner districts rely most on incidental teaching, and is there a program offer for them?

    Why it matters to Relay

    California is watch-only for Relay and everything here caps at SCAN, but two threads are worth the line. AB 1381 extends educator-discipline grounds to disclosure failures, which is the kind of credentialing-conduct rule that migrates between states. The reported $30 million for teacher residency and National Board certification, if the single-engine attribution holds, is a data point on what a large state is willing to spend on residency models — the same model Relay builds — at a moment when the board is tracking residency funding fights in Tennessee and Connecticut that died for want of appropriation.

    What it does

    Surfaced by the cross-engine sweep from the Governor's legislative updates of 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-20; the Governor's pages were NOT read directly by this session, so these are recorded at the sweep's confidence, not this run's. Marked VERIFIED by two engines: AB 1381, signed 2026-09-20, makes failure to disclose prior employment or to conduct a background check a form of unprofessional conduct for purposes of the Commission on Teacher Credentialing; AB 167, signed 2026-09-18, the higher-education budget trailer bill; AB 713, VETOED 2026-09-20, on undocumented students' eligibility for public postsecondary employment; and AB 917, VETOED 2026-09-20, on permanent status for small districts through county offices of education. Marked ATTRIBUTED by a single engine and therefore weaker: AB 113, reported as a Budget Act amendment signed 2026-09-18 carrying $30 million for teacher residency and National Board certification and $5 million for transcript-related work; and proposed educator apprenticeship standards posted 2026-09-18 by the San Diego County Office of Education and the Child Care Resource Center. NO bill number, dollar figure or date in the attributed group should be relied on without a primary read. SWEEP ADDITION, ATTRIBUTED ONLY (2026-09-22): the cross-engine sweep reports that Governor Newsom also signed SB 960 and AB 2694 around 2026-09-20, authorizing California community college districts to establish two to twelve new bachelor's degree programs starting in 2028, tied to a five-tier accountability framework based on district graduation, retention and transfer rates, and removing the bar on community colleges awarding bachelor's degrees already offered at the University of California or California State University. This is reported by Inside Higher Ed (2026-09-21) and CalMatters; NEITHER BILL NUMBER APPEARS on the Governor's own 2026-09-20 legislative update, which this board fetched and read in full this run and which does list AB 2206 and AB 1381. The signings are therefore recorded as ATTRIBUTED, with the date unconfirmed, and are not asserted as fact. Adjacent-tier in any case: higher-education governance rather than educator preparation, with the teacher-pipeline link running through the companion AB 2206 career-and-technical-education credential provisions tracked separately at x:6dada068.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. A large state funding teacher residencies at scale is a citable comparison in states where Relay's residency partners are arguing for appropriations.

    Leader brief

    California signed a law making it professional misconduct for an educator to hide prior employment, and vetoed two other education bills

    This item sits in the ACT lane because the mechanical scorer promoted it there this run; the underlying facts have not changed since it was last reviewed. Brief written on promotion. The Governor signed AB 1381 on September 20, making failure to disclose prior employment or to conduct a background check a form of unprofessional conduct for credentialing purposes. He signed the higher-education budget trailer bill on September 18 and vetoed two bills: one on undocumented students' eligibility for public postsecondary employment and one on permanent status for small districts. A single search engine also reported a budget amendment carrying $30 million for teacher residency and National Board certification; that one is weaker and unconfirmed. None of the Governor's pages was read directly this run, so these facts carry the search engines' confidence rather than ours.

    • California is watch-only, so nothing here is operational. The disclosure-failure rule is the kind of educator-conduct provision that migrates between states, and the reported residency funding, if real, is a data point on what a large state is willing to spend on the model Relay uses.

    Questions to ask

    • If educator-conduct disclosure rules spread to Relay's states, do Relay's own placement and background-check practices already meet that bar?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay's Pennsylvania candidates in unpaid student-teaching placements are eligible if enrolled through a PDE-approved program at a Pennsylvania institution — the three-year in-state service commitment is a retention lever for partner districts, and the annual September deadline belongs on the recruiting calendar.

    What it does

    Pennsylvania Department of Education release of 2026-04-16 (read raw this run): the PA Student Teacher Support Program, administered by the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA), pays $10,000 stipends for the 2026-27 school year to student teachers in unpaid placements who are enrolled at a Pennsylvania institution of higher education in a PDE-approved educator preparation program, hold a 3.0 GPA and required clearances, and agree to teach at a participating Pennsylvania LEA or non-public school for at least three years; cooperating teachers receive up to $2,500. Placements may be in districts, intermediate units, non-public schools, career and technical schools, or charter, regional charter and cyber charter schools. In 2025-26 PHEAA received more than 3,500 applications and funded 2,300 stipends; the Governor's 2026-27 budget proposal adds $5 million, for $35 million annually. Applications for the 2026-27 round were due 2026-09-15 (first-come, first-served).

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Pennsylvania's $10,000 student-teaching stipend round closed September 15; the next one is a year out

    This item sits in the ACT lane because the mechanical scorer promoted it there this run; the underlying facts have not changed since it was last reviewed. Brief written on promotion. Pennsylvania pays $10,000 stipends to student teachers in unpaid placements who are enrolled at a Pennsylvania institution in a state-approved preparation program, hold a 3.0 grade point average and required clearances, and commit to teaching in Pennsylvania for three years. Cooperating teachers receive up to $2,500. Awards are first-come, first-served. In 2025-26 the agency received more than 3,500 applications and funded 2,300 stipends. The 2026-27 application round closed September 15. The Governor's budget proposal would add $5 million, bringing the program to $35 million a year.

    • This is a recruiting-calendar item rather than a policy one. Relay's Pennsylvania candidates in unpaid placements are eligible if they are enrolled through a state-approved program at a Pennsylvania institution, and because awards are first-come, first-served, the timing of the application matters as much as eligibility. The three-year service commitment is also a retention mechanism partner districts benefit from.

    Questions to ask

    • Is the annual September deadline on Relay's Pennsylvania recruiting calendar for next year's round?

    • Are Relay's Pennsylvania candidates enrolled in a way that makes them eligible, and does anyone confirm that before the window opens?

    What it does

    Two Professional Standards Board proposals published in the September 1, 2026 Delaware Register of Regulations (Vol. 30, Issue 3), both under 14 Del.C. sections 1203, 1204(a), 1205(b) and 1220, both taking written comment at the Department of Education's Office of the Secretary (Attn: Regulation Review, 401 Federal Street, Suite 2, Dover) or through the online form at de.gov/doeregs until 4:30 p.m. on October 1, 2026. (1) 1521 Elementary Teacher, the standard certificate for Delaware elementary teachers: strikes unnecessary definitions in Section 2.0; in Section 4.0 replaces the prior ETS test codes with the current codes and adds a subsection stating the dates after which the outdated tests will no longer be accepted; clarifies the application requirements in Section 5.0; simplifies Section 10.0; the Board states no cost to the state or local boards. The full proposed 1521 text is not printed in the Register and the separately posted copy is a JavaScript-only page that could not be read this run, so the synopsis is the verified scope. (2) 1528 Elementary Montessori Teacher, a NEW standard certificate required to teach grades K-6 in a Delaware public Montessori school, with two acceptance carve-outs written into Section 1.2: the Early Childhood Montessori certificate for grades K-2, and the 1521 Elementary Teacher Standard Certificate, which 'may be accepted instead' for grades K-6. Requires a bachelor's degree from a regionally accredited institution plus a Montessori teacher-education program accredited by the Montessori Accreditation Council for Teacher Education, and 6 college credits (each equating to 15 hours) in evidence-based reading instruction; it is not a content-area certificate and is not accepted in non-Montessori schools. Both are Board proposals; adoption follows the comment period and Secretary and State Board action.

    Implications

    • Compliance. The 1521 amendments replace the ETS test codes and set dates after which the outdated tests will no longer be accepted. Any Delaware candidate holding a passing score on a superseded test needs to know that date; Relay's Delaware advising should confirm the sunset dates from the posted text before the comment window closes.

    • Program. The new Montessori certificate explicitly accepts the 1521 Elementary Teacher certificate in its place for grades K-6 in public Montessori schools, so Relay's Delaware elementary completers stay eligible for those placements without a separate MACTE-accredited credential.

    • Advocacy. A 17-business-day comment window on a certification rule in an authorized state is a direct opportunity: the question worth raising is whether the sunset dates give in-progress candidates enough runway to retest under the current codes.

    Leader brief

    Delaware is updating the elementary teacher certificate's required tests and creating a Montessori certificate; comments are open until October 1

    Delaware's Professional Standards Board, the body that writes teacher-certification rules, has published two proposals. The first updates the Elementary Teacher certificate rule so it names the current versions of the required ETS tests and, for the first time, sets dates after which the older versions of those tests will no longer count. The second creates a new certificate for teachers in public Montessori elementary schools, which requires a Montessori-accredited training program and coursework in evidence-based reading instruction, but it states that the ordinary Elementary Teacher certificate can be accepted instead. Written comments on both are due by 4:30 p.m. on October 1, 2026.

    • Delaware is a state where Relay is authorized to prepare teachers, and the Elementary Teacher certificate is what Relay's Delaware elementary candidates earn. The test-code change is mostly housekeeping, but the new cut-off dates could catch a candidate who passed an older version of a test and has not yet been certified. The Montessori rule is good news in a small way: Relay graduates holding the standard certificate remain eligible to teach in public Montessori schools. The full text of the elementary-certificate proposal has not yet been read, so the exact cut-off dates are still to be confirmed.

    Questions to ask

    • Do any current Delaware candidates hold passing scores on older test versions, and would the proposed cut-off dates affect them before they are certified?

    • Is it worth submitting a short comment by October 1 asking for adequate runway for candidates already in the pipeline?

    • Should Relay's Delaware advising materials be updated to the new test codes now, ahead of adoption?

    No additional coverage recorded.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay's operating licenses run through this rule twice: MSCHE (institutional accreditor and Title IV gatekeeper) and CAEP (educator-prep accreditor) are both Secretary-recognized under Part 602, so the proposed outcome metrics and the credential-inflation review factor would reshape the standards both apply to Relay.

    What it does

    Notice of proposed rulemaking rewriting the Secretary's accrediting-agency recognition regulations at 34 CFR part 602 (conforming changes to parts 600 and 668) to implement Executive Order 14279. Verified from the Federal Register text this run, the NPRM: requires accreditors to hold member institutions to program-level student-outcome expectations — completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns — assessed "without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex"; requires accreditation decisions to be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology (proposed 602.18, with a religious-mission exception); adds academic-freedom and intellectual-diversity review, cost-benefit analysis, and program-length review to 602.17; REMOVES the 602.15(a)(4) requirement that programmatic accreditors seat educators, practitioners, and employers on evaluation and decision-making bodies; lowers barriers to recognizing new accreditors and to institutions switching accreditors (new 602.12(e): qualifying experience may be national, State, or programmatic); and makes it a recognition-review factor whether an agency joined a "concerted effort to unnecessarily restrict the qualifications necessary for a student to sit for a licensure or certification examination" or inflated entry requirements through "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" (proposed 602.31(g)(1)). Docket ED-2025-OPE-1042, RIN 1840-AD82. Comments close 2026-09-21 (~21 business days), via regulations.gov only — no fax or email.

    Update 2026-09-23: the FTC's Office of Policy Planning and Bureau of Competition filed a comment on Monday September 21 — the last day of the window — strongly endorsing the proposal, and the Commission issued a press release on September 22 (read raw this run). The comment argues that accreditation monopolies drive up tuition, limit choice and stifle innovation because incumbent accreditors have an incentive to impose rigid requirements and oppose flexible standards, citing that 21 of 27 commissioners on the Middle States Commission on Higher Education are university administrators or faculty. The comment states that the situation for PROGRAMMATIC accreditors — the category that covers educator preparation — is 'often worse,' because they are guided by incumbent members of the profession with incentives to raise educational costs and create barriers to lower-cost alternatives.

    Implications

    • Compliance. MSCHE and CAEP would be re-reviewed against rewritten recognition criteria; whatever standards survive flow down into Relay's next reaffirmation cycles, with program-level completion, licensure pass-rate, and earnings data as the evidence currency.

    • Program. Program-level economic-returns metrics put graduate-EPP tuition-to-earnings ratios under accreditor scrutiny — Relay's employment and certification outcomes become either an accreditation asset or an exposure, program by program.

    • Risk. Proposed 602.31(g)(1) treats "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" for entering a profession as a mark against an accreditor's recognition — a federal thumb on the scale against graduate-level entry expectations for teaching, rhyming with the state-level deregulation the board is already tracking (IN Pub. L. 150, CO SB26-126).

    • Advocacy. Comment window open to 2026-09-21. Relay can speak as a graduate EPP with strong licensure outcomes; coordination with AACTE and with MSCHE/CAEP comment strategies is the near-term decision.

    • Advocacy. A sitting federal competition authority has now argued on the record that programmatic accreditors — the category that includes educator-preparation accreditation — create barriers to lower-cost alternatives. That framing, if it survives into the final rule's preamble, is favorable to alternative-route providers and worth tracking as the rationale, not just the rule.

    Leader brief

    Federal proposal rewrites the rules for college accreditors

    Update September 21: TODAY IS THE LAST DAY to file a comment. The Education Department's rewrite of the rules governing how it recognizes accreditors closes its public comment period at the end of today, September 21, confirmed this morning against the Federal Register's own record. After today the only remaining influence on this rule is through our accreditors and through sector associations. The U.S. Department of Education proposed new rules for how it recognizes accreditors — the organizations that certify colleges and control access to federal student aid. The proposal would push accreditors to judge institutions on measurable results for each program: how many students finish, how many pass licensure exams, and what graduates earn. It would also make it easier for new accreditors to enter the market and for institutions to switch accreditors, and it directs the Department to weigh, when reviewing an accreditor, whether that accreditor helped raise the education requirements needed to enter a profession. Public comments are open until September 21, 2026.

    • Both of Relay's accreditors — Middle States (institutional) and CAEP (educator preparation) — are recognized under the rules being rewritten, so the standards Relay is held to in future reviews would change. Program-level results reporting would become the currency of accreditation, and the provision against raising professional entry requirements could add federal pressure against graduate-degree expectations for teachers.

    Questions to ask

    • This closes today. Is anyone filing on Relay's behalf, and if not, is that a deliberate choice or an oversight?

    • Do we submit a comment by September 21, and on which provisions — the program-level earnings metrics, the credential-inflation test, or both?

    • Are our program-level completion, certification pass-rate, and graduate-earnings data ready to stand as accreditation evidence?

    • If switching accreditors becomes cheap and new accreditors enter, does our own accreditation strategy change?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Indiana is an authorized Relay jurisdiction and secondary mathematics is a shortage field Relay prepares for. Revised educator standards flow into the licensure assessment and into what a preparation program must cover for state approval, so this is a direct program-design input with an open comment window.     What it does

    Announced in the Indiana Department of Education's Office of Educator Preparation section of the September 4, 2026 SAMS newsletter: a committee of educator-preparation program representatives and K-12 educators has recommended updates to the Indiana Educator Standards for Middle School Mathematics (5-9) and Mathematics (5-12). The draft standards are open for public comment through 5:00 p.m. ET on Friday, October 2, 2026, via two Jotform links (one per standard set) that also carry the participation instructions. IDOE states the input will be used to refine the standards and that final recommendations will be presented to the Indiana State Board of Education. Contact named: Renee Baratta. Educator standards, distinct from the K-12 academic standards, define the content knowledge teacher candidates must demonstrate for licensure and drive both licensure-test blueprints and preparation-program design.

    Implications

    • Program. Revised mathematics educator standards will reset what Indiana expects a licensed 5-9 or 5-12 math teacher to know, and preparation programs are approved against those standards. Relay's Indiana math coursework and clinical expectations should be checked against the drafts before the window closes.

    • Advocacy. An 18-business-day public comment window on the standards themselves is a rare direct input; a program-level response from Relay's Indiana faculty carries weight because the drafting committee included preparation-program representatives.

    Leader brief

    Indiana is rewriting the standards for what middle-school and high-school math teachers must know, and is taking public comment until October 2

    The Indiana Department of Education has released draft updates to its educator standards for Middle School Mathematics (grades 5-9) and Mathematics (grades 5-12). Educator standards are different from the standards students are taught to: they spell out what a teacher candidate has to know and be able to do to be licensed, and they shape both the licensure exam and what preparation programs must teach. A committee of preparation-program representatives and K-12 teachers drafted the updates. Public comment is open through 5 p.m. Eastern on Friday, October 2, after which final recommendations go to the State Board of Education.

    • Relay prepares mathematics teachers in Indiana, so whatever these standards become will shape Relay's Indiana math curriculum, its candidates' licensure testing, and the basis on which the state reviews the program. The drafts themselves have not yet been read. The comment window is short enough that a decision on whether to respond is needed in the next two weeks.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay submit comments as a program, and is there anything in Relay's Indiana completer or placement data that would strengthen them?

    • If the standards change materially, what is the lead time to revise coursework before the state's next program review?

    CommentComment

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the rule that decides whether Relay's Texas EPP may recommend candidates for certification at all — 19 TAC §229.1(a) bars any program not accredited under Chapter 229 from recommending a candidate. Texas is named in the rubric as a deep-partnership jurisdiction, the window is open, and the changes cut in both directions. The threshold drop and the inserted warning year are relief: more headroom at the Accredited line and one more year to recover before probation, which matters because §229.4(b)(5)(A) revokes approval after three consecutive probation years. The mandatory $4,500 continuing review is new downside attached to the very first sub-80% year, converting what is today a status label into an immediate review obligation and a bill. The three-separate-people governance requirement is the sleeper: it is a structural condition on the EPP, not a data request, and Relay should confirm it can name three distinct individuals as legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair for its Texas program before the August 1 reporting date arrives.

    What it does

    The State Board for Educator Certification proposes amendments to all six operative sections of 19 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 229, the rules that assign every Texas educator preparation program (EPP) its annual accreditation status under the Accountability System for Educator Preparation (ASEP). Four changes carry real consequence. (1) The Accredited threshold drops: §229.4(b)(1) would require 80% of possible ASEP Index points, replacing the current 85% — the bracketed deletion '[85%]' appears in the proposed rule text. (2) The status ladder is restructured. Today a program between 80% and 85% is Accredited-Warned and anything under 80% is Accredited-Probation; under the proposal the first year below 80% is Accredited-Warned and only the second and later consecutive years below 80% are Accredited-Probation (§229.4(b)(3)(A), (b)(4)(A)) — one additional year before probation attaches. (3) New §229.5(b) makes a continuing EPP review under §228.13 MANDATORY whenever a program is assigned Accredited-Warned or Accredited-Probation, satisfied by an in-process review if one is already under way. The fiscal note prices that review at $4,500 per program, paid by the EPP: of nine programs that scored below 80% on the 2024-2025 ASEP Index, five had been Accredited the prior year and one was already due its five-year review, so TEA models four discretionary reviews, $18,000 in new EPP cost and $18,000 in new state revenue. (4) New reporting: Figure 19 TAC §229.3(f)(1) adds 'EPP contact information' — names, email addresses and phone numbers of the EPP's legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair, due by August 1 each year through the Educator Certification Online System, and the figure states these 'must be three separate people.' New §229.2(19) and (23) define 'governing body' (including at minimum its chairperson) and 'legal authority' (the person with final decision-making authority — dean, director, owner, executive director, superintendent or program director). §229.7(b)(4) and (c) then route accreditation-status notices to all three roles and let the legal authority request an informal review. Also proposed: the first year a redesigned principal or teacher survey replaces a prior survey is report-only and not used for accreditation (§229.4(a)(2), (a)(5)), because both surveys are being revised to track the updated T-TESS observation rubric; and beginning in 2026-2027, candidates are evaluated against the Chapter 228 Subchapter F field-supervision frequency and duration requirements effective September 1, 2026 (§229.4(a)(4)(A)(ii)). New definitions align 'host teacher' and 'intern mentor teacher' with §228.2. The comment period runs August 14 through September 14, 2026; SBEC will also take registered oral and written comment at its September 2026 meeting. DETAIL ADDED 2026-09-21 from the Item 6 agenda PDF (september18agendaitem6.pdf, 1.45 MB, read raw with pdftotext this run): the item is styled DISCUSSION AND ACTION and gives SBEC 'an opportunity to adopt, SUBJECT TO STATE BOARD OF EDUCATION (SBOE) REVIEW,' amendments to 19 TAC Chapter 229 Subchapters A, B, C and E. Stated scope: adjustments to the Accountability System for Educator Preparation (ASEP) Manual; clarified processes and timelines for new certification tests, surveys and observation requirements; updated sources for population identification; increased ASEP communications; and time and supports for EPPs with a lowered ASEP status. EFFECTIVE DATE, quoting the packet: 'The proposed effective date would be December 27, 2026 (20 days after filing as adopted with the Texas Register). The proposed effective date is based on the SBEC and SBOE meeting schedules' — so the December date is contingent on BOTH SBEC adoption and SBOE review, not on the 09-18 vote alone. FISCAL DETAIL not previously on this row: the packet prices a discretionary review at $4,500 per program and estimates that of the nine programs scoring below 80% on the ASEP Index in 2024-2025, four would receive a discretionary review under the proposed rules, amounting to $18,000 in new state revenue and $18,000 in new costs to EPPs. The packet repeats that 'no changes are recommended since published as proposed, but additional changes may be recommended at the time of the meeting based on public comment.' The VOTE OUTCOME REMAINS UNVERIFIED — see the action note.

    Implications

    • Compliance. New annual submission by August 1: names, emails and phone numbers of the EPP's legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair, filed through the Educator Certification Online System — and the figure requires three separate people. Confirm Relay's Texas EPP can satisfy the three-distinct-persons condition and decide who is named to each role.

    • Compliance. Accreditation-status notices would go by email to all three named roles, and the legal authority gains standing to request an informal review — so the internal routing for a 14-day informal-review deadline under §229.7(b)(3) needs to be settled in advance, not when a notice lands.

    • Risk. A single ASEP Index year below 80% would trigger a mandatory continuing EPP review under §228.13 at $4,500, paid by the EPP. Under current rules a first sub-80% year produces probation status but no automatic review; the proposal adds cost and an oversight cycle at the first miss.

    • Program. Field-supervision frequency and duration for candidates in clinical teaching, residency or internship shift to the Chapter 228 Subchapter F requirements effective September 1, 2026 for the 2026-2027 evaluation year. The 95% compliance standard in §229.4(a)(4)(A) is unchanged and the small-group exception does not apply to it.

    • Advocacy. Nineteen business days to file written comment, plus registered oral comment at the September SBEC meeting. The most useful comment is narrow: the preamble describes the §229.4(b)(3)(A) restructuring but does not separately itemize the §229.4(b)(1) drop from 85% to 80% that the rule text marks, and asking SBEC to confirm the Accredited threshold on the record protects every program's planning assumption.

    Leader brief

    Texas votes September 18 on the rewrite of the rules that grade Relay's teacher-preparation program; comments close September 14

    Update September 21: the Texas board took up this item at its September 18 meeting, but three days on the agency has published no result — only the agenda, which confirms the adoption vote was scheduled. There is no adopted rule document and no minutes. We therefore do not know whether the 80 percent accreditation bar, the warning year and the mandatory paid continuing review were adopted, amended or held. Staff had recommended adopting the rules exactly as proposed, and any adoption would still go to the State Board of Education for review, with a proposed effective date of December 27, 2026. We will check again at the next run.

    • Relay's Texas program will be rated under these rules for the next accountability cycle. The lower threshold and the warning year reduce the risk of an abrupt probation status; the new timelines for tests and surveys change what data the program must track. This is the last week to put anything on the record before the vote.

    Questions to ask

    • If the rules were adopted as proposed, our Texas programs have roughly three months before the standard changes. Do we want to begin preparing on the assumption that they passed, rather than waiting for the agency to post the record?

    • Does Relay Texas want to submit a written comment by September 14 or register a speaker for September 18, and on which provisions?

    • Has the program checked its current Accountability System for Educator Preparation index against the new 80 percent line and the warning-year sequence?

    • Who owns tracking the State Board of Education review step and the December 27 effective date?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Georgia is one of Relay's authorized jurisdictions and Relay's Georgia programs are approved by the same Professional Standards Commission this act directs. The new 20-2-200(b) standard is a program-approval requirement, not a district mandate: it changes what an approved elementary-preparation program must teach, which is Relay's curriculum surface directly. The GACE alignment change moves the certification assessment Relay's Georgia completers sit for.

    What it does

    House Bill 1030, passed by both chambers and effective 2026-07-01, enacts the 'Math Matters Act' at O.C.G.A. 20-2-153.2 and amends the Professional Standards Commission's certification statute at O.C.G.A. 20-2-200. On the school side it requires the State Board of Education to adopt content standards for middle and high school advanced math courses, requires every local education agency to establish advanced math courses, sets minimum core math instruction time in grades four and five, mandates parent notification and annual reporting, and prohibits waivers. On the educator-preparation side — the part that reaches Relay — it does two things. First, it requires the Professional Standards Commission to revise the standards for acquiring and maintaining teacher certification in elementary education to include developmentally appropriate evidence-based math instruction, and requires the Georgia Assessments for Certification of Educators (GACE), or any successor certification assessment, to be aligned with evidence-based literacy instruction AND evidence-based math instruction. Second, it adds a new program-approval standard at O.C.G.A. 20-2-200(b): the Commission must create standards ensuring that postsecondary students completing ELEMENTARY education teacher certification programs graduate with training that effectively teaches the four strands of mathematical proficiency (real-world problem solving, procedural fluency, conceptual understanding, productive dispositions), implements evidence-based math instruction, provides effective instruction and interventions for students needing intervention, and uses student data to make instructional decisions. That standard sits alongside the existing 20-2-200(b)(2) mandatory-coursework requirements (differentiated instruction; fundamental reading skills including phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension) and the existing 20-2-200(b)(3) approval of alternative-certification programs. UPDATE 2026-08-21: the rulemaking this act ordered is now real. At its July 9, 2026 meeting the Professional Standards Commission initiated amendments to Rule 505-3-.14 (Elementary Education P-5 Program), 505-3-.27 (Mathematics Education Program), and 505-3-.92 (K-5 Mathematics Endorsement) to add the Math Matters Act requirements. The proposed 505-3-.14 text (verified from the posted rule PDF) writes the four strands of mathematical proficiency, evidence-based math instruction, intervention, and data-based instructional decisions directly into program content standard 3. Public comment runs 2026-07-31 through 2026-08-29 (written comments to the GaPSC Executive Secretary via RulesComments@GaPSC.com or mail); the Commission takes up adoption at its September 10 meeting, with an effective date of October 15, 2026 if adopted.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Relay's Georgia elementary preparation curriculum must be able to evidence the four strands of mathematical proficiency, evidence-based math instruction, math intervention, and data-based instructional decision-making when the Professional Standards Commission revises its program-approval standards.

    • Program. Elementary math methods coursework and clinical assessment rubrics are the concrete artifacts a GaPSC reviewer will ask for; building them ahead of the rule is cheaper than retrofitting under a review deadline.

    • Advocacy. The Commission has to write these standards. A graduate-level preparation provider has a narrow, well-timed opening to comment on how 'four strands' training is evidenced before the rule text hardens.

    • Advocacy. A live, short comment window: if Relay wants the math program standards workable for graduate-level and alternative-route providers, written comments are due to RulesComments@GaPSC.com by August 29, before the September 10 adoption vote.

    • Risk. If the GACE alignment date is in fact 2028, Georgia completers face an assessment change mid-pipeline; if it was 2025, the alignment obligation is already overdue. The tracker cannot yet say which, and program planning should not assume either.

    Leader brief

    Georgia has told its teacher-certification agency to rewrite elementary preparation standards around math — including for us

    Update September 18: still nothing published from the September 10 meeting on HB1030 rules; the posted minutes file does not open. Georgia's Math Matters Act ordered the Professional Standards Commission — the agency that approves Relay's Georgia programs — to rewrite elementary preparation standards around math. That rewrite is now on paper: the Commission published proposed rule amendments adding the law's math requirements (the four strands of mathematical proficiency, evidence-based math instruction, intervention, and using student data) to the elementary program standards, the public comment window closed August 29 and the Commission votes on adoption September 10. If adopted, the rules take effect October 15, 2026. Update, September 11: the Commission met on September 10 as scheduled; no report or minutes were posted by the morning of September 11, so the adoption result is unconfirmed until we check again on Monday, September 14. Update, September 14: still no published result from the September 10 vote after a fourth check; the rules are still listed as proposed with an October 15 effective date. Update, September 15: still no posted result from the September 10 vote after a fifth check; the October 15 effective date stands if the rules were adopted. As of September 16 the Commission still has not posted the result of its September 10 vote. Update, September 17: seventh check, still no posted result from the September 10 vote.

    • This is the moment the requirement becomes concrete for our Georgia elementary program: once adopted, program reviewers can ask us to evidence math training against the new standard. The comment window is the one chance to shape the wording before it is fixed.

    Questions to ask

    • Should our Georgia elementary math methods coursework be mapped against the proposed standard now, so we know the gap before the rule takes effect October 15?

    • The comment window closed August 29 — if Relay did not file, the remaining lever is the September 10 adoption meeting and the implementation guidance that follows. Do we want a presence there?

    Scopewhole enrolled text, 4 sections; the certification/preparation provisions (Section 2, O.C.G.A. 20-2-200) read in full

    • Section: Section 2; Cite: O.C.G.A. 20-2-200(b)(6); Change: New standard: the Professional Standards Commission must ensure postsecondary students completing elementary education teacher certification programs graduate with training in the four strands of mathematical proficiency, evidence-based math instruction, intervention for students who need it, and use of student data for instructional decisions.; Direction: restricts; Relay relevance: Adds a curriculum requirement every Georgia-approved elementary preparation program must satisfy, Relay's included.

    • Section: Section 2; Cite: O.C.G.A. 20-2-200(a)(4)(B); Change: The GACE, or any other assessment the Commission requires for teacher certification, must be aligned with evidence-based math instruction in addition to evidence-based literacy instruction. The effective date printed in the enrolled text is ambiguous between 2025 and 2028 (markup lost in extraction).; Direction: restricts; Relay relevance: Changes the content of the certification assessment Relay's Georgia completers must pass; the timing is not yet established.

    • Section: Section 1; Cite: O.C.G.A. 20-2-153.2; Change: Creates the Math Matters Act: advanced math course standards and LEA offerings, minimum core math instruction time in grades 4-5, parent notification, annual reports, and an express prohibition on waivers.; Direction: restricts; Relay relevance: District-side demand signal — defines the math practice Relay's Georgia graduates will be hired to deliver.

    • Section: Section 3; Cite: HB1030 Sec. 3; Change: Act becomes effective July 1, 2026.; Direction: procedural; Relay relevance: Already in force at the date of this run.

    Why it matters to Relay

    The flexibility lets a certified teacher earn the bilingual extension by passing a test instead of enrolling in a registered program's coursework, which reduces demand for exactly the kind of extension coursework a New York educator-preparation provider sells, while widening the pool of bilingual-certified teachers in the districts Relay serves. One more year of it is now near-certain; the question for Relay is whether it becomes permanent in 2027. Never on the board; found by the sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 1 Register.

    What it does

    Emergency/proposed rulemaking EDU-26-26-00007-EP (Filing No. 542), adopted by the Board of Regents on an emergency basis effective June 16, 2026 and published in the July 1, 2026 State Register with a 60-day comment period (closed around August 30). Amends §§80-2.9, 80-4.3 and 80-5.18 to move the sunset of flexibilities first adopted in January 2024, November 2024 and October 2025 from August 31, 2026 to August 31, 2027: certified teachers applying for the Supplementary certificate in ESOL (or ESOL-certified teachers applying for a Supplementary certificate in another area) may satisfy either the examination requirement or the enrollment-and-education requirement; certified teachers and pupil personnel professionals applying for the Supplementary Bilingual Education extension may pass the Bilingual Education Assessment in lieu of matriculating in a registered bilingual-extension program and completing its coursework, with a single renewal allowed for extensions first obtained this way. The stated rationale is the continued influx of recently arrived and asylum-seeking English language learners. The June emergency action expires September 13, 2026; the notice anticipated a further emergency re-adoption at the July Regents meeting, but no re-adoption notice appears in the August 5 through September 9 Register issues read this run (the item stays on the pending-actions index). Permanent adoption is anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Update 2026-09-14: the June 16 emergency action expired September 13. No re-adoption notice appeared in the State Register through the September 9 issue, and the September 14-15 Regents agenda (Higher Education Committee and Full Board item lists read this run) carries no item on §§80-2.9, 80-4.3 or 80-5.18. Either a re-adoption was filed without a Regents agenda item (check the September 16 and 23 Register issues) or the test-in-lieu-of-coursework flexibility has lapsed until the October permanent adoption.

    Implications

    • Program. Through August 31, 2027, certified teachers can add the bilingual education extension by passing the Bilingual Education Assessment rather than completing a registered program's coursework; any Relay bilingual-extension enrollment in New York competes with that route for another year.

    • Partnership. Partner districts with large newcomer populations gain a faster, cheaper path to bilingual-certified staff, which can change what they ask Relay for (assessment preparation and bilingual pedagogy PD rather than extension coursework).

    • Risk. A flexibility renewed three times since 2024 and now extended to 2027 is on a path to permanence; the 2027 sunset is the next decision point.

    Leader brief

    New York is extending, for a fourth year, a shortcut that lets certified teachers earn bilingual and ESOL credentials by passing a test instead of taking coursework

    Since 2024 New York has let already-certified teachers add a bilingual education extension by passing the state's bilingual assessment rather than enrolling in a university program, and let teachers seeking the supplementary English-as-a-second-language certificate choose between the exam and the coursework route. Those shortcuts were due to expire August 31, 2026. In June the Board of Regents extended them on an emergency basis to August 31, 2027, citing the continued arrival of asylum-seeking students, and it expects to make the extension permanent in October. Update, September 14: the emergency version expired September 13 and we found no renewal in the state register or on this week's Regents agenda, so the shortcut may be lapsed until the permanent rule is adopted in October. Update, September 17: the September 16 State Register carries no notice re-adopting the emergency rule, so the shortcut appears to have lapsed on September 13 and to stay lapsed until the permanent rule takes effect in late October, unless a re-adoption appears in the September 30 Register.

    • Where Relay offers or plans bilingual-extension or ESOL coursework in New York, the test route is a lower-cost competitor for another year, and districts with newcomer populations may prefer to route staff through it. The extension also enlarges the bilingual-certified workforce in Relay's partner schools.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay's New York enrollment depend on bilingual-extension or ESOL coursework that the test route displaces?

    • Is there a service Relay could offer around the test route itself, such as preparation or bilingual pedagogy training for teachers who certify by exam?

    Federal role restructuring: 'Returning Education to the States' campaign continues

    The standing storyline of this cycle: federal role shrinking, state discretion growing. With Ed-Flex now covering five Relay jurisdictions, Title program

    SourceED press · Open the primary source
    StatusUPDATED

    Why it matters to Relay

    The standing storyline of this cycle: federal role shrinking, state discretion growing. With Ed-Flex now covering five Relay jurisdictions, Title program requirements Relay's partner districts operate under can increasingly be waived at the state level — the compliance baseline varies by state more than it used to.

    What it does

    ED's 'Returning Education to the States' push continues and hit a numeric milestone: with Arizona, Nevada, and South Carolina approved on Aug 21, 25 states now hold Ed-Flex authority — the ESSA-reauthorized power for a state education agency to waive certain federal statutory/regulatory requirements for its districts without case-by-case ED signoff (civil rights, IDEA, and parental-involvement requirements are non-waivable). Verified from ED's participating-states list: five Relay jurisdictions now hold the authority — Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana, and Illinois (approved May 13, 2026, through 2030-31). Secretary McMahon's tour also stopped in Virginia this week. Added 2026-09-14: Education Week (09-11, page read this run) reports how the 'returning education to the states' competitive priority worked in this year's National Professional Development grant round (training teachers of English learners): applicants were encouraged to obtain letters of support from governors or state chiefs for extra points, states handled the requests inconsistently (some reviewed applications in depth, some lacked capacity, at least one is barred from issuing such letters), and the Department intends to make final NPD selections by September 30 (per Education Week). Update 2026-09-25 (ED release read raw this run): ED approved Mississippi's Returning Education to the States (RES) waiver on 09-24, the seventh state after Iowa, Louisiana, Indiana, Vermont, Arkansas and South Dakota. The ESEA Title VIII waiver lets Mississippi consolidate $14 million in federal state-level activities funds through 2029 and align them with its own plan; across the seven states, $123 million is now consolidated. Indiana is the one Relay jurisdiction among the seven.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Half the states can now waive some federal education rules on their own

    The U.S. Department of Education approved three more states for 'Ed-Flex,' bringing it to 25 states — half the country. Ed-Flex lets a state education agency waive certain federal program requirements for its school districts without asking Washington first (civil-rights and special-education protections cannot be waived). Five states where Relay operates now hold this authority: Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana, and Illinois.

    • Federal program rules our partner districts operate under are becoming more state-variable: the same federal funding stream can carry different strings in different Relay states. This shifts where our policy attention needs to sit — state agencies, not just ED.

    Questions to ask

    • Do our district partnerships in the five Ed-Flex Relay states know which requirements their state has actually waived?

    • Should state-level waiver activity become a standing item in how we track these five states?

    CommentComment

    Why it matters to Relay

    Georgia's educator-preparation program rules for elementary and mathematics are being rewritten around the Math Matters Act on a October 15 effective date, and a state AI-for-educators endorsement now exists with two RESAs approved to deliver it. Relay's Georgia programs and any Georgia partner pipeline work sit inside both changes, and the AI endorsement is a named credential Relay could build toward rather than a general trend.

    What it does

    GaPSC's July 31, 2026 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (read raw this run) set a package of certification and educator-preparation rule changes all dated effective October 15, 2026, with comments due August 29 and adoption scheduled for the Commission's September 10 meeting. Chapter 505-2 Certification: AMENDS 505-2-.08 Provisional Certificate, 505-2-.11 International Exchange Certificate, 505-2-.26 Certification and Licensure Assessments, 505-2-.34 Add a Field, 505-2-.46 Military Support Certificate and 505-2-.106 Academic Content Concentrations; INITIATES 505-2-.198 Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement, 505-2-.199 Artificial Intelligence for Educators Micro-Endorsement, 505-2-.200 Safety and Hunter Education Endorsement and 505-2-.201 Lifeguarding and Aquatic Safety Micro-Endorsement. Chapter 505-3 Educator Preparation: REPEALS and re-INITIATES 505-3-.64 Instructional Technology Program (rebuilt on the 2024 ISTE standards) and 505-3-.68 School Nutrition Director Program; AMENDS 505-3-.14 Elementary Education (P-5) Program, 505-3-.27 Mathematics Education Program and 505-3-.92 K-5 Mathematics Endorsement to add the requirements of the Math Matters Act (HB1030) passed in the 2026 session, and 505-3-.112 Dyslexia Endorsement to adopt the International Dyslexia Association's 2025 definition. The .34 amendment allows a test-in option for Elementary Grades P-5. Three of the amendments (.08, .26, .106) bar obtaining the Special Education Reading academic content concentration by assessment alone. The Professional Association of Georgia Educators' Capitol Report of September 21 states the Commission approved or amended these rules at the September 10 meeting with an October 15 effective date, and that Middle Georgia RESA and Northwest Georgia RESA both received developmental approval to offer the Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement and the Foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Education Micro-Endorsement. That adoption is ATTRIBUTED, not verified: GaPSC's rules page still lists only the April 15 and July 1, 2026 Final Notices of Effective Rules, the September 2026 minutes file is still a soft-404, and the Georgia Administrative Code is current only through rules filed September 2, 2026, so 505-2-.198 still reads 'Reserved' there.

    Implications

    • Compliance. If the Elementary Education (P-5), Mathematics Education and K-5 Mathematics Endorsement program rules take effect October 15 as noticed, any Relay Georgia elementary or math preparation offering must map to the Math Matters Act content requirements written into 505-3-.14, 505-3-.27 and 505-3-.92.

    • Program. 505-2-.34 adds a test-in option for Elementary Grades P-5, which changes the add-a-field route Georgia candidates can use alongside coursework and is worth modeling against Relay's own P-5 pathway.

    • Program. The Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement (505-2-.198) and Micro-Endorsement (.199) become real Georgia credentials on October 15, with Middle Georgia RESA and Northwest Georgia RESA already approved to deliver them — a defined standard Relay could design toward rather than a general AI-in-education trend.

    • Risk. The adoption itself rests on a stakeholder association's meeting report. Relay should not act on the October 15 date as settled until GaPSC posts the Final Notice of Effective Rules or the September minutes.

    Leader brief

    Georgia approves new teacher-certification rules, including a first state AI endorsement for educators, effective October 15

    The Georgia Professional Standards Commission, the state body that sets teacher certification and teacher-preparation program rules, approved a package of rule changes at its September 10 meeting. The changes take effect October 15. Two of them create new credentials: an Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement and a shorter micro-endorsement version. Others rewrite the rules governing elementary (grades P-5) and mathematics teacher preparation programs to carry out the Math Matters Act, a law Georgia passed earlier in 2026. A separate change lets candidates add an elementary P-5 teaching field by passing a test. Two regional service agencies, Middle Georgia and Northwest Georgia, have already been approved to offer the new AI endorsement. One caution: this approval is reported by the Professional Association of Georgia Educators, which attends the meetings, and the Commission itself has not yet posted its formal notice or its September minutes. The underlying proposal, the rule numbers and the October 15 date are confirmed from the Commission's own July notice.

    • Georgia is now the clearest case of a state writing artificial intelligence into its formal educator-credential structure rather than issuing guidance, and it is doing so with named providers already approved. Separately, Georgia's elementary and mathematics preparation program standards change on October 15, which affects how any Relay program or partner pipeline in Georgia must be structured. The work in front of Relay is compliance and program design, not advocacy: the comment period closed August 29.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay want to offer, or partner to offer, Georgia's new Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement, given that two regional service agencies already have approval?

    • Which Relay Georgia offerings touch the elementary P-5 or mathematics program rules, and who owns mapping them to the Math Matters Act requirements before October 15?

    • Should someone confirm the adoption directly with the Commission rather than waiting for the formal notice to be posted?

    Track

    NY: AI employment-decision disclosure extended to school districts and BOCES (Chapter 86 of 2026)

    Ecosystem-level rather than a direct Relay obligation — Relay is a private institution and not a covered entity. It matters because it reshapes hiring on the

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionNew York
    ClassBill
    StagePassed
    RecommendationTrack · impact 68
    Latest actionS08831 signed, Chapter 86, 2026-02-13. Assembly same-as A09487 (Otis) was substituted by S08831 on 2026-01-21. Summary and sponsor memorandum read from nyassembly.gov this run. · 2026-02-13
    SourceNew York State Assembly / LegiScan (enacted chapter) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level rather than a direct Relay obligation — Relay is a private institution and not a covered entity. It matters because it reshapes hiring on the receiving end of Relay's New York pipeline: every district and BOCES that hires Relay graduates now has to disclose whether an automated tool screened the application, and maintain an inventory of the AI it uses. Expect districts to slow or narrow their use of AI screening tools while they build the disclosure apparatus, which changes how candidate applications actually get read.

    What it does

    Enacted as Chapter 86 of the Laws of 2026. Amends the State Technology Law, Education Law, and Civil Service Law to extend automated-employment-decision-tool disclosure and artificial-intelligence inventory requirements — already applicable to State agencies — to counties, cities, towns, villages, school districts, boards of cooperative educational services (BOCES), county vocational education and extension boards, district corporations, SUNY, CUNY, and community colleges. Covered entities must publish annual disclosure of automated employment-decision tools in use on their websites and maintain an AI inventory. The chapter repeals and restructures provisions of Chapter 711 of the Laws of 2025 and amends its effective date.

    Implications

    • Program. New York district and BOCES hiring processes gain a disclosure and inventory layer around automated screening. Relay career-services guidance to New York graduates should reflect that applicants can now see whether an automated tool was used.

    • Compliance. Relay is not a covered entity under the chapter. SUNY, CUNY, and community colleges are — relevant if Relay partners with them on shared hiring or placement infrastructure.

    Why it matters to Relay

    California is a watch state (SCAN cap). If the summary holds, the bill draws the line between community-college baccalaureates as a credential on-ramp and community colleges as teacher-preparation providers, which keeps the preparation market with universities and approved programs. Status verified; substance attributed.

    What it does

    Assembly Bill 2206 (Fong), an act amending Education Code sections 44203, 44225, 44227, 44252, 44252.2, 44256, 44258.2, 44258.7, 44259, 44259.1, 44265, 44269, 44300 and 44325 relating to teacher credentialing, topic 'Teacher credentialing: community college baccalaureate degrees'; last amended 2026-08-21, enrolled 2026-09-01, location Governor. Per the sweep's summary (text not read this run), it addresses how community-college bachelor's degrees qualify for credential purposes, including reading, writing and mathematics coursework, and bars community colleges from offering an integrated program combining the baccalaureate with professional preparation for a teaching credential.

    HEA Title II report cards on teacher preparation: ED proposes revised information collection — comment closes Oct 20

    The IPRC is a report Relay actually files, in every state it operates. What gets removed or reworded changes Relay's annual reporting burden and the public data

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionFederal
    ClassRule
    StageComment period open
    RecommendationTrack · impact 67
    Latest actionNotice published 2026-08-21; comments due 2026-10-20 (docket ED-2026-SCC-2707, OMB control 1840-0744) · 2026-08-21
    WindowOctober 20, 2026 · 17 business days
    Sourcefederal_register · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    The IPRC is a report Relay actually files, in every state it operates. What gets removed or reworded changes Relay's annual reporting burden and the public data programs are judged on — worth pulling the draft instruments from the docket to see which items are cut.

    What it does

    ED's Office of Postsecondary Education opened comment on the information collection behind the HEA Title II report cards — the State Report Card and the Institution and Program Report Card that every teacher preparation program, Relay's included, files annually (data feeding the Secretary's Report to Congress on Teacher Quality and states' at-risk/low-performing TPP designations). The notice's summary line calls it an 'extension without change,' but the collection block says 'Type of Review: Revision' and states the request 'removes several items no longer needed and updates some reporting instructions' — the two statements conflict, and the notice does not list which items are removed. Burden estimate: 2,283 annual responses, 185,000 burden hours. Comments due October 20, 2026 via regulations.gov docket ED-2026-SCC-2707.

    Implications

    • Compliance. The Title II IPRC is an annual Relay filing; removed items and revised instructions change what the reporting team must produce, starting with the next collection cycle if approved.

    • Advocacy. A 60-day PRA window (to Oct 20) is the routine opportunity to comment on burden and on which program elements should stay public — but first the draft instruments in docket ED-2026-SCC-2707 need to be pulled to see what 'removes several items' means.

    Leader brief

    The federal report card every teacher-prep program files is being revised

    The U.S. Department of Education is updating the paperwork behind the Higher Education Act Title II report cards — the annual reports every teacher preparation program (including Relay) and every state must file about enrollment, completion, and licensure-test pass rates. The notice says some items are being removed and instructions updated, but does not say which; the details sit in the public docket. Comments are open until October 20.

    • This is the reporting our programs are publicly measured by. Fewer items could mean less annual burden — or the loss of data points that currently work in our favor. Low urgency, but worth knowing what changed before the comment window closes.

    Questions to ask

    • Who should pull the draft report-card instruments from the docket and confirm what is being removed?

    • If the removed items affect how program performance is shown publicly, do we want to file a comment by October 20?

    Why it matters to Relay

    LASO is how Texas districts access state talent money, and the Strategic Talent Systems strand has carried the residency and educator-pipeline supports Relay's Texas partners use. This is a district-facing application, so the Relay angle is partnership readiness before September 23 and a hand-off to the grant finder for the strand-level detail when the portfolio posts.

    What it does

    To the Administrator Addressed letter dated September 3, 2026 from TEA's System Innovation Division: the Learning Acceleration Support Opportunities (LASO) consolidated application for 2026-27 (Cycle 5) offers 21 opportunities bundled around Strategic Planning, Curriculum & Instruction, Strategic Talent Systems, More Time, and Innovative School Models, totaling up to $400 million in grants, allotments and in-kind supports. The application opens September 23, 2026 and closes December 1, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. CT; portfolio details, timeline, webinar registration and resources are to be posted on the LASO webpage. The individual opportunities were not enumerated in the letter.

    Sourcelegiscan_in · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is Indiana's EPP accountability and public-reporting regime, and it applies to any entity the Department approves to offer a course of study leading to an initial license — the category Relay would occupy in Indiana. The 'located in Indiana' qualifier on 'teacher candidate' is the provision worth understanding, because it decides whether an out-of-state institution's Indiana candidates are inside or outside the reporting population. What this act CHANGED is not established: Indiana's enrolled PDF prints amendments without recoverable strike-through markup, and IC 20-28-3-1 carries codified deadlines from 2015 and 2016 that are plainly pre-existing. Reported at TRACK rather than ACT for that reason.

    What it does

    Senate Bill 199, enacted as Public Law 120, amends Indiana Code 20-28-3-1 effective upon passage. As it reads after the act, the Department of Education arranges the statewide system of professional instruction for teacher education, accredits and reviews teacher preparation programs, approves content-area licensure programs within accredited programs, and specifies the license types for completers. 'Teacher candidate' means an individual recommended for an initial teaching license from a teacher preparation program LOCATED IN INDIANA; 'teacher preparation program' includes a teacher education school or department, a transition-to-teaching program under IC 20-28-4, and any other entity approved by the Department to offer a course of study leading to an initial teaching license. Every program must report annually against Department standards and benchmarks — which must include content-area and pedagogy licensure test score data by program — and must publish that report on its OWN website as well as the Department publishing it. Required reporting adds attrition, retention and completion rates of teacher candidates for the previous three calendar years plus the underlying data behind retention rates; completers per content area disaggregated by cumulative GPA range; and the number of candidates per content area who fail a content-area licensure examination and do not retake it. The Department also publishes average scaled scores on basic-skills, content-area and pedagogy examinations, average attempts per test and first-attempt pass percentage, and a matrix rating system for programs built on three years of data.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Any Indiana-approved preparation program must publish its own performance report on its own website annually and supply three-year attrition, retention and completion data with the underlying retention calculations, plus completer counts by content area disaggregated by GPA range.

    • Risk. The matrix rating system publishes comparative program ratings from three years of licensure-test and completion data. A small Indiana candidate cohort can move a published rating sharply, and the statute carries no small-group exception comparable to the Texas ASEP rules.

    Leader brief

    Indiana amended its teacher-preparation reporting and rating rules; what changed is not yet clear

    Indiana enacted a law in March amending the statute that governs how the state accredits teacher-preparation programs and what each program must publish about itself every year. Under the statute as it now reads, any program the state approves must report three years of student attrition, retention and completion figures, licensing-exam results broken out by subject and by grade point average, and must post that report on its own website, not just the state's. The state also publishes a comparative rating for every program. We read the enacted text but could not determine which parts this year's law actually changed, because Indiana publishes its enacted bills in a format that does not show the edits and the state's data service requires a key we do not have.

    • If Relay operates an approved preparation program in Indiana, this is a public-reporting and public-rating obligation that runs annually and that a small cohort can distort. The immediate question is factual rather than strategic: we need to establish what our Indiana status and cohort size actually are before deciding whether any of this needs a response.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we hold an Indiana program approval today, and if so how many candidates are in the reporting population?

    • Is it worth the effort to pin down exactly what this law changed, or is knowing the current obligations enough for now?

    What it does

    Posted September 8, 2026 by NYSED's Office of Teacher and Leader Development: beginning September 15, eligible educator candidates with demonstrated financial need may apply through the voucher survey on the NYSTCE webpage for one NYSTCE Registration Voucher (offsets the cost of registering for a New York State Teacher Certification Examination) and one NYSTCE Right Start Learning Course Voucher (access to an eligible exam-preparation course) per academic year.     Why it matters to Relay

    New Tennessee money for exactly the leadership-pipeline and mentoring work Relay sells to districts; the districts and charters that join the grant are potential buyers. The Department of Labor's name on a TSL award is also a small data point in the ED-to-DOL program shift.

    What it does

    The Tennessee Department of Education was awarded more than $7.9 million through the federal Teacher and School Leader Incentive Program (TSL), which the release attributes to the U.S. Department of Education and the U.S. Department of Labor; Tennessee was one of about twenty grantees this round. Its Instructional Leadership & Educator Development Grant will fund eligible districts and public charter schools to build educator leadership and mentoring pathways, strengthen educator evaluation, implement strategic staffing, and pay educator incentives in high-need schools, monitored with evaluation and human-capital data. The release does not give the grant period, the participating districts, or how subgrants will be made.

    Implications

    • Partnership. Participating Tennessee districts and charters will be buying leadership, mentoring and evaluation support; worth asking TDOE how districts join and whether outside providers are used.

    • Funding. About twenty TSL grantees were funded this round nationally; other Relay states' SEAs or districts may be among them.

    Leader brief

    Tennessee gets $7.9 million federal grant for teacher and principal leadership pipelines

    Tennessee's education department won a $7.9 million federal grant from the Teacher and School Leader Incentive Program, one of about twenty awards nationwide. The money will go to districts and charter schools serving high-need students to build leadership and mentoring pathways for teachers, improve teacher evaluation, place staff strategically, and pay incentives to educators.

    • This funds the kind of teacher-leader and principal development Relay offers, in a state where Relay works. The districts that take part will need partners to deliver it, so it is a possible sales or partnership opening once Tennessee says which districts are in.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay approach the Tennessee Department of Education now about how districts will join and whether outside providers are part of the design?

    • Were any of the other roughly twenty grantees in Relay's states, and do we know who they are?

    Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for as a graduate

    At a glance
