    SourcePrimary court order: California v. U.S. Dept. of Education, No. 1:25-cv-10548-AK (D. Mass.), Doc. 176, filed 2026-09-17 (Kelley, D.J.) — PDF read in full this run via the California Attorney General press-documents archive. Coverage: Education Week 2026-09-18; Associated Press via WBUR 2026-09-18. · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for as a graduate institution and educator-preparation provider, which makes this the run's most consequential item. The directive that suppressed those competitions is now vacated and declared unlawful, and the court expressly framed vacatur as restoring the ordinary priorities that govern the FORTHCOMING FY2026 awards — the same awards the Department said on 2026-09-09 it was preparing to make (16 SEED and 12 TQP). That converts a watch item into a live eligibility question with a short fuse: the competitions are imminent and the legal cloud over DEI-adjacent program design has lifted, at least as to this directive. What the ruling does NOT do is return terminated money, and it does not enjoin the Department from adopting a new, properly reasoned policy. Relay's decision is about posture on the next competition, not recovery of the last one.

    What it does

    VERIFIED FROM THE PRIMARY ORDER this run: California v. U.S. Department of Education, No. 1:25-cv-10548-AK (D. Mass.), Document 176, filed 2026-09-17, 70 pages, Hon. Angel Kelley — retrieved as a PDF from the California Attorney General's press-documents archive and read in full with pdftotext. This SUPERSEDES the wire-attributed account this row previously carried. Holding: Plaintiff States' Motion for Summary Judgment is GRANTED, Defendants' Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment is DENIED, and the Motion to Strike is DENIED AS MOOT. Relief, quoting the order: pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 706 and 28 U.S.C. 2202 the Court 'VACATES and SETS ASIDE, in its entirety, the Department's February 5, 2025, Directive, titled "Eliminating Discrimination and Fraud in Department Grant Awards," as arbitrary and capricious and not in accordance with law'; and pursuant to 28 U.S.C. 2201 it is DECLARED that the Directive is unlawful because it violates the APA. The Court DECLINED to enter the permanent injunction plaintiffs also sought, reasoning that the declaratory judgment and principles of preclusion make injunctive relief unnecessary against a hypothetical future policy document. Facts as found in the order: the plaintiffs are eight States (California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Colorado, Illinois, Maryland, New York and Wisconsin); defendants are the Department, Denise Carter in her official capacity as former Acting Secretary, and Secretary Linda McMahon; the February 5, 2025 Directive implemented Executive Order 14173 (2025-01-21) and Executive Order 14190, 'Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling,' 90 Fed. Reg. 8,853 (2025-02-03); and 'as of March 12, 2025, Defendants terminated 104 out of 109 total grants pursuant to the February 2025 Directive, including forty from Plaintiff States.' The order also records that 'since June 5, 2025, the Department has not relied on the February 2025 Directive in issuing any termination or non-continuation decisions for TQP and SEED grants.' On the reach of the remedy, the court reasoned that vacatur 'would leave in place the statutory and regulatory framework for TQP and SEED grants, as well as the most recently promulgated agency priorities, which ordinarily govern the Department's grant award process, including the forthcoming FY2026 grant awards.' TWO CORRECTIONS to the previously reported account: (1) the court's own figure is 104 of 109 TQP and SEED awards, not the 31 SEED / 72 TQP split Education Week drew from its own database of canceled grants; (2) the effect on the pending FY2026 awards comes from the VACATUR of the Directive, not from a separate injunction barring use of the executive order — the order denies injunctive relief. The order does not itself restore terminated funds; the court had previously held that recovery of the money lies with the Court of Federal Claims.

    Implications

    • Funding. The FY2026 TQP and SEED competitions are the near-term opportunity. With the February 2025 Directive vacated, the ordinary statutory framework and most recent agency priorities govern the award process — the court said so explicitly.

    • Risk. The court denied a permanent injunction. A new directive, issued with adequate reasoning and process, could reimpose similar conditions. This is a reprieve on one instrument, not a durable rule.

    • Compliance. Program descriptions written defensively during the directive's life may now understate what Relay actually does; conversely, nothing here immunizes a proposal from a future policy. Design to the statute, not to either directive.

    • Advocacy. The reasoning — that mass termination on DEI grounds was arbitrary and capricious and contrary to the TQP, SEED and GEPA statutes — is directly citable in Relay's EDGAR comment, which closes 2026-09-23 and concerns the Department's discretion to terminate grants for convenience.

    Leader brief

    The court order behind last week's teacher-training grant ruling is now in hand, and it is stronger than the news coverage suggested

    We have now read the actual court decision rather than press accounts of it. On September 17 a federal judge in Massachusetts threw out, in full, the Education Department's February 2025 order that directed the cancellation of education grants tied to diversity, equity and inclusion work. The court found the directive arbitrary and unlawful. The decision records that the Department cancelled 104 of 109 Teacher Quality Partnership and SEED grants under it — the two federal programs Relay is eligible for. Two details matter and were not clear from the coverage. First, the judge deliberately did NOT issue an injunction, holding that striking the directive down was enough; that means the Department could write a new, better-reasoned policy. Second, the judge specifically said that clearing the directive away restores the normal rules governing the upcoming 2026 grant awards — the awards the Department said on September 9 it was about to make.

    • The practical effect is that the next round of federal teacher-preparation grant competitions is expected shortly and is no longer operating under the cancelled directive. This is an opportunity window, not a settled victory: no terminated money comes back, and nothing stops a future administration policy done properly. The same reasoning is also useful to us this week, because the Department is finishing a separate rule about its power to cancel grants, and comments close Wednesday.

    Questions to ask

    • Are we positioned to compete in the upcoming federal teacher-preparation grant round, and who owns that decision this week? And do we cite this ruling in our comment on the grant-cancellation rule before Wednesday?

    At a glance

    ClassAgency

    SourceNYCPS 'Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and Screen Time' (primary, verified 2026-09-03); Chalkbeat New York, The 74, K-12 Dive, Politico (coverage) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    NYCPS is Relay's largest placement and hiring partner, and this policy now sets the operating envelope for every Relay candidate and graduate teaching there: AI may support planning and operational work, but not grading, behavior monitoring, or any placement, promotion or graduation decision, and special-education documents stay with qualified professionals. That line should be mirrored in how Relay teaches AI use to NYC-bound candidates and in any practice tools Relay puts in their hands. The K-8 ban on student-facing generative AI closes New York's elementary and middle grades to AI-tutoring pilots of the kind tested in the Oreopoulos trials; the five high-school pilots and the mandatory AI-literacy modules are where an AI-in-instruction partnership could still land. The Technology in Schools Coalition is the venue for influencing the April 2027 recommendations. Across Relay's large districts the split is now explicit: NYC bans student AI through grade 8 and narrows teacher use, DC's OSSE permits AI grading with oversight, and Florida's State Board votes September 16 on a district AI-policy mandate.

    What it does

    New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) has enacted, for the 2026-27 school year, a moratorium on student-facing generative AI in grades 2-K through 8 and a set of screen-time limits, published on its 'Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and Screen Time' page (read this run). Mechanisms, from the primary text: (1) BANS software that uses student-facing generative AI in grades 2-K through 8. (2) LIMITS high-school use to approved, vetted programs — five centrally approved pilots (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, Intel AI-Ready Schools), any high school may apply, one pilot per student, dosage set per tool (15 to 45 minutes a week or one period a week); career-readiness pathways (CTE, FutureReadyNYC, certification programs) may use required AI tools under teacher supervision. (3) REQUIRES every high-school student to complete two 45-minute AI literacy modules (how AI works, data privacy and bias, appropriate school use), with a longer course for pilot and career-pathway students. (4) SETS screen-time rules: no 1:1 screen time in 2-K through grade 2; recommended maximum of 30 minutes a day of 1:1 screen time in grades 3-5 and 45 minutes in grades 6-8; teacher-led use of computers, tablets and smart boards for whole- or small-group instruction stays allowed. (5) CARVES OUT assistive technology and screen time provided under an IEP or 504 plan, tools students with disabilities and English language learners need, assessments (screeners and diagnostics), remote-instruction days, and centrally approved instruction such as e-books, robotics, coding and simulations. (6) EXTENDS the rules to community-based organizations instructing during school hours in NYCPS buildings or contracted settings, and to contracted early-childhood programs. (7) For TEACHERS and staff: AI use for instructional planning and operational tasks continues, subject to the ERMA (Enterprise Request Management Application) data-privacy and security review and procurement rules; AI MAY NOT be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or placement, promotion, graduation and other decisions about students; special-education documents are developed by qualified professionals, and counseling, crisis intervention and therapeutic support only by qualified staff; teachers remain responsible for the accuracy and appropriateness of what they produce. (8) GOVERNANCE: NYCPS is forming a Technology in Schools Coalition (students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners, experts) to recommend the future of classroom technology use, with a report due April 2027; ERMA review is to expand beyond privacy and security to algorithmic bias, equity impact and instructional effectiveness. Per Chalkbeat (2026-09-02): the moratorium runs for at least this school year; the city is disabling AI features in 38 existing citywide ed-tech contracts (list not released; Amira and the digital HMH Into Reading named by the mayor's education adviser), products whose AI cannot be turned off will be dropped, and principals may resume ed-tech purchases with an added IT/legal/contracts review for requests under $25,000; Mayor Mamdani called it the 'broadest generative AI moratorium in the nation.' Per K-12 Dive: ed-tech leaders expect national ripple effects from a one-year ban in the largest U.S. district. Update 09-16 (per Chalkbeat New York): YouTube is now blocked on all school-issued student devices, in school and at home, effective 09-09, with a Google Classroom teacher-share exception — disclosed at a 09-15 City Council oversight hearing one day after Council members Krishnan and Dinowitz called for the restriction.

    Implications

    • Program. Relay's NYC-facing coursework and coaching on AI use should match the teacher-side rules now in force: planning and operational use permitted under ERMA-approved tools; grading, behavior monitoring, and placement/promotion/graduation decisions barred; special-education documents and counseling reserved to qualified professionals.

    • Partnership. The Technology in Schools Coalition is forming now and reports in April 2027. An advisory seat or a standing relationship with it is a timing decision for this fall.

    • Risk. Student-facing generative AI, AI tutors included, is barred in 2-K through grade 8 for at least 2026-27. Any Relay pilot or partner work that puts AI tutoring in front of NYC elementary or middle-grade students must stop or move to the five approved high-school pilots.

    • Compliance. Any Relay-supplied software used with NYC students or staff must clear ERMA (data privacy and security now; algorithmic bias, equity impact and instructional effectiveness planned), and community-based programs Relay partners with inside NYCPS buildings are bound by the same AI and screen-time rules.

    Leader brief

    New York City's AI policy is now official: no student AI tools through eighth grade, and firm limits on how teachers may use AI

    New York City's school system posted its artificial-intelligence and screen-time policy on the evening of September 2, and it applies to the school year that starts September 10. Students from the earliest grades through eighth grade get no access to generative AI tools, including chatbots and AI tutors, for at least this year. High-school students may use AI only in five approved pilot programs or in career-training courses, and every high-school student must complete two short AI-literacy lessons. The youngest students get no individual screen time, and older elementary and middle-school students have daily limits. Teachers may keep using approved AI tools to plan lessons and handle administrative work, but may not use AI to grade, monitor behavior, or make decisions about students; special-education paperwork and counseling stay with qualified staff. The city is also forming a coalition of educators, parents, students and experts to recommend where the policy goes next, with a report due in April 2027. On September 15 the district told the City Council it has also blocked YouTube on every school-issued student device since September 9, in school and at home, except for videos a teacher shares through Google Classroom.

    • New York City is our largest partner, so these rules now define what our candidates and graduates may and may not do with AI in their classrooms, and how we teach AI use should match the city's line. Any work that puts AI in front of younger students in the city is off the table for this year; the high-school pilots and the required AI-literacy lessons are the openings that remain. The new coalition is where the next version of the policy will be shaped.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want a seat or an advisory role on the city's new Technology in Schools Coalition, and who would represent Relay?

    • Should candidates and graduates heading into New York City classrooms get a short briefing on the teacher-side rules before school opens on September 10?

    • Does any current or planned Relay work in New York City depend on student-facing AI in elementary or middle grades, and if so, what is the fallback?

    This is the most directly Relay-facing item the run surfaced, and the wired sources missed it entirely — it came from the cross-engine sweep and was then

    At a glance

    Latest actionDiscussion-only item at the 2026-09-18 SBEC meeting. Agenda packet (september18agendaitem8.pdf, 131 KB) read raw with pdftotext this run. The packet states: 'TEA staff anticipate presenting proposed revisions related to EPP continuing approval, review, monitoring, and support to the SBEC at a future meeting for approval to be published in the Texas Register.'     SourceTX SBEC (agenda Item 8) · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the most directly Relay-facing item the run surfaced, and the wired sources missed it entirely — it came from the cross-engine sweep and was then confirmed against the agency's own packet. Chapter 228 continuing approval is the mechanism by which Relay's Texas program remains an approved EPP; Chapter 229, which the board already tracks, is the accountability rating that feeds it. Two of the questions on the table would change Relay's exposure directly: contingent renewal with differentiated cure periods replaces a blunt approve/sanction decision with a graded one, and risk-based monitoring under 228.13(c) determines how often and how hard a program is examined. The timing is the point. There is no rule text and no comment period, which means this is the pre-rulemaking window when an agency is still deciding what to propose — the stage at which a provider's input is cheapest to give and most likely to land. Once this reaches the Texas Register as proposed text, the room narrows to a formal comment.

    What it does

    Item 8 of the 2026-09-18 State Board for Educator Certification meeting, styled DISCUSSION ONLY, opened a redesign of 19 TAC Chapter 228 — the rules under which an approved Texas educator preparation program keeps its approval. Read raw from the agenda packet this run. The packet frames it as supporting 'development of a redesigned approach to continuing approval review, monitoring, and program support,' and lists the specific policy questions staff put to the board: (1) Continuing approval definitions, processes and renewal decisions — proposed updates to the Continuing Approval Review process 'including how to operationalize the quality review'; options for CONTINGENT RENEWAL decisions and DIFFERENTIATED CURE PERIODS graded to the nature and severity of noncompliance; and treatment of programs initially approved to offer PREP-funded preparation routes. (2) Use of risk factors — the role of risk factors in continuing-approval reviews, monitoring and compliance oversight, and updates to the risk factors in 19 TAC 228.13(c)(1)-(3) and how they prioritize agency review and intervention. (3) Technical assistance — the role of technical assistance following review outcomes, and 'approaches for developing a technical assistance service.' (4) Related updates such as revisions to EPP NEW ENTITY APPROVAL requirements to align with the continuing-approval changes. Statutory basis cited includes Texas Education Code 21.0443, which requires SBEC to set standards for approval and renewal of EPPs and to review each EPP at least once every five years. Staff named as responsible: Melissa Yoder, Director of Quality Preparation; Josh Jones, Director of EPP Field Support and Operations; William Sea, Director of EPP Continuous Improvement. NO RULE TEXT EXISTS YET and none of these are decisions — this is the direction-setting stage.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Contingent renewal and differentiated cure periods would change what a finding against Relay's Texas EPP actually costs — potentially a graded remedy rather than a cliff, but also more frequent intermediate determinations.

    • Risk. Updated risk factors in 19 TAC 228.13(c)(1)-(3) set how often and how intensively TEA reviews a program. Where Relay's Texas program lands against revised factors is worth knowing before the factors are written, not after.

    • Program. Continuing approval of programs offering PREP-funded routes is explicitly on the table, which bears on any Relay pathway that uses or might use PREP funding.

    • Advocacy. No comment period exists yet. Direct engagement with the named TEA staff during the drafting stage is the available route, and it closes when proposed text is published.

    Leader brief

    Texas is starting to rewrite the rules for how teacher-preparation programs keep their state approval, and there is no comment period yet

    At its September 18 meeting, the Texas board that regulates educator certification held a discussion — no vote — on redesigning how programs like ours keep their approval to operate in Texas. Staff asked the board for direction on several things that would affect us: whether renewals could be made conditional with different correction periods depending on how serious a problem is, how the agency decides which programs to scrutinize and how often, whether to build a technical assistance service for programs after a review, and whether to change the requirements for approving new providers. Agency staff said they expect to bring proposed rule language back to the board at a future meeting, with no date announced. We read the agency's own meeting packet for this.

    • This is the stage before there is anything to comment on. Once proposed language is published, our options narrow to a formal comment on someone else's draft. Right now the agency is still deciding what to write, and the staff responsible are named in the packet. Separately, this connects to the Chapter 229 accountability rules we are already tracking in Texas — the accountability rating feeds the approval decision this redesign would restructure.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want to engage Texas agency staff directly while the rules are still being drafted, and if so, who from Relay is the right person to do it? What would we actually ask for on conditional renewals and on how often programs get reviewed?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay's Illinois licensure work runs on 21B-20 and 21B-30, and Public Act 104-0803 (HB5552, signed 2026-08-07) amended the same part of the School Code after this revisory bill was enrolled on 2026-05-31. Which text controls where the two overlap is the open question — worth confirming once the Governor acts rather than assuming the revisory is inert.

    What it does

    Senate Bill 3731, the First 2026 General Revisory Act, passed the House 115-0 on 2026-05-31, passed both houses the same day and was sent to the Governor 2026-06-29. A revisory act's function is to combine multiple amendments made to the same statutory section in a single session into one operative text; Illinois revisory acts are non-substantive by design. The enrolled bill runs 742 sections; 34 fall inside the tracker's topic taxonomy, including the School Code educator licensure sections 105 ILCS 5/21B-20 (types of licenses) and 105 ILCS 5/21B-30 (licensure application and requirements), the Evidence-Based Funding section 105 ILCS 5/18-8.15, the Teachers of Illinois scholarship program, and the pension section 40 ILCS 5/16-150.1. Under Article IV, Section 9(b) of the Illinois Constitution the Governor has 60 calendar days from presentment to sign, veto or amendatorily veto, after which the bill becomes law without signature; presentment was 2026-06-29, putting the default date at 2026-08-28. No gubernatorial action was recorded as of this run.

    Implications

    • Compliance. The operative text of 105 ILCS 5/21B-20 and 21B-30 — the sections governing Illinois license types and licensure requirements — is being consolidated. Any Relay Illinois documentation that cites those sections should be checked against the final text after 2026-08-28.

    • Risk. Public Act 104-0803 amended the same School Code part on 2026-08-07, after this bill was enrolled. A revisory act is meant to be non-substantive, but the interaction with a later public act is not something to assume away.

    Leader brief

    The Illinois housekeeping bill touching our licensure statutes is now law (Public Act 104-0852)

    Illinois passes a 'revisory' bill each session whose only job is to merge the various amendments made to the same statute into one clean text. This year's version was signed by the Governor on August 21 and took effect the same day, as Public Act 104-0852 — a week before the August 28 date on which it would have become law automatically. It touches the two School Code sections that define Illinois teaching license types and licensure requirements — the same part of the code amended on August 7 by the teacher-licensing rewrite we track separately (Public Act 104-0803).

    • Nothing here is intended to change policy. It does mean the authoritative wording of the Illinois licensure sections our program documentation cites is now settled, and it is worth one read against the enacted August 7 law rather than assumed identical.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want a check of the final Illinois licensure text against Public Act 104-0803 now that both are law, or is that a level of detail we accept carrying?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Reshapes what NY teachers and leaders must be prepared to teach and assess; expect downstream changes to educator-prep expectations and Regents agenda items. Relay's largest jurisdiction.

    What it does

    Update 2026-09-15: the Board acted. Per the NYSED release of September 14 (read raw this run), the Board of Regents authorized the Department to move forward with the next phase of NY Inspires: beginning with students graduating in 2028, New York transitions to one State high school diploma and students will no longer be required to pass a prescribed set of Regents examinations to graduate; Regents exams continue as statewide measures of achievement of the learning standards; districts and schools develop local assessment strategies drawing on multiple sources of evidence (initial guidance, a template and a webinar are already released); the Department will develop new high-school accountability assessments for ESSA purposes; the current Advanced Designation becomes a seal or endorsement. The Department will bring proposed regulatory amendments to the Regents by February 2027 to implement the changes in 2027-28, and ESSA-plan and secondary-accountability changes come to the Regents later this fall. Per Chalkbeat (09-14), Regents pressed staff on how locally designed assessments will be kept consistent and rigorous and on what current 9th-11th graders will face; staff said 'high-level local assessment strategies' would be released publicly next school year, and Chalkbeat reports a final vote on the regulations expected in June. EdTrust-New York (09-14, attributed from its feed; the page blocks plain clients) called on NYSED and the Regents to pause the elimination of Regents exams as a graduation requirement until equity concerns and a statewide assessment strategy are addressed. Earlier record: Full Board action item BR (A) 4 (revised), memo dated 2026-09-11 from Angelique Johnson-Dingle and Michael Bennett, read this run from the Regents agenda: the Board is asked to direct Department staff to take the necessary steps — regulatory amendments, field memoranda and related work — to sunset separate diploma assessment requirements (the '4+1' Regents-examination rule) and move to one New York State high school diploma beginning in the 2027-28 school year, Phase 2 of the NY Inspires plan announced November 2024. Students graduating in January 2028 or later would earn one diploma without passing Regents examinations; the local diploma disappears and 'advanced designation' becomes a seal or endorsement, with districts authorized to add their own seals. Districts would develop local assessment strategies (initial high-level strategies to be shared publicly during 2027-28); Regents examinations would remain as measures of the learning standards and the Department proposes new high-school accountability assessments, with ESSA-plan amendments coming to the Regents 'later this fall'. Earlier record: plan announced 2026-08-04; Chalkbeat reported 09-03 that the Class of 2027 is the last cohort under the exam requirement. Added 2026-09-24: per Chalkbeat New York, a New York City Education Department official told a City Council hearing on 2026-09-22 that if the Regents vote in June 2027 to end the exam requirement, the Class of 2028 would graduate by completing the 44 required credits, with no separate replacement assessment system in place; the same rules would apply to current freshmen and sophomores (roughly 212,000 students were in grades 9-11 last year). New credit requirements, a new diploma and new assessments arrive with the Class of 2031. Per the outlet; the hearing record was not read this run.

    Implications

    • Program. Every secondary teacher Relay prepares for New York will be assessing against local assessment strategies and a new accountability assessment rather than teaching to Regents exit exams from 2027-28; curriculum and clinical-practice expectations for the MAT secondary tracks should track the regulatory amendments as they are drafted.

    • Partnership. Partner districts must publish initial local assessment strategies during 2027-28, which is a professional-education need (assessment literacy, capstone and portfolio design) Relay can supply.

    Leader brief

    New York's Board of Regents has voted to end Regents exams as a graduation requirement and move to one state diploma, starting with the Class of 2028

    On September 14 the Board of Regents authorized the State Education Department to carry out the rest of its NY Inspires plan. Beginning with students who graduate in 2028, New York will issue a single state diploma and will no longer require students to pass a set list of Regents examinations to earn it. The exams continue as statewide measures of what students learned, and districts will build their own local assessment strategies from classroom work, performance tasks and state tests. The Department will bring the actual regulations to the Board by February 2027, with federal accountability changes coming this fall and implementation in the 2027-28 school year. At the meeting, Regents pressed staff on how locally designed assessments will stay consistent across districts and on what current high-school students will face; staff acknowledged those answers are not yet settled. EdTrust-New York asked the state to pause the change until an assessment strategy exists.

    • The decision is now made; the work moves to regulation-writing and district implementation. Relay's New York secondary candidates and the districts they teach in are heading into a system where graduation rests on local evidence of learning rather than a state exit exam, and every district has to design and publish an assessment strategy before 2027-28. That is a change in what teachers must know how to design and grade, and a professional-education need Relay can supply.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay's New York MAT secondary coursework add explicit preparation in local assessment design (portfolios, capstones, performance tasks) ahead of 2027-28?

    • Is there a partnership offer to district leaders who must draft and publish local assessment strategies, now that the timeline is set?

    • Who at Relay follows the fall accountability items and the February 2027 regulatory package, and do we submit comments when the regulations are published?

    This is the single largest employer of Relay's graduates setting the terms of instructional practice they will be evaluated on, and it landed three weeks ago

    At a glance

Both the announcement and the standing policy page were fetched raw and read this run. In effect for the 2026-27 school year; the moratorium is stated as a one-year measure. · 2026-09-02
    SourceNew York City Public Schools — Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and Screen Time (policy page); NYCPS announcement, posted 2026-09-02, updated 2026-09-11 · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the single largest employer of Relay's graduates setting the terms of instructional practice they will be evaluated on, and it landed three weeks ago without reaching this board — no NYCPS source is wired. Two things follow directly. First, any Relay coursework, clinical assignment, or edTPA-style performance task that has candidates put students in front of a generative-AI tool is now out of bounds in every 2-K-through-8 placement in the city, and in high school is confined to five named products. Second, the high-school AI-literacy requirement is a teaching task with no established preparation behind it: every NYC high school must deliver two 45-minute modules on how AI works, data privacy, and bias, and the teachers delivering them were not prepared to. That is a preparation gap in Relay's home market that Relay is positioned to fill, and the one-year framing means the district will revisit this before the 2027-28 year with evidence it is actively collecting.

    What it does

    New York City Public Schools has imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence for grades 2-K through 8, effective for the 2026-27 school year, and layered graduated screen-time limits on top of it. Read from the NYCPS policy page this run, the grid is: grades 2-K through 2, student-facing AI banned and no one-to-one screen time at all; grades 3 through 5, banned, with no more than 30 minutes of daily one-to-one screen time recommended; grades 6 through 8, banned, with no more than 45 minutes recommended; grades 9 through 12, AI limited to approved, vetted programs, with screen time left to the school and course. The district's announcement puts the reach at nearly 600,000 students, about two-thirds of total enrollment. High schools get a required floor and a narrow ceiling: every high-school student must complete two 45-minute AI-literacy modules covering how AI works, data privacy and bias, and appropriate school use, while actual student use of generative AI is confined to five centrally approved pilots (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools), each with a published expected weekly dosage from 15 minutes to one class period, and to career-readiness pathways such as Career and Technical Education and FutureReadyNYC where the tools are used under teacher supervision. Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots; applications are reviewed case by case and a student may participate in only one pilot. Carve-outs: the policy does not reach assistive technology provided through a student's Individualized Education Program or 504 Plan, and it exempts assessments, out-of-school learning, and centrally approved instruction such as e-books, robotics, coding, and simulations from the screen-time caps. Teacher-led whole-group and small-group use of devices remains allowable throughout. Tool selection for the pilots ran through the district's Enterprise Request Management Application data-privacy and security review; NYCPS says it is developing a limited evaluation plan for the pilots.

    Implications

    • Program. Relay's NYC clinical placements in grades 2-K through 8 cannot include student-facing generative-AI activities; any course assignment that assumes students will use such a tool needs to be re-specified before candidates hit those classrooms.

    • Program. The mandatory two-module high-school AI-literacy requirement creates immediate in-service demand: NYC high-school teachers must teach how AI works, data privacy, and bias without existing preparation for it.

    • Compliance. Only five tools (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, Intel AI-Ready Schools) are approved for student use in grades 9-12, each through a case-by-case school application, with one pilot per student — a constraint Relay's NYC faculty need to know before recommending any tool to a candidate's host school.

    • Partnership. NYCPS says it is building a limited evaluation plan for the pilots and frames the moratorium as one year; the evaluation and the renewal decision are both openings for a preparation partner with data on what candidates and mentors actually need.

    • Risk. Relay's own AI-in-instruction positioning now runs against its largest district partner's stated posture for two-thirds of that district's students; messaging that presumes classroom AI use will read badly in NYC through at least the 2026-27 year.

    Leader brief

    New York City has banned classroom AI for younger students for this school year — and created teaching work nobody is trained for

    On September 2 the Mayor and the Schools Chancellor announced that for the 2026-27 school year, students in pre-K through eighth grade in New York City public schools may not use generative artificial intelligence — the kind that writes text or makes images on request. The district puts the reach at close to 600,000 students, about two-thirds of its enrollment. The district also set daily limits on how long younger students may work alone on a screen: none at all in pre-K through second grade, thirty minutes in grades three to five, forty-five minutes in grades six to eight. High schools are treated differently: students there may use AI only inside five specific approved products, or in career-and-technical coursework under a teacher's supervision, and every high-school student must complete two forty-five-minute lessons on how AI works, what it does with their data, and where it goes wrong. Students who need technology for a disability or as an English learner keep it — the policy explicitly does not touch those tools. The ban is written as a one-year measure.

    • Our largest placement market has just drawn a line through a set of classroom practices, and we did not see it coming — no New York City schools source feeds this tracker. Anything we teach or assign that puts a K-8 student in front of an AI tool has to come out of the New York City version of our program for this year. At the same time the district has created a teaching job it has no trained teachers for: every high school now has to deliver AI-literacy instruction. That is squarely our work, and the one-year clock means the district will be deciding what comes next while it is still collecting evidence.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we treat New York City's line as a constraint to comply with, or as the opening position in a conversation where we bring evidence about what teachers actually need?

    • Should we build and offer AI-literacy preparation for New York City high-school teachers now, while the requirement is new and unmet, or wait to see whether the district builds it internally?

    • How much of our current public positioning on AI in instruction assumes classroom student use, and what does it cost us in New York City if we leave it unchanged this year?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level only. It regulates district practice, not preparation providers, and it expressly carves out teacher preparation, lesson planning and professional use from the device limits. It matters as context for what Relay's Tennessee elementary graduates will walk into: a statutory presumption of teacher-led, low-screen instruction in K-5 classrooms.

    What it does

    HB2393 / SB2310, Public Chapter 808, effective 2026-07-01, adds a new section to Tenn. Code Ann. Title 49, Chapter 6, Part 3. Every LEA and public charter school serving any of grades K-5 must adopt a policy governing age-appropriate and instructional use of digital devices to minimize unnecessary screen time while preserving instructional effectiveness. The policy must prioritize in-person, teacher-led instruction and non-electronic materials as the primary mode of instruction in K-5; limit district-issued devices for K-5 students to instructional purposes with a clear educational benefit; prohibit K-5 students from accessing social media platforms through school-provided internet during the instructional day; ensure electronic assessments and instructional tools used in K-5 are developmentally appropriate and aligned to state academic standards; and give parents transparency about the devices used and their instructional purpose. Carve-outs preserve device use for targeted instructional support, intervention and remediation; accommodations required under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, or the Americans with Disabilities Act; universal screeners, dyslexia screenings and state-adopted benchmark or legally required assessments; teacher preparation, lesson planning and professional use; public virtual schools; homebound instruction; remote instructional days; and hybrid learning days.

    Implications

    • Program. Tennessee K-5 clinical placements now sit under a statutory low-screen, teacher-led instructional presumption; elementary methods and clinical guidance should reflect the environment candidates are placed into.

    Leader brief

    Tennessee capped screen time in K-5 classrooms

    A Tennessee law effective July 1 requires every school district and charter school serving kindergarten through fifth grade to adopt a policy that puts in-person, teacher-led instruction first, limits school-issued devices to uses with a clear educational benefit, and blocks social media on school internet during the school day. Special education accommodations, reading screeners, required testing, virtual schools, and teachers' own lesson planning are all exempt.

    • Nothing here regulates us. It does describe the classroom our Tennessee elementary graduates are entering: less technology, more direct teaching.

    Questions to ask

    • Does our elementary clinical guidance in Tennessee assume more instructional technology than these classrooms will now have?

    NJ S3814 / A4800 — out-of-State institution licensure rewrite, with a placement-impact test

    This is the sharpest direct-regulation item on the board. Relay Graduate School of Education is a New York–chartered institution with a physical New Jersey

    At a glance

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the sharpest direct-regulation item on the board. Relay Graduate School of Education is a New York–chartered institution with a physical New Jersey presence, which places it squarely inside the definition of an out-of-State institution. The bill converts New Jersey program approval from a regulatory process into a competitive one: incumbent New Jersey institutions get notice, a public comment period, and a Presidents' Council recommendation on Relay's petitions, and the statutory denial standard is that the program not 'unduly impact existing in-State programs.' The clinical-placement clause is the part to read twice — a teacher-preparation program runs on district clinical placements, and the bill makes competition for those placements an explicit ground for both denial and revocation. Three-year licenses replace open-ended authorization, so this also creates a recurring renewal exposure.

    What it does

    Requires any out-of-State institution of higher education seeking to offer a credit-bearing course, degree-completion program, or full degree program with a physical presence in New Jersey to petition the Secretary of Higher Education for licensure. The petition must carry home-state licensure evidence, accreditation status, three years of financial statements, prospective-faculty qualifications at least equal to comparable in-State programs, evidence that the curriculum aligns with New Jersey professional licensure and certification requirements, and an impact analysis on existing in-State institutions. The impact analysis must identify comparable in-State programs, show unmet need and unmet demand, justify any duplication, and — for programs requiring clinical or field placements — show the program will not displace or reduce placements, sites, or supervisors available to students in existing in-State programs. The Secretary circulates a summary of every petition to all New Jersey institutions of higher education, opens 30 days of public comment, and refers the petition plus comments to the New Jersey Presidents' Council for written recommendation within 60 days. Licensure is granted only where offerings meet State quality standards, are fiscally viable, serve demonstrable need, and 'will not unduly impact existing in-State programs.' Licenses run three years maximum and are reauthorized only on continued need, reporting compliance, and positive outcomes. Licensees file annual reports on enrollment, completion, curriculum and faculty changes, student outcomes, and a summary of clinical and field placements arranged. The Secretary may suspend or revoke a license where the institution fails a minimum performance level, misrepresents data, or 'adversely impacts the access of students enrolled in an in-State institution of higher education to clinical and field placements.' Effective immediately on enactment.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Relay's New Jersey authorization would move to a three-year renewable license with annual reporting on enrollment, completion, student outcomes, and every clinical and field placement arranged. Confirm what Relay's current NJ Office of the Secretary of Higher Education approval covers and what a re-petition under this framework would require.

    • Risk. The impact analysis and the revocation clause both turn on clinical and field placements. A teacher-prep program that recruits district placements in the same counties as in-State programs has to be able to document that it is not displacing them — an evidentiary burden Relay should be ready to meet before it is imposed.

    • Risk. The New Jersey Presidents' Council — the presidents of in-State institutions — gets a formal written recommendation on each out-of-State petition. Competitors are placed inside the approval path.

    • Advocacy. The bill is on Second Reading with no scheduled floor date and the Assembly companion has had no committee action. That is the window: amendments narrowing the placement-displacement standard, or a carve-out for programs meeting an documented educator-shortage need, are far cheaper to seek now than after passage.

    • Partnership. The 'unmet need / unmet demand' test is met with labor-market data, employer needs assessments, and State workforce reports. New Jersey district partners documenting teacher-shortage demand would be the strongest evidence in a Relay petition.

    Leader brief

    New Jersey: out-of-state programs like Relay would need a renewable state license (S3814 / A4800)

    New Jersey is advancing a bill that would require out-of-state institutions operating in the state, which includes Relay as a New York-chartered school, to hold a state license renewable every three years. Applications would be judged partly on whether the program harms New Jersey's own institutions, the presidents of those institutions would get formal input on each application, and competing with in-state programs for student-teaching placements would itself be grounds for denial or revocation. The bill passed its first Senate committee unanimously in March and can be brought to a floor vote at any point through January 2028.

    • Relay's authority to operate in New Jersey would shift from a standing approval to a contested renewal every three years, with annual reporting and with competitors formally inside the process. The practical burden is evidence: Relay would need to document that its programs meet demand others are not filling and that its clinical placements do not displace anyone else's.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay seek amendments now, such as a carve-out for shortage-area programs or a narrower placement test, while the bill is still cheap to change, and who carries that conversation in Trenton?

    • Could we document today, district by district, that Relay placements fill unmet demand? If not, how quickly can that evidence base be built?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Two hooks, one immediate and one to watch. A3072's grant program sits in the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education — the same office that would license Relay under S3814 — and a higher-ed AI grant line is a competition Relay could enter. The mandate bills matter more slowly: if New Jersey requires every district to adopt an AI policy and requires AI instruction with State model curricula, Relay's New Jersey graduates need preparation to teach into that, and Relay's own program design has a new State standard to align to. None of the eight has passed both houses; this is early-warning, not compliance.

    What it does

    A coherent docket of eight bills in the 222nd Legislature, all live in the two-year session. Two pairs would mandate district policy: A5184/S4469 require every board of education to adopt an artificial-intelligence policy and direct the Department of Education to establish a model policy; A1323/S3883 require boards of education and boards of trustees to adopt a policy on surveillance systems with AI capabilities (A1323 has cleared the Assembly and is in the Senate Education Committee). Two would create curriculum mandates: A4352/S2862 require districts to provide AI instruction and direct the Secretary of Higher Education to develop AI model curricula. Two carry money: A2616 directs the Office of Information Technology to develop a New Jersey generative-AI program and implement AI education courses with county governments, appropriating $1.5 million; A3072 establishes an Artificial Intelligence Grant Program in the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education.

    Implications

    • Funding. A3072 would create an Artificial Intelligence Grant Program inside the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education — a fundable line Relay's NJ operation could pursue. Worth flagging to the grant finder as a pipeline item if it advances.

    • Program. A4352/S2862 would put AI instruction and State model curricula into New Jersey districts. Relay's NJ preparation coursework would need to prepare teachers to deliver it.

    • Compliance. A5184/S4469 mandate district-level AI policy with a DOE model. Relay's clinical placement partners would be operating under it before Relay's own curriculum catches up.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Adjacent rather than core — this is school accountability, not educator preparation — but it is New York, where Relay's largest program sits, and it redraws the map of which schools are in which intervention status. Relay's partner schools and the placements its candidates serve are disproportionately in the CSI and receivership population, so a re-tiering of that system changes which schools face which interventions, and the new Transfer High School receivership pathway reaches a school type that serves over-age and under-credited students. The deadline is the reason this surfaces now: five business days, by email, with no formal State Register process to extend it.

    What it does

    NYSED proposes amendments to Sections 100.19 and 100.21 of the Commissioner's Regulations, the accountability determinations and accountability calculation rules. Read raw from the NYSED accountability newsroom page this run. Per that page, the amendments 'strengthen the connection between identified needs, meaningful support, and continuous improvement,' and specifically: the Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI) support model is differentiated across multiple tiers of increasingly rigorous support — CSI-A, CSI-B, School District Superintendent Receivership, and Independent Receivership; a new alternative pathway to School District Superintendent Receivership provides rigorous intervention and progress monitoring for Transfer High Schools; interventions and exit criteria are modified for each CSI tier and for the Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI) model; and definitions and language on accountability calculations and receivership are updated. Supporting materials named on the page: the regulatory-amendments proposal slide deck with script presented at the July 2026 Regents meeting, and an Accountability and Receivership Amendments fact sheet; full text is on the Board of Regents webpage. The full regulatory text was NOT read this run — only the Department's own summary. DATING NOTE: the cross-engine sweep surfaced this as a 2026-09-18 item; the NYSED page is dated 2026-07-31. The September 28 deadline is confirmed; the item is new to this board, not new to the world.

    Implications

    • Partnership. Re-tiering CSI into CSI-A, CSI-B and two receivership levels changes which Relay partner schools carry which intervention obligations, and therefore what kind of support a partnership needs to offer.

    • Program. A dedicated receivership pathway for Transfer High Schools touches a school type serving over-age and under-credited students, where clinical placements have distinct demands.

    • Advocacy. Comments go by email to REGCOMMENTS@nysed.gov and close 2026-09-28 — a short, low-formality window if Relay wants a view on the record.

    Leader brief

    New York is rewriting how it identifies and intervenes in struggling schools, and comments close September 28

    The New York State Education Department has proposed changes to the regulations that determine which schools are identified as needing comprehensive support and what happens to them. The proposal creates a graded ladder — two levels of comprehensive support and two levels of receivership, where the state or an outside receiver takes over management — instead of the current arrangement, and adds a new route into receivership designed for transfer high schools, which serve students who are older than typical or behind on credits. It also changes how schools exit each level. Comments are taken by email until September 28. The proposal was published July 31; we are picking it up now.

    • Many of the New York schools Relay partners with and places candidates in sit in exactly the categories this redraws. A change in which schools are identified, and in what an identified school is required to do, changes what our partners need from us and what our candidates walk into.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we have a view worth putting on the record by September 28, and do our New York school partners know this is open? Should someone map which of our partner schools would change status under the new tiers?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Chapter 231 is the assignment side of the certification system: it governs which certificate lets a district place a teacher in which role. Relay's interest is indirect but real — assignment rules determine what a Relay-prepared certificate is actually good for in a Texas district, and clarifying amendments sometimes narrow placements that providers and districts had been treating as available. Carried at SCAN until the proposed text and the comment window are published.

    What it does

    Item 5 of the 2026-09-18 SBEC meeting: a proposed amendment to 19 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 231 (Requirements for Public School Personnel Assignments), Subchapter A, Section 231.1, Criteria for Assignment of Public School Personnel. Per the meeting agenda read through a real browser this run, the proposed amendment 'would clarify requirements related to the criteria for school districts to make personnel assignments based on the correlating certification requirements.' The full text of the proposed change was not read this run beyond the agenda's description, and the board's action on the item is not published.

    Implications

    • Program. Assignment criteria determine where a Relay-certified graduate can be placed in a Texas district; a clarification here can change the practical value of a certificate area.

    Why it matters to Relay

    TQP and SEED are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for (IHE plus EPP plus Title IV); the release says the pending award slates were selected under the literacy priority, so award announcements are imminent and the priority will shape the next competitions. Hand to the grant finder for the award lists.

    What it does

    Department of Education press release (2026-09-09, read this run) describing how the Secretary's evidence-based literacy priority is applied across grant programs. Stated forthcoming awards: 12 new Teacher Quality Partnership (TQP) grants totaling roughly $70 million and 16 new Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED) grants totaling roughly $90 million, both 'in the coming weeks', with TQP framed as preparing teachers to deliver literacy instruction and SEED as supporting certification pathways and literacy coaching. Already awarded: four Innovative Approaches to Literacy grants ($16M+, this week), $256 million in Comprehensive Literacy State Development continuation awards to 24 states, nearly $500 million across 49 Education Innovation and Research grants over two years (17 to state agencies), and $3.7 million for a National Center on Academic Interventions. IES is refocusing its largest FY2027 competitions on state-identified needs with literacy as a core priority. The release frames the shift as ending funding for the prior administration's DEI-related efforts.

    Implications

    • Funding. 12 TQP (~$70M) and 16 SEED (~$90M) awards are about to be announced; if Relay applied in either FY2026 competition, the decision is weeks away, and the literacy priority was the selection lens.

    • Program. The Secretary's literacy priority now runs through TQP, SEED, EIR, CLSD and IES; future Relay proposals in these programs should lead with Science of Reading alignment in teacher preparation.

    • Risk. The release ties the priority to ending 'DEI-laden' spending; proposal language and program descriptions will be read against that framing.

    Leader brief

    Washington is about to announce the two federal grant slates Relay competes in, and says it picked winners for reading instruction

    Update September 18: the award list still has not appeared, and a federal court has now ruled that the Department's 2025 cancellation of the previous round of these same grants broke the law, which puts the coming slate in a more contested legal setting. The U.S. Department of Education said on September 9 that it will announce 12 new Teacher Quality Partnership grants (about $70 million in total) and 16 new Supporting Effective Educator Development grants (about $90 million) in the coming weeks. These are the two federal programs that fund teacher-preparation providers like Relay directly. The Department says it chose projects that prepare teachers to teach reading using evidence-based methods, and that this literacy priority now runs through its other grant programs and its research agency as well.

    • If Relay has an application pending in either program, the answer is imminent. For future applications, the Department has told the field what it wants to fund: reading instruction grounded in the science of reading, framed explicitly against diversity-related spending.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay have a pending Teacher Quality Partnership or SEED application, and who is watching for the award notice?

    • Should Relay's next federal proposals foreground its literacy preparation, and is the evidence base for that ready?

    Why it matters to Relay

    A federal statutory definition of the science of reading, with three-cueing written out of it, becomes the reference point state literacy and educator-preparation rules converge on — including the New York teacher-preparation literacy rules Relay's New York programs must meet, which are up for adoption in October. It also sets the content bar for Relay's literacy coursework and its Teacher Professional Education literacy offerings in every state.

    What it does

    The House passed H.R. 7890 on 2026-09-16 under suspension of the rules, as amended, by voice vote; the engrossed text was read in full this run. The bill amends the Elementary and Secondary Education Act's comprehensive literacy provisions (20 U.S.C. 6641-6644, the Comprehensive Literacy State Development program) in four ways. First, it adds a new subparagraph (M) to the definition of comprehensive literacy instruction providing that the term 'does not include the use of a three-cueing model.' Second, it defines 'science of reading' in statute as an interdisciplinary body of evidence-based research that identifies phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and writing as essential components of skilled reading, that establishes the importance of background knowledge, oral language and the reading-writing connection, that explains why some students struggle, and that does not use three-cueing; and it defines 'three-cueing model' as an approach using meaning, structure/syntax or visual cues as the primary basis for teaching word recognition, or teaching visual memory as the primary basis for word recognition. Third, it requires a state applying for a Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant to describe the extent to which its state literacy plan is aligned to the science of reading, and conditions the grant priority on that alignment. Fourth, it applies the same alignment condition to both subgrant priorities, birth-through-kindergarten-entry and kindergarten-through-grade-12. The Act appropriates no money and creates no new program; it changes what existing literacy dollars may support and adds a rule of construction preserving IDEA, Section 504 and ADA rights and barring federal officials from directing curriculum or instruction. The changes apply to funds awarded on or after enactment. The bill now goes to the Senate, where no action is scheduled. UPDATE 2026-09-21: per the GPO bill-status record read raw this run, the House action of 2026-09-16 (passed by voice vote under suspension, as amended, after forty minutes of debate on a motion by Mr. Walberg; motion to reconsider laid on the table) was followed on 2026-09-17 by receipt in the Senate, two readings, and referral to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

    Implications

    • Compliance. If enacted, a federal statutory definition of the science of reading would sit underneath state educator-preparation literacy rules, including New York's proposed 8 NYCRR 52.21 and 80-3.7 requirements, giving Relay's literacy coursework a single national reference standard to align to.

    • Program. The explicit exclusion of three-cueing from comprehensive literacy instruction sets a content floor for Relay's literacy methods courses and for the literacy modules in its Teacher Professional Education coaching line.

    • Funding. Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant priorities would turn on science-of-reading alignment, so state literacy plans that fund district coaching and professional development become a more selective market for providers that can document that alignment.

    • Advocacy. The bill is in the Senate with no action scheduled, which is the open window for comment from educator-preparation providers on how the statutory definition interacts with preparation-program requirements.

    Leader brief

    The House has written the science of reading into federal law, and written three-cueing out of it

    Update September 21: the bill moved. After passing the House on September 16, it was sent to the Senate on September 17 and referred to the Senate's education committee. That is a procedural step, not a signal that it will pass, but it does mean there is now a committee that could take it up and a place to direct comment. On September 16 the House of Representatives passed the Science of Reading Act of 2026 by voice vote. The bill changes the federal law that governs the main federal literacy grant program for states. It puts a definition of 'the science of reading' into the statute for the first time, naming phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and writing as the essential components, and it says explicitly that comprehensive literacy instruction does not include three-cueing, the practice of teaching children to guess unfamiliar words from pictures, context or sentence structure. States applying for federal literacy money would have to describe how their literacy plans align to that definition, and the grants and subgrants would give priority to plans that do. The bill spends no new money and does not tell schools what curriculum to use. It now goes to the Senate, where nothing has been scheduled.

    • Relay teaches literacy methods in its degree programs and sells literacy coaching through its professional-education line, so a single federal definition of acceptable literacy instruction becomes the reference point for both. It also reinforces the direction New York is already taking with its proposed literacy requirements for teacher-preparation programs, which are expected to be adopted in October. Where states rewrite their literacy plans to match, district spending on coaching and professional development follows the same standard.

    Questions to ask

    • The bill is now in front of a Senate committee rather than sitting unreferred. Does that change whether we want to state a position, and to whom?

    • Should Relay state a public position while the bill is in the Senate, given that the definition would reach teacher-preparation content in the states where we operate?

    • Are our literacy courses and coaching materials documentably free of three-cueing practices, and could we show that to a state reviewing its literacy plan?

    • If states rewrite literacy plans to prove alignment, do we want to be positioned as the provider that helps districts meet the new standard?

    Why it matters to Relay

    A statutory 25-student cap in every New Jersey district would raise teacher demand district-wide, the same staffing pressure the NYC class-size law created for Relay's New York partners, and the 100%-State-funded clause would make it an aid-formula fight. Watch for a hearing or Senate companion; as introduced by two minority sponsors it is parked.

    What it does

    Introduced 2026-09-10 and referred to the Assembly Education Committee (sponsors Alex Sauickie and Robert Clifton, both Republicans; LegiScan API and the introduced text read this run). The bill supplements N.J.S.A. Title 18A chapter 36. Section 1 caps state-funded universal preschool classes at 15 children. Section 2 codifies the existing State Board class-size regulations for 'high poverty' districts (40% or more at-risk pupils under C.18A:7F-45): 21 students in K-3, 23 in grades 4-5, 24 in grades 6-12, with physical-education and performing-arts exceptions. It then extends a cap of 25 students in every K-12 class to all other districts, with exceptions for PE and performing arts, multi-grade academies, and other 'personalizing' practices; special-class special-education sizes stay with State Board rules; a district with unassigned students may exceed 25 by placing them or split classes. Section 2(f) has the State pay 100 percent of the cost districts incur to reach the 25-student cap. Collective-bargaining agreements in force are not affected. Effective immediately, first applicable to the second full school year after enactment. The sponsor's statement blames S-2 (P.L.2018, c.67) state-aid cuts for larger classes. No fiscal estimate is attached; two minority-party sponsors in a Democratic-controlled Assembly and no companion bill found.

    Why it matters to Relay

    The PSPB is the advisory body through which New York's teacher-education and certification rules are vetted before the Regents act, and one-quarter of its educator seats are reserved for institutions that prepare teachers, including at least one president or chief academic officer. The change itself is administrative — it fixes a chronic vacancy problem — but the deletion of the full-time-teaching-experience minimum and the shift to proportional seats change who can sit on the body that reviews certification rules. New York is Relay's deepest jurisdiction; the item to watch is the September 14-15 Regents agenda for the permanent adoption and any accompanying appointments. Found by the cross-engine sweep; the NY State Register is not a wired source.

    What it does

    Notice of emergency rule making I.D. No. EDU-22-26-00017-E, published in the September 2, 2026 State Register (filed and effective 2026-08-17; a re-adoption of the emergency rule first taken at the May 2026 Regents meeting, effective May 19). Amends section 3.14(a) and (h) of the Rules of the Board of Regents governing the Professional Standards and Practices Board for Teaching (PSPB), the body established in 1998 to advise the Regents and the Commissioner on teacher education, certification and practice. Changes: the board's size moves from a fixed thirty members to 'at least 25', with thirteen members a quorum; the fixed category counts are replaced with proportions — at least two-thirds of members must be educators practicing in New York (certified teachers, school or district administrators, faculty engaged in preparing teachers, or presidents or chief academic officers of institutions that prepare teachers), of whom at least half must be practicing certified teachers, at least one-sixth practicing certified administrators, and at least one-quarter representatives of higher-education institutions that prepare teachers including at least one president or chief academic officer; and the requirement that 15 of the 23 educator members have full-time experience as certified teachers is deleted. The notice states the amendment was presented to the Higher Education Committee in May, that the earliest non-emergency adoption after the 60-day SAPA comment period is the September 2026 Regents meeting, and that the permanent rule would take effect September 30, 2026 on publication of the Notice of Adoption. Update 2026-09-14: the September Regents agenda (item BR (CA) 4, memo dated 2026-09-03, read this run) submits the amendment to the Full Board for permanent adoption on the September 15 consent agenda. The memo states that the Department received no comments during the State Register comment period, so no Assessment of Public Comment is required and the text is unchanged from the emergency version; the recommended vote makes the rule effective September 30, 2026, with a Notice of Adoption in the September 30 Register. A companion consent item, BR (CA) 1, fills one vacant teacher seat on the board (Marguerite Dimgba, term to June 30, 2029) and attaches the current membership list.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. The board that advises the Regents on certification rules is being resized and its educator seats redefined by proportion; institutions that prepare teachers keep at least one-quarter of educator seats, including a president or chief academic officer. If seats open under the new structure, Relay's New York leadership is eligible to be nominated.

    • Program. No direct change to certification requirements; the effect is on who reviews future changes. Track the September Regents adoption and any appointment slate.

    Leader brief

    New York is changing the makeup of the advisory board that reviews teacher-certification rules; the Regents are expected to make it permanent this month

    The Board of Regents runs a standing advisory board, the Professional Standards and Practices Board for Teaching, that reviews proposed teacher-education and certification rules before the Regents vote on them. An emergency rule already in effect shrinks the board from a fixed thirty members to at least twenty-five, sets thirteen as a quorum, replaces fixed seat counts with proportions (two-thirds practicing educators; of those, half classroom teachers, a sixth administrators, a quarter from colleges and universities that prepare teachers, including at least one president or chief academic officer), and drops the requirement that most educator members have full-time classroom experience. The Regents are expected to adopt it permanently at their September 14-15 meeting. Update, September 14: the Regents are adopting the rule permanently on their September 15 consent agenda; nobody filed a public comment, and it takes effect September 30.

    • Nothing in this changes what Relay's New York candidates must do to be certified. What changes is who sits on the body that reviews future changes, and institutions like Relay hold a guaranteed share of those seats. The practical question is whether the reorganization opens seats, and whether Relay wants a voice on the board that sees certification proposals first.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay want to seek a seat on the Professional Standards and Practices Board, and who would be the right nominee?

    • Is anyone at Relay watching the September 14-15 Regents agenda for the permanent adoption and any appointments?

    HHS proposes rescinding the Head Start Performance Standards — English-only instruction, staff-qualification rollback, a ban on requiring credentials in hiring; comments close Oct 6

    Relay does not operate Head Start programs, so nothing binds Relay directly — but §1301.12(c) is the strongest federal skills-based-hiring-over-credentials

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionFederal
    ClassRule
    StageComment period open · Proposed rule (NPRM) published 2026-08-07; comment window open, closes 2026-10-06. Provisions verified from the Federal Register full text 2026-08-18.
    RecommendationTrack · impact 58
    Latest actionProposed rule published 2026-08-07; 60-day public comment period open · 2026-08-07
    WindowOctober 6, 2026 · 7 business days · Comment deadline 2026-10-06 (34 business days out)
    SourceFederal Register · Open the primary source
    CommentComment

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay does not operate Head Start programs, so nothing binds Relay directly — but §1301.12(c) is the strongest federal skills-based-hiring-over-credentials signal yet in the education workforce, landing the same month CT, DE, and GA routed teacher-pipeline money to undergraduate-only pathways.

    What it does

    HHS's Administration for Children and Families proposes to rescind and replace the Head Start Program Performance Standards in full ('Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs', NPRM 2026-16134, published 2026-08-07; docket ACF-2026-0595; comments close 2026-10-06). Verified from the rule text this run: proposed §1301.04(a) requires programs to prioritize teaching English to children who do not speak it, rescinding the current §1302.31(b)(2) requirement to support bilingualism for dual-language learners, on the authority of Executive Order 14224 (English as the official language); §1301.17(d) exempts Indian Head Start agencies where the language furthers tribal heritage. The Performance Standards would retain no staff-qualification or professional-development requirements beyond statute — regulatory qualifications for directors, family child care providers, coaches, family service staff, and health staff are removed (statutory requirements for preschool teachers, assistant teachers, Early Head Start teachers, and education managers at Head Start Act §648A(a) and §645A(h) survive), and the coordinated-coaching-strategy requirement is dropped. New §1301.12(c) bars programs from requiring or incentivizing postsecondary credits, hours, or credentials in hiring unless the program demonstrates they are necessary for the position, with mandatory non-degree alternatives (assessments, industry-recognized credentials, work experience). Proposed §1301.18 broadens waiver authority, including teacher-qualification waivers under §648A(a)(4); the administrative cost cap drops from 15% to 5%. The regulatory impact analysis models roughly $18.8M/yr (low scenario) in salary reductions from lowered qualifications. Source upgrade 2026-08-19: the NPRM now arrives via the federal_register source directly (ACF agency scope added 2026-08-18), replacing the EdWeek discovery lead as the tracking route; facts unchanged, deadline 2026-10-06 reconfirmed from the Federal Register API this run (34 business days).

    Implications

    • Risk. New §1301.12(c) forbids requiring or rewarding postsecondary credentials in Head Start hiring unless proven necessary — a federal precedent for suppressing employer demand for credentials in the education workforce. If the model travels to K-12-adjacent programs, it works against every credential-bearing preparation provider.

    • Partnership. Districts and community organizations running Head Start in Relay's communities face staffing-model changes; the removal of professional-development and coaching mandates reshapes the early-childhood support landscape Relay-prepared leaders work in.

    • Advocacy. Comment window open to 2026-10-06 (34 business days) via regulations.gov docket ACF-2026-0595 — 279 comments filed in the first 11 days. Early-childhood and English-learner coalitions are mobilizing; a Relay position could ride a coalition letter rather than a solo filing.

    Leader brief

    Washington proposes to rewrite Head Start's rulebook: English-only instruction, and a ban on requiring degrees in hiring

    The federal Department of Health and Human Services, which runs Head Start (the federal early-childhood program for low-income families), has proposed replacing the program's entire rulebook. The proposal would require programs to prioritize teaching in English rather than supporting children's home languages, would delete almost every staffing-credential requirement not written into the underlying law, and — most unusually — would forbid Head Start programs from requiring or even rewarding college credits or credentials when hiring, unless a program can prove the job's skills can only be learned through that credential. The public can comment until October 6.

    • Relay does not run Head Start programs, so nothing here binds Relay directly. The concern is the direction of travel: the federal government is telling one part of the education workforce that degrees and credentials should not be required or rewarded in hiring — in the same month that Connecticut, Delaware, and Georgia routed new teacher-pipeline money to undergraduate-only routes. If that hiring philosophy spreads toward K-12, it weakens the market for credential-bearing preparation.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay comment before October 6 — directly or through coalition partners — given it is not directly regulated, and what would it say?

    • Does the growing skills-based-hiring trend change how Relay makes the case for its degrees and credentials to employers and policymakers?

    Ecosystem-level for Relay, with one structural caveat worth recording. The eligibility conditions — bachelor's-degree intent, and entry in the fall directly
