    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level for Relay, with one structural caveat worth recording. The eligibility conditions — bachelor's-degree intent, and entry in the fall directly after high school graduation — confine this to undergraduate pathways, so Relay's Delaware operations cannot capture these dollars. At a cap of 35 awards and $2,500 each, the programme is roughly $87,500 a year statewide and will not move teacher supply on its own. Its value here is as the second instance this run of a state routing new teacher-pipeline money exclusively through undergraduate, four-year pathways, alongside Connecticut's Public Act 26-149.

    What it does

    Signed by the Governor on 2026-07-23 after unanimous passage (House 37-0 with 4 absent on 2026-03-10; Senate 21-0 on 2026-06-25). The act adds section 3438A to Title 14 of the Delaware Code, creating a Teacher Academy scholarship for individuals who completed a Teacher Academy and are enrolled in a Delaware college or university. A 'Teacher Academy' is defined as a Career and Technical Education program offered in Delaware public schools, including charter and vocational-technical schools, that prepares students for careers in elementary and secondary education. The award is $2,500 for one year only, payable in two equal semester instalments. To be eligible an applicant must have completed a Teacher Academy and be enrolled full-time in an educator preparation program in Delaware — defined as a program approved by the Department of Education under section 1280 of Title 14 — with the intent to earn a BACHELOR'S degree, and must enter that program in the fall semester directly after high school graduation. Applicants for the existing educator support scholarship under section 3438 are automatically considered, with no separate application. Applicants must apply for all financial aid for which they are eligible, including the Federal Pell Grant, and must accept all aid offered except loans. The scholarship is available from the 2026-2027 school year, capped at no more than 35 awards per year, with expansion contingent on interest and funding. If applicants exceed funding, the Department of Education develops competitive award criteria.

    Implications

    • Risk. Eligibility requires intent to earn a bachelor's degree and entry into the preparation program in the fall directly after high school graduation, which excludes graduate-level providers. Relay cannot serve as the receiving institution for these awards in Delaware.

    • Program. The scholarship attaches to Delaware's Teacher Academy CTE pathway, including academies in charter and vocational-technical schools. That pathway is a defined, state-recognised feeder population, and its graduates remain reachable later at the graduate level even though this award is not.

    • Funding. At most 35 awards of $2,500 — about $87,500 per year statewide — with expansion tied to interest and funding. The scale means the signal value exceeds the fiscal value.

    Leader brief

    Delaware: a small new scholarship for high-school teacher-academy graduates, undergraduate only (DE HB12)

    Delaware's Governor signed a bill on July 23, passed unanimously by both chambers, creating a $2,500 one-year scholarship for students who complete a 'Teacher Academy' — a career and technical education programme in Delaware public, charter, or vocational-technical high schools that prepares students for teaching careers — and then enrol full-time in a Delaware teacher-preparation programme. Students must be pursuing a bachelor's degree and must start in the autumn immediately after finishing high school. It starts with the 2026-27 school year and is capped at 35 awards a year, roughly $87,500 in total.

    • There is nothing for us to capture here directly: the bachelor's-degree requirement and the enrol-straight-from-high-school condition put this entirely in the undergraduate lane. The reason it is worth a minute of leadership attention is the pattern rather than the programme. Delaware and Connecticut both created or reworked teacher-pipeline funding this year in ways that route money exclusively through four-year undergraduate preparation. The amounts are small, but the design assumption behind them is not.

    Questions to ask

    • Delaware's teacher-academy students are a defined pipeline the state has now invested in. Is there a case for engaging that pipeline further upstream, on a horizon where they later become graduate-level candidates?

    • Do we want a considered position on state teacher-pipeline funds being written for undergraduate pathways only, before the next state does the same?

    New Jersey is a deep Relay jurisdiction and 6A:10 governs how every Relay completer and every partner-school teacher is evaluated, including the

    Why it matters to Relay

    New Jersey is a deep Relay jurisdiction and 6A:10 governs how every Relay completer and every partner-school teacher is evaluated, including the student-achievement component that has driven SGO practice since 2013. Replacing SGOs with curriculum-derived measures of student learning changes what first-year teachers are coached to produce and what Relay's clinical faculty prepare candidates for. Also relevant: the observer-certification and co-observation calibration language touches Relay's school-leadership programs. This is the first-discussion stage; the formal proposal with a comment window comes later. Found by the cross-engine sweep; NJ State Board agendas are not a wired source.

    What it does

    New Jersey Department of Education agenda item for the September 9, 2026 State Board of Education meeting (First Discussion): proposed readoption with amendments of N.J.A.C. 6A:10, Educator Effectiveness, the chapter implementing the TEACHNJ Act (P.L. 2012, c. 26) evaluation system for teachers, principals, assistant and vice principals and other certificated staff; the chapter otherwise expires July 6, 2027. The summary describes the amendments as grounded in the 2024 Governor's Task Force on Educator Evaluation and the 2025 Evaluation Working Group and as shifting the rules toward a performance-based system prioritizing instructional feedback, professional growth, and a direct link between evaluation results and professional-development planning. Specific changes in the summary read this run: the term 'student growth objective' (SGO) is replaced throughout by 'measures of student learning', newly defined as a metric of student achievement or growth derived from the district-approved curriculum and aligned to the New Jersey Student Learning Standards, which may include teacher-set goals, performance assessments including portfolios and internships, teacher-developed, standardized and district assessments (aligned to N.J.S.A. 18A:6-119), moving away from predictive-model measures; observation terminology is aligned ('announced'/'unannounced'); co-observation is amended to add 'perform the calibration' as a required step; supervisors conducting observations must have completed certification training; corrective-action-plan provisions are retained with clarified indicators; defunct or time-limited provisions are deleted. The readoption follows the State Board's discussion, proposal and adoption levels, with formal publication and a 60-day comment period after proposal. Read this run from the Department's accessible first-discussion document (dated September 9, 3,000+ lines including full rule text): the required observation counts do not change (tenured teachers two observations with post-conferences and one pre-conference; nontenured three; tenured principals two, nontenured three). New requirements: a 'comprehensive strategy session' before the first observation for teachers in their first year in a district or on a corrective action plan, aligning the improvement-plan goals with the specific practice indicators to be observed; pre- and post-observation conferences become 'collaborative discussions' tied to the individual professional development plan, with evidence of applying that plan added to what evaluators review. Measures of student learning: teachers without a student growth percentile go from two-to-four objectives to exactly two measures; teachers with a percentile need at least one, with the chief school administrator setting the number; a highly effective tenured teacher may use a Commissioner-approved activity that includes a growth measure to satisfy one required measure; schoolwide measures may be allowed. District Evaluation Advisory Committees return as a requirement. Charter and renaissance schools remain outside the chapter. Chapter sunset July 6, 2027.

    Implications

    • Program. Replacing student growth objectives with curriculum-derived 'measures of student learning' changes the student-achievement artifact every New Jersey teacher, including Relay's first-year completers, must produce; Relay's New Jersey coursework and coaching on SGOs would need to shift once adopted.

    • Program. The new pre-observation 'comprehensive strategy session' for first-year teachers is a concrete coaching artifact Relay's New Jersey residents and completers will meet in year one; coursework on evaluation should describe it once the rule advances.

    • Program. The observer-certification and co-observation calibration requirements bear on Relay's principal and leadership programs in New Jersey, which train the people who conduct these observations.

    • Advocacy. First discussion is the earliest point to shape the text; the formal comment window opens only after the proposal level, likely in the coming months.

    Leader brief

    New Jersey is starting to rewrite its teacher-evaluation rules, replacing 'student growth objectives' with measures drawn from the curriculum

    New Jersey's rules for evaluating teachers and principals expire next July, and the Department of Education has drafted a renewal with changes. The State Board of Education will hold its first discussion of the draft on September 9. The most visible change replaces 'student growth objectives', the goal-setting exercise every teacher has completed since 2013, with 'measures of student learning' drawn from the district's own curriculum and state standards, which can include teacher-designed assessments, portfolios and projects. The draft also emphasizes feedback and professional growth over ratings, requires observers to be trained and calibrated, and cleans out obsolete provisions. Formal public comment comes later, after the Board advances the proposal. The full draft, read September 10, keeps the number of required classroom observations unchanged, adds a required planning session before the first observation for first-year teachers and teachers on improvement plans, and sets the number of student-learning measures at two for teachers without state test-score growth data.

    • Every Relay graduate teaching in New Jersey is evaluated under these rules, and Relay's New Jersey program teaches candidates how to meet them. If the change goes through, the coursework and coaching built around student growth objectives will need to be rewritten, and Relay's leadership programs, which prepare the principals who conduct observations, will need to reflect the new observer-training requirements. Nothing is final yet; this is the beginning of a process that runs into 2027.

    Questions to ask

    • Who at Relay New Jersey should follow the State Board's discussion and read the full draft?

    • Does Relay want to comment when the formal window opens, and is there a position on curriculum-based measures versus the current growth objectives?

    • What lead time would the New Jersey program need to revise its evaluation-related coursework if the rules are adopted in early 2027?

    Leader brief

    Delaware rewrote its school funding formula in June and this tracker never caught it

    Two Delaware bills, Senate Bills 302 and 303, were signed by the Governor on June 30. Together they authorize a new hybrid school funding formula and create a standing Public Education Funding Commission to oversee its implementation. An advocacy organization reports the state has committed $100 million to the transition and that a new coalition launched on September 22 to push for sustained investment. We surfaced this from that commentary and confirmed both bills are enacted through a legislative database. We have not read the bill text — the public text pages are behind a bot challenge and the Delaware legislature's own lookup did not resolve — so how the formula actually works is still unknown to us.

    • Delaware is a jurisdiction where Relay already tracks a teacher scholarship program. A formula rewrite plus a permanent funding commission is the frame every future Delaware education appropriation passes through, including anything touching educator preparation. Nothing is urgent, but the gap is real and this should be read properly rather than carried as a headline.

    Questions to ask

    • How much does Relay's Delaware work depend on state funding decisions that this formula now governs?

    • Is it worth reading the two acts in full on the next run, or is Delaware peripheral enough to leave as context?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level only for Relay: the scholarship is restricted to public institutions of higher education in New Jersey, so Relay's students cannot use it even if public schools land on the shortage list. Its interest is as a paraprofessional-to-credential pipeline that could feed New Jersey school staffing.

    What it does

    A2534 would establish the Jersey Strong Public Service Scholarship Program at the Higher Education Student Assistance Authority, developed with the Department of Labor and Workforce Development. The bill text was read this run. A participant who completes one year of full-time employment in a public-service sector experiencing critical workforce shortages becomes eligible for a scholarship toward two academic years of attendance, capped at $25,000; two years of employment yields eligibility for four academic years, capped at $50,000. Scholarships apply only toward the cost of attendance at a public institution of higher education in New Jersey. Applicants must be state residents and U.S. citizens who graduated from a New Jersey high school within the past year or will graduate within six months, and must be employed full-time in an eligible sector. Within 90 days of enactment the Commissioner of Labor and Workforce Development would publish the list of eligible shortage sectors, which the bill says 'may include employment in hospitals or public schools or employment as a crossing guard or first responder,' revisited every four years. The Authority would also match participants who are not already employed in an eligible sector with open positions paying at least the state minimum wage. It was reported from the Assembly Higher Education Committee 2026-09-17 and re-referred to the Assembly Community Development and Women's Affairs Committee.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level, and the reason to cluster rather than list them: the direction of travel is what matters, not any one bill. Four Relay states are legislating AI into K-12 in the same session, and none of the four is a teacher-preparation bill. That gap is the signal — states are mandating AI literacy and AI policy for districts faster than they are addressing whether new teachers are prepared to deliver it. Relay's opportunity is in the gap, not the bills.

    What it does

    Four separate AI-in-education bills moved in authorized Relay jurisdictions. Pennsylvania HB2314 (Ciresi, D, with 15 cosponsors including Republicans) would fund a public education campaign on artificial intelligence and consumer AI literacy; it passed the House 198-3 on 2026-06-03 and sits in the Senate Communications & Technology Committee. Delaware HB404 would amend Title 14 to create an Artificial Intelligence and Extended Reality in Schools Pilot Program; it passed the House 36-4 on 2026-06-30 after clearing House Appropriations, and awaits Senate action when the 153rd General Assembly reconvenes in January. District of Columbia B26-0491, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Education Act of 2025 (Pinto), was referred to the Committee of the Whole 2025-12-02 with no action since. New York S10049 (Jackson, Fahy) would extend the Dignity for All Students Act definition of cyberbullying to cover intentionally using AI to mimic or alter a person's likeness or voice; it passed the Senate 60-0 on 2026-05-28 and is in the Assembly Education Committee. Added 2026-09-02: a Chalkbeat national review reports at least 13 states have passed AI-in-education laws, most of them delegating the hard calls to state agencies and districts, and that roughly three-quarters of states have published AI guidance that largely skirts academic dishonesty; half of the ten largest districts discourage AI-detection tools (per Chalkbeat; not independently verified). Added 2026-09-03: CRPE's 'Leading Through Uncertainty' report (survey and interviews across 39 states and territories and 18 partner organizations) finds state AI action still ad hoc and fragmented — vision statements, guidance, advisory bodies and AI-literacy support are common, operational help with tool evaluation, procurement and evidence is rare; a companion CRPE profile describes how SCORE, a Tennessee intermediary, convenes state-level AI strategy for the State Board and Department of Education, vets tools for districts, and co-funds pilots through the Tennessee AI Ecosystem Project. Outside the footprint but on the same trend: Florida's State Board of Education votes 2026-09-16 on a rule requiring every district and charter board to fold AI into its internet-safety policy by 2027-07-01 — parent notification when a teacher approves an AI tool, an opt-out with alternatives, extra age-appropriateness review in PreK-5, teacher and administrator training on AI safety and compliance, a bar on AI simulating friendship or meeting social-emotional needs, and a 30-day retention of student interactions — with parallel rules for the 28 state colleges and a Board of Governors syllabus-disclosure rule for the universities (per The 74 / Florida Phoenix, from a draft rule; not independently verified).

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

The agenda item and the CDE program page were fetched raw and read this run. The Department must post the approved list by 2026-09-30 per statute; as of this run the CDE page was last reviewed 2026-09-08 and the approved list is not yet posted. SCAN lane is the California pending-watch gate cap, not a judgment that the item is minor. · 2026-09-09

    SourceCalifornia State Board of Education September 2026 agenda, Item 09 (DOCX read this run); CDE Literacy Professional Development Programs page (read this run); outcome per EdSource/The74 · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    California is a pending-watch jurisdiction for Relay and this item is capped at SCAN on that gate alone — but it is the most directly analogous action on this board to what Relay sells. A state assembled a rubric, ran a competitive review with an external evaluator, scored providers of literacy training for practicing teachers on 18 criteria, ranked them publicly by evidence, and attached $200 million to the result. Two things are worth carrying forward regardless of Relay's California posture. First, the mechanism: an evidence-ranked approved-provider list with a public score is a template other states can copy, and Relay would be a candidate for such a list wherever it appears. Second, the near-term date is real: the Department must post the approved list by September 30, six business days out, and that posting is what converts an agenda recommendation into the verified outcome.

    What it does

    Assembly Bill 121 (2025), Chapter 8, appropriated $200 million for local educational agencies to provide professional development on effective means of teaching literacy, and its section 15 added Education Code section 33319.6, directing the State Board of Education to approve — and the Department of Education to post by September 30, 2026 — criteria and a list of in-service literacy professional-development programs for transitional kindergarten through grade five. Read from the agenda item this run: the Board approved the underlying criteria on November 5, 2025; Marin County Office of Education contracted WestEd to run the review; 50 program submissions arrived by the February 20, 2026 deadline, two were withdrawn and two were ineligible for lacking a required Intent to Submit, leaving 46 programs eligible; a 29-member review committee, chosen from 50 applicants and balanced across TK-5 teachers, site and district administrators, coaches, and higher-education faculty, evaluated them against an 18-criterion rubric after a March 16, 2026 calibration meeting, with escalation to second and third review rounds for borderline programs. Thirty-seven of the 46 submissions rated eligible for the proposed list; nine failed the minimum thresholds. In response to public comment, the staff recommendation arrived as a ranked two-tier list rather than an alphabetical one, scored as (Strong x 3) + (Moderate x 2) + (Minimal x 1) out of 54 possible points: Tier 1 holds 31 programs scoring 30 or above, Tier 2 holds 6 scoring 28 or below. The top-ranked program is the California Association for Bilingual Education's BEACONS; Amplify Education's Science of Reading courses rank 31st, at the bottom of Tier 1. Per EdSource (republished by The74 on 2026-09-21), the Board approved the 31 Tier 1 programs and declined the six in Tier 2, and directed the Department to publish detailed per-program information for districts — an outcome this board records as attributed, not verified, because the Department's own approved list was not yet posted when this run checked. Districts may still spend the funds on a program not on the list if they verify its alignment with the criteria. Recipients must report to the Department by September 1, 2029 on how many teachers were trained and which programs were used.

    Implications

    • Program. California scored literacy professional-development providers on an 18-criterion rubric with published per-program scores; the criteria and the rubric are public and are a usable external benchmark for Relay's own literacy in-service offerings.

    • Risk. If evidence-ranked approved-provider lists spread to states where Relay does operate, placement on such a list — and the published score attached to it — becomes a market gate rather than a marketing claim.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Illinois is a deep Relay jurisdiction, and this is the first Illinois instrument that puts education systems explicitly inside a state AI-risk governance structure. Nothing binds anyone yet — the cabinet has no members and issues recommendations — but recommendations from a governor's cabinet are the usual upstream of procurement rules and, in other states this year, of educator AI training requirements. Worth watching who is named to it.

    What it does

    Governor JB Pritzker signed Executive Order 2026-07 on September 22, 2026 establishing an Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet drawn from academia, law, ethics, governance and industry. The release (read raw this run) gives the cabinet four charges: advise state government on preparing for and responding to AI-related incidents and capture lessons learned; under 'Protection of Public Assets & Infrastructure,' create policies and procedures to safeguard public assets — the release lists public buildings, water systems, EDUCATION SYSTEMS and information infrastructure — from AI-driven threats; assess the feasibility, timelines and challenges of recommended AI policy measures; and evaluate steps to strengthen AI safety and accountability, including in state procurement. Members will be named in the coming weeks after input from agency leaders. The order is advisory and creates no requirement on districts or preparation programs by itself.

    Implications

    • Compliance. No obligation today. If the cabinet's recommendations reach state procurement or district AI policy, Relay's Illinois programs and any AI tooling used with Illinois candidates would sit inside that frame.

    • Risk. Illinois already has AI employment-decision and Big Tech accountability laws; an AI cabinet with an education-systems mandate is the plausible route to educator-facing AI rules, which have moved fast in other states this year.

    Leader brief

    Illinois creates a governor's AI cabinet, and education systems are named in its mandate

    Governor Pritzker signed an executive order on September 22 creating an Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet — a cross-sector group from academia, law, ethics, governance and industry. Its charges include advising on AI incident preparedness and, specifically, writing policies to safeguard public assets from AI-driven threats. The order's list of public assets names education systems alongside public buildings, water systems and information infrastructure. Members have not been appointed yet; they are expected in the coming weeks. The cabinet advises and recommends; it imposes nothing on districts or preparation programs by itself.

    • Illinois is one of Relay's deepest jurisdictions and this is the first Illinois instrument that puts education inside a state AI-risk structure. Recommendations from a governor's cabinet typically become procurement rules, and in several states this year they have become educator AI training requirements. There is nothing to comply with today. Who gets named to the cabinet is the thing to watch.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay want visibility into this cabinet, given that Illinois is a core jurisdiction and education systems are explicitly in scope?

    • If Illinois follows Georgia and Tennessee toward educator AI training requirements, is Relay positioned to deliver that preparation?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Title II-A state-activity funds are one of the streams that pay for state educator-preparation and induction work Relay competes for; this survey is the federal record of how states spend them. An extension without change is routine — the value is the signal that the collection continues under the current Department, and the window if Relay wants to ask for finer-grained reporting on preparation-program spending.

    What it does

    The Department proposes an extension without change of information collection 1810-0756, the annual Survey on State Education Agency Use of Funds Under Title II, Part A (ESEA section 2104(a) reporting). The survey asks each of the 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico (52 responses, 416 burden hours a year) how Title II-A state-activity funds are used, how they improve equitable access to teachers for low-income and minority students, and, where applicable, teacher, principal and school-leader evaluation and retention data. Notice published 2026-09-03; comments due 2026-11-02 via regulations.gov docket ED-2026-SCC-2905. Verified from the Federal Register API and full text this run.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Two openings and one compliance note. The state must publish a list of professional development providers for high-quality math instruction by 2027-01-01 and decide whether to stand up MathConn — an explicit, dated route onto a state-sanctioned provider list in an authorized jurisdiction. The mathematics-specialist guidelines run through the Connecticut Educator Preparation and Certification Board, the body that governs preparation and certification in the state. The 10-222c rewrite tightens what Relay's Connecticut graduates must disclose when they are hired.

    What it does

    Substitute House Bill 5323, signed 2026-06-04 as Public Act 26-139, 14 sections. Section 10 (effective from passage) requires the Commissioner of Education, by 2027-01-01, to redesign Connecticut's high school mathematics pathways around four named tracks — science, technology, engineering and mathematics; data science and statistics; quantitative reasoning; and workforce and applied mathematics — and, in consultation with the Connecticut Educator Preparation and Certification Board established under Conn. Gen. Stat. 10-150b, to develop guidelines for the role of mathematics specialists supporting math interventions in schools. The same section requires the Commissioner, by 2027-01-01, to develop a list of professional development providers to support implementation of high-quality mathematics instruction and to explore the feasibility of launching MathConn, a professional learning series for educators. Section 2 (effective 2026-07-01) directs the Connecticut Advisory Council for School Administrator Professional Standards, with the Connecticut Association of Schools, to establish a new school administrator mentorship pilot program, report the implementation plan by 2027-07-01, run the pilot in identified districts from the 2027-28 school year, and report results with recommendations by 2029-01-01. Section 11 (effective 2026-07-01) rewrites Conn. Gen. Stat. 10-222c, the pre-employment review every board of education, charter governing council, magnet operator and nonpublic supervisory agent must run before offering a position with direct student contact; the bracketed text in the enrolled act removes the exception that had let an applicant omit an abuse, neglect or sexual misconduct investigation where the investigation found all allegations unsubstantiated.

    Implications

    • Partnership. Connecticut must name math professional development providers by 2027-01-01. Getting considered means engaging the Commissioner's office well before that date.

    • Program. The four named math pathways and the mathematics-specialist role define what Connecticut districts will be staffing for; a math-specialist oriented offering has a described demand shape.

    • Compliance. Relay's Connecticut completers now face a broader pre-hire disclosure obligation under 10-222c, including investigations that ended unsubstantiated.

    Leader brief

    Connecticut is building a state list of math professional development providers, due January 2027

    Connecticut signed a education omnibus in June. The piece that matters most to us: by January 1, 2027 the state Commissioner of Education must redesign high school math into four tracks, write guidelines for what a school-based mathematics specialist does, and — the actionable part — publish a list of professional development providers who can support high-quality math instruction, plus decide whether to launch a state professional learning series called MathConn. A separate section tightened what job applicants must disclose about past misconduct investigations before a school can hire them, removing an exception for investigations that cleared the applicant.

    • A state naming approved professional development providers is a listing we either compete for or are absent from, and the decision date is roughly four months out on our planning calendar. The hiring-disclosure change is a small but real thing our Connecticut graduates will encounter.

    Questions to ask

    • Is Connecticut math professional development a market we want on that list, or is our capacity better spent in the deeper-partnership states?

    • Who do we know in the Connecticut Commissioner's office, and is there a warm route before the provider list is drafted?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Retention-side, not preparation-side: a state-funded housing incentive for the workforce Relay's Colorado partners employ. Worth one line as an example of the 'raft' of housing-based retention tools districts are adopting; no educator-prep mechanism.

    What it does

    The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority runs CHFA Schools to Home, a General Assembly-authorized shared-appreciation down-payment program for full-time employees of Colorado public schools, districts, charter schools, institute charters, BOCES and innovation zones: a fixed-rate first mortgage plus a deferred second mortgage for down payment or closing costs of up to 25 percent of the first loan, repaid with a share of appreciation to the Public School Permanent Fund (verified from the CHFA page). Per Chalkbeat Colorado (09-14), the program launched July 1 under a 2025 state law (SB25-167 per the article's link), 85 employees have used it, initial funding is expected to support about 125 purchases at roughly $80,000 average assistance, and the Treasury invested $10 million of Permanent Fund money.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Adjacent-tier and not an educator-preparation rule, but it is a staffing-demand signal in an authorized jurisdiction where the board already tracks certification items (the DE Teacher Academy scholarship and the Professional Standards Board's Elementary Teacher certificate amendments). A five-year push to add roughly ten percent to charter capacity is a five-year push to staff it, and the named priorities — dual-language, literacy-focused, alternative and therapeutic models — are teacher-supply categories that are hard to fill. The first competitive subgrant round falls in year one, beginning 2026-10-01.

    What it does

    Delaware has been awarded a five-year, $16 million federal Charter Schools Program grant. Quoting and summarizing the state release read raw this run: the grant is to 'expand access to high-quality public charter school options while strengthening the support, oversight and accountability systems that help schools deliver strong outcomes for students.' The grant period begins 2026-10-01. AT LEAST 90 PERCENT of the award will fund competitive subgrants for the planning, implementation, replication and expansion of charter schools addressing documented student and community needs, with awards turning on applicant quality and readiness, community need, financial sustainability and evidence of demand. Subject to proposals meeting those requirements, grant-supported activities carry a five-year target of increasing statewide charter enrollment CAPACITY by about 10 percent; the release states roughly 19,000 Delaware students are currently enrolled across 23 charter schools. Identified needs the state names: alternative and therapeutic educational models, workforce-connected pathways, rural educational opportunities, dual-language programs, literacy-focused programs, and flexible pathways for students who are over-age or under-credited, with a focus on expanding access for educationally disadvantaged students, multilingual learners and students with disabilities.

    Implications

    • Partnership. New and expanding Delaware charter schools funded from year-one subgrants will be hiring against a five-year capacity target — a concrete pipeline demand signal in a state where Relay already tracks certification policy.

    • Program. The state's named priority areas (dual-language, literacy-focused, alternative and therapeutic settings) are precisely the preparation specialties that are scarce, which is where a preparation provider has leverage.

    H.R. 10436 'Reaching English Learners Act' — would create a new competitive Higher Education Act Title II grant for teacher-preparation programs that prepare candidates to teach English learners, with a 50% non-federal match and a clinical placement requirement

    This is a Title II teacher-preparation grant written in language that fits Relay directly: the eligible-institution definition names postbaccalaureate and

    SourceGovInfo (GPO) — BILLS-119hr10436ih introduced text, read raw 2026-09-23. Surfaced by the wired govinfo_bills feed. · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is a Title II teacher-preparation grant written in language that fits Relay directly: the eligible-institution definition names postbaccalaureate and alternative-route certification programs, the required partner is a high-need LEA, and the required clinical component is a mentored placement — Relay's model. If it moves, it is a fundable line for building or strengthening English-learner preparation across Relay's programs. It is newly introduced with no committee action, so this is a watch-and-position item, not a response item. The 50 percent non-federal match is the constraint worth noting early.

    What it does

    Introduced September 16, 2026 by Rep. Grijalva (with Reps. Vargas, Norton, and Wilson of Florida) and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce. The bill adds a new Subpart 6 and Section 259, 'Teaching English Learners Grant,' to Part B of Title II of the Higher Education Act (20 U.S.C. 1031 et seq.). It directs the Secretary to award competitive grants of up to five years to 'eligible partnerships' — an eligible institution of higher education partnered with a high-need local educational agency or high-need early childhood program — to improve teacher candidates' preparation to instruct English learners. The definition of eligible institution explicitly includes programs leading to an undergraduate degree, a master's degree, or a postbaccalaureate program required for certification or licensure, 'including any requirements for certification obtained through alternative routes to certification.' Grantees must provide at least 50 percent of activity costs from non-federal sources, in cash or in kind, and the grant may only supplement, never supplant, non-federal funds. Funds must be used to develop or strengthen a preparation program that meets the state's licensure requirements to teach English learners and embeds evidence-based strategies including bilingual, immersion and dual-language education; to build candidate skills in helping English learners meet state academic standards and attain English proficiency, identifying and serving English learners with disabilities, addressing social and emotional needs, and engaging families; and to provide preservice clinical experience meeting HEA Section 202(d)(2), including, to the extent practicable, clinical learning in classrooms serving English learners and mentoring by a teacher certified to teach English learners. The Secretary must give preference to partnerships recruiting candidates from underrepresented populations or former English learners. Applications require a self-assessment of the existing preparation program and of local personnel needs. Grantees must report completion, licensure and placement rates for candidates plus the systemic effect on the partnership; the Secretary must publish findings and best practices within 180 days of the last grant period. The bill carries no stated authorization amount in the sections read. No cosponsor additions, committee action or scheduled markup as of this run.

    Implications

    • Funding. If enacted and appropriated, this is a five-year competitive grant Relay could pursue in partnership with a high-need district to build or strengthen English-learner preparation, subject to a 50 percent non-federal match in cash or in kind.

    • Program. The required uses map onto curriculum work Relay would have to do anyway in states adding English-learner or bilingual requirements — evidence-based EL instruction, EL students with disabilities, and mentored clinical placements in classrooms serving English learners.

    • Partnership. Eligibility runs through a partnership with a high-need LEA or high-need early childhood program, so any pursuit starts with choosing the district partner, not with the application.

    • Advocacy. The bill's eligible-institution language already names alternative routes to certification; keeping that language intact through committee is the specific thing worth watching.

    Leader brief

    A new House bill would fund teacher-preparation programs to train teachers of English learners, and its eligibility language explicitly covers alternative-route programs like Relay's

    Representative Grijalva and three colleagues introduced the Reaching English Learners Act in the House on September 16. It would add a new competitive grant program to the Higher Education Act, the federal law that governs college and teacher-preparation funding. Grants would run up to five years and would go to partnerships between a teacher-preparation institution and a high-need school district or early childhood program. The money would build or strengthen programs that prepare teacher candidates to teach English learners, including coursework in evidence-based instruction, serving English learners with disabilities, and family engagement, plus a mentored student-teaching placement in classrooms that serve English learners. Grantees would have to cover at least half the cost from non-federal sources, in cash or in kind. The bill was referred to the House education committee and has had no further action; it names no dollar amount in the operative sections.

    • The eligibility definition specifically includes postbaccalaureate programs and programs leading to certification through alternative routes, which is the category Relay occupies — this is not a bill written only for traditional schools of education. If it advances, it would be a fundable path for English-learner preparation work across Relay's programs, and the required district partnership means the partner choice would come first. Nothing is actionable yet: the bill was introduced a week ago with no committee action.

    Questions to ask

    • Is English-learner preparation a capability Relay wants to build out deliberately, independent of whether this particular bill passes?

    • If Relay were to pursue this, which district partner and which programs would be the natural fit, and could the 50 percent non-federal match be met in kind?

    • Is it worth signalling support for the bill's alternative-route eligibility language while it is still in committee?

    Why it matters to Relay

    If enacted, districts could spend Title IV-A formula dollars on educator AI professional development, an allowable-use category Relay's Teacher Professional Education line could sell into; it also gives the federal AI-in-education debate a vehicle that has cleared committee, unlike H.R. 10315 (introduced only). A board gap: the July committee action predates the tracker's federal-bill wiring and was surfaced by the cross-engine sweep (Opus) this run.

    What it does

    Introduced 2026-05-12 by Rep. Randy Fine (R-FL) and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce; the Committee's 2026-07-21 release (read raw this run) lists it among ten bills the Committee 'advanced' at that day's markup. The bill text (introduced version, read in full this run — a single operative section) amends four allowable-use provisions of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act's Title IV, Part A Student Support and Academic Enrichment program: state activities for student instruction (section 4104(b)(3)(A)(i)) and for teachers and school leaders (4104(b)(3)(C)), and local activities for student instruction (4107(a)(3)) and for teachers and school leaders (4109(a)). Each amendment adds instruction in, or giving teachers, paraprofessionals, librarians, specialized instructional support personnel and administrators the knowledge and skills to use and teach, artificial intelligence 'safely, effectively, and responsibly, including through professional development.' It appropriates nothing and creates no new program; it widens what existing Title IV-A dollars may buy. No reported (RH) text is on govinfo as of this run, so the Committee release is the only record of the vote.

    Implications

    • Program. Educator AI professional development would become an explicit allowable use of Title IV-A funds at the state and district level — a purchasable category for Relay's Teacher Professional Education offerings if the bill is enacted.

    • Advocacy. The bill is the only federal AI-in-education measure that has cleared a committee; its allowable-use language (no new money) is the template other bills, including H.R. 10315, would be measured against.

    Leader brief

    House committee bill would let schools spend existing federal enrichment money on AI training for teachers

    A House bill, H.R. 8747, would change the federal K-12 law (the Elementary and Secondary Education Act) so that states and districts may use their existing Title IV-A 'Student Support and Academic Enrichment' grant money to teach students to use artificial intelligence responsibly and to train teachers, paraprofessionals, librarians and administrators to use and teach it. The bill adds no new money. The House Education and Workforce Committee advanced it on July 21 as part of a ten-bill package; it has not been scheduled for a House vote and has no Senate counterpart that we found. It was not on our board until the cross-engine sweep surfaced it this run.

    • If it became law, districts would have an explicit federal funding category for AI professional development for educators, which is a service Relay already offers to districts. The near-term effect is on the conversation: this is the one federal AI-in-schools bill that has moved past committee, so district and state AI plans may start to reference it.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay's professional-education catalog have an AI-for-educators offering that a district could buy with Title IV-A funds if this passed, and should one be ready before it does?

    • Is this a bill Relay would want to be visible on — for example through AACTE or district partners — given that it adds no funding but names educator AI training as a federal priority?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Connecticut is rewriting the formula that funds every district Relay's Connecticut partners operate in, with a choice-system working session that touches charter funding; the January report will set the 2027 legislative session's education-finance agenda.     What it does

    Per the Governor's commission page (read raw this run): Executive Order 26-3 (2026-04-16) created the Blue-Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability and tasked it with 'a top-to-bottom overhaul of how the state funds its public schools' — the funding landscape, other states' models, districts' primary cost drivers, and proven delivery strategies — with a final report of recommendations due 2027-01-15. The full Commission meets 2026-09-17 at 10:00 a.m. in the Legislative Office Building with the Education Cost Sharing (ECS) working session held in-person during the meeting (agenda 'coming soon' at run time); parallel working sessions run on accountability (09-22, 10-13), the choice system (09-16, 10-01, 10-08) and special education (09-24). Members include two legislators, the Office of Policy and Management secretary, superintendents, a district finance director, a regional education service center director and a paraprofessionals' union president. Public listening sessions run twice weekly by registration and a public survey is open.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Governance rather than regulation: nothing here changes a program-approval or certification standard. It changes who convenes the agencies that set them, and it puts the annual public accounting of Georgia's teacher-preparation and alternative-certification investments under a new office with a workforce mandate. Worth tracking as the venue where Georgia educator-pipeline policy will now be argued.

    What it does

    House Bill 1302, effective 2026-07-01, restructures how Georgia governs education and workforce policy. It reconstitutes the Office of Student Achievement as the Office of Education and Workforce Strategy and replaces the former name throughout Titles 20, 34 and 50; repeals the Alliance of Education Agency Heads and reassigns its functions; renames the High Demand Apprenticeship Program the Top State for Talent Pre-Apprenticeship and Apprenticeship Program; designates the Technical College System of Georgia as the state apprenticeship agency for Georgia with related authority over registered apprenticeship programs; requires a combined Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act Plan and Perkins State Plan; repeals the sunset on HOPE scholarship access for dual enrollment students; and establishes an Education Data Governance Board whose members include the Professional Standards Commission, the University System of Georgia, the Technical College System of Georgia, the Georgia Student Finance Commission, the Department of Early Care and Learning, the Office of Planning and Budget and the Department of Labor. That board becomes the primary interagency forum for governing cross-agency education and workforce data systems, including the statewide longitudinal data system and interagency data-sharing agreements. The act also moves the Georgia education workforce report — which reports on the state's investments in teacher preparation, educator professional development, education leadership development, in-field teaching, geographic teacher shortages and alternative routes to teacher certification — under the new office's authorship while leaving it under the Professional Standards Commission's administrative control.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. The Office of Education and Workforce Strategy is the new address for Georgia educator-pipeline policy; the Alliance of Education Agency Heads no longer exists as a venue.

    • Risk. A workforce-framed office authoring the report on alternative routes to teacher certification can shift how graduate-level and alternative preparation is characterized in state policy narrative.

    Leader brief

    Georgia reorganized the agencies that set education and workforce policy

    Effective July 1, 2026, Georgia renamed its Office of Student Achievement the Office of Education and Workforce Strategy, abolished the Alliance of Education Agency Heads that used to coordinate the state's education agencies, and created a new Education Data Governance Board that includes the Professional Standards Commission — the agency that approves our Georgia programs. The state's technical college system becomes Georgia's official apprenticeship agency. None of this changes any rule we have to follow; it changes who is in the room.

    • Georgia's annual public report on what the state is getting from its investments in teacher preparation and alternative certification routes now sits under an office with a workforce mandate. That is where the framing of graduate-level preparation in Georgia policy will be set.

    Questions to ask

    • Does our Georgia relationship map still point at the right offices after this reorganization?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Pennsylvania is an authorized Relay jurisdiction and charter schools are a large share of Relay's partner footprint; a tuition-formula rewrite of this scope changes what every Pennsylvania charter and cyber charter receives per student and what every district pays. No preparation or certification content. Adjacent-tier finance item, surfaced because the House put it in floor position rather than leaving it in committee.

    What it does

    Amends Public School Code §1725-A (charter funding) and §1725.1-A (cyber charter funding). From 2027-28, the non-special-education charter tuition base moves from the district's budgeted per-ADM expenditure of the prior year to the audited total expenditure per ADM, with tuition already paid to charter entities and the ADM of charter-enrolled students deducted from the district figures (new cl. 2.1), and the result grown by the average of the statewide average weekly wage and employment cost index increases (new cl. 2.2). Special-education tuition from 2027-28 is recomputed on the same adjusted base with charter special-education payments and ADM netted out (new cl. 3.1). The Department, not districts, calculates and posts per-student amounts from annual financial reports by June 15 each year (cl. 7(ii); a 5% growth placeholder applies if a district's report is late). For cyber charters, the 2026-27 tuition already deducts cyber tuition paid, tax assessment and collection, 80% of student activities and 80% of operations and maintenance of plant, multiplied by a §2502.56 factor capped at 1; the bill extends those deductions and the wage-index growth to 2027-28 and later (new (e)(4)), and caps cyber special-education tuition from 2027-28 at the lesser of the adjusted amount or 1.71 times the non-special-education amount (new (f.1)). Cyber provisions take effect immediately; the rest on 2027-07-01. Sixteen House Democratic sponsors (Prokopiak, Madden, Borowski, Khan and others). History: introduced 2026-06-12, reported as amended from House Education 2026-06-16, first consideration and re-committed to Rules the same day; on 2026-09-08 re-reported as committed and laid on the table, one of about 85 bills the House placed on the table on its first day back. A companion in the same batch, HB2602 (Schweyer), would require cyber charter students to be visible on camera for synchronous attendance and adds wellness-check and child-protection provisions.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay signs the Title IV program participation agreement (Federal School Code 042086), so the new §487(a)(30) undertaking would become one of its standing PPA conditions if enacted — a compliance certification with no educator-preparation content. Section 3's July 31 certification applies only to Title VI (international education) participants, which Relay is not. Ecosystem-level otherwise; Senate path unclear, no companion recorded.

    What it does

    The House passed H.R. 4795 on September 3, 2026, 237-169 (Roll no. 295). Read from the engrossed text (BILLS-119hr4795eh): Section 2 AMENDS the Higher Education Act's program participation agreement (HEA §487(a), 20 U.S.C. 1094(a)) by adding a new paragraph (30) under which every participating institution agrees it 'will not engage in a nonexpressive commercial boycott of a major strategic partner of the United States.' 'Major strategic partner' is defined by cross-reference to section 4 of Public Law 113-296 (the United States-Israel Strategic Partnership Act of 2014) and entities licensed, regulated or organized under such a country's laws; 'nonexpressive commercial boycott' means a commercial action (including refusals to deal and terminating business activities) intended to limit commercial relations with such a partner and 'not based on a valid business reason,' excluding actions covered by the exceptions regulations under the Anti-Boycott Act of 2018 (50 U.S.C. 4842(a)(2)). Because §487(a) is the agreement every Title IV institution signs, this condition would apply to all of them. Section 3 ADDS new HEA §639 to Title VI (international education programs): an institution participating or applying under Title VI must certify by July 31 each year that it permits its students and faculty to take part in academic programs in a major strategic partner on the same terms as in other foreign countries, and admits that partner's students and faculty to its own programs on the same terms as other foreign institutions; a missed certification makes the institution ineligible for Title VI funds in the next fiscal year, including continuation funds on prior awards. Section 3 also adds a sense-of-Congress §639A. The engrossed bill carries no effective-date provision, so §487(a)(30) would take effect on enactment; the certification cycle begins with the first July 31 after enactment. Next step is the Senate, where no companion action is recorded.

    Implications

    • Compliance. If enacted, Relay's program participation agreement would carry a new standing undertaking not to engage in a 'nonexpressive commercial boycott' of Israel or Israeli-organized entities; procurement and vendor decisions touching that definition would need a documented 'valid business reason' record.

    • Risk. The definition turns on intent and 'valid business reason,' terms the bill leaves to ED to interpret; a PPA breach can put Title IV participation at issue, so the exposure is disproportionate to the operational footprint.

    Leader brief

    The House passed a bill that would add an anti-boycott-of-Israel promise to every college's federal student-aid agreement

    Update September 21: this bill is no longer sitting in the House. It went to the Senate on September 14 and was referred to the Senate's education committee, alongside the science-of-reading bill. On September 3 the House of Representatives passed H.R. 4795, 237 to 169. Every institution that takes federal student aid, Relay included, signs a program participation agreement with the U.S. Department of Education listing the conditions of that aid. This bill would add one more condition: the institution promises not to take part in a 'nonexpressive commercial boycott' of Israel, meaning business decisions (such as refusing to buy from or ending contracts with Israeli companies) that are intended to limit dealings with Israel and lack a valid business reason. A second part of the bill requires an annual certification about academic exchanges with Israel, but only from institutions in the federal international-education grant programs, which Relay is not. The bill now goes to the Senate, where nothing is scheduled.

    • Nothing changes unless the Senate passes it and the President signs it. If that happens, the practical work is small but the stakes are not: the promise would live in the same agreement that keeps federal aid flowing, so a purchasing or partnership decision that touched the definition would need a documented business reason on file. There is no educator-preparation content in the bill.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want general counsel to note this now as a standing item for the next program-participation-agreement review, or wait for Senate movement?

    • Is there any current vendor or partnership decision that could be read as within the bill's definition, so we know our exposure before the question is asked?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level only. Colorado is an authorized jurisdiction but not a deep-partnership state, and the item is authorizer governance and homeschool-program funding rather than educator preparation. The CDE rulemaking this fall is the next primary event.

    What it does

    Per Chalkbeat Colorado (2026-09-10): the State Board of Education began rulemaking on publicly funded homeschool-enrichment programs at its 2026-09-09 meeting, the second step of the state's response after Senate Bill 26-023 (May 2026) created an approval process for part-time homeschool programs (CDE release, attached); the board is to finalize rules by the end of December for the 2027-28 school year. Colorado Department of Education staff presented two rule versions (one would limit operation to public providers), which can be combined or amended. A separate rule discussed the same day would require enrichment programs to provide 180 class hours per semester, roughly double today's typical 90, to draw half-time per-pupil funding (about $6,000 a year on average). Of 54 programs that applied for approval this summer, five were approved or partially approved and 11 await decisions; most others were rejected, incomplete, or lost their authorizer when Education reEnvisioned BOCES dissolved in August (prior entry attached). Public commenters asked the board to pursue recovery of past misspent funds. Update 2026-09-14 (CDE news release of 2026-09-11, read this run): at its September meeting the State Board approved notices of rulemaking for three sets of rules. (1) New rules for part-time programs for homeschool students, noticed as two alternatives so the board can take public feedback before choosing: Option A requires a local education provider to operate the program directly (private entities may only supply contracted courses); Option B lets a provider contract with a private nonprofit to operate the program under added authorizing, contracting, financial-separation and oversight requirements. A rulemaking hearing is scheduled for the October meeting with the rules back before the board in November; the statutory deadline is the end of calendar 2026. (2) Updates to 1 CCR 301-39 (administration of the Public School Finance Act) implementing SB 26-023: private-school students barred from part-time public programs, minimum instructional hours for part-time funding raised from 90 to 180, online-school schedule and attendance alignment; deadline Dec. 31, 2026. (3) Updates to the Exceptional Children's Educational Act rules on facility-school placements (FAPE and LRE responsibilities, placement, residency and reimbursement). The same meeting remanded the MESA K-8 charter application to Jeffco (7-2) and denied Koson Schools' Littleton STEM High appeal (6-3).

    NY A11693 / S10671 — would bar AI-enabled humanoid robots from any instructional role in districts, charter schools and BOCES, and require every one of them to adopt a written policy

    The clause worth Relay's attention is the definitional one, not the robots. In defining 'instructional capacity' the bill enumerates what teaching is for

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionNew York
    ClassBill
    StageIn committee
    RecommendationTrack · impact 50
    Latest actionIntroduced by the Committee on Rules at the request of M. of A. Carrie Woerner, read once and referred to the Committee on Education 2026-09-02. Same-as S10671. No committee action. · 2026-09-02
    SourceNew York State Assembly bill page (summary, actions, and full introduced text) read raw this run; sponsor detail from the LegiScan API cache · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    The clause worth Relay's attention is the definitional one, not the robots. In defining 'instructional capacity' the bill enumerates what teaching is for statutory purposes — delivering and leading instruction, tutoring, small-group support, and assessing and grading student work — and reserves it to people. That is the first New York bill this board has seen that draws the line by function rather than by tool, and the same enumeration is the natural template for any later bill about software rather than hardware. As drafted the bill reaches a narrow class of physical devices few of Relay's partner schools own, so the direct operational effect today is close to nil; the durable content is the definition. Momentum is minimal: referred to Education on September 2, no action in either house.

    What it does

    The bill adds a new section 3039 to the Education Law requiring every school district, charter school, and board of cooperative educational services to adopt and implement a written policy governing the use of humanoid robots in schools, and requiring that policy to prohibit the use of an artificial-intelligence-enabled humanoid robot in an instructional capacity. Read from the introduced text this run, an 'artificial intelligence-enabled humanoid robot' is a physical robotic device that (i) is designed or marketed to simulate human appearance, expression, movement, voice, or social interaction, and (ii) uses artificial intelligence or machine learning to generate autonomous or interactive responses through speech, gestures, facial expressions or other communication. 'Instructional capacity' is defined as using such a device to deliver, lead, facilitate or direct classroom instruction; to provide one-on-one or small-group academic instruction, tutoring or educational support; to assess, evaluate or grade student work or academic performance; or otherwise to perform duties ordinarily performed by teaching staff. The title of the act reaches 'humanoid robots and artificial intelligence avatars in instructional settings.'

    Implications

    • Compliance. If enacted, every district, charter school and BOCES in New York would owe a written humanoid-robot policy — an administrative requirement Relay's school partners would carry, not Relay.

    • Risk. The bill's enumeration of 'instructional capacity' — delivering, leading, tutoring, and grading — is a statutory definition of teaching work reserved to humans, and it is the definition a later software-focused bill would most likely reuse.

    Leader brief

    A New York bill would say a robot cannot be the teacher — and in doing so, defines what teaching is

    This bill would require every school district, charter school, and regional service board in New York to adopt a written policy on humanoid robots, and that policy would have to forbid using an AI-powered humanoid robot to teach. It defines teaching broadly for this purpose: leading a class, tutoring one student or a small group, grading student work, or otherwise doing what a teacher ordinarily does. It was referred to the Assembly education committee on September 2 and has not moved.

    • Almost no school we work with owns a device this bill would reach, so the practical effect right now is negligible. What is worth noting is the definition. New York lawmakers are starting to write down, in statute, which parts of teaching must be done by a person. That list — instruct, tutor, assess, grade — is the list any future bill about AI software would likely start from, and it is a list we have a stake in.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want a position on which instructional functions should be legally reserved to people, before the question arrives as a bill about software rather than robots?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Three things make this Relay's business rather than general Delaware news. First, the Department has named 'Higher Education Leaders' as one of twelve stakeholder audiences for the feedback process and has published both a form and an email address — a preparation provider with a Delaware presence has a standing invitation to the table, and October is the stated month for partner engagement. Second, a teacher retention target of 72 to 75 percent by 2028 sits on the same slide as the academic targets, which puts educator supply inside an accountability framework rather than beside it; Tier 4 explicitly contemplates state-directed 'leadership or staffing supports,' meaning the state would be intervening in who staffs a struggling school. Third, the companion early-literacy and pre-retention framework makes K-3 reading instruction the hinge on which retention decisions turn, and that is a preparation question before it is an accountability question. The board already tracks two Delaware items — the Professional Standards Board's Elementary Teacher certificate amendments and the $16M federal Charter Schools Program grant — and this is the third Delaware thread in a month.

    What it does

    The Delaware Department of Education has published a working draft of a School Performance and Support Framework that would, for the first time, attach a defined escalating state response to the performance data the state already collects. Read from the Department's own 28-slide stakeholder deck this run, the framing is that Delaware already has the Delaware School Success Framework to identify schools under the Every Student Succeeds Act, Multi-Tiered Systems of Support to organize instruction and intervention, and assorted literacy, mathematics, leadership and coaching supports — but no single statewide continuum connecting identification to response. The new framework supplies that continuum across five tiers: Tier 1 is the universal expectation with the lowest intervention and an emphasis on strengthening core instruction and leadership; Tiers 2 and 3 add targeted supports; Tier 4 begins state involvement with state-directed instructional and operational actions, leadership or staffing supports, and monthly performance and implementation plans; and Tier 5 is receivership, under which a state-appointed receiver or recovery leader operates with defined authority under a state receivership order and a public recovery plan, with frequent public monitoring and a phased return of authority to the local board after sustained progress. The deck lists the conditions for Tier 5 as sustained underperformance after Tier 4 intervention, required actions and benchmarks failing to produce improvement, leadership, governance, operational or financial conditions substantially impeding improvement, or existing Tier 4 authority proving insufficient. A companion 'Early Literacy Success and Pre-Retention Framework' is included in the same draft; the deck states 'K-3 prevention first; retention is a last resort' and flags K-3 exemptions, student mobility, family communication, and the decision process as detail still to be settled. The framework is anchored to Delaware's 2028 Strategic Plan targets, which the deck states as grade 3 reading 38 percent to 53 percent, grade 8 mathematics 26 percent to 35 percent, graduation rate 89 percent to 91 percent, chronic absenteeism 15 percent to 13 percent, teacher retention 72 percent to 75 percent, and a Delaware School Success Framework composite of 264 to 300. The Department states explicitly that this is a working draft, that final recommendations have not been made, and that some elements require legislative and regulatory action. Per Spotlight Delaware's 2026-09-22 report, fewer than half of Delaware's third through eighth graders read and do mathematics at a proficient level and 18 percent of eleventh graders are proficient in mathematics; the Delaware State Education Association's president, Tameka Mays, is reported as expressing mixed views, and the Delaware Chief School Officers' Association president, Lake Forest Superintendent Steven Lucas, as supportive of working with the Department.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. The Department's feedback process is open now and names higher-education leaders as a stakeholder audience, with October designated for partner engagement — a defined route to comment on how staffing and early-literacy preparation appear in the framework, through de.gov/spsffeedback or school.performance@doe.k12.de.us.

    • Program. The companion Early Literacy Success and Pre-Retention Framework puts K-3 reading instruction at the center of a retention decision; the quality of early-literacy preparation Delaware teachers receive becomes an accountability input, not just a program feature.

    • Partnership. Tier 4 contemplates state-directed leadership and staffing supports and Tier 5 a state-appointed receiver; schools in those tiers are, by construction, schools with acute staffing and instructional-leadership needs and a state actor authorized to address them.

    • Risk. The Department says some elements require legislative action and plans recommendations for the session opening in January; the content could shift materially between this draft and the bill, so nothing here should be treated as settled Delaware policy.

    Leader brief

    Delaware wants the power to take over failing school districts, and is asking for feedback now

    Delaware's Education Secretary, Cindy Marten, presented a draft plan to the State Board of Education on September 17 that would create five levels of state response to schools whose results do not improve. The first three levels are support. At level four the state starts directing what a school does, including decisions about its leadership and staffing, and puts it on monthly improvement plans. At level five the state takes over the district, appoints someone to run it, and hands authority back to the local school board only after sustained improvement. A companion piece would make holding third-graders back a last resort if early reading help does not work. The state's own numbers give the context: fewer than half of students in grades three through eight read or do math at grade level. This is a draft, not a decision. The Department is collecting feedback through the fall and plans to send legislative recommendations in December, before the session that opens in January.

    • Delaware has publicly invited higher-education leaders into this feedback process, and October is the month it has set aside for partners. That is an open door we can walk through. Two parts of the draft are directly our work: the state's own goal of lifting teacher retention from 72 to 75 percent sits inside this accountability plan, and the early-reading piece means the quality of how Delaware teachers are prepared to teach reading becomes a factor in whether children are held back. Schools at the top two levels of intervention will have acute staffing and instructional-leadership needs by definition.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want to submit feedback during Delaware's October partner window, and if so, what is the one thing we would most want changed or added?

    • Delaware is now our third active policy thread this month alongside the elementary certification rules and the federal charter grant — is our Delaware presence sized to the attention the state is getting?

    • If the state gains authority to direct staffing in struggling schools, is that a risk to how our graduates are placed, an opportunity to supply them, or both?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Routine paperwork housekeeping, carried at SCAN because it is the administrative plumbing of Title IV cash management rather than a change to it. It matters to Relay only as a graduate institution participating in Title IV: the HCM2 machinery is the mechanism by which a Department that has grown markedly more willing to attach conditions to federal money can slow an institution's cash. Nothing here changes those forms. Worth a line, not a response.

    What it does

    Notice under the Paperwork Reduction Act: the Department is proposing an extension WITHOUT CHANGE of the currently approved information collection for the Request for Title IV Reimbursement or Heightened Cash Monitoring 2 (HCM2). HCM2 is the payment method the Department imposes on Title IV institutions it judges to need closer oversight; under it an institution must disburse its own funds to students first and then request reimbursement with documentation. The notice submits the collection to the Office of Management and Budget for review and approval and opens comment through 2026-10-05. Published date, type and comment-close date were read raw from the Federal Register API this run; no substantive change to the forms is proposed.
