    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the companion ruling to the teacher-training grant decision issued the same day, and for Relay it matters less as research money than as a limit on the mechanism. The apportionment-footnote device is how spending conditions get attached to federal education dollars without notice-and-comment; a court saying the device does not carry that power constrains the same playbook that could be pointed at Teacher Quality Partnership, Supporting Effective Educator Development or Title II funds Relay competes for. It also sits directly alongside the EDGAR rewrite now in its final comment days, which would give the Department that discretion by regulation rather than by footnote — the judicial and regulatory tracks are moving in opposite directions on the same question. The nearest dated event is the Department's 2026-09-28 status report to the court.

    What it does

    Per Education Week (Mark Lieberman, 2026-09-18, read raw this run) — the court order itself was NOT read and is UNVERIFIED here: Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts ruled on 2026-09-17 that she is skeptical of the Office of Management and Budget's claim of authority to use binding apportionment footnotes to impose policy priorities on federal agencies, quoting her order that the Court 'does not find that this "modest" and "subtle" footnote reference ... authorizes the sweeping power to utilize binding apportionment footnotes to advance the Executive Branch's policy objectives.' Apportionment is the routine process by which OMB releases congressional appropriations to agencies. Education Week reports OMB attached footnotes to Institute of Education Sciences (IES) apportionments requiring IES to comply with the administration's anti-DEI executive order and with an OMB-approved spending plan. Education Week reports OMB released some fiscal 2025 IES funds more than a year later than usual and continues to withhold more than $465 million in fiscal 2026 funds that IES was due to access six months ago (those expire 2027-09-30). On the delayed apportionments Burroughs declined a definitive ruling and instead ordered the Education Department to report on 2026-09-28 whether it is on track to obligate the remaining $180 million of fiscal 2025 IES funds by the 2026-09-30 expiry, warning the Court may reconsider whether there has been undue delay if it appears defendants have misled it. Plaintiffs, per Education Week: the National Center for Learning Disabilities, Knowledge Alliance, BNP Education Partners and the Massachusetts Teachers Association, who sued 2026-06-30. Case caption, docket number and the order's precise disposition are UNVERIFIED: a CourtListener v4 search of the District of Massachusetts run raw this run returned zero results and the docket API requires authentication. ADDED 2026-09-21 from the cross-engine sweep (NOT independently verified from a docket this run): two engines identify the case as NCLD et al. v. OMB et al. in the District of Massachusetts, with plaintiffs the National Center for Learning Disabilities, Knowledge Alliance, BNP Education Partners and the Massachusetts Teachers Association, and characterize the disposition as a partial summary judgment barring OMB from attaching extra-statutory conditions to appropriated IES research funds. Unlike the companion teacher-training case, whose order this run retrieved and read in full, NO ORDER FOR THIS CASE WAS LOCATED — the California Attorney General's press-docs archive serves the teacher-training order because California is a plaintiff there, and it is not a party here. The case caption is therefore ATTRIBUTED, not verified. The sweep also flags an Inside Higher Ed report of 2026-09-21 that the National Science Foundation is over $1 billion behind on grants and that IES says it will obligate the expiring funds; that outlet's figures differ from Education Week's ($180M FY2025 remaining) and from a Hechinger figure the sweep cites ($289M unspent), so NO dollar figure here should be treated as settled except the ones quoted to a named outlet.

    Implications

    • Risk. The IES evidence base Relay and its state partners cite in program design and accreditation narratives is being funded late or not at all; a FY2026 hold of $465M is a multi-year gap in the research pipeline, not a one-year dip.

    • Advocacy. A ruling against policy-conditioning by apportionment footnote is a citable precedent in Relay's EDGAR comment, which closes 2026-09-23 — the rule would relocate that same discretion into regulation.

    • Funding. Nothing in this ruling releases money to any grantee. The practical question is whether the $180M in FY2025 IES funds is obligated by 2026-09-30; the Sept 28 status report is the tell.

    Leader brief

    A second court has told the White House budget office it cannot attach policy strings to education money by memo

    On the same day a judge struck down the cancellation of teacher-training grants, a second federal judge in Massachusetts rejected the White House Office of Management and Budget's use of footnotes on its funding releases to force the Education Department's research arm to follow the administration's diversity-equity-and-inclusion executive order. Education Week reports that more than $465 million Congress appropriated for education research in fiscal 2026 is still being withheld, and that the judge has ordered the Education Department to tell the court by September 28 whether it will actually spend $180 million of last year's research money before it expires on September 30. We are reporting this from Education Week's account; we have not been able to read the court's own order.

    • The practical significance for Relay is not the research money itself. It is that a court has limited the quiet administrative mechanism used to attach conditions to federal education grants — the same kind of grant Relay competes for. At the same time, the Education Department is finishing a rule change (comments close September 23) that would give it that discretion openly. Courts are closing one door while the rulemaking opens another.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want our comment on the Education Department's grant-rules rewrite to cite this ruling, given that we have two days to decide? And how much of our program-evidence strategy depends on federal education research that may arrive late or not at all for the next two years?

    Why it matters to Relay

    The endorsement itself is outside Relay's programs (JROTC instructors are certified through the military, not an educator-preparation program). The item is on the board for the comment exchange: a request to extend New Jersey's limited CE/CEAS alternate-route pilot past 2027 was put to the Department in a certification rulemaking and drew a scope answer rather than a position, which leaves the pilot's future an open question for New Jersey's alternate-route providers.

    What it does

    Notice of Adoption (R.2026 d.097) for the amendment to N.J.A.C. 6A:9B-11.8 proposed February 17, 2026 (58 N.J.R. 1057(a)) and adopted without change by the State Board of Education on August 7, 2026; effective September 8, 2026, expiring April 6, 2030. The amendment deletes former paragraph (a)1, which required a candidate for the standard certificate with a military science endorsement to document 20 years of military service; as adopted, eligibility rests solely on holding a current certification or letter of eligibility from the appropriate branch of the U.S. military authorizing the person to serve as a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (JROTC) instructor. The Department's stated purpose is alignment with the 2024 revision of 10 U.S.C. 2031, which reduced the federal minimum from 20 to eight years. Five commenters (NJSBA, NJEA, an Air Force JROTC regional director, two individuals) supported the change. One commenter asked that the limited certificate of eligibility (CE) and limited CEAS pilot program be extended beyond 2027 or made permanent; the Department answered that the pilot is beyond the scope of this rulemaking.

    Implications

    • Program. No effect on Relay's New Jersey programs: the rule changes eligibility for one endorsement that is granted on a military credential, not on preparation-program completion.

    • Risk. The limited CE/CEAS pilot, New Jersey's most recent alternate-route experiment, is now on record as a question the Department has not answered; its 2027 sunset is a date to watch for any provider that places candidates through the CE route.

    Leader brief

    New Jersey finalized a small certification rule change for JROTC instructors, and a commenter used it to ask about the future of the state's alternate-route pilot

    New Jersey's State Board of Education has finalized a rule that drops the requirement that Junior ROTC instructors document 20 years of military service before they can be certified to teach military science in public schools; the state now defers to each military branch's own instructor certification, which federal law changed to an eight-year minimum in 2024. The rule took effect September 8. During the comment period, one commenter asked the Department to extend or make permanent a separate pilot that lets districts hire some teachers on a limited certificate before they finish full preparation. The Department replied that the pilot was outside the scope of this rule.

    • The JROTC change does not touch Relay. The exchange about the limited-certificate pilot matters more: it is one of New Jersey's routes into teaching for people who have not completed a preparation program, it is scheduled to end in 2027, and the Department has not said what happens next.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay New Jersey enroll or partner with candidates who enter through the limited certificate pilot, and would its expiration in 2027 change enrollment?

    • Is there a position Relay would want on record if the Department opens a rulemaking on the pilot's future?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Fails the liveness gate — dead for this General Assembly — and is surfaced as recorded legislative appetite by the same convention the board uses for the Texas early-literacy bills. The content is unusually close to Relay: a state residency grant explicitly open to 501(c)(3) preparation providers, at $44,500 a resident, with statutory credit toward the clinical experience licensure requirement. It cleared Senate Education unanimously and died on money, not on policy, which is the profile of a bill that returns in the 115th General Assembly.

    What it does

    HB1977 (White, Behn) / SB2156 (Haile, Akbari) would have enacted the 'Tennessee Teacher Residency Program Act' at Tenn. Code Ann. 49-5-1201 et seq., directing the Department of Education to award grants of up to $44,500 per teacher resident for up to 100 residents per academic year, covering program operating costs, resident stipends and mentor teacher stipends. Its definition of an eligible residency program expressly included a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization conducting teacher preparation using a residency model in partnership with an LEA, an institution of higher education, or an approved educator preparation provider. Program requirements: one full academic year of rigorous EPP coursework integrated with a concurrent full year of guided clinical apprenticeship under a mentor teacher, competitive admissions, effectiveness-based mentor selection, paid and trained mentors, cohorts, progress measures, an employment expectation from the partnering or a high-need LEA, a three-year teaching commitment with stipend reimbursement by the residency program if the resident does not complete it, and one year of post-completion support. Completion of a qualifying residency would have satisfied the clinical experience required by 49-5-5604. The fiscal note put state expenditures at $4,547,600 for FY26-27 and subsequent years. The Senate Education Committee recommended passage with amendment 8-0 on 2026-03-11; the House companion was recommended for passage by the Education Committee and referred to Finance, where it was placed behind the budget on 2026-04-08 and last calendared for 2026-04-20. Neither bill advanced before the 114th General Assembly adjourned.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. A Tennessee residency grant open to nonprofit preparation providers has cleared a chamber committee unanimously once. The interval before the 115th General Assembly convenes in January 2027 is when sponsor relationships and fiscal framing are built, not after refiling.

    • Funding. $44,500 per resident for up to 100 residents is the price point Tennessee legislators were willing to put on a residency seat. That number is a useful anchor for any Relay Tennessee residency proposal, public or philanthropic.

    Leader brief

    Tennessee nearly funded teacher residencies at $44,500 a seat — open to nonprofits like us — and it died on money, not policy

    A Tennessee bill this spring would have created a state teacher residency grant program: up to $44,500 per resident for as many as 100 residents a year, covering program costs, the resident's stipend, and the mentor teacher's stipend. Its definition of an eligible residency program expressly included a 501(c)(3) nonprofit running a residency in partnership with a school district, a university, or an approved preparation provider — which describes us. The design was a full year of coursework alongside a full year in a classroom under a paid, trained mentor, a job expectation at the end, and a three-year teaching commitment. The Senate education committee approved it unanimously. It then went to the finance committee, was 'placed behind the budget,' and never came back before the legislature adjourned. The fiscal note was about $4.5 million a year.

    • Nothing changes operationally today; the bill is dead. What it tells us is that Tennessee legislators were willing to price a residency seat at $44,500 and to write nonprofit preparation providers into the eligibility language, and that the obstacle was budget timing rather than opposition to the model. The next Tennessee legislature convenes in January 2027, and bills of this shape usually return.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want to be involved before this is refiled — with the sponsors, or with the fiscal case — rather than reacting to it next January?

    • Is $44,500 per residency seat a number we can build a Tennessee program around, and would we want to if the money appeared?

    • The eligibility language naming 501(c)(3) providers is unusually favorable to us. Is protecting that language worth engagement effort in its own right?

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is New York building a funded statewide intermediary for exactly the work Relay does — registered teacher apprenticeships, grow-your-own pipelines, and alternative credentialing routes. Two readings matter and they point opposite ways. As opportunity: $50M of technical assistance and apprenticeship intermediation that Relay's New York programs could plug into, and a named partner to be at the table with. As risk: a single designated nonprofit becomes the State's contracting channel for educator-pipeline work, and Relay is not it. Either way the decision about who sits inside that structure gets made before the money moves, not after.

    What it does

    Establishes a State educator development workforce initiative and authorizes it to contract with EDHUBNY, a named nonprofit intermediary, to address workforce shortages across New York's child-serving system — early childhood, early intervention, special education, and K-12. The contract provisions carry performance measures, reporting requirements, and fiscal controls, and the initiative may collaborate with other State agencies. EDHUBNY reports to the Governor, the Senate Temporary President, the Assembly Speaker, and the Ways & Means and Finance chairs. Appropriates $50,000,000 from the general fund. The sponsor's memorandum states the mechanism explicitly: registered apprenticeships, coordinated with grow-your-own strategies, strategic staffing and retention models, and streamlined credentialing pathways. Effective January 1, 2027.

    Implications

    • Funding. $50M general-fund appropriation for educator apprenticeship intermediation and credentialing pathways in Relay's deepest jurisdiction. No competitive solicitation is contemplated in the bill — the money flows through a contract with a named nonprofit.

    • Partnership. EDHUBNY is the designated contractor. Whether Relay is a subrecipient, a program partner, or outside the structure is decided in the contract design phase, which begins only if the bill advances. Establishing the relationship now costs little and is the whole ballgame later.

    • Program. The bill's mechanism — registered apprenticeships plus streamlined credentialing pathways — is the model Relay already operates. Relay's New York apprenticeship and residency data is directly relevant evidence for sponsors building the case.

    • Advocacy. No statutory deadline, but a real calendar: the bill dies December 31, 2026. The live window is the January 2027 session opening and the FY2028 executive budget, typically released mid-January. Sponsor outreach happens in the fall or not at all.

    • Risk. A single-intermediary structure can consolidate State educator-pipeline funding away from direct program providers. Worth reading the eventual contract language on whether prep providers can access technical assistance and apprenticeship funds directly.

    Leader brief

    New York: a proposed $50 million educator-workforce fund routed through one nonprofit (A10196-B / S09397-A)

    Two New York legislators have proposed a $50 million state initiative to grow the educator workforce through teacher apprenticeships, grow-your-own pipelines, and streamlined credentialing, run through a single named nonprofit intermediary called EDHUBNY. That is very close to the work Relay already does in New York, and the bill routes the money through one contract rather than a competitive grant. The bill did not pass this session and dies at the end of 2026 unless revived, so the meaningful window is this fall, ahead of the January session and the next state budget.

    • This cuts both ways. Inside the structure, Relay could plug into $50 million of apprenticeship and credentialing funding in its deepest state; outside it, Relay could watch state pipeline funding consolidate into a channel it does not touch.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we have a relationship with EDHUBNY today, and what would it take to be a named partner rather than a bystander if this advances?

    • Should Relay put its New York apprenticeship results in front of the sponsors this fall, while the bill's next-session fate is being decided?

    Every ED discretionary grant Relay holds or pursues (SEED, TQP-structure partnerships) would sit under codified termination-for-convenience and

    At a glance

    RecommendationScan · impact 61
    Second opinionModel scorer: Scan · impact 61; reviewer: Act · impact 82
    Latest actionComment window closed 2026-09-23 per the Federal Register notice (deadline unchanged; final comment count not re-read this run). Docket ED-2026-OPEPD-2542, RIN 1875-AA14. · 2026-08-24

    SourceFederal Register · Open the primary source
    CommentComment

    Why it matters to Relay

    Every ED discretionary grant Relay holds or pursues (SEED, TQP-structure partnerships) would sit under codified termination-for-convenience and continuation-at-discretion terms — the regulatory codification of the 2025 grant-termination fights — while the 75.500(f) merit certification reaches into grantee hiring and admissions practice and 75.228 puts competitive pressure on indirect-cost recovery. The 77.1 evidence-framework change also alters how applicants prove moderate/strong evidence in competitions.

    What it does

    Notice of proposed rulemaking amending the Education Department General Administrative Regulations (34 CFR parts 75, 76, 77, 79; 2 CFR parts 3474, 3485), docket ED-2026-OPEPD-2542, RIN 1875-AA14. Verified from the Federal Register text this run: revised 75.901 gives "clear notice to all recipients of the Department's ability to terminate discretionary awards for convenience," citing the 2025 per curiam opinions in Department of Education v. California and NIH v. American Public Health Association and reasoning that grant agreements are "ultimately contractual in nature," and adds FAR-modeled temporary-suspension provisions. Revised 75.253 removes subsection (c) and codifies the Secretary's discretion to reduce or deny continuation awards using any relevant information, with the General Education Provisions Act declared inapplicable to those decisions; revised 75.230 states that approving an application does not obligate future funding; new 75.251(d) lets ED adjust awards based on unspent balances. New 75.228 authorizes competitive preference for applicants proposing indirect-cost rates below their negotiated rate. New 75.500(f) requires grantees to certify that hiring, admissions, promotion, and compensation under the grant are merit-based "without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or proxies thereof" and that employment practices do not compel statements of belief. Revised 77.1 realigns the evidence-tier definitions (strong/moderate/promising) to ESEA statute, removes What Works Clearinghouse references, and adds an "evidence framework" definition allowing third-party-funded evidence reviews. 75.562(c)(2) keeps the 8% MTDC cap for training grants without a negotiated rate and bars the de minimis rate on training programs. Styled an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action; ED intends to finalize in late 2026. Comments close 2026-09-23, via regulations.gov.

    Implications

    • Risk. Termination-for-convenience plus discretionary continuation determinations (GEPA inapplicable) would let ED end or shrink any Relay federal award mid-project for alignment-with-priorities reasons, with reduced procedural recourse.

    • Compliance. The 75.500(f) certification obligates grantees to attest merit-based hiring/admissions/promotion practices 'without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or proxies thereof' and to avoid compelled belief statements — Relay's hiring and admissions language for grant-funded work would need review against it.

    • Funding. Competitive preference for below-negotiated-rate indirect costs (new 75.228) pressures Relay to discount indirect recovery to stay competitive; unspent-balance adjustments (75.251(d)) tighten multi-year budget management.

    • Advocacy. Comment window open through 2026-09-23 — Relay (directly or through AACTE) can seek clarity on continuation-award criteria, the scope of "proxies thereof," and evidence-framework governance.

    Leader brief

    Update September 21: two business days remain — comments close Wednesday, September 23, confirmed this morning against the Federal Register's own record. This is the rule that would let the Department cancel grants 'for convenience' and exercise more discretion over continuation awards. A federal court ruled on September 17 against a related mechanism the administration had been using to attach conditions to education money without a rule, which makes this rulemaking the administration's remaining route to the same discretion. The U.S. Department of Education proposed rewriting its general grant rules (called EDGAR) — the terms that govern every discretionary grant the Department makes, including the kinds Relay holds. The headline changes: the Department would write into regulation its power to end any grant early 'for convenience' (that is, without the grantee doing anything wrong), and to reduce or deny each year's continuation funding at the Secretary's discretion. Grantees would also have to certify that hiring and admissions under the grant are strictly merit-based and that employees are not required to make statements of belief. Public comments are due September 23; final rules are expected late this year.

    • Federal grant revenue becomes less predictable: a multi-year award could be ended or reduced at any annual renewal, with limited appeal rights. Grant-funded hiring and admissions language would need legal review against the new merit certification. And applications proposing lower overhead (indirect) rates could earn preference points — a real tradeoff between competitiveness and cost recovery.

    Questions to ask

    • We have two days. Do we comment, and do we cite the September 17 apportionment ruling?

    • Should Relay file a comment (directly or via AACTE) by September 23, and on which provisions — the continuation-award discretion, the merit certification, or both?

    • Do budget scenarios for current federal awards assume continuation funding that this rule would make discretionary?

    The counter-pattern to CT PA 26-149, DE HB12, and GA HB310: this is the first pipeline-money bill in a Relay state this cycle whose eligibility a graduate

    Why it matters to Relay

    The counter-pattern to CT PA 26-149, DE HB12, and GA HB310: this is the first pipeline-money bill in a Relay state this cycle whose eligibility a graduate provider could reach as written. It died on money, not design — a Joint Favorable from Education says the committee liked the mechanism. The January 2027 session (odd-year, budget-writing) is the natural refiling window.

    What it does

    Backlog read (deferred since 2026-08-13; full text read this run). The bill would have created the 'Student Teacher Investment and Professional Educator Network for Development' (STIPEND) program: from fall 2026, the Connecticut State Department of Education funds each teacher preparation program $1,000 per week of student teaching for every enrolled student teacher placed in a Connecticut public school, and the program disburses the stipend to the student teacher. Clawbacks both directions: programs repay pro rata for uncompleted placements, and recipients repay at least 50% if not employed as a certified teacher in a Connecticut public school for two of the three years after graduation. Eligibility runs through 'teacher preparation program, as defined in section 10-10a' — provider-neutral, no undergraduate-only screen. History verified from cga.ct.gov: Joint Favorable from Education (change of reference), then died in Appropriations when the 2026 session adjourned May 6. A committee bill (Joint Education Committee, primary sponsor) with ten co-sponsors, nine Democrats and one Republican (per the LegiScan API).

    Implications

    • Advocacy. If refiled in January 2027, the provider-neutral eligibility is worth defending as drafted — the CT/DE/GA pattern shows how easily these programs get scoped to undergraduate pathways.

    • Program. As drafted, Relay students placed in CT public schools would have drawn $1,000/week during student teaching, routed through Relay as the preparation program — an operational role (semester headcount reporting, pro-rata reimbursement) as well as a benefit.

    Leader brief

    Connecticut nearly funded $1,000/week for student teachers — and graduate programs like Relay's would have qualified

    Connecticut's legislature considered paying every student teacher in a public-school placement $1,000 per week, with the money flowing through their preparation program. The education committee approved it, but it died in the budget committee when the session ended in May. Unlike the teacher-pipeline programs Connecticut, Delaware, and Georgia did fund this year — all limited to undergraduate pathways — this one was written so any approved preparation program, including a graduate school like Relay, could participate.

    • A funded version would materially change the economics of student teaching in Connecticut for Relay candidates, and Relay would administer the payments. The bill's death was about budget, not opposition to the design.

    Questions to ask

    • Should Relay (directly or through partners) support refiling in the January 2027 budget session, and advocate to keep the provider-neutral eligibility language intact?

    • If a version passes, is Relay's Connecticut footprint positioned to take on the reporting and disbursement role the bill assigns to preparation programs?

    Fails the liveness gate and is surfaced as recorded legislative appetite under the same convention the board uses for the Texas early-literacy bills and the

    Why it matters to Relay

    Fails the liveness gate and is surfaced as recorded legislative appetite under the same convention the board uses for the Texas early-literacy bills and the Tennessee residency act. Two design choices matter more than the bill's death. First, eligibility required federal Pell Grant eligibility — Pell is an undergraduate award, so a graduate-level candidate would sit outside the eligible population; that interaction has not been verified against federal student-aid rules this run and should be before it is relied on. Second, the provider had to be a University System institution or an eligible private postsecondary institution 'located in this state.' Together those two clauses point the money at in-state undergraduate pathways. That is now the third instance of the same structure in a Relay state this month, after Connecticut Public Act 26-149 and Delaware House Bill 12, and the pattern is the finding — not this one bill.

    What it does

    House Bill 310, the 'Student Teacher Promotion Act,' would have written two grant programs into O.C.G.A. 20-2-252. The Georgia Student Finance Commission would provide grants to no more than 500 student teachers per school year beginning July 1, 2026, capped at $5,000 per student teacher and disbursed in monthly installments BY THE STUDENT'S OWN preparation provider; to qualify a student teacher had to be eligible for the federal Pell Grant program and actively engaged and in good standing in the student teaching component of the program. The State Board of Education would provide one-time $2,500 signing-bonus grants beginning January 1, 2027 to former student-teacher grant recipients who completed their program and finished 30 calendar days of employment under a contract with a Georgia public school; the Department of Education was to publish an application process and seek applications from schools and districts by October 1, 2026. The bill defined 'educator preparation provider' as an institution of the University System of Georgia or an eligible private postsecondary institution as defined in O.C.G.A. 20-3-519 LOCATED IN THIS STATE and approved by the Professional Standards Commission, and 'student teacher' as a college or university student enrolled in such a program. Both programs sunset after December 31, 2028 and both were contingent on a specific appropriation. The committee substitute passed the House 151-6 on 2026-02-24 and was favorably reported by Senate Education and Youth on 2026-03-25; on 2026-03-31 the Senate carried a motion to table the remaining legislation on the Rules calendar 39-10 and the bill went no further.

    Implications

    • Risk. Three Relay states in one month — Connecticut, Delaware, and now Georgia — have written new teacher-pipeline money in a form that reaches undergraduate, in-state pathways and not graduate providers. Georgia's version does it through Pell eligibility and a 'located in this state' provider definition rather than by naming four-year degrees.

    • Advocacy. A bill that passes a chamber 151-6 with primary sponsors from both parties and clears the receiving committee dies on floor calendar time, not on policy. It is the likeliest of Georgia's failed 2026 education bills to return in January 2027, and the eligibility language is the thing to influence before refiling, not after.

    Leader brief

    A Georgia bill to pay student teachers died on the clock — and its eligibility rules would have excluded us

    Georgia's House voted 151 to 6 for a bill creating $5,000 grants for up to 500 student teachers a year plus a $2,500 bonus once they started teaching. It cleared the Senate education committee and then died on the last days of the session when the Senate voted to clear its calendar. Two details matter for us. Students had to be eligible for the federal Pell Grant, which is an undergraduate award, and the money had to flow through a preparation program run by a Georgia public university or a private institution located in Georgia. Georgia's legislature works in two-year cycles that ended with this session, so the bill would have to start over in January 2027.

    • This is the third state this month — after Connecticut and Delaware — to put new teacher-pipeline money into a channel that reaches in-state undergraduate programs and not graduate providers like Relay. No single bill decides anything, but three in a month is a pattern in how states are choosing to spend teacher-recruitment dollars, and it argues for engaging on eligibility language while bills are being drafted rather than after they pass.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want a position on eligibility language in state student-teacher stipend bills, and who would carry it in Georgia before January 2027?

    • Is the Pell-eligibility screen actually disqualifying for our candidates? We should confirm that against federal student-aid rules rather than assume it.

    • Across Connecticut, Delaware and Georgia, roughly how much new pipeline funding has been routed somewhere we cannot reach?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Dead on liveness, surfaced as recorded appetite, and the substance is worth more than the outcome. The mechanism is a statutory ceiling on a licensing agency: subsection (c) would have forbidden the Professional Standards Commission from requiring anything beyond a bachelor's degree, four years of experience that may be entirely private-school, two courses or eighty hours of professional development, and two GACE assessments. That is a low-cost substitute for a Relay Georgia pathway. It is simultaneously a Relay opportunity, because the experience-based program still had to be COMMISSION-APPROVED, and eighty hours of professional development is precisely the shape of Relay's Teacher Professional Education line. The same double edge appears in Indiana's enacted Public Law 150 this run, which is the more important fact: Georgia filed the idea, Indiana passed it.

    What it does

    Senate Bill 484 would have added O.C.G.A. 20-2-206.1, requiring the Professional Standards Commission to issue a PROFESSIONAL certificate — not a provisional or emergency one — upon an offer of employment by a Georgia school system or public school, to a candidate who holds a bachelor's degree or higher from a regionally accredited institution; has at least four years of verifiable teaching experience in kindergarten through grade five in a public OR PRIVATE school (for elementary candidates) or four years in grades six through twelve in a public or private school or at least 72 semester hours of verifiable postsecondary teaching (for secondary candidates); completes an 'experience based teacher preparation program'; and passes the Georgia educator ethics assessment and the GACE content assessment for the field sought. An 'experience based teacher preparation program' was defined as a Commission-approved program of study consisting of EITHER six semester hours — one three-hour course covering pedagogy, the science of reading, evaluation, ethics, classroom management and professional practice, and one three-hour course covering child, adolescent and young adult development and psychology and special education — OR eighty hours of professional development covering the same content. Subsection (c) would have barred the Commission from imposing any requirement 'in addition to or in lieu of' those listed. Subsection (d) would have barred districts from treating such a teacher differently in any manner, including refusing admission to a job fair or other recruitment activity. Sponsored by five Republican senators; read and referred to Senate Education and Youth on 2026-02-11 with a committee hearing calendared for 2026-02-24, and no further recorded action.

    Implications

    • Risk. A route to a full Georgia professional certificate on six semester hours or eighty hours of professional development, with the licensing agency statutorily barred from adding requirements, would substitute directly for a graduate preparation pathway in Georgia.

    • Program. The experience-based program had to be approved by the Professional Standards Commission, and the eighty-hour professional development option maps onto Relay's existing Teacher Professional Education line. If this returns, being an approved provider is the response, not opposition.

    • Advocacy. Four years of qualifying experience could be entirely in private schools, and the bill barred districts from treating such teachers differently including at job fairs. Those are the provisions to engage on if the bill is refiled in January 2027.

    Why it matters to Relay

    The Department of Education is a named defendant and its PRWORA notice is among those vacated, which is what puts this on an educator-preparation board rather than a social-services one. Two threads matter to Relay. First, Head Start and adult education are early-childhood and adult-workforce employers whose staffing this verification regime would have disrupted directly; a program that must check the status of everyone it serves is a program with less capacity for everything else, including hosting and supervising candidates. Second, and more durable: the court did not bar the agencies from trying again. It held the notices were legislative rules that skipped notice and comment, and expressly left HHS, ED, DOL and HUD free to promulgate new PRWORA rules through proper rulemaking. That converts an adverse policy into a probable future comment window, which is the form in which this board can actually act on it. Nothing is required of Relay now.

    What it does

    Title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 bars some categories of noncitizens from receiving defined federal, state and local public benefits. Quoting the order read this run: shortly after PRWORA's enactment the relevant federal agencies issued guidance interpreting that prohibition as excluding various programs, including those constituting 'widely available services' (61 Fed. Reg. 45,985, Aug. 30, 1996), but 'beginning in July 2025, these agencies took an about-face by issuing new notices that purport to reinterpret PRWORA as applying to a swath of federal programs that had previously been excluded.' Twenty states and the District of Columbia sued. The court had already granted a preliminary injunction, holding that the PRWORA Notices of the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Education and the Department of Labor were final agency action reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, that they implemented legislative rules and were therefore subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking, and that they posed irreparable harm to the plaintiffs given the impracticality and cost of compliance. The parties then agreed to proceed directly to summary judgment. The disposition, quoted from the order's final page: 'The PRWORA Notices are declared unlawful under the APA and are ordered set aside and vacated. Defendants are enjoined from implementing or enforcing the PRWORA Notices or the interpretations contained therein against Plaintiffs by any other means.' One express limit, also quoted: 'this injunction does not prohibit HHS, ED, DOL, HUD, and their respective heads from promulgating new rules related to PRWORA after a period of notice-and-comment rulemaking as required under the APA.' Per the New York Attorney General's release of the same date — attributed, not drawn from the order — the vacated rules threatened Head Start, Title X family planning clinics, food banks, domestic violence shelters, adult education and community health centers, and would have required those programs to check the immigration status of everyone they serve, turning away not only undocumented immigrants but some people with legal status including student visa holders, temporary workers and exchange visitors.

    Implications

    • Risk. The order rests on procedure, not substance: the agencies were told they skipped notice-and-comment, and are expressly free to re-promulgate through proper rulemaking. Treat this as a threat deferred, not removed.

    • Advocacy. A re-promulgated PRWORA rule from the Department of Education would arrive with a comment window; that is the point at which a preparation institution with placements in Head Start and adult-education settings has standing to say what verification would cost.

    • Partnership. Head Start and adult-education providers in the twenty plaintiff states and DC are relieved of a verification burden that would have consumed administrative capacity — capacity that clinical placement and mentoring draw on.

    Leader brief

    A federal court has struck down the rule that would have made Head Start check every family's immigration status

    In July 2025 four federal agencies, including the Department of Education, reinterpreted a 1996 welfare law to cover a wide range of programs that had always been exempt from it. The practical effect would have been that programs like Head Start, adult education, food banks and community health centers had to verify the immigration status of everyone they served and turn away anyone who could not prove it — which, the states argued, would have caught citizens and lawful residents who simply lack government identification. Twenty states and the District of Columbia sued. On September 21 a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled for them, declared the agencies' notices unlawful, and threw them out. We located and read the full twenty-five-page order rather than relying on coverage. One caveat matters: the judge ruled the agencies broke the rules for how policy must be made, not that the policy itself is forbidden, and explicitly said they may try again if they go through the proper public comment process.

    • Nothing is required of us today. Head Start and adult education programs employ early-childhood and adult educators and host candidates, and they have just been relieved of an administrative burden that would have consumed a great deal of their capacity. The part to watch is the opening the judge left: if the Department of Education comes back through formal rulemaking, there will be a public comment period, and that is the moment we could say something useful about what verification would cost the programs our people work in.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we want to be positioned to comment if the Department of Education re-issues this through formal rulemaking, and who would own that?

    • Do we have visibility into how many of our placements and alumni sit in Head Start or adult-education settings, which is what would tell us how much this actually matters to us?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Texas is a deep Relay jurisdiction and Workforce Pell is now live there. It does not touch educator preparation directly — no approved program to date is a teaching credential — but it is the federal mechanism now channeling Pell money into short-term credentials, and whether any teacher-pipeline or paraprofessional pathway can qualify is the question worth watching.

    What it does

    The Education Department announced on September 22, 2026 that it approved Workforce Pell grant programs at Kilgore College and Weatherford College in Texas. Workforce Pell extends Pell Grant eligibility to short-term, career-focused programs; the Working Families Tax Cuts Act set the eligibility criteria, the Department ran negotiated rulemaking, and the final rule was published May 18, 2026 and took effect July 1, 2026. The approval sequence so far: Iowa Central Community College (emergency medical technicians) on August 4, Ivy Tech Community College in Indiana (clinical medical assistants) on August 19, three programs at Nebraska's Metropolitan Community College on September 16, and now the two Texas colleges. Governors, working with state workforce boards, identify the programs that meet the high-skill, high-wage and in-demand criteria.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Federal short-term Pell grants reach Texas community colleges, though none of the approved programs prepares teachers

    Workforce Pell lets students use federal Pell Grants for short, career-focused programs for the first time. The rule took effect July 1. On September 22 the Education Department approved programs at two Texas community colleges, Kilgore and Weatherford — power lineman, phlebotomy, pharmacy technician, HVAC and machining. Texas is the fourth state approved, after Iowa, Indiana and Nebraska. Governors, working with state workforce boards, pick which programs are put forward as high-skill, high-wage and in-demand.

    • Nothing here touches teacher preparation today; every approved program so far is a trade or allied health credential. What matters is that the machinery now exists and is reaching a state where Relay works. If a state ever puts a paraprofessional or teacher-pipeline credential forward, this is the route it would travel.

    Questions to ask

    • Is it worth asking whether Texas or any other Relay state would consider a teacher-pipeline credential for a Workforce Pell nomination?

    • Do any of Relay's district partners run paraprofessional programs that could plausibly meet the high-skill, high-wage, in-demand test?

    Why it matters to Relay

    The mandated curricula are what Relay's NYC candidates and graduates teach from day one; the expansion to elementary math and, by 2027, all middle-school literacy and math keeps narrowing the set of programs Relay's methods coursework should assume. The liaison and platform changes are operating context for residents in NYC schools.

    What it does

    Per Chalkbeat, beyond the AI policy: (1) the Mamdani administration CONTINUES and EXTENDS the Adams-era curriculum mandates — all elementary schools teach one of three approved literacy curricula, every school uses one of nine approved reading-intervention programs, nearly all high schools use a set Algebra 1 curriculum, elementary schools in four community districts must adopt city-approved math curricula this fall, and all middle schools are to be mandated to set literacy and math curricula by fall 2027; (2) New York State's financial-literacy mandate begins this year for grades 5-12 (K-4 the following year); (3) every school must designate a school-avoidance liaison by 2026-10-31 (two-hour training, no additional pay); (4) middle schools must seat at least two students on their School Leadership Teams; (5) a virtual student OMNY card pilot at seven schools; (6) the student-data platform ATS is being replaced by OASIS, with a rocky summer rollout in pupil transportation. The Regents-exam phase-out is carried on its own TRACK row. Coverage added 2026-09-07: per New York Focus (republished by Chalkbeat), NYC teachers report that the mandated curricula and intervention blocks leave no time for full-length novels; of the three approved reading curricula, EL Education and Wit and Wisdom require full books while HMH Into Reading and Into Literature do not; NYCPS says students have access to whole books in classrooms and the citywide digital library (digital checkouts up 14% last year).

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the statewide statutory version of the policy New York City imposed administratively on September 2 (see the NYCPS moratorium row), and the two moving together is the signal worth holding: a district policy and a bill with ten Senate sponsors including one Republican, both pointed at the same restriction, in the state where Relay's largest program sits. The bill goes further than the city in two respects that touch preparation directly — a statutory 'right to analog learning' and a state registry that educational technology providers would have to register with. For Relay the practical content is that New York is moving toward a floor on non-digital instruction, which is a pedagogical skill set, not just a compliance rule. Momentum is genuinely low; nothing has moved in either house.

    What it does

    The Fostering Optimal Classroom Use of Screens Act would add a new Article 2-B (sections 30 through 39) to the Education Law and amend section 2-d. Read from the introduced text this run, the article's structure is: definitions (section 30), screen time limitations (31), right to analog learning (32), standards for school-issued devices (33), prohibited practices (34), an educational technology registry (35), updated learning standards (36), construction (37), rulemaking (38), and enforcement (39). Per the sponsors' summary, it would limit use of internet-enabled and electronic devices and prioritize non-digital teaching methods; prohibit use by younger students and limit and restrict certain uses by older students; require written opt-in policies for school-issued devices; prohibit social media applications, gaming, and artificial intelligence on school-issued devices; and require registration by educational technology providers. The bill imports its artificial-intelligence definitions from General Business Law section 1700 — 'artificial intelligence' from subdivision one and 'AI companion' from subdivision four — rather than defining them fresh. Both houses' versions are at introduction: the Assembly version sits in Education, the Senate version in Rules.

    Implications

    • Program. A statutory right to analog learning and a prioritization of non-digital teaching methods would make low-tech instructional planning an assessed competency for New York candidates, not a stylistic preference.

    • Compliance. An educational technology provider registry would create a state gate for any tool Relay recommends, builds, or embeds in New York coursework and clinical practice.

    • Risk. The bill would bar artificial intelligence outright on school-issued devices statewide, going beyond New York City's grade-banded moratorium; Relay's New York program should not build toward classroom AI use while both are live.

    Leader brief

    A statewide New York bill would do what New York City just did — and go further

    Two identical bills, one in each house of the New York legislature, would put limits on classroom screen use into state law: caps on how much screen time students get, a stated right to learn without a screen, a requirement that schools get written parental opt-in for school-issued devices, and an outright ban on social media, games, and artificial intelligence on those devices. Companies that sell educational technology in New York would have to register with the state. The Senate version has ten sponsors including one Republican. Neither version has had any committee action — the Assembly version was referred to its education committee on September 2, the Senate version to its rules committee on August 21.

    • On its own this bill is early and may go nowhere. What makes it worth watching is the pairing: New York City put a version of this into effect administratively at the start of September, and now there is a statewide bill with bipartisan Senate sponsorship pointed the same way. If both hold, teaching well without a screen becomes a skill New York expects of new teachers, and that is something we would need to teach deliberately rather than assume.

    Questions to ask

    • If New York formalizes a preference for non-digital instruction, is our current preparation strong enough on planning and delivering lessons without technology?

    • Should we be watching this bill only, or treating the city policy and the state bill together as a single direction we should plan around?

    Why it matters to Relay

    District-finance mechanics rather than an educator-preparation surface, but New York is Relay's deepest jurisdiction and charter operators are significant employers of Relay graduates. If enacted it would blunt the fiscal argument districts make against charter growth. Sponsored by Assembly Majority Leader Peoples-Stokes, which raises the ceiling on it — but two sessions in committee with no movement is the honest read.

    What it does

    Amends Education Law section 3602 to add a new subdivision 42 creating a state apportionment for school districts required to pay charter school tuition under section 2856. Eligible districts would report total charter tuition paid in the base year, and the aid would equal the positive difference between base-year tuition and 2025-26 tuition — that is, it reimburses growth in a district's charter tuition bill above the 2025-26 level. Takes effect immediately on enactment. Still in the Assembly Education Committee: referred 01/14/2025 and re-referred 01/07/2026 with no further action. Bill text and action history verified from the New York State Assembly page on 2026-08-08.

    Implications

    • Partnership. Charter-sector fiscal stability in New York supports hiring demand from charter partners that employ Relay graduates.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay's MAT students are borrowing under exactly these caps as of this admissions cycle. Whether private lenders price graduate-education loans at all — and how they treat nonprofit graduate schools of education, whose earnings profiles are modest — is now a live enrollment-economics question. Pairs with the borrowing-caps principal-pipeline reporting (EdWeek) and the ICR-to-RAP repayment shift already on the board.

    What it does

    Per the abstract: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) eliminated federal GradPLUS loans for new borrowers effective 2026-07-01, replacing two decades of uncapped federal graduate lending with annual limits of $20,500 ($50,000 for eleven professional fields) plus new aggregate caps. Turner estimates the displaced financing at roughly $8 billion per year across ~370,000 affected borrowers and examines whether and how private lenders will substitute — including which fields and institution types private capital is likely to serve or skip. Working paper, not peer-reviewed. Added 2026-09-14: NAICU reports (09-11, page read this run) that the Department has told institutions to calculate a continuing student's 'expected time to credential' for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act interim exception — the rule that lets students enrolled and borrowing as of June 30, 2026 keep pre-OB3 loan limits for the lesser of three years or the time left in their program — in credit hours rather than the elapsed-time method in the 34 CFR 685.102 definition; NAICU notes the Department has published no guidance confirming the change beyond what Inside Higher Ed reported on August 17 (per NAICU).

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Coverage

    • per Federal Register 2026-19536: Federal Direct PLUS Loan Request for Supplemental Information (ICR revision, comments to Oct 26) (2026-09-24)

    Why it matters to Relay

    Personnel, but consequential personnel. Georgia's literacy statute now has a named owner whose formal liaison list includes the Professional Standards Commission — the body that on September 10 approved the Dyslexia Endorsement amendment and the Math Matters Act rewrites of the elementary and math preparation rules. Whoever coordinates literacy across GaDOE, the university and technical college systems, the RESAs and GaPSC shapes what educator-preparation literacy requirements look like in practice in a state where Relay operates.

    What it does

    The Governor's Office of Education and Workforce Strategy announced on September 22, 2026 that Stacey Lutz will serve as Georgia's Interim State Literacy Director and Lindsay McVicar as Workforce Director (release read raw this run). Lutz is responsible for maintaining, implementing, aligning and evaluating the statewide literacy plan, and for recommending continuous improvements to literacy and reading education programs across state, regional and local agencies. The release names her as primary liaison on literacy and reading education with the Department of Education, the Department of Early Care and Learning, the Department of Public Health, the University System of Georgia, the Technical College System of Georgia, Georgia's Regional Educational Service Agencies, the PROFESSIONAL STANDARDS COMMISSION and GOEWS, to guide implementation of the Georgia Early Literacy and Dyslexia Act and related policy. Lutz retired in 2024 as Director of Strategic Programs and Evaluations at the Governor's Office of Student Achievement and returned in July 2025 as State Literacy Coach Coordinator; at GOSA she built Growing Readers, Georgia's first statewide K-5 literacy coaching system, scaled across all 16 RESAs, and in 2018 founded the Governor's School Leadership Academy. She is a former school administrator and National Board-Certified Teacher.

    Implications

    • Partnership. Georgia's literacy coordination now runs through a named office with a formal liaison line to the Professional Standards Commission; that is the entry point for any Relay conversation about Georgia literacy preparation requirements.

    • Program. Lutz built Growing Readers, the statewide K-5 literacy coaching system running through all 16 RESAs — the same RESAs now approved to deliver GaPSC's new AI-for-educators endorsement. The state's delivery infrastructure for both literacy and AI credentialing is the RESA network, not the universities.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay is a Title IX recipient (Title IV participant, federal school code 042086), so a statutory definition of sex would bind its nondiscrimination policies, grievance procedures and any sex-separated facilities or programs, and it would reach every district and charter partner. House passage is plausible given the sponsor count; Senate prospects are the open question. Same treatment as H.R. 4795 at this stage: SCAN with promotion on passage.

    What it does

    Reported 2026-09-08 with an amendment in the nature of a substitute (H. Rept. 119-798, Union Calendar No. 698); introduced 2026-05-13 by Rep. Arrington (R-TX) with 22 original and 22 additional cosponsors listed in the reported print (party affiliations not stated in the text and not asserted here). Section 2 amends §901(c) of the Education Amendments of 1972 (20 U.S.C. 1681(c)) to add three definitions: 'sex' refers to an individual's biologically determined sex as either male or female; 'female' and 'male' are defined by the reproductive system that at some point produces the large or small gamete. Section 3 makes the Act effective on enactment and applies it to education programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance on or after that date. The definitions would govern Title IX's nondiscrimination requirement for every recipient of federal education funds, K-12 and postsecondary.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Decides who administers the federal programs Relay lives on. The Office of Postsecondary Education runs Title II teacher-quality partnership grants, TEACH grants, and educator-prep reporting; OESE runs Title I and Title II-A. If those functions move to Labor or elsewhere, Relay's grant competitions, reporting obligations, and program officers all change hands. Direct counterweight to the 'Returning Education to the States' track already on this board.

    What it does

    Bipartisan Senate bill barring the Secretary of Education from entering or implementing interagency agreements that move the functions of four ED offices — Elementary & Secondary Education, Postsecondary Education, Special Education & Rehabilitative Services, and Indian Education — to other federal agencies. Covers grant administration, technical assistance, enforcement, data collection, and grantee monitoring. Exempts arrangements in effect on Feb 1, 2025 and their like-for-like renewals. Section 2 adds quarterly public cost reporting on every interagency agreement signed since Feb 1, 2025, and withholds the Secretary's travel funds until those reports are delivered. Update 2026-09-03: a House companion, H.R. 10232, was introduced 2026-09-02 by Rep. Mannion (D-NY) with Rep. Fitzpatrick (R-PA) and Rep. Scott (D-VA) and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce (verified from the GPO introduced text). Its section 1 carries the same prohibition covering the same four offices (Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, Postsecondary Education, Indian Education, Elementary and Secondary Education), the same February 1, 2025 grandfather clause for existing arrangements and like-for-like renewals, and section 2 the same quarterly cost analysis to the HELP, Education and Workforce, and both Appropriations committees.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Washington: bipartisan bills in both chambers to keep the Education Department's functions in the Department (S. 5046 / H.R. 10232)

    A bipartisan group of senators is advancing a bill to stop the U.S. Department of Education from transferring its core offices to other federal agencies, including the offices that run the federal grant programs Relay depends on. A Senate committee approved it in early August and it awaits a floor vote. On September 2 a matching House bill was introduced by a Democrat from New York, a Republican from Pennsylvania, and a Democrat from Virginia, so the effort now has a foothold in both chambers. It is Congress's direct counterweight to the ongoing campaign to move the Department's functions elsewhere.

    • If the Department's functions move, the grant competitions, program officers, and reporting rules Relay works with change hands mid-stream; this bill would prevent that. Its progress is the best single indicator of whether Congress will let the restructuring proceed.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we have a current picture of which Relay funding streams would be disrupted if Department of Education functions moved, or does contingency planning wait on this bill's fate?

    • Is watching enough here, or should Relay add its voice through the associations that represent educator-preparation programs?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Georgia is an authorized Relay jurisdiction and this is the second early-literacy statute there in two years, passed by leadership without meaningful opposition. Where these acts usually land is on instructional materials, screening and intervention requirements, and educator training in the science of reading — the last of which is teacher-preparation surface. Read the enacted text before treating this as settled: the vote record is verified, the content is not.

    What it does

    Enacted as Act 391 with an effective date of 2026-05-05, on near-unanimous votes — 170-2 in the House on 2026-02-24 and 49-0 in the Senate on 2026-03-31, with the House agreeing to the Senate substitute 168-0 the same day. Carried by House Education Chair Chris Erwin (R) with Speaker Jon Burns (R) among seven primary sponsors, which places it in the leadership package rather than the member-bill lane. Georgia's 2026 statute follows SB93 of 2025, which barred the three-cueing system from high-quality instructional materials and structured-literacy programs effective 2025-07-01. The operative text of HB1193 was NOT read this run — legis.ga.gov is JavaScript-gated and returned no text to a plain client, so the substantive provisions are UNVERIFIED and this row reports only the passage record and vote tallies, which are API-sourced.

    Implications

    • Compliance. If the act carries educator-preparation or reading-endorsement provisions, Relay's Georgia program approval is implicated. Verify against the enacted text before assuming either way.

    • Program. Georgia now has two stacked early-literacy statutes (SB93 2025, HB1193 2026). Relay's Georgia reading coursework should be checked against both, not just the newer one.

    A New York opt-in would route new private-school tuition and tutoring dollars into the K-12 market Relay's NYC partners recruit and place in; it is also the second live opt-in fight in a Democratic-governor Relay state after Illinois, and the Treasury regulations due this month are the trigger for both decisions. Ecosystem-level; no Relay regulatory surface.

    What it does

    Per Chalkbeat New York (2026-09-16, read raw this run): a coalition of union officials (including United Federation of Teachers president Michael Mulgrew) and civil-rights leaders urged Governor Hochul on 09-16 to reverse her plans to opt New York into the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit created by the 2025 reconciliation law (Internal Revenue Code section 25F), which from January 2027 lets taxpayers claim a dollar-for-dollar credit for donations of up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations that fund private-school tuition, tutoring and other education costs. Hochul's office has said it is waiting for Treasury Department regulations, expected later in September, to check for 'poison pills' before deciding. Primary check: the IRS Federal Scholarship Tax Credit page (read raw this run; 'Participating states for 2027 (as of September 14, 2026)', page updated 09-16) lists 30 states that have made an advance election for 2027 — Colorado, Georgia, Indiana, Tennessee and Texas among Relay's states — and New York is not on it; neither are Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island or DC.

    Relay is a nonprofit whose graduates go to work in public schools, which is the population PSLF exists for, and Relay is itself a PSLF-qualifying employer that

    At a glance

    StageComment period open

    Latest actionPublished in the Federal Register 2026-09-22 (Vol. 91, No. 182, p. 60119); filed 2026-09-21. Full notice text fetched raw and read this run. Comments to OMB via reginfo.gov on or before 2026-10-22. Federal Student Aid contact: Linnea Hengst, 202-453-6737. · 2026-09-22
    WindowOctober 22, 2026 · 19 business days
    SourceFederal Register (API + full notice text read this run), Docket ED-2026-SCC-2443, OMB Control Number 1845-0110 · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay is a nonprofit whose graduates go to work in public schools, which is the population PSLF exists for, and Relay is itself a PSLF-qualifying employer that certifies employment for its own staff. The vacated attestation would have put every one of those employers — districts, charter networks, Relay itself — in the position of swearing under penalty of perjury about the legality of their own activities before a borrower's payments could count. Its removal restores the prior form and the prior certification burden. The comment window is real and open for 21 business days; the substantive question a commenter can still raise is whether the Department's removal is complete, since the notice says no other changes were made and the underlying executive order has not been rescinded.

    What it does

    Federal Student Aid is asking OMB to approve a revision to the Public Service Loan Forgiveness and Temporary Expanded PSLF Certification and Application form (OMB 1845-0110), and the revision is a removal. Quoting the notice read this run: 'The Department is now removing the attestation from the PSLF form in order to comply with the court order. No other changes have been made at this time.' The attestation in question required a borrower's employer to swear, under penalty of perjury, that it had not engaged in any activity with a substantial illegal purpose on or after July 1, 2026. It was added to implement Executive Order 14325 ('Restoring Public Service Loan Forgiveness,' signed March 7, 2025), which made individuals employed by organizations whose activities have a substantial illegal purpose ineligible for PSLF; the requirement was written into 34 CFR 685.219(i) by final regulations published October 31, 2025 (90 FR 48966). On Tuesday, June 30, 2026 — one day before the rule was to take effect — a federal judge vacated it. The Department has requested emergency processing for the revision. The collection covers an estimated 913,713 annual responses and 456,857 annual burden hours. Borrowers use the form to have qualifying public-service employment certified and progress toward forgiveness recorded; they are encouraged to file annually and required to file at 120 qualifying monthly payments. This notice is the 30-day OMB stage of the collection this board already tracks at the 60-day ED stage (fedreg:2026-14053, comments closed 2026-09-11). Caveat on the notice's own text: it dates the NPRM to 'August 18, 2026' while citing 90 FR 40154 and a comment close of 'September 17, 2025' — the year on the NPRM date appears to be an error in the notice, and this board does not restate it as fact.

    Implications

    • Compliance. Relay's HR and financial-aid staff certify PSLF employment for Relay employees and field questions from alumni; the form they are certifying on is changing back, and the change is being processed on an emergency basis, so the operative version could shift within weeks.

    • Advocacy. A 30-day comment window is open through 2026-10-22 on a form used by an estimated 913,713 filers a year — the cheapest available route for a teacher-preparation institution to put its graduates' experience of PSLF certification on the record.

    • Risk. Executive Order 14325 remains in force even though the implementing rule was vacated on 2026-06-30; the Department could return with a differently-drafted attestation, so the removal should be read as the current state, not a settled one.

    • Funding. PSLF eligibility is part of the economic case Relay's programs make to prospective teachers; a certification requirement that would have reached employers was a live threat to that case and is, for now, withdrawn.

    Leader brief

    The loan-forgiveness form our graduates depend on is losing the employer loyalty-oath question, and the public can comment until October 22

    Public Service Loan Forgiveness cancels the remaining federal student debt of people who work ten years in public service, including public-school teaching. A 2025 executive order directed the Education Department to disqualify people employed by organizations engaged in activities with a 'substantial illegal purpose,' and the Department put that into effect by adding a line to the forgiveness form requiring the employer to swear, under penalty of perjury, that it had done no such thing. On June 30 of this year — one day before that rule would have started — a federal judge struck it down. The Department has now formally asked the White House budget office to approve taking the line back off the form, and says it has made no other change. The public may comment through October 22. About 914,000 people file this form each year.

    • This is a direct financial matter for the teachers we prepare and for Relay as an employer that certifies its own staff's service. Had the rule stood, every district, charter network, and nonprofit employing our graduates would have had to make a sworn legal statement about itself before those graduates' payments counted. That burden is being lifted. It is worth noting the executive order behind it has not been withdrawn, so a redrafted version could return.

    Questions to ask

    • Is it worth filing a short comment before October 22 describing what the certification process actually costs our alumni and our staff, given how rarely a preparation institution's voice appears in these records?

    • Do we need to notify alumni that the form is changing, and if so, when — the Department has asked for emergency processing, so the timing is not fully predictable?

    • How much weight does loan forgiveness carry in our recruiting case, and what is our position if the Department returns with a redrafted eligibility restriction?

    NY A11702 / S04449-A — would delete New York City's exclusion from transitional aid for charter school payments in Education Law 3602(41), effective April 1, 2027

    New York City is where Relay's largest program places, and the city's charter sector is a major employer of its graduates. Transitional aid for charter payments

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionNew York
    ClassBill
    StageIn committee
    RecommendationScan · impact 46
    Second opinionModel scorer: Scan · impact 46; reviewer: Track · impact 55
    Latest actionIntroduced by the Committee on Rules at the request of M. of A. Marcela Mitaynes, read once and referred to the Committee on Education 2026-09-02. Same-as S04449-A. No committee action. · 2026-09-02
    SourceNew York State Assembly bill page (summary, actions, and full introduced text) read raw this run; sponsor detail from the LegiScan API cache · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    New York City is where Relay's largest program places, and the city's charter sector is a major employer of its graduates. Transitional aid for charter payments exists to cushion districts against the fiscal effect of students moving to charters; New York City has been carved out of it since the provision was written. Ending the carve-out would relieve fiscal pressure that has, in the city, consistently been argued as a reason to restrain charter growth. The connection to Relay is indirect and runs through hiring demand, not through any rule Relay must follow. Momentum is minimal — one referral, no action, and the effective date is more than six months out even on a successful path.

    What it does

    The bill amends the opening paragraph of subdivision 41 of section 3602 of the Education Law — the transitional aid apportionment for charter school payments, as most recently amended by section 10-d of part A of chapter 56 of the laws of 2025 — by striking the bracketed exclusion 'other than a city school district in a city having a population of one million or more.' Read from the introduced text this run, the effect of that deletion is that New York City, the only district meeting the population threshold, would become eligible for the same apportionment other districts already receive: an amount equal to the greater of the sum of paragraphs (a), (b) and (c), or paragraph (e), of that subdivision, for the 2007-08 school year and thereafter. The bill carries no appropriation and no dollar figure of its own; the amount would follow from the existing formula. Section 2 sets the effective date at April 1, 2027, with a retroactivity clause deeming it in force from that date if enacted later. The board separately tracks NY A01996 (legiscan:1917961), a different bill on state aid to offset charter school tuition payments.

    Implications

    • Funding. Removing New York City's exclusion would route formula aid to the district that hosts the largest concentration of Relay's graduates, easing a fiscal argument regularly used against charter expansion there.

    • Partnership. Reduced fiscal friction between New York City and its charter sector would be a favorable backdrop for the charter partners that hire Relay's candidates, though the effect is on hiring demand rather than on any preparation requirement.

    Leader brief

    A New York bill would end the rule that keeps New York City out of state aid for charter enrollment

    When students move from a district school to a charter school, the district still sends money with them. New York State gives districts a transitional payment to cushion that, but the law has always excluded any district in a city of more than a million people — which means New York City alone. This bill deletes that exclusion, so New York City would receive the payment on the same terms as everywhere else. It sets an effective date of April 1, 2027. The bill was referred to the Assembly's education committee on September 2 and has not moved since.

    • This does not change anything we are required to do. It matters because the money New York City loses to charter enrollment is one of the standing arguments against charter growth in the city, and the city's charter schools employ a large share of our graduates. If that pressure eases, the hiring environment our candidates enter gets somewhat better. It is an early-stage bill with no action behind it yet.

    Questions to ask

    • Is New York City charter hiring demand something we should be forecasting formally, given how much of our placement depends on it?

    SourceOSSE (DC) release + booklet PDF · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    DC is a Relay jurisdiction and this is the staff-side rulebook its LEAs will adopt or adapt, including a 'yellow' allowance for AI-assisted grading and 'green' lesson planning that New York City is reportedly closing or narrowing the same week. Two things for Relay: the training-before-use expectation is a professional-development market OSSE says it will supply itself, and the red/yellow/green line is a ready-made rubric for how Relay teaches DC candidates to use AI.

    What it does

    Verified from the OSSE booklet PDF and the September 1 release: OSSE issued its first model policy on staff use of artificial intelligence, offered as customizable guidance (not law) for DC local education agencies. Its stoplight framework PROHIBITS staff AI use for physical surveillance of students and staff, educational-trajectory decisions, student discipline decisions, teacher and staff performance evaluation, and IEP/Section 504 eligibility evaluations (red); PERMITS WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT digital-activity monitoring on LEA devices, drafting IEP language, reviewing and grading student work, and supplemental coaching of teachers (yellow); and PERMITS WITH AWARENESS AND HUMAN REVIEW lesson-plan drafting, tutoring and individualized learning plans, customized student materials, data analysis, school communications, and logistics (green). It recommends approved enterprise tools only; FERPA, COPPA, CIPA, IDEA, HIPAA and DC's Protecting Students Digital Privacy Act of 2016 compliance for any personally identifiable information; training before use, renewed annually; and demonstrated AI literacy. It does not cover student use or tool procurement. Origin: a February 2026 OSSE survey of 39 LEAs found fewer than half had staff AI guidance (45%, per the release). OSSE says additional AI professional development for educators is coming. Companion documents on the OSSE technology page: an AI Policy Template (docx) and the survey results brief.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

The Secretary must study which states receive funds and how they use them, and report to the House Education and Workforce and Senate HELP committees within one year of enactment. No authorization amount is stated; 'artificial intelligence' takes the 15 U.S.C. 9401 definition and school terms follow ESEA section 8101.
