    IL HR1026 — House Minority Leader files a resolution directing the Auditor General to audit Grow Your Own Illinois, citing a cost of over $70,000 per new teacher produced

    Grow Your Own Illinois is the closest thing the state has to a public alternative to what Relay does — recruit non-traditional candidates, support them

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionIllinois
    ClassBill
    StageIntroduced
    RecommendationScan · impact 44
    Second opinionModel scorer: Scan · impact 44; reviewer: Track · impact 65
    Latest actionFiled with the Clerk 2026-09-09 by Rep. Tony M. McCombie. One action only; not yet assigned to a committee. Bill status page and full introduced text fetched raw from ilga.gov and read this run. · 2026-09-09
    SourceIllinois General Assembly bill status and full text, read raw this run · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Grow Your Own Illinois is the closest thing the state has to a public alternative to what Relay does — recruit non-traditional candidates, support them financially, and get them credentialed and placed. A legislative audit that fixes an official cost-per-teacher figure for that program creates a public benchmark every teacher-preparation provider in Illinois will subsequently be measured against, Relay included. The resolution is a single-sponsor filing by the House Minority Leader with no committee assignment, so its odds are low and the board should not treat an audit as imminent. But the number it puts in the record — over $70,000 per teacher produced, on 42 to 85 graduates a year against a $6 million appropriation — is now a citable legislative finding whether or not the resolution moves, and the cost-effectiveness frame it introduces is the frame Relay's Illinois program should expect to be argued about in.

    What it does

    House Resolution 1026 directs the Illinois Auditor General to conduct a management, performance, and fiscal audit of Grow Your Own Illinois, the state's flagship teacher-pipeline program. The resolution's own findings, quoted from the introduced text, frame the case: the program began as a 2004 grassroots campaign, was codified by the 2005 Grow Your Own Teacher Education Act, was funded at $1.5 million in FY06 and now carries a $6 million appropriation, and moved from the State Board of Education to the Illinois Board of Higher Education under SB 2487 of the 96th General Assembly effective July 1, 2010. The operative charge: Grow Your Own 'reports graduating between 42 and 85 teachers per year for the past several years giving an annual cost per new teacher created of over $70,000, the highest of any teacher-focused student aid program in the State.' The resolution also asserts that the Illinois Student Assistance Commission 'is probably the entity best equipped to handle the operations' of the program — a relocation the resolution does not itself enact. The audit is directed to determine, at minimum, the program's operating cost and a breakdown of expenditures since 2018 (staff salaries, benefits and travel; buildings, rent and structural costs; student financial aid by type, including cash assistance, scholarships and housing stipends; and wrap-around services by type), and student outcomes (how many students were accepted, how many successfully graduated from their teaching program while in the program, and how many did not). The Illinois Board of Higher Education, the State Board of Education, Grow Your Own Illinois, and subordinate entities are directed to cooperate fully and promptly, and the Auditor General is directed to commence as soon as possible and report under Section 3-14 of the Illinois State Auditing Act.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. An official cost-per-completer benchmark for Illinois teacher-pipeline spending would be the comparison point for Relay's Illinois program; knowing Relay's own figure before that benchmark is set is cheaper than contesting it afterward.

    • Risk. The resolution introduces a per-teacher cost-effectiveness frame for evaluating teacher-preparation subsidy in Illinois; that frame can travel to other programs and appropriations regardless of whether this audit is ever conducted.

    • Partnership. The resolution proposes moving Grow Your Own's operations to the Illinois Student Assistance Commission; a change of administering agency would change who Relay's Illinois partners deal with on pipeline funding.

    Leader brief

    Illinois Republicans want the state auditor to open the books on the state's own teacher-pipeline program

    The leader of the Republicans in the Illinois House filed a resolution on September 9 asking the state's Auditor General to audit Grow Your Own Illinois, a state program that recruits and financially supports people from local communities to become teachers. Her case is cost: the resolution says the program spends about $6 million a year and produces between 42 and 85 new teachers, which works out to more than $70,000 per teacher — the most expensive teacher-focused student aid program in the state. The audit would look at where the money goes and how many participants actually finish their teaching program. The resolution also suggests the program should be run by a different state agency. This is a single filing by a member of the minority party with no committee assigned yet, so it is unlikely to advance on its own.

    • Grow Your Own is the state-run version of work we do. If this audit happens, Illinois will publish an official cost-per-teacher figure for that program, and that number becomes the yardstick anyone can apply to us. Even if the resolution goes nowhere, the argument it makes — judge teacher-preparation spending by cost per teacher actually produced — is now on the legislative record in a state where we operate.

    Questions to ask

    • Do we know our own fully-loaded cost per Illinois completer well enough to speak to it if the comparison is drawn publicly?

    • Is a cost-per-teacher comparison one we want to compete on in Illinois, or is there a better measure we should be putting forward before someone else sets the terms?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level. Notable mainly as the point where New York's AI-in-schools debate reaches instructional delivery rather than employment screening or disclosure, which is where the state's enacted AI provisions have sat so far.

    What it does

    Two New York bills introduced in late July 2026 address humanoid robots in schools. A11662 (referred to Education 2026-07-31, one sponsor) would prohibit humanoid robots and AI systems from being used in schools with limited exceptions and student privacy protections. S10671 (referred to Rules 2026-07-29, six sponsors) would instead require each school district, charter school and BOCES to adopt a written policy governing humanoid robot use, and would bar AI-enabled humanoid robots in an instructional capacity. Both are introductions with no committee action.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level, but it hardens the evidence bar for the AI-tutoring and edtech tools Relay's partner districts buy — and the same evidence-first framing now shows up in the state AI-PD markets Relay could serve (TN Ch. 1056, GA's proposed AI endorsement).

    What it does

    ED's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education issued a Dear Colleague Letter (verified from the letter itself) distinguishing recreational from instructional technology and telling states and districts to judge edtech by demonstrated learning outcomes: incorporate evidence of effectiveness into procurement, prefer products with RCTs and positive outcomes, review implementation, and drop tools that do not improve learning. Providers are urged to publish rigorous independent evaluations. It names five questions every edtech product should answer and cites outcomes-based contracting work in Louisiana, Arkansas, Indiana, Michigan, and Texas. Non-binding guidance; builds on the July 2025 McMahon AI Dear Colleague Letter's five principles.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay reports to IPEDS as a Title IV graduate institution, so ACTS reaches its admissions data (applicants, admits, enrollees by race-sex pair, by field) and the 200-hour burden estimate is the Department's own figure for what compliance costs. The remand means the collection is under active litigation; the next event is the court's response, not a comment window.

    What it does

    Notice published 2026-09-14 (91 FR 58104, docket ED-2025-SCC-0382; read from the Federal Register text this run). NCES revises the supplementary information of its November 13, 2025 notice on the Admissions and Consumer Transparency Supplement (ACTS) to IPEDS 'in accordance with the remand in Massachusetts v. U.S. Dep't of Educ., No. 1:26-cv-11229 (D. Mass. 2026)'. The document re-argues the implementation timeline (collection launched with the 2025-26 IPEDS Winter Collection, a December 18, 2025 to March 18, 2026 window), the consumer-transparency purpose under the August 2025 Presidential Memorandum, why the collection is not duplicative (disaggregation by race-sex pair and by admissions-test-score quintile, not race and sex separately), and its burden estimate (a settled estimate of 200 hours per institution, down from a 480-hour worst case). For graduate students it states that the Department collects 'a similar set of ACTS data regarding graduate student admissions', further disaggregated by broad field of study because graduate admissions are administered at the college or department level; the contextual variables collected for undergraduates are not collected for graduate applicants. No new comment period; the notice changes the record, not the instrument.

    Why it matters to Relay

    A Pennsylvania Act 48 lane for AI-in-teaching professional development that schools could buy from approved outside providers, colleges and nonprofits named explicitly. Relevant to Relay only if it offers or plans AI PD in Pennsylvania as an Act 48-approved provider; momentum is low (single-sponsor minority bill, introduced this week, grants only if funded).

    What it does

    Adds Section 1205.9 to the Public School Code. A school entity (district, charter, cyber charter, regional charter, intermediate unit, or career and technical school) MAY train its professional employees on AI in education; training must cover at least instructional uses and limits of AI, verifying AI-generated content, academic integrity and assessment, student privacy and cybersecurity, and bias, accessibility and ethics, plus the entity's own AI policy. Training approved by the Pennsylvania Department of Education counts toward Act 48 continuing professional education (sections 1205.2 and 1205.5), and the school entity must make reasonable efforts to schedule it in paid hours or in-service time. To the extent funding is made available, the Department must run a grant program for the training costs, with an application process and award guidelines; grantees may contract with institutions of higher education, intermediate units, nonprofits or other PD providers approved under 1205.2(c), and the Department must publish awards, uses and teachers trained each year. Training is permissive, not mandated, and no appropriation is made. Effective 60 days after enactment.

    Implications

    • Program. If enacted and funded, Pennsylvania schools could pay approved Act 48 providers for AI-in-education training; Relay would need Act 48 provider approval for the content to count.

    • Partnership. Grant-funded contracts are open to institutions of higher education and nonprofits, a route for Relay's Pennsylvania partner districts.

    Leader brief

    Pennsylvania bill would give teachers continuing-education credit for AI training

    A Pennsylvania House Democrat introduced a bill on September 24 that would let schools train teachers on using artificial intelligence in teaching and have that training count toward the continuing-education hours Pennsylvania teachers must earn to keep their certificates. If the legislature funds it, the state education department would also give schools grants to pay for the training, which schools could buy from colleges, nonprofits, and other approved providers. The bill has just been sent to the House Education Committee.

    • It would create a paid market for AI teacher training in Pennsylvania that outside providers like Relay could serve, but only as a state-approved continuing-education provider and only if lawmakers put money behind it. Passage is uncertain.

    Questions to ask

    • Does Relay have, or want, Pennsylvania approval as a continuing-education provider for teachers?

    • Is AI-in-teaching training something Relay intends to offer schools as a product?

    California is a pending-watch jurisdiction for Relay, so this caps at SCAN. It matters as the clearest current example of a state budget squeezing teacher headcount, which is the demand side of the pipeline Relay supplies.

    What it does

    Per the California School Boards Association (September 22, read raw this run): CSBA filed a lawsuit on September 22 challenging the state's withholding of $3.9 billion in Proposition 98 constitutionally guaranteed K-14 funding from the 2026-27 budget, roughly $643 per student, and the California Teachers Association filed a complementary suit. CSBA CEO Vernon Billy characterized it as a third consecutive year of Prop 98 manipulation; the new suits complement CSBA's existing litigation over the 2024-25 and 2025-26 budgets. CSBA attributes roughly 1,000 statewide teacher layoffs to the shortfall.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level only: Indiana is an authorized jurisdiction, and a voucher program moving toward universal eligibility shifts where the state's teaching jobs and district enrollment sit over time.

    What it does

    Per Chalkbeat Indiana (2026-09-17, read raw this run) reporting new state data: enrollment growth in Indiana's Choice Scholarship voucher program slowed for the second consecutive year, adding about 4,000 students in 2025-26 to reach roughly 80,000 total, against about 6,000 added the prior year and nearly 17,000 in 2023-24 after the 2023 eligibility expansion. For the first time more vouchers went to households earning above $100,000 than below. Roughly 7,000 students from families earning more than $200,000 received a voucher in 2025-26, up from about 5,400 the year before. The 2025-26 income ceiling was 400 percent of the reduced-price-meal threshold, about $238,000 for a family of four; the 2025 legislative session removed income limits entirely, effective July 2026, so the effect of universal eligibility will not appear until next year's data. The majority of participants have never attended a public school.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Ecosystem-level, but the mechanism matters more than the headline. HBCUs prepare a disproportionate share of the nation's Black teachers and several run educator-preparation programs, so the money lands in the teacher pipeline. It is a reallocation, though, not an addition: Hispanic-serving institutions and other minority-serving institutions — many of which also run teacher-prep — lose the same dollars. For Relay the signal is about how this Department is willing to move higher-education money between institution categories on a constitutional theory, which is the kind of reasoning that could reach future educator-preparation grant competitions.

    What it does

    The Education Department announced on September 22, 2026 more than $174 million in one-time funding for Historically Black Colleges and Universities and more than $61 million for Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities, announced by Secretary Linda McMahon at a White House HBCU Summit. ED's own press release calls these 'additional funding' and does not say where the money comes from. Inside Higher Ed reported on September 23, citing the Department directly, that the funds are redirected from programs that generally served Hispanic-serving and other minority-serving institutions: the HBCU money comes from a Hispanic-serving institutions grant program aimed at increasing Hispanic and low-income students in STEM and building two-year-to-four-year transfer and articulation agreements; tribal colleges receive about $14.4 million from that same STEM program and $47.2 million from programs for Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-serving institutions, Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-serving institutions, and Native American-serving nontribal institutions. This repeats last year's pattern: in September 2025 ED cancelled most minority-serving-institution grants on the position that their enrollment-share eligibility criteria are unconstitutionally discriminatory, then redirected $495 million to HBCUs and tribal colleges; DOJ backed that interpretation in December. Congress blocked ED from defunding the MSI programs outright but allowed the money to be moved into the Strengthening Institutions Program. ED told Inside Higher Ed it has urged Congress to fix the constitutional issue and worked with OMB to identify legal options in the meantime. Two-year total to HBCUs and tribal colleges: roughly $612 million.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Federal-oversight context: ED has stepped back from monitoring the Title I money that funds much district spending on coaching and professional development, which lowers compliance pressure on districts but also the federal check on how the funds are used. Adds to the ED-restructuring thread on the board. No Relay action.

    What it does

    GAO report 'K-12 Education: Actions to Improve Oversight of Key Federal Programs and Address High Chronic Absenteeism', released 2026-09-23 (highlights read this run). Findings: in 2026 the Department of Education discontinued its most comprehensive monitoring of ESEA programmatic and fiscal requirements; because it is not currently assessing compliance with Title I fiscal requirements, about two-thirds of the nearly $27 billion in FY2025 ESEA funding is at higher risk of undetected fraud, waste or abuse. Thirty-six states include chronic absenteeism in their accountability systems. ED computes chronic-absenteeism rates by dividing a full-year count of chronically absent students by single-date enrollment, which produces implausible rates (some over 100 percent); over 30 percent of low-performing and shared-time schools showed implausible rates against under 2 percent of others. GAO asks Congress to spell out ESEA monitoring requirements and makes three recommendations to ED, including resuming comprehensive monitoring; ED agreed with one and disagreed with two.

    Why it matters to Relay

    This is the upstream document behind Georgia's entire 2026 educator-workforce package — HB1107, HB1030, HB1302, and the two bills that died this session. The reporting deadline passed more than eight months ago, so the recommendations either exist or were not delivered, and either answer is worth knowing. Two priorities point straight at Relay: an explicit call for outcome data on out-of-state preparation programs' Georgia graduates at one, three, five and ten years, which is a future accountability exposure; and a call for innovative entry pathways naming apprenticeships and tutors-to-teachers, which is a Relay product surface. The report is the cheapest available read on what Georgia will legislate next.

    What it does

    Senate Resolution 237, adopted by the Georgia Senate 53-0 on 2025-04-02, urges the Professional Standards Commission to lead a collaborative effort with the Department of Education, the Department of Early Care and Learning, the Teachers Retirement System, the Office of Student Achievement, the University System of Georgia, the Technical College System, the Georgia Student Finance Commission and education associations, and to give the Governor and General Assembly comprehensive recommendations to strengthen the K-12 education workforce. The resolution names five priorities: encouraging innovative entry pathways such as enhanced student teaching models, apprenticeship programs and 'tutors to teachers' pathways; collecting and reporting outcome data for graduates of ALL teacher education programs, both in state and out of state, covering placement, effectiveness and retention at one, three, five and ten years; exploring partnerships with postsecondary institutions to improve teacher education programs, including recommendations on the effectiveness and amount of funding to compensate student teachers and on reinstating HOPE access; improving public awareness of the profession's benefits; and teacher and school leader retention strategies including mentorship and school leader professional development. Recommendations were to go to the Governor on a timeline set by the Office of Planning and Budget and to the Senate no later than December 1, 2025, together with any proposed legislation, policy or budget changes needed to implement them. A resolution is not law and creates no compliance obligation.

    Implications

    • Advocacy. Request the Commission's SR237 report directly. It should name Georgia's intended pathway designs and its position on compensating student teachers, which is the fight HB310 lost this session.

    • Risk. The resolution asks for placement, effectiveness and retention data on graduates of out-of-state teacher education programs at one, three, five and ten years. If Georgia builds that reporting, Relay's Georgia completers become a published cohort.

    • Program. 'Enhanced student teaching models, apprenticeship programs, and tutors to teachers pathways' is a description of program designs Relay can already staff. Knowing which the Commission recommended tells us which Georgia will fund.

    Leader brief

    Georgia's 2026 teacher-workforce laws trace back to one Senate resolution — and its report is worth asking for

    In April 2025 the Georgia Senate unanimously adopted a resolution directing the state's teacher licensing body, the Professional Standards Commission, to work with the university system, the state finance commission and others and hand the Governor and Senate a full set of recommendations for strengthening the teaching workforce, due by December 1, 2025. The resolution asked specifically about new routes into teaching such as apprenticeships and tutor-to-teacher pathways, about paying student teachers, and about collecting long-term outcome data on graduates of teacher preparation programs both inside and outside Georgia. We could not confirm this run whether the report was delivered; the Commission's news page did not load.

    • Georgia passed four significant educator-workforce laws in 2026 and this resolution is the visible origin of that agenda, which makes the report the best available preview of what Georgia does next. One of its requests would eventually publish outcome data on out-of-state preparation programs' Georgia graduates — Relay would be in that group. Getting the document is a phone call, not a project.

    Questions to ask

    • Who on our side owns the Georgia Professional Standards Commission relationship, and can they simply request the SR237 report?

    • If Georgia does begin publishing one-, three-, five- and ten-year outcomes for out-of-state preparation programs, are we confident in how our Georgia completers would show up?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Advisory only, but it is the document Connecticut's districts and the State Department of Education will cite when they ask for AI professional learning, and its 'time for professional learning' principle is an argument Relay's Teacher Professional Education line can use with Connecticut partners; the annual report will also be where legislative AI-in-education proposals get previewed.

    What it does

    Draft resolution posted for the Commission's 2026-09-14 regular meeting (1:00-3:00 pm, online; agenda and draft PDF read this run; the draft carries an 'Adopted Monday, September 14, 2026' signature line for Chair Mark Raymond, the State CIO, but the vote had not occurred at run time). The resolution adopts an adaptive AI advisory framework aligned with the Connecticut AI Responsible Use Framework and Public Act 26-15, with six principles: human oversight and judgment in instructional and administrative decisions; a clear educational purpose for any AI tool; AI literacy built on critical evaluation and informed skepticism; workforce enablement, including 'creating time for professional learning by reducing unnecessary administrative burdens'; opportunity and access; data minimization; and vendor transparency on data practices, model training and limitations. It commits the Commission to an annual 'State of Artificial Intelligence in Connecticut Education' report to the Governor and General Assembly, an AI Advisory Working Group that can issue interim memoranda, and an AI-disruption scenario exercise at least every 18 months. Section 6 states the framework carries no regulatory authority. The same agenda includes proposed comments to the FCC on E-rate dockets 26-133 and 13-184.

    No implications recorded.

    Leader brief

    Ten Senate Democrats led by Cory Booker introduced a bill on September 17 whose stated purpose is to remove college cost as a barrier to becoming a teacher, aimed at a well-prepared and diverse teaching workforce. The bill's text has not been published yet, so how it would do that (grants, loan forgiveness, or program funding) is not known.

    • If it funds aspiring teachers' preparation costs, it would touch the students Relay enrolls. With no Republican cosponsors this late in the session, passage this year is unlikely; its value is as a marker of where Democratic education policy is heading.

    Questions to ask

    • Once the text is published, does it reach graduate-level and alternative-route preparation, or only undergraduate programs?

    • Is this a bill Relay would want to be associated with publicly, given its bipartisan relationships?

The value is as a live read on how the Department's recognition process is being used while its own rewrite of the accreditor-recognition rules at 34 CFR 602 sits at the final-rule stage — the ABA renewal, with that commenter roster, is the test case.

    What it does

    The National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity meets September 23-24, 2026, 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. EST; the final agenda was read raw this run. Wednesday: a consent-agenda compliance report on the American Physical Therapy Association's Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education, then Renewal of Recognition reviews for the American Bar Association's Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar and the American Psychological Association's Commission on Accreditation, plus the Accrediting Bureau of Health Education Schools. Thursday: Renewal of Recognition for the Transnational Association of Christian Colleges and Schools' Accreditation Commission and the Accreditation Commission for Acupuncture and Herbal Medicine, and a staff update on agencies seeking initial recognition. The ABA item draws an unusually long third-party comment roster including Defending Education, two representatives of the America First Policy Institute, the America First Legal Foundation, the Manhattan Institute, the Ethics and Public Policy Center, AccessLex, the Association of American Law Schools, the Law School Admission Council and the New York City Bar Association. No educator-preparation accreditor is on this agenda. Update 2026-09-24 (per Inside Higher Ed, 09-23; no committee record posted yet): after about seven hours on the Department's recommendation to deny recognition to the ABA Council of the Section of Legal Education, a motion to extend recognition 12 months with two compliance reports and a bar on accrediting new programs failed on an 8-8 tie decided by the chair, Jay P. Greene; a motion to deny recognition also deadlocked; the committee then voted 8-7 to table the item. The 'separate and independent' criterion was the sticking point. Whether the item resumed on Sept 24 was not known at this run. Update 2026-09-25 (per Inside Higher Ed, 09-25; no committee record posted): on Thursday morning NACIQI voted to make no recommendation on renewing or denying recognition of the ABA accreditation council, leaving Under Secretary Nicholas Kent to decide without one; the Department had recommended non-renewal. The committee then voted 7-4, on a motion by Steve Taylor, to recommend suspending recognition of the American Psychological Association's Commission on Accreditation after third-party comments alleging failures to address antisemitism in accredited programs; Department staff had recommended renewal. APA is a programmatic accreditor, so a suspension would not affect institutions' federal student aid eligibility. Still no educator-preparation accreditor on this agenda.

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Why it matters to Relay

    PSLF is part of the financial case for teaching that Relay's candidates and alumni rely on, and forbearance months lost to servicer backlogs are a live grievance on this board (the PSLF credit-reversal row). A ten-sponsor minority bill at introduction marks the position rather than moving it; it joins H.R. 10206 (Grad PLUS restoration) as the second September bill to reopen the OBBBA loan settlement.

    What it does

    Introduced 2026-09-04 by Rep. Bill Foster (D-IL) with nine original cosponsors including Rep. Fitzpatrick (R-PA), Adams, Bishop, Carson, Clarke (NY), Craig, Figures, Garcia (IL) and Norton; referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce. Section 2(a) rewrites HEA §455(m)(1)(A)(iii) so that a borrower's first 60 monthly payments under an income-driven or (d)(1) plan count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) 'without regard to the amount of such payment,' with later payments required to be at least the 10-year standard amount; it also adds payments under the standard repayment plan in §455(d)(7)(A)(i) as qualifying. Section 2(b) adds §455(m)(3)(C): months in administrative forbearance count as payments while the borrower is employed in public service. Section 2(c) requires the Secretary to notify every Direct Loan borrower of the changes within 180 days and applies the 60-payment rule to borrowers who have made fewer than 120 qualifying payments at enactment.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay is a graduate school whose MAT candidates finance the degree with federal graduate loans, so the July 1, 2026 end of Grad PLUS and the new graduate caps already bear on enrollment. This is the first standalone restoration bill found this cycle. With a single minority-party sponsor and no cosponsors it marks the debate rather than moving it; the signals to watch are cosponsor growth, a Senate companion, or attachment to a larger higher-education package.

    What it does

    Introduced 2026-09-01 by Rep. Shomari Figures (D-AL-2) and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce; no cosponsors as of the 2026-09-03 status update. The bill's stated purpose is to terminate federal student loan limits and restore Federal Direct PLUS Loans for graduate and professional students. Section 2 amends HEA section 455(a) (20 U.S.C. 1087e(a)): it strikes the clause limiting graduate and professional PLUS eligibility to periods of instruction 'ending on June 30, 2026', strikes subparagraph (3)(C) and paragraphs (4) and (6) (the provisions the bill's title identifies as the loan limits), renumbers the remaining paragraphs and makes conforming changes. No effective-date clause beyond the amendments themselves; no appropriation.

    Implications

    • Funding. If enacted, graduate and professional students would regain Direct PLUS borrowing up to cost of attendance and the new graduate loan limits would be repealed, restoring the financing route Relay's candidates used before July 1, 2026.

    • Advocacy. A restoration bill gives graduate-school and educator-preparation coalitions a vehicle to endorse; the near-term value is in signaling, since the bill has no cosponsors and sits in a committee controlled by the other party.

    Leader brief

    A House bill would bring back Grad PLUS loans and repeal the new graduate borrowing caps, but it has one sponsor and no cosponsors

    Representative Shomari Figures of Alabama introduced a bill on September 1 that would undo two changes that took effect on July 1, 2026: the end of Grad PLUS loans (federal loans that let graduate students borrow up to the full cost of attendance) and the new annual and lifetime caps on graduate borrowing. It was sent to the House education committee the same day. As of September 3 no other member had signed on.

    • Relay's master's candidates borrow through the federal graduate loan programs, so the July changes affect how they pay for the degree. This bill would restore the old rules, but a bill with a single sponsor from the minority party is unlikely to move on its own. Its value for now is as a marker: it shows the issue has a champion and gives coalitions something concrete to support.

    Questions to ask

    • Has the July 1 change in graduate borrowing shown up yet in Relay's enrollment or financing conversations, and is that worth documenting for advocacy partners?

    • Should Relay, directly or through its associations, signal support for restoration bills like this one, or wait for a vehicle with bipartisan sponsorship?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay is a graduate school of education whose value proposition is practice-based preparation; this report is a policy argument aimed at the sector Relay belongs to, and two of its four recommendations (outcome-tied funding and accreditation; expanded alternative certification) match levers already moving in ED's accreditor-recognition and Title II report-card proposals. Sector-reputation and advocacy context, not a regulatory event.

    What it does

    Per the American Enterprise Institute (report by Daniel Buck, published 2026-09-09, read raw this run — web page and PDF): a review of syllabi from eight graduate schools of education (over 400 readings from 75 courses) sorts assigned readings into traditional, progressive, critical and therapeutic categories and concludes the programs are 'deeply partisan,' grounded largely in progressive and critical frameworks. The author states the sample is neither representative nor comprehensive (there are over 1,600 education schools). The recommendations to states: eliminate financial incentives that encourage teachers to pursue graduate degrees of limited demonstrated value; tie ed-school funding and accreditation to measurable outcomes; expand high-quality alternative certification pathways; encourage intellectual diversity and rigor within graduate schools of education. UPDATE 2026-09-21: AEI published a companion commentary, 'What Teachers Should Learn: An Alternative Graduate School Curriculum' (2026-09-18), which moves the project from critique to a proposed replacement reading list and course sequence for graduate schools of education. Read raw this run; the AEI landing text frames it as answering 'what exactly should teachers learn if not Freire and French critical theory?' The full alternative curriculum's contents were NOT read this run beyond that framing.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay runs the National Principal Academy Fellowship and principal-supervisor partnerships, so evidence on what actually converts assistant principals into principal candidates speaks to both program design and the size of the market. It pairs with the board's earlier Tennessee finding that half of licensed would-be leaders are not actually available to lead.

    What it does

    Per an Annenberg Institute EdWorkingPaper posted September 2026 by Anna Moyer and Ellen Goldring (abstract read raw this run): using the 2024 Tennessee Educator Survey, the authors estimate that 60 percent of assistant principals in the Tennessee sample aspire to the principalship. Encouragement from their principal and early-career status are the strongest predictors. Black assistant principals are more likely to aspire than white ones, a pattern concentrated among Black men, and high-school assistant principals are less likely to aspire than elementary and middle-school ones. The authors argue districts should differentiate development by career stage and school level, and that principals can deliberately build the future leader pool by encouraging their assistant principals. Working paper, not peer-reviewed.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Context behind two rows already on the board, the Illinois and New York opt-in fights. The regulations, when published, settle how far the credit reaches into tutoring and supplemental services, which is adjacent to the district-services market Relay sells into. Watch for the Treasury rule itself; it would enter as a primary.

    What it does

    Per The 74, the Treasury Department is preparing regulations for the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit created last year, the White House is reviewing them, and they are expected before the end of September. The credit lets taxpayers give up to $1,700 a year to a scholarship-granting organization in a participating state and take it off their tax liability; scholarships can pay for private tuition, tutoring and therapy services. Thirty states have opted in, per the outlet, with Colorado's Gov. Polis the only Democratic governor signed up and New York's Gov. Hochul committed but under union pressure. Open questions named: whether married couples can give $3,400, and whether homeschoolers and microschool students qualify (left largely to states). Members of the House and Senate introduced a bill last week to repeal the opt-in requirement, per the outlet; bill numbers were not given and were not verified this run. Education Week published an explainer the same week.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay is an institution of higher education and would be an eligible applicant for the section 762 faculty-training grants if enacted, an accessibility and universal-design professional-development stream that fits Relay's own faculty development. A minority-party HEA bill introduced in September of an election year is parked; logged for the appetite it records, not for movement.

    What it does

    Introduced 2026-09-01 by Rep. DeSaulnier and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce (verified from the GPO bill text). The bill rewrites the Higher Education Act's Title VII Part D disability programs: it replaces section 762 (20 U.S.C. 1140b) with competitive five-year grants to institutions of higher education for training faculty, staff, and administrators in universal-design-for-learning teaching methods, accommodations, secondary-to-postsecondary transition practices, and accessible distance education, reserving at least five awards for institutions that provide professional development and technical assistance; creates an Office of Accessibility; adds provisions on accessible instructional materials and technology, postsecondary programs for students with intellectual disabilities, and national technical-assistance and coordinating centers; requires data submission on students with disabilities; and funds training of realtime writers for captioning. Authorization amounts run through a new section 765C. Introduced-and-referred; no committee action scheduled.

    Why it matters to Relay

    The second federal AI-in-education bill on the board alongside H.R. 8747, and the more ambitious one: this is a framework bill rather than an ESEA Title IV-A allowable-use amendment. If it carries educator AI professional development, that is Relay's surface. AFT and ACE endorsements give it institutional backing but it is a minority bill referred to three committees a week ago with no text printed, so the realistic read is a marker for the next Congress, not near-term law.

    What it does

    Introduced September 21, 2026 by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR-1) with seven original cosponsors (Reps. Lieu, Foushee, Gottheimer, Krishnamoorthi, Panetta, Thompson of Mississippi, and Wilson of Florida), and referred the same day to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, additionally, to Science, Space, and Technology and to Ways and Means. VERIFIED from the GovInfo bill-status XML, read raw this run. The official title: 'To establish a human-centered Federal framework for artificial intelligence in education and the workforce, promote the ethical and responsible teaching and learning of artificial intelligence, provide for equitable access to artificial intelligence-ready workforce development, safeguard student and worker data privacy, and for other purposes.' NO TEXT VERSION HAS BEEN PRINTED — GovInfo lists none as of this run — so the bill's operative provisions cannot be read yet. Per the sponsor's own press release of September 22 (read raw this run), ATTRIBUTED: the bill establishes national workforce strategies, coordinates evidence-based programs across the Departments of Education and Labor, directs safety research at federal science agencies, creates enforceable safeguards, and invests in professional development. The release lists endorsements from the American Federation of Teachers, the American Council on Education, the Center for American Progress, the Alliance for Learning Innovation, the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence, SIAM and Workday. Claims circulating about specific mechanisms — AI risk assessments at federally funded institutions, a bar on student data for commercial model training, ED/FTC breach reporting, and dedicated educator AI professional-development grants — are UNVERIFIED against bill text and should not be relied on until a text version is printed.

    Implications

    • Program. If the professional-development investment the sponsor describes survives into text, it would be a federal funding line for educator AI training — the same ground Georgia is now credentialing through its new endorsement and Tennessee through its mandatory AI course.

    • Compliance. A framework bill reaching 'federally funded institutions' would likely cover Relay directly on data privacy and risk assessment; nothing can be sized until text is printed.

    • Advocacy. AFT and ACE endorsements are already attached. If Relay has a position on educator AI preparation, the pre-text window is when framework language is still being drafted.

    This lands on the causal claim underneath a strategy several of Relay's states are funding right now: that recruiting early, in high school, widens and

    At a glance

    Field Value

    Second opinionModel scorer: Scan · impact 30; reviewer: Scan · impact 53

    Why it matters to Relay

    This lands on the causal claim underneath a strategy several of Relay's states are funding right now: that recruiting early, in high school, widens and diversifies the pipeline. The board already carries grow-your-own and early-recruitment vehicles in multiple jurisdictions — NY's $50M EDHUBNY educator-development workforce package, GA's workforce directives to the Professional Standards Commission, and CA's apprenticeship statute among them. The Texas result does not say early exposure is worthless; it says the yield sits in retention and in who shows up, not in the number who ultimately enter. That is a usable distinction for Relay when a state partner proposes a high-school pipeline program and asks what to expect from it, and it is a finding worth having read in full before it is cited either way.

    What it does

    Danielle Sanderson Edwards and Matthew A. Kraft, 'Can Early Exposure to the Teaching Profession Increase Teacher Supply and Diversity? New Evidence on the Teacher Pipeline' (September 2026). The authors exploit the staggered expansion of high school education courses across Texas and, per the abstract read raw this run, find little evidence that these courses increased new teacher supply or diversity — despite course takers being substantially more diverse than the teacher workforce. The abstract further reports that high school education course takers who do become teachers are similarly effective as their peers and more likely to be retained. Posted as EdWorkingPapers ai26-1582 and circulated as NBER working paper w35776; the two postings are the same paper and are clustered here. Only the abstract was read this run — the identification strategy, effect sizes and subgroup results were NOT read, so no quantitative claim beyond the abstract's own wording is made here.

    Implications

    • Program. If the supply effect is near zero but the retention effect is positive, a high-school exposure program is better justified as a retention and fit-screening investment than as a headcount fix — a different design and a different success metric.

    • Advocacy. State partners weighing grow-your-own appropriations will meet this paper; Relay is better positioned having read it in full than having it quoted at us.

    Leader brief

    A new study finds high school 'intro to teaching' courses did not actually produce more or more diverse teachers

    Researchers at Brown and the National Bureau of Economic Research studied what happened as Texas high schools rolled out courses introducing students to teaching as a career. The students who took those courses were much more diverse than the current teaching workforce, which is what the strategy is designed to address. But the researchers found little evidence that the courses actually increased the number or the diversity of people who went on to become teachers. They did find that the students who took such a course and then became teachers were about as effective as other new teachers and stayed in the job longer. This is a working paper, not yet peer-reviewed, and we have read only its summary.

    • Several states where Relay works are funding early-recruitment and grow-your-own programs on the premise that reaching students earlier widens the pipeline. This evidence suggests the return shows up in who stays, not in how many arrive. That is still a real return, but it changes what such a program should be designed for and measured on.

    Questions to ask

    • Where are we currently attached to high-school-level recruitment work, and is it being justified to funders on a supply promise this evidence does not support? Should we read the full paper before a state partner cites it at us?

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relay's leadership lines (National Principal Academy Fellowship, principal-supervisor work) sell into this pipeline. The finding cuts two ways: districts' 'we have plenty of licensed candidates' objection weakens, but the study says preparation alone doesn't expand real supply — useful framing for how Relay pitches leadership programs, in Tennessee especially.

    What it does

    Per the abstract (EdWorkingPapers 26-1560, Aug 2026): using statewide Tennessee administrative and survey data, 53% of educators holding administrative licenses but not in leadership roles are 'unavailable' — not pursuing and not intending to pursue leadership. The unavailable pool is older and more experienced; cited reasons are role stress and unrealistic expectations, family incompatibility, insufficient pay, and scarce openings. The effective principal supply is far smaller than license counts imply; the authors point to pay and working conditions, not preparation volume, as the binding constraint.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Reference material, not an action, and it is reported as ECS's compilation rather than as verified state-by-state fact. Its value to Relay is the certification column: which states require charter teachers to be certified, and which permit waivers or percentage thresholds, is precisely the variable that determines whether a charter network in a given state must hire credentialed teachers or may hire and credential later. That is a market map for a teacher-preparation provider, and it now exists in a refreshed public form.

    What it does

    The Education Commission of the States has published the 2026 edition of its 50-state comparison of charter school policies, with a companion page of individual state profiles. Per the resource read this run: 46 states and the District of Columbia have charter school laws; North Dakota's, created in 2025, are the newest; the Kentucky Supreme Court has ruled that state's charter school laws unconstitutional. Forty states and the District of Columbia allow existing public schools to convert to charter status. Of the states with charter policies, only two do not allow enrollment preferences to be set, and 19 allow approval preference in charter applications for specific school types — most often schools serving students at risk of academic failure or economically disadvantaged students. The certification data point is the one that touches educator preparation: 23 states require charter school teachers to be certified, with some allowing a waiver or specifying a percentage of a school's teachers who must hold certification.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Philadelphia is Relay Pennsylvania's principal placement district; the report describes the instructional environment Relay's literacy-methods coursework prepares candidates for, and the phonics gap it names is exactly the foundational-skills instruction a preparation program can supply where the adopted curriculum does not.

    What it does

    Per Chalkbeat: a School District of Philadelphia research report, built on focus groups with more than 100 K-8 teachers, principals and administrators, finds that nearly all K-2 educators reported the EL Education curriculum's phonics instruction is not direct or explicit enough, that teachers lack time and materials for full-book reading, and that the curriculum carries no dedicated Tier 2 lessons for students below grade level; some teachers have returned to Saxon or Fundations against district directive. The district says it has adjusted pacing, added flex days and K-2 foundational-skills support, and increased professional development. Year-one state reading scores fell (about one-third proficient against a board goal of over half by 2030); year-two scores are delayed at the state level.

    The AI-in-education evidence turns cautionary (per Future Ed, CRPE, Bellwether, Brookings)

    Relevant to Relay as a program-design question rather than a policy one. The legislative wave in the row above is mandating AI literacy and district AI policy

    At a glance

    Field Value
    JurisdictionFederal
    ClassPress
    Stage—
    RecommendationScan · impact 18
    Second opinionModel scorer: Scan · impact 18; reviewer: Scan · impact 31
    Latest actionFifteen items published between 2026-07-20 and 2026-09-17 · 2026-09-09
    SourceFuture Ed, CRPE, Bellwether, Brookings, Chalkbeat, The 74, K-12 Dive, Education Next · Open the primary source

    Why it matters to Relay

    Relevant to Relay as a program-design question rather than a policy one. The legislative wave in the row above is mandating AI literacy and district AI policy at the same moment the research base is turning cautionary on teacher reliance on AI. A preparation program has to teach new teachers to use these tools well and to know when not to — and the evidence for the second half is arriving first. Also worth noting that CRPE and Bellwether are both pushing state agencies toward procurement standards, which is where the district-facing rules will come from.

    What it does

    A cluster of AI research and commentary from the last three weeks runs against the adoption narrative. Future Ed reports (2026-07-20) on one of the first randomized trials of AI in real classrooms, finding student engagement drops when teachers rely on it. CRPE published a strategic research agenda for AI-driven transformation (2026-07-30) naming the absence of shared success measures, governance lagging the technology, and a market shaped by ed-tech vendor priorities. Bellwether issued a state education agency resource guide on driving procurement of effective AI tools (2026-07-21). Brookings argued that AI is changing education faster than research can keep up (2026-07-21) and that education and research policy must address AI's 'borrowed expertise' (2026-07-20). Trade coverage runs alongside: Chalkbeat on AI-generated material entering the Teachers Pay Teachers marketplace (2026-08-03), The 74 on AI-assisted rating of students beyond A-F grades (2026-08-05), K-12 Dive on teaching source evaluation under AI overviews (2026-08-05), and Education Next on AI as college-choice advisor (2026-08-03). All reported as commentary; none independently verified this run. Added 2026-08-18: The 74 reports survey evidence (College Board and others) that generative AI use is cutting into how students learn — five distinct mechanisms, per the outlet. Added 2026-08-19: Bellwether published two substantial pieces — 'Learning Systems,' on shaping AI's role in education, and 'Agency in the Algorithm,' on how districts and advocacy organizations can build parent voice on AI — and Brookings proposed student-inclusive school AI councils (all per the outlets; none independently verified). The randomized-trial evidence in the companion row (Oreopoulos et al., three NBER experiments) now anchors the empirical side of this cluster. Added 2026-09-02: K-12 Dive reports a Century Foundation survey of more than 2,000 voters (Morning Consult, May 2026) finding 85% concerned about students using AI to complete assignments without learning the material, 81% about teachers being pressured to use AI tools without proven benefit, and majorities across parties wanting government guardrails on classroom technology (per K-12 Dive; survey not independently verified). Added 2026-09-03: Chalkbeat reports an American Psychological Association report calling for higher standards for education technology (gamification features such as badges and tokens singled out as harmful) rather than blanket screen bans; K-12 Dive summarizes research finding AI can evaluate some components of critical thinking in student work but not others (both per the outlets; not independently verified). Added 2026-09-14: K-12 Dive reports the same APA report's headline recommendation — measure ed tech by what students do on screens, what it replaces and whether it helps learning, not by minutes, with added caution and age-appropriate guardrails for generative AI (per K-12 Dive). Education Next's Frederick Hess writes up Fordham's 'High Tech, Low Standards' survey of 1,000 high-school students and 1,000 recent graduates: three-quarters report daily use of 'illicit' technology during school hours (per Education Next; report not independently read).

    Implications

    No implications recorded.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Feeds the teacher-compensation thread the board already carries. Relevant to Relay only as context on where district dollars go, and as a framing that state legislatures may pick up in the next session.

    What it does

    Per the Fordham Institute (Aaron Garth Smith, September 22, read raw this run): between 2002 and 2023 the average inflation-adjusted teacher salary fell even as real per-student funding rose 36 percent, while non-teaching staff — instructional aides, counselors, social workers — grew 23 percent. The piece attributes the shift to special education, technology, wraparound services and administration, argues the opportunity cost is high because teachers are the strongest in-school factor in student outcomes, and calls on state lawmakers to steer scarce dollars toward teacher compensation. Commentary, not a study.

    Why it matters to Relay

    Adds to the cautionary-evidence cluster the board already tracks on AI in education. Relevant as the evidentiary counterweight while states, including Georgia this run, are writing AI into educator credentials.

    What it does

    Per Education Next (Benjamin Riley, September 23, read raw this run): unlike earlier ed-tech, generative AI has no adoption problem — students use it heavily — but the empirical base on its learning effects remains thin. The piece cites a Stanford research-landscape analysis finding that of more than 800 studies of AI in education, roughly 20 produced credible causal evidence, and frames the emerging finding as students automating cognition and learning less. Commentary, not a study.

    Sources and methods

    Methods

    Relevance checks, impact dimensions and recommendations

    Relevance gates

    Check Rule
    JurisdictionFederal, or one of Relay's authorized jurisdictions (CO, CT, DE, GA, IL, NJ, NY, PA, RI, TN, TX, DC, IN; CA = pending_watch, surfaces at SCAN max). Other states only via COMMENTARY when a national trend.
    Topic relevanceMatches >=1 taxonomy topic (config/topics.yaml). Context-tier-only matches cap at SCAN unless momentum is exceptional.
    Current activityLEGISLATION: current session and not dead (adjourned-without-action = ARCHIVE with a one-line note if core-tier). REGULATION: comment window open, pending finalization, or effective date in the future. AGENCY: live unless superseded or withdrawn (a board agenda, memo, guidance, budget proposal, or press release stays live as context). COMMENTARY older than 30 days: ARCHIVE.
    Duplicate coverageSame underlying policy event across sources (a bill + its press coverage + a think-tank take) clusters into ONE surfaced item; the primary source leads, secondaries attach as 'coverage'.

    Impact dimensions

    Dimension Weight Highest score
    Relay surface30%Directly regulates Relay's operations: EPP approval/accountability, cert/licensure rules, residency/apprenticeship funding, Title II, program-approval standards
    Momentum20%Enacted/final, or passed a chamber / final-rule stage imminent; 0-1 = introduced-and-parked, think-piece
    Jurisdiction depth15%Federal with direct effect, or a state where Relay has deep partnerships (NY, NJ, TX, TN, IL); 2-3 = other authorized states; 1 = CA watch / national trend
    Ecosystem reach15%Reshapes funding or staffing across many districts Relay serves (formula rewrite, class-size mandate, salary floor)
    Actionability10%Relay can respond NOW: open comment period, testimony window, program-design opportunity, partnership angle
    Signal quality10%Primary source verified this run; 0-1 = single secondary source, unconfirmed

    Recommendations

    Recommendation Impact Meaning
    Act70–100Direct Relay impact with an open response window — surface at top with the deadline and a suggested next step.
    Track50–69Moving and plausibly impactful — follows in the digest with stage + next expected event.
    Scan30–49Context worth one line (vibes lane).

    Relay Policy Watch — Digest 2026-09-25

    Friday weekday refresh. Run on claude-opus-5-5, the model the routine specifies, so there is no model drift this run. Effort and permission mode are not self-observable and are not reported.

    What actually happened today

    Today is the last business day to comment on New York's science-of-reading rule for teacher preparation. Comments on 8 NYCRR 52.21 and 80-3.7 are due Sunday, September 27, so a filing has to go to OHERegcomments@nysed.gov today. This is still the open window closest to Relay's own programs. Comments on New York's school accountability rewrite (8 NYCRR 100.19 and 100.21) close Monday, September 28. The same day, ED owes the federal court in the IES apportionment case a report on whether it will obligate the remaining $180 million of fiscal 2025 IES funds before they expire on September 30.

    Tennessee won a $7.9 million federal Teacher and School Leader Incentive grant. The Tennessee Department of Education announced on September 24 that its Instructional Leadership & Educator Development Grant will fund districts and public charter schools serving high-need students to build educator leadership and mentoring pathways, strengthen evaluation, staff strategically and pay educator incentives. Tennessee was one of about twenty grantees this round. The release names the U.S. Department of Labor alongside ED as the funder, and it does not say how districts join. This is the most Relay-relevant item of the day: new money in a deep-partnership state for the leadership-pipeline work Relay sells. It sits at TRACK in both scorings (Claude 69, Jev 66). A reasonable next step is to ask TDOE how participating districts will be chosen and whether outside providers are part of the design.

    Pennsylvania introduced an AI-training bill that runs through teachers' continuing-education credit. HB2788 (Rep. Pielli, referred to House Education on September 24) would let schools train teachers on AI in education, count state-approved training toward Act 48 hours, and, if the legislature funds it, give schools grants to buy that training from colleges, nonprofits and other approved providers. I read the full text (PN 3907). It is permissive and unfunded, so its chances are modest. Its companion HB2787 would bar schools from using AI to diagnose, counsel or treat students' mental health.

    The federal accreditation panel finished its meeting. On September 24 NACIQI voted to make no recommendation on the American Bar Association's law-school accreditor, leaving the decision to Under Secretary Nicholas Kent, and voted 7-4 to recommend suspending the American Psychological Association's accreditor over complaints about antisemitism in accredited programs. ED staff had recommended renewal for the APA (per Inside Higher Ed). No educator-preparation accreditor was on the agenda. The pattern matters for Relay only through ED's pending rewrite of the recognition rules (34 CFR 602), which stays at ACT.

    Smaller federal items: ED approved Mississippi's Returning Education to the States waiver, the seventh, which brings consolidated state-activity funds to $123 million across seven states (Indiana is the one Relay state among them). A Washington federal judge reportedly enjoined ED's termination of up to $1 billion in school mental-health grants in 15 states. Only Law360 reports this, and the order was not retrieved, so it is on the board at SCAN with the attribution stated. Sen. Booker also introduced S. 5566, with a bipartisan House companion, H.R. 10551, to create an ED program of educational assistance for dependents of long-serving public employees, educators among them. No text has been printed.

    ACT (21)

    NY proposes science-of-reading requirements for teacher preparation programs (8 NYCRR 52.21, 80-3.7) — literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, 15 of 100 field-experience hours and the full student-teaching placement spent on evidence-based literacy instruction, SWD literacy credits 6 → 9; comments close Sept 27, adoption expected October

    Jev: ACT 80 · Claude: ACT 86 · NY · REGULATION

    What it does. Proposed rulemaking EDU-30-26-00007-P, published in the July 29, 2026 State Register (no hearing; 60-day comment period, so comments are due September 27, 2026; the Register text and the NYSED full-text index both list the rule and neither prints a calendar deadline, so the date is computed from publication). Amends §52.21 program-registration requirements for teacher preparation programs in bilingual education, early childhood (birth-grade 2), childhood (grades 1-6), ESOL, literacy, and special education (blind/visually impaired, deaf/hard-of-hearing, speech and language disabilities, students with disabilities at every level). Requires the study of literacy skills or methods of teaching reading in those programs to align with the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including theories of literacy development, evidence-based instruction, assessment and intervention through a multi-tier framework, and dyslexia, dysgraphia and other language-based learning disabilities (definitions, detection, screener administration, evidence-based instruction, accommodations for ELLs); removes the 'methods of reading enrichment and remediation' language. Clinical requirements for candidates first enrolling Fall 2028 or later: at least 15 of the 100 field-experience clock hours must include evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with one or more students with reading difficulties, and candidates must teach reading and writing throughout the student teaching or residency experience (70 days or longer), assessing learning in whole-group and small-group settings; literacy programs must spend at least 25 of 50 practicum hours the same way. Programs must comply by September 1, 2028 or at new-program registration, whichever is first. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs must add three semester hours in language acquisition and literacy development (six to nine total) for candidates first enrolling Fall 2029 or later; §80-3.7 makes the same 6 → 9 change for the individual-evaluation certification pathway from September 1, 2033. The notice states SWD programs in childhood and adolescence will no longer be registered on or after September 1, 2029. Cost statement names $1,335 CUNY tuition per three-credit course and $7,100 per adjunct literacy course as illustrative private-party costs. Permanent adoption anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Grounded in the Hunt Institute Path Forward initiative (NY joined Fall 2023) and the December 2024 NYS Dyslexia and Dysgraphia Task Force report.

    Relay angle. This is a direct rewrite of what Relay's registered New York programs in childhood education, students with disabilities and any ESOL/bilingual-extension offerings must teach and how their clinical placements must be structured, with a September 1, 2028 compliance date and a residency-specific clause: the entire student teaching or residency experience must include teaching and assessing reading and writing. The comment window is the first and only formal input point before the Regents adopt in October. Never on the board: the rule was published July 29 while the NYSED newsroom source was down and the State Register is not a wired source; found by the cross-engine sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 29 issue.

    Stage. Proposed rule, comment window open through 2026-09-27; permanent adoption expected at the October 2026 Regents meeting (effective 2026-10-21 on publication); program compliance by 2028-09-01. The July Regents item that authorized publication was not read this run (the Register notice carries the substance).

    Response window. Comments due 2026-09-27, a Sunday; the practical filing date is Friday 2026-09-25, today (0 business days). Send to OHERegcomments@nysed.gov (William P. Murphy, Deputy Commissioner, Office of Higher Education, 89 Washington Ave., Room 975 EBA, Albany, NY 12234, 518-473-3781). (0 business days out.)

    Implications.

    • compliance — Every affected Relay New York program (childhood, students with disabilities, and ESOL or bilingual extension if registered) must show literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including dyslexia and dysgraphia content, by September 1, 2028 or at the next new-program registration, whichever comes first.

    • program — For candidates enrolling Fall 2028 or later, 15 of the 100 pre-student-teaching field hours must involve evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with a struggling reader, and the residency itself must include teaching and assessing reading and writing throughout, in whole-group and small-group settings; Relay's residency design and partner-school placements will need to guarantee that exposure for secondary-leaning placements too.

    • program — SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs gain a three-credit language-acquisition-and-literacy course for Fall 2029 entrants (six to nine credits total); the notice also says SWD childhood and adolescence programs stop being registered after September 1, 2029, which bears on how Relay's special-education offerings are structured in New York.

    • advocacy — Comments are open through September 27 to the Office of Higher Education; a program-level comment from Relay could address the residency-wide literacy clause for adolescence and secondary placements, the clock-hour accounting, and the 2028/2029 phase-in.

    • funding — The cost statement anticipates new coursework and literacy-expert instructors for registered programs; Relay would bear curriculum-development and faculty cost for the affected New York programs.

    Source. NYS Register 2026-07-29 (proposed rule making, PDF) and 2026-09-09 (Action Pending Index) — cross-engine sweep (Opus; verified by this session)

    PA Student Teacher Support Program 2026-27 round closed Sept 15 — $10,000 stipends (first-come, first-served) for student teachers at PA institutions who commit to three years of teaching in-state; $2,500 for cooperating teachers; 2,300 stipends paid in 2025-26

    Jev: ACT 68 · Claude: SCAN 34 · DISAGREE · PA · AGENCY

    What it does. Pennsylvania Department of Education release of 2026-04-16 (read raw this run): the PA Student Teacher Support Program, administered by the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA), pays $10,000 stipends for the 2026-27 school year to student teachers in unpaid placements who are enrolled at a Pennsylvania institution of higher education in a PDE-approved educator preparation program, hold a 3.0 GPA and required clearances, and agree to teach at a participating Pennsylvania LEA or non-public school for at least three years; cooperating teachers receive up to $2,500. Placements may be in districts, intermediate units, non-public schools, career and technical schools, or charter, regional charter and cyber charter schools. In 2025-26 PHEAA received more than 3,500 applications and funded 2,300 stipends; the Governor's 2026-27 budget proposal adds $5 million, for $35 million annually. Applications for the 2026-27 round were due 2026-09-15 (first-come, first-served).

    Relay angle. Relay's Pennsylvania candidates in unpaid student-teaching placements are eligible if enrolled through a PDE-approved program at a Pennsylvania institution — the three-year in-state service commitment is a retention lever for partner districts, and the annual September deadline belongs on the recruiting calendar.

    Source. PA Department of Education newsroom (cross-engine sweep: Opus + Gemini; release read raw by this session)

    ED proposes full rewrite of accreditor-recognition rules (34 CFR 602) — comment window closed Sept 21, now at drafting

    Jev: ACT 63 · Claude: ACT 87 · US · REGULATION

    What it does. Notice of proposed rulemaking rewriting the Secretary's accrediting-agency recognition regulations at 34 CFR part 602 (conforming changes to parts 600 and 668) to implement Executive Order 14279. Verified from the Federal Register text this run, the NPRM: requires accreditors to hold member institutions to program-level student-outcome expectations — completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns — assessed "without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex"; requires accreditation decisions to be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology (proposed 602.18, with a religious-mission exception); adds academic-freedom and intellectual-diversity review, cost-benefit analysis, and program-length review to 602.17; REMOVES the 602.15(a)(4) requirement that programmatic accreditors seat educators, practitioners, and employers on evaluation and decision-making bodies; lowers barriers to recognizing new accreditors and to institutions switching accreditors (new 602.12(e): qualifying experience may be national, State, or programmatic); and makes it a recognition-review factor whether an agency joined a "concerted effort to unnecessarily restrict the qualifications necessary for a student to sit for a licensure or certification examination" or inflated entry requirements through "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" (proposed 602.31(g)(1)). Docket ED-2025-OPE-1042, RIN 1840-AD82. Comments close 2026-09-21 (~21 business days), via regulations.gov only — no fax or email.

    Update 2026-09-23: the FTC's Office of Policy Planning and Bureau of Competition filed a comment on Monday September 21 — the last day of the window — strongly endorsing the proposal, and the Commission issued a press release on September 22 (read raw this run). The comment argues that accreditation monopolies drive up tuition, limit choice and stifle innovation because incumbent accreditors have an incentive to impose rigid requirements and oppose flexible standards, citing that 21 of 27 commissioners on the Middle States Commission on Higher Education are university administrators or faculty. The comment states that the situation for PROGRAMMATIC accreditors — the category that covers educator preparation — is 'often worse,' because they are guided by incumbent members of the profession with incentives to raise educational costs and create barriers to lower-cost alternatives.

    Relay angle. Relay's operating licenses run through this rule twice: MSCHE (institutional accreditor and Title IV gatekeeper) and CAEP (educator-prep accreditor) are both Secretary-recognized under Part 602, so the proposed outcome metrics and the credential-inflation review factor would reshape the standards both apply to Relay.

    Stage. Proposed rule; comment window closed 2026-09-21. The FTC's competition staff filed a supporting comment on the closing day and publicized it September 22. Next expected event: the final rule; ED has not published a date. NACIQI, which applies the current recognition criteria, is in session today and tomorrow on six renewals — the two tracks are running in parallel.

    Response window. Closed 2026-09-21. No remaining input route before the final rule. (0 business days out.)

    Implications.

    • compliance — MSCHE and CAEP would be re-reviewed against rewritten recognition criteria; whatever standards survive flow down into Relay's next reaffirmation cycles, with program-level completion, licensure pass-rate, and earnings data as the evidence currency.

    • program — Program-level economic-returns metrics put graduate-EPP tuition-to-earnings ratios under accreditor scrutiny — Relay's employment and certification outcomes become either an accreditation asset or an exposure, program by program.

    • risk — Proposed 602.31(g)(1) treats "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" for entering a profession as a mark against an accreditor's recognition — a federal thumb on the scale against graduate-level entry expectations for teaching, rhyming with the state-level deregulation the board is already tracking (IN Pub. L. 150, CO SB26-126).

    • advocacy — Comment window open to 2026-09-21. Relay can speak as a graduate EPP with strong licensure outcomes; coordination with AACTE and with MSCHE/CAEP comment strategies is the near-term decision.

    • advocacy — A sitting federal competition authority has now argued on the record that programmatic accreditors — the category that includes educator-preparation accreditation — create barriers to lower-cost alternatives. That framing, if it survives into the final rule's preamble, is favorable to alternative-route providers and worth tracking as the rationale, not just the rule.

    Source. Federal Register

    NY Regents extend the incidental-teaching flexibility for a seventh year (8 NYCRR 80-5.3) — certified teachers may teach up to 10 classroom hours a week outside their certificate area in 2026-27 when no certified teacher can be found; Higher Education Committee recommended emergency adoption Sept 15; comments open Sept 30

    Jev: ACT 71 · Claude: TRACK 68 · DISAGREE · NY · REGULATION

    What it does. Higher Education Committee item HE (A) 1 (memo dated 2026-09-03 from William P. Murphy, read this run from the Regents agenda). The Committee is asked to recommend, and the Full Board to adopt as an emergency rule effective September 15, 2026, an amendment to section 80-5.3 extending through the 2026-27 school year the flexibility that lets a certified teacher teach up to 10 classroom hours a week (the permanent rule allows five) in a subject not covered by their certificate, after the district determines through documented recruitment that no certified or qualified teacher is available. The same one-year extension was adopted in December 2020, October 2021, September 2022, September 2023, November 2024 and November 2025; the memo's stated rationale is 'ongoing staffing challenges'. A Notice of Emergency Adoption and Proposed Rule Making is to be published in the State Register on September 30, 2026 for a 60-day comment period (through about November 29); permanent adoption is anticipated at the January 2027 Regents meeting, with a further emergency re-adoption expected before then because the emergency action lapses first.

    Relay angle. Incidental teaching is the state's alternative to certifying more teachers in shortage subjects: every hour a district covers this way is an hour it does not need a teacher with an additional certificate or extension, which is the coursework and pathway business of a New York educator-preparation provider. Seven straight renewals make the 'temporary' flexibility a fixture; the January 2027 permanent-adoption step and the 60-day comment window from September 30 are the places to say whether Relay wants a sunset or a certification-linked condition.

    Implications.

    • program — Districts can keep covering shortage-subject sections with out-of-field certified teachers for another year, which reduces near-term demand for additional-certificate and extension coursework in those subjects.

    • advocacy — The 60-day comment window from September 30 and the January 2027 permanent-adoption step are the opportunities to ask for a sunset, a reporting requirement, or a link between incidental assignments and enrollment in a certification pathway.

    • partnership — Districts using incidental teaching heavily are the districts with the deepest shortage-subject needs; that is the target list for residency and additional-certification partnerships.

    Source. Regents September 2026 Higher Education Committee agenda, HE (A) 1 (cross-engine sweep: Opus + Codex; PDF read by this session); 2026-09-16: Higher Education Committee report read by this session
