    CO SB26-126 — out-of-state teacher licensure opened: 7-year recency limit repealed, 30-day Compact licensing with no added coursework, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 67)

    Jev: ACT 74 · Claude: ACT 71 · CO · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 67 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act amends C.R.S. 22-60.5-201 to widen two routes into a Colorado teacher license for people licensed elsewhere. First, it removes the requirement that the three years of successful, evaluated out-of-state teaching experience supporting a professional teacher license have occurred within the previous seven years, so older experience now counts. Second, it adds a new subsection (6) requiring the Department of Education to issue an INITIAL teacher license within thirty days of receiving a complete application from a person licensed by a state participating in the Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact, where the applicant holds an unencumbered eligible license equivalent to a Colorado eligible license, is not subject to current disciplinary action, suspension, investigation or restriction, and has cleared a Colorado criminal history record check. Critically, subsection (6)(b) bars the department from requiring any additional coursework, examinations or program completions beyond those three conditions as a condition of INITIAL license issuance, while expressly preserving its authority to require them for license RENEWAL. The department must determine which Colorado endorsement areas most closely correspond to the applicant's out-of-state license, and must publish an annual table mapping licenses from each reciprocal-agreement state to Colorado endorsement areas. Subsection (6) self-repeals once the department begins issuing licenses under the Compact itself.

    Relay angle. This cuts both ways for Relay and the honest read holds both. Subsection (6)(b) forbids Colorado from requiring additional program completions of Compact-state licensees at initial issuance, which is a straightforward reduction in demand for Colorado-specific preparation among already-licensed teachers. At the same time, a national, multi-state, primarily-online provider benefits more than an in-state one from a regime where a license earned in one state travels cleanly: Relay completers licensed elsewhere gain a fast, thirty-day path into Colorado classrooms, and the removal of the seven-year recency limit helps career-changers and returners, a population Relay's model already serves. The annual endorsement-crosswalk table is a concrete artifact worth obtaining as soon as CDE first publishes it — it will state, officially, how licenses Relay's completers hold map onto Colorado endorsements.

    Implications.

    • risk — Subsection (6)(b) prohibits Colorado from requiring additional coursework, examinations or program completions of Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact licensees at initial issuance. For already-licensed teachers moving into Colorado, that removes a route by which preparation providers pick up incremental enrollment.

    • program — Relay completers licensed in a Compact state now have a statutory thirty-day path to a Colorado initial license. A multi-state footprint becomes a recruiting argument in Colorado in a way it was not before.

    • program — Repeal of the seven-year recency limit on the three-years-experience route reopens the professional-license path for career-changers and re-entrants whose classroom experience is older — a population that maps onto Relay's candidate profile.

    • compliance — The department may still require additional coursework, examinations or program completions as a condition of license RENEWAL. Advising should distinguish the initial-issuance bar from renewal requirements rather than treating Compact entry as a permanent exemption.

    • advocacy — CDE must publish an annual table mapping each reciprocal state's licenses to Colorado endorsement areas. Obtaining the first published table establishes how Relay completers' credentials are officially classified, and the table's construction is a reasonable point of engagement.

    Source. Colorado General Assembly (leg.colorado.gov bill page SB26-126; Final Act text, bill_files/114203; Session Laws Ch. 67)

    IL HB5321 — only accredited graduate credit with an instructor of record may count for teacher salary advancement (Public Act 104-0795)

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 87 · IL · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Adds a new Section 24-8.2 to the Employment of Teachers Article of the Illinois School Code, signed 2026-08-07 as Public Act 104-0795 and effective the same day. For continuing education coursework completed on or after July 1, 2026, a school district, special education cooperative, or other public educational employer may recognize that coursework for salary advancement ONLY IF it (1) is graduate-level, degree-eligible credit offered through a regionally accredited institution of higher education and documented on an official academic transcript, and (2) includes an instructor of record. The Act defines 'graduate-level, degree-eligible credit' as transcripted credit applicable toward a master's, education specialist, or doctoral degree, and defines 'instructor of record' as a credentialed educator holding at least a master's degree, academically qualified in the content area, who provides substantive instructional support throughout the course and returns individualized written feedback aligned to course objectives. It applies only to licensed classroom teachers holding a Professional Educator License under Section 21B-20 who are covered by a collective bargaining agreement, and expressly excludes administrators. Carve-outs: nothing requires an employer to create a salary schedule or advancement pathway that does not already exist, nothing precludes bargaining over other compensation-related advancement, and implementation — documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, compliance monitoring — is left to each employer rather than to State Board rulemaking. Passed unanimously at every recorded vote: House 105-0-0 (2026-04-16), Senate 57-0-0 (2026-05-21), House concurrence 112-0-0 (2026-05-28).

    Relay angle. This regulates the market for Relay's Illinois products directly, and it cuts both ways. Relay is a Middle States-accredited, master's-degree-granting institution, so its MAT and advanced-certificate coursework is exactly the transcripted graduate credit the Act preserves as salary-bearing — competitors selling ungraded, self-paced, non-transcripted seat-hour PD are now barred from Illinois salary lanes. The same clause is a risk to Relay's other Illinois line: Teacher Professional Education, the job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD product, does not carry transcripted graduate credit and so cannot support a lane change under the new Section unless it is delivered through the degree-granting side with an instructor of record.

    Implications.

    • risk — Relay's Teacher Professional Education line (job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD) is not graduate-level, degree-eligible transcripted credit. Where Illinois district contracts were sold partly on teachers earning salary-lane movement, that value proposition no longer holds for coursework completed on or after 2026-07-01. Audit the Illinois PD contracts and any marketing language that implies lane credit.

    • program — The clean response is a credit-bearing delivery path: route Illinois PD sequences through the degree-granting side so participants receive transcripted graduate credit with a named instructor of record who grades and gives written feedback. The Act's instructor-of-record definition (master's degree, content-qualified, substantive support throughout, individualized written feedback) is a design spec, not a formality.

    • partnership — Section 24-8.2(f) leaves documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, and compliance monitoring to each district and special education cooperative individually. Illinois partners now need a per-district answer on what evidence they will accept — an opening to supply that documentation package rather than wait to be asked for it.

    • funding — For the MAT and advanced-certificate lines this is favorable demand policy: Illinois teachers seeking lane movement are pushed toward accredited graduate credit, which is what Relay sells. Worth testing in Illinois enrollment messaging for the coming cycles.

    • compliance — The Act imposes no direct obligation on Relay as an institution — the duty runs to the employer recognizing the credit. Relay's exposure is entirely commercial and reputational: being able to evidence regional accreditation, transcripting, and instructor of record on demand.

    Source. Illinois General Assembly (ilga.gov bill status + enrolled full text)

    IN Public Law 150 (SB204) — a STEM bachelor's plus nine credits now earns a grades 5-12 initial teaching license, treated by statute as equal to finishing a preparation program

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 82 · IN · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Senate Bill 204, enacted as Public Law 150, amends Indiana Code 20-28-5-16.5 effective July 1, 2026. As amended, the Department of Education SHALL grant an initial practitioner license to an individual who: holds a bachelor's degree with a grade point average of at least 2.5 on a 4.0 scale from an accredited postsecondary institution with a major in any combination of science, technology, engineering or mathematics; completes at least nine academic credits covering high-impact practices in lesson planning, instructional design, instructional activities, learning modalities and (where applicable) laboratory experiments, use of digital media, learning management software and technology, teaching inductive and deductive reasoning, metacognition, problem framing, interpreting results and data-based decision making, diagnostic, direct, indirect, formative and summative assessment, feedback loops, engagement and peer-to-peer and small-group strategies, constructive feedback and preventing disruptive behavior, early intervention strategies and professional standards, and teaching students with disabilities; demonstrates subject-matter proficiency by written examination under IC 20-28-5-12(b)(2); completes the training in IC 20-28-5-12.3; and participates in one or more of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives, or full-term student teaching, as determined by the Department. A licensee under this section may teach only in grades 5 through 12 as determined by the Department, may not be granted the license to teach special education, and — by express statutory command — 'shall be treated in the same manner as an individual who receives an initial practitioner license after completing a traditional teacher preparation program,' including during the transition from an initial practitioner to a practitioner license. The section was originally added by P.L.194-2025; this act amends it.

    Relay angle. Indiana is an authorized Relay jurisdiction, and this is a nine-credit statutory substitute for the thing Relay sells. A candidate with a STEM bachelor's and a 2.5 GPA can reach a grades 5-12 Indiana license without enrolling in a preparation program at all, and the statute forbids treating that licensee differently from a program completer. That is a direct competitive threat to a graduate teacher-preparation pathway in exactly the shortage fields where alternative certification demand concentrates. It is also an opening: the nine credits have to be taught by someone, the coursework list reads like a syllabus Relay already teaches, and Indiana law does not say who may offer it. One caveat on our own side of the ledger — Relay's Indiana operating footprint is an open verification item in the org profile, so the size of the exposure is not yet established.

    Stage. Enacted and in force. Signed into law as Public Law 150 on 2026-03-12; the amended IC 20-28-5-16.5 is effective July 1, 2026, so the route is live now. Next expected event is Department of Education implementation — the statute leaves the Department to determine the grade range and which of the four experience options applies, and no Indiana rulemaking notice was located this run.

    Implications.

    • risk — A nine-credit, no-program route to a grades 5-12 Indiana license, statutorily equal to a preparation-program completion, undercuts the value proposition of a graduate teacher-prep pathway for STEM candidates in Indiana.

    • program — The nine required credits map closely onto content Relay already delivers. Indiana law does not name an approved provider for them, which makes a for-credit nine-hour sequence for STEM degree holders a concrete product question rather than a speculative one.

    • compliance — The license may not be issued for special education and is capped at grades 5-12, so Relay's special-education advanced certificate line and any K-4 pathway are outside the substitution.

    • advocacy — The Department of Education decides which of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives or full-term student teaching satisfies the clinical requirement. That determination is where preparation quality is either preserved or hollowed out, and it is made administratively, not legislatively.

    Source. legiscan_in

    CO HB26-1090 — teacher, EPP-student and charter-hire criminal-disclosure certifications rewritten into four categories, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 68)

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 77 · CO · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 68 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act rewrites the criminal-conviction certification that three different populations must sign under penalty of perjury, and it makes the same change in all three places: teacher-license applicants (C.R.S. 22-60.5-103(2)(a)), students in educator preparation programs (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3(2)(a)), and applicants offered employment by a charter school (C.R.S. 22-30.5-110.7(2)). The prior form required disclosure of every misdemeanor regardless of date, excluding only traffic offenses. The act replaces that with four categories: (A) any felony, regardless of date; (B) any misdemeanor for which an element of the offense was that the victim was an at-risk person as defined in section 18-6.5-102 or a child under eighteen, regardless of date; (C) any other misdemeanor where the application is submitted within seven years after the disposition of the conviction, still excluding traffic offenses and infractions; and (D) any misdemeanor enumerated as grounds for denial, annulment, suspension, or revocation of a license, certificate, endorsement, or authorization under 22-60.5-107(2)(b), regardless of date. New language requires that each conviction in these four categories be listed individually, with the offense, the date of conviction, and the court entering judgment. Each of the three statutes also gains a savings clause stating the change does not alter the department's obligation to evaluate criminal convictions under C.R.S. 24-5-101. A provision in the introduced bill that would have required the department to waive the program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for applicants with two or more years of Colorado private school teaching experience does NOT appear in the final act — it was removed before enactment.

    Relay angle. Section 2 amends the record check that Relay's own Colorado educator-preparation students execute, so this is a Relay compliance surface rather than an ecosystem observation: the certification language and the itemized-listing requirement changed, and the act has been in force since yesterday. Section 3 does the same for charter-school hiring, which is the placement channel for much of Relay's network. The stripped private-school waiver is the quieter finding: had it survived, Colorado would have let two years of private-school experience substitute for completing a preparation program, a direct substitution for what Relay sells. It did not survive, and that is worth recording as a live legislative appetite rather than a settled question.

    Implications.

    • compliance — Relay's Colorado educator-preparation record-check certification (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3) must match the new four-category language and the requirement that each conviction be listed individually with offense, date and court. The act is already in force, so any form still using the old 'all misdemeanors regardless of date' text is out of date now, not at some future compliance date.

    • program — Candidates previously deterred by having to disclose decades-old minor misdemeanors now disclose non-traffic misdemeanors only within a seven-year window, which modestly widens the admissible Colorado applicant pool. Offenses against at-risk persons or children, and licensure-disqualifying misdemeanors, remain lifetime-disclosable.

    • risk — The introduced version would have waived program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for two years of Colorado private-school experience. It was removed before enactment, but the proposal establishes that an experience-for-preparation substitution has sponsors in Colorado and may return in a later session.

    • partnership — Section 3 changes the same certification for charter-school employment offers, so Relay's Colorado charter partners are updating the identical form on the identical timeline — a low-cost, concrete reason to compare notes with placement partners.

    Source. Colorado General Assembly (leg.colorado.gov bill page HB26-1090; Final Act text, bill_files/114467; Session Laws Ch. 68)

The cohort was identified from ISBE's annual Unfilled Positions Report, limited to eligible districts in Evidence-Based Funding Tiers 1-3 with the highest numbers of unfilled teaching positions; the selected districts account for about 77% of reported vacancies statewide while making up 12% of Illinois local education agencies.     CT Public Act 26-149 — aspiring educators scholarship redefined and opened statewide (up to $10k/yr), teacher-shortage areas now include underrepresented subgroups

    Jev: ACT 70 · Claude: TRACK 69 · DISAGREE · CT · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Substitute Senate Bill 220, signed 2026-06-04 as Public Act 26-149. Section 2 rewrites C.R.S.-equivalent Conn. Gen. Stat. 10-156ii, renaming the 'aspiring educators diversity scholarship' the 'aspiring educators scholarship' and changing who qualifies: the geographic restriction to graduates of alliance-district high schools is replaced with graduation from any public high school in the state, while the beneficiary definition narrows from 'diverse students' to 'aspiring educators', meaning individuals in a population subgroup that is underrepresented in the teaching profession AND identified as a teacher shortage area by the Commissioner of Education under section 10-8b. The award remains up to $10,000 per year while the recipient is enrolled and in good standing in a teacher preparation program at any FOUR-YEAR institution of higher education. The department must develop an administration policy by 2027-01-01 and award annually from the fiscal year ending 2027-06-30 onward; the Commissioner must develop repayment criteria for recipients who do not go on to teach as certified teachers in Connecticut. Section 3 rewrites section 10-8b so the Commissioner must annually by December 1 identify teacher shortage areas in three categories — subject, geographic, and population subgroups underrepresented in the profession — certify them to the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, and by March 1 distribute shortage-area information covering at least the prior five years to the president of every institution of higher education in the state offering a teacher preparatory program. Section 4 (effective 2027-01-01) establishes an American Sign Language education working group charged with recommending curriculum guidance, ASL teacher certification standards including a proficiency benchmark, an alternative certification pathway for native ASL users and interpreters, and reciprocity with other states' ASL certifications, plus guidance to educator preparation programs on expanding ASL programs, creating incentives such as tuition support and credit enhancement, and establishing bridge, endorsement or alternative programs. Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in a public school rather than only those employed by a local or regional board of education, reaching charter school paraeducators, with up to $300,000 of unexpended FY2026 funds transferred by 2026-07-15.

    Relay angle. Two Relay-relevant asymmetries. The scholarship — the money in this act — is restricted to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education, which excludes a graduate school of education, so Relay's Connecticut candidates cannot reach these dollars. But Section 3's distribution duty runs to every institution offering a teacher preparatory program, which does include Relay Connecticut, and the newly required identification of underrepresented population subgroups as formal shortage areas is a designation Relay's recruitment work is well positioned to speak to. Section 4's charge to advise educator preparation programs on alternative-route and bridge programs for native ASL users is the clearest programme-design opening in the act, though it does not begin until January 2027.

    Implications.

    • risk — The up-to-$10,000 aspiring educators scholarship is limited to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education. Relay's Connecticut candidates are structurally outside it, and the same exclusion appears in Delaware's new Teacher Academy scholarship — a pattern worth naming rather than treating as two coincidences.

    • advocacy — From December 1 each year the Commissioner must formally identify population subgroups underrepresented in teaching as shortage areas. That designation drives scholarship eligibility, and it is a decision Relay's recruitment and completer data speak to directly.

    • program — Section 4's working group must advise educator preparation programs on bridge, endorsement and alternative-route programs for native ASL users and certified interpreters seeking teacher certification — an alternative-certification design space matching what Relay already operates. It convenes from 2027-01-01.

    • compliance — By March 1 annually the department must send five years of shortage-area data to every Connecticut institution offering a teacher preparatory program. Relay Connecticut should be on that distribution list and should confirm it is.

    • partnership — Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in public schools including charter schools, strengthening a paraeducator-to-teacher pipeline population that alternative-route providers recruit from.

    Source. Connecticut General Assembly (cga.ct.gov, Public Act 26-149 full text)

    California watch: Newsom signs AB 1381 making it unprofessional conduct for an educator to withhold prior-employment disclosures, signs the higher-education budget trailer AB 167, and vetoes AB 713 and AB 917

    Jev: ACT 70 · Claude: SCAN 34 · DISAGREE · CA · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Surfaced by the cross-engine sweep from the Governor's legislative updates of 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-20; the Governor's pages were NOT read directly by this session, so these are recorded at the sweep's confidence, not this run's. Marked VERIFIED by two engines: AB 1381, signed 2026-09-20, makes failure to disclose prior employment or to conduct a background check a form of unprofessional conduct for purposes of the Commission on Teacher Credentialing; AB 167, signed 2026-09-18, the higher-education budget trailer bill; AB 713, VETOED 2026-09-20, on undocumented students' eligibility for public postsecondary employment; and AB 917, VETOED 2026-09-20, on permanent status for small districts through county offices of education. Marked ATTRIBUTED by a single engine and therefore weaker: AB 113, reported as a Budget Act amendment signed 2026-09-18 carrying $30 million for teacher residency and National Board certification and $5 million for transcript-related work; and proposed educator apprenticeship standards posted 2026-09-18 by the San Diego County Office of Education and the Child Care Resource Center. NO bill number, dollar figure or date in the attributed group should be relied on without a primary read. SWEEP ADDITION, ATTRIBUTED ONLY (2026-09-22): the cross-engine sweep reports that Governor Newsom also signed SB 960 and AB 2694 around 2026-09-20, authorizing California community college districts to establish two to twelve new bachelor's degree programs starting in 2028, tied to a five-tier accountability framework based on district graduation, retention and transfer rates, and removing the bar on community colleges awarding bachelor's degrees already offered at the University of California or California State University. This is reported by Inside Higher Ed (2026-09-21) and CalMatters; NEITHER BILL NUMBER APPEARS on the Governor's own 2026-09-20 legislative update, which this board fetched and read in full this run and which does list AB 2206 and AB 1381. The signings are therefore recorded as ATTRIBUTED, with the date unconfirmed, and are not asserted as fact. Adjacent-tier in any case: higher-education governance rather than educator preparation, with the teacher-pipeline link running through the companion AB 2206 career-and-technical-education credential provisions tracked separately at x:6dada068.

    Relay angle. California is watch-only for Relay and everything here caps at SCAN, but two threads are worth the line. AB 1381 extends educator-discipline grounds to disclosure failures, which is the kind of credentialing-conduct rule that migrates between states. The reported $30 million for teacher residency and National Board certification, if the single-engine attribution holds, is a data point on what a large state is willing to spend on residency models — the same model Relay builds — at a moment when the board is tracking residency funding fights in Tennessee and Connecticut that died for want of appropriation.

    Implications.

    • advocacy — A large state funding teacher residencies at scale is a citable comparison in states where Relay's residency partners are arguing for appropriations.

    Source. Office of the Governor of California (via cross-engine sweep)

    What actually happened today

    Three things are worth a leader's attention.

    Georgia's certification-rules package is approved. After ten consecutive runs of negative checks, the Professional Standards Commission's July package is reported approved at the September 10 meeting, effective October 15. It creates an Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement and a micro-endorsement, adds a test-in route for Elementary P-5, and writes the Math Matters Act into the elementary, mathematics and K-5 math-endorsement preparation rules. Two regional service agencies are already approved to deliver the AI endorsement. The approval is attributed to the Professional Association of Georgia Educators, not verified from GaPSC — the Commission has posted no final notice and its September minutes file still returns HTML instead of a PDF — so the row stays at TRACK with the gap named. Everything else about the package, including the October 15 date, is verified from GaPSC's own July 31 notice, read in full this run.

    The FTC put its weight behind the accreditation rewrite. On September 21, the closing day of the comment window, the FTC's Office of Policy Planning and Bureau of Competition filed a comment endorsing ED's rewrite of the accreditor-recognition rules, and publicized it the next day. The comment argues accreditation monopolies raise tuition and block lower-cost alternatives, and says the situation for programmatic accreditors — the category that covers educator preparation — is 'often worse.' That is a federal competition authority arguing on the record for exactly the position that favors alternative-route providers. Worth tracking as the rationale, not just the rule.

    The HBCU announcement is a reallocation, not new money. ED's press release announced $174M for HBCUs and $61M for tribal colleges as 'additional funding' without saying where it came from. Inside Higher Ed, sourcing the Department directly, reports it is redirected from Hispanic-serving and other minority-serving institution programs — the same maneuver ED ran with $495M last year after cancelling MSI grants on a constitutional theory DOJ later endorsed. Several institutions on both sides of that transfer run educator-preparation programs.

    ACT (21)

    NY proposes science-of-reading requirements for teacher preparation programs (8 NYCRR 52.21, 80-3.7) — literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, 15 of 100 field-experience hours and the full student-teaching placement spent on evidence-based literacy instruction, SWD literacy credits 6 → 9; comments close Sept 27, adoption expected October

    Jev: ACT 80 · Claude: ACT 86 · NY · REGULATION

    What it does. Proposed rulemaking EDU-30-26-00007-P, published in the July 29, 2026 State Register (no hearing; 60-day comment period, so comments are due September 27, 2026; the Register text and the NYSED full-text index both list the rule and neither prints a calendar deadline, so the date is computed from publication). Amends §52.21 program-registration requirements for teacher preparation programs in bilingual education, early childhood (birth-grade 2), childhood (grades 1-6), ESOL, literacy, and special education (blind/visually impaired, deaf/hard-of-hearing, speech and language disabilities, students with disabilities at every level). Requires the study of literacy skills or methods of teaching reading in those programs to align with the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including theories of literacy development, evidence-based instruction, assessment and intervention through a multi-tier framework, and dyslexia, dysgraphia and other language-based learning disabilities (definitions, detection, screener administration, evidence-based instruction, accommodations for ELLs); removes the 'methods of reading enrichment and remediation' language. Clinical requirements for candidates first enrolling Fall 2028 or later: at least 15 of the 100 field-experience clock hours must include evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with one or more students with reading difficulties, and candidates must teach reading and writing throughout the student teaching or residency experience (70 days or longer), assessing learning in whole-group and small-group settings; literacy programs must spend at least 25 of 50 practicum hours the same way. Programs must comply by September 1, 2028 or at new-program registration, whichever is first. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs must add three semester hours in language acquisition and literacy development (six to nine total) for candidates first enrolling Fall 2029 or later; §80-3.7 makes the same 6 → 9 change for the individual-evaluation certification pathway from September 1, 2033. The notice states SWD programs in childhood and adolescence will no longer be registered on or after September 1, 2029. Cost statement names $1,335 CUNY tuition per three-credit course and $7,100 per adjunct literacy course as illustrative private-party costs. Permanent adoption anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Grounded in the Hunt Institute Path Forward initiative (NY joined Fall 2023) and the December 2024 NYS Dyslexia and Dysgraphia Task Force report.

    Relay angle. This is a direct rewrite of what Relay's registered New York programs in childhood education, students with disabilities and any ESOL/bilingual-extension offerings must teach and how their clinical placements must be structured, with a September 1, 2028 compliance date and a residency-specific clause: the entire student teaching or residency experience must include teaching and assessing reading and writing. The comment window is the first and only formal input point before the Regents adopt in October. Never on the board: the rule was published July 29 while the NYSED newsroom source was down and the State Register is not a wired source; found by the cross-engine sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 29 issue.

Proposed rule, comment window open through 2026-09-27; permanent adoption expected at the October 2026 Regents meeting (effective 2026-10-21 on publication); program compliance by 2028-09-01.     IL HB5552 — School Code omnibus rewriting educator licensure, testing exemptions and the Preparation & Licensure Board, signed as Public Act 104-0803

    Jev: ACT 88 · Claude: ACT 95 · IL · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Omnibus School Code rewrite signed by Governor Pritzker on 2026-08-07 as Public Act 104-0803, effective the same day. It amends the departments and functions of the Illinois State Board of Education, the teacher supply and demand report, the State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board, the qualifications of educators, provisional educator endorsements on Educator Licenses with Stipulations, educator testing exemptions, the Teacher Performance Assessment Advisory Committee, and teacher and principal model evaluation templates. It also touches evidence-based funding, charter school renewals, waivers and modifications of mandates and administrative rules, school district audits and statements of affairs, the Illinois Purchased Care Review Board, and provisions for students who are parents, expectant parents, or victims of domestic or sexual violence. It renames the Teacher Certificate Fee Revolving Fund the Teacher Licensure Fee Revolving Fund, replaces 'foreign language' with 'world language' and 'ethnic school' with 'community-based heritage language school', repeals the Community Service Education Act, and makes conforming changes to the Postsecondary and Workforce Readiness Act, the State Finance Act, and various public-university governance Acts. Roll calls as printed in the ILGA action list: House Third Reading 071-034-000 (2026-04-09), Senate Third Reading 043-014-000 (2026-05-20), House concurrence in Senate Committee Amendment No. 1, 074-037-000 (2026-05-27).

    Relay angle. The statutory machinery governing Relay's Illinois program is now rewritten and in force, not pending. The section-by-section read of the enrolled text (see text_analysis) stands: the direction is predominantly loosening — a new provisional educator endorsement for out-of-state and out-of-country trained applicants, content-test reciprocity, coursework exemptions, and assessment exemption windows extended a year. The State Educator Preparation and Licensure Board's appointments move from the State Board of Education to the State Superintendent, which is governance rather than standards. Because the Act is effective immediately, the provisional-endorsement and reciprocity pathways are available to candidates now, and the open question moves entirely to ISBE's implementing rules.

    Implications.

    • program — The new provisional educator endorsement (105 ILCS 5/21B-20(2)(P)) and the 21B-35 reciprocity exemptions are live as of 2026-08-07 — no waiting period. Fold both into Illinois admissions and candidate advising now; the recruiting window for out-of-state-trained teachers opened this month, not in September.

    • compliance — Relay's Illinois program approval now sits under a board whose members and secretary are appointed by the State Superintendent rather than the State Board of Education. Update the relationship map; the approval standards themselves are unchanged in the sections read.

    • advocacy — The veto question is closed. Remaining advocacy surface is downstream ISBE rulemaking — the rules implementing the provisional endorsement, the content-test reciprocity exemption, and the coursework-checklist exemption. Watch the Illinois Register for those proposals.

    • risk — Districts may now seek waivers from the mandate that student-performance data be a significant factor in teacher and principal evaluations (the 2-3.25g deletion). If uptake spreads, evaluation practice in partner districts could drift away from Relay's training content.

    Jev: ACT 81 · Claude: ACT 83 · TN · LEGISLATION

    What it does. HB2426 / SB2404, passed 2026-04-21 and approved by the Governor in May 2026 as Public Chapter 1133. Section 2 adds a new section to Tenn. Code Ann. Title 49, Chapter 5, Part 56 directing the State Board of Education to promulgate rules creating a pathway for privately operated child care programs (as defined in 49-1-1102) and licensed child care agencies (as defined in 71-3-501) serving children from birth to kindergarten enrollment to be approved as CLINICAL PRACTICE SITES for an educator preparation program offering a birth-to-kindergarten endorsement on the initial license. The pathway is conditional: the educator preparation program must operate a registered apprenticeship program approved by the Department of Education, and the site must be either a DHS-licensed child care agency or a child care program certified, approved or otherwise authorized by the Department of Education, and must meet the State Board's clinical-experience requirements and standards. Rules are to be promulgated under the Uniform Administrative Procedures Act. Section 1 creates an early educator workforce development resource task force chaired by the Commissioner of Labor and Workforce Development, which must catalog existing state-supported routes into early education (Tennessee Promise, Tennessee Reconnect, career and technical education and dual enrollment, registered apprenticeships for aspiring early educators, federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act funds, and Workforce Pell), assess gaps including those left by discontinued programs, and report findings and recommendations to the Governor and legislative committees by 2026-12-31, at which point the task force ceases to exist. Members serve without compensation and the task force may draw on nonprofit or community-based organizations for stakeholder engagement and data collection. Section 3 makes Section 1 and the rulemaking authority in Section 2 effective on becoming law (2026-05-22); Section 2 takes effect for all other purposes on 2026-07-01.

    Relay angle. Tennessee is one of the five states where Relay has deep partnerships, and this act sets a condition on who may host clinical practice for a birth-to-K endorsement: only an educator preparation program operating a Department-approved registered apprenticeship unlocks the new private child care site pool. That is a direct program-design lever — the apprenticeship is the key, not the endorsement. The task force's December 31 report is the second surface: it is explicitly permitted to draw on nonprofit organizations, and it will name the gaps that later funding follows.

    Stage. Enacted; rulemaking authority live since 2026-05-22, substantive provisions since 2026-07-01. Next expected event: State Board of Education rules under the Uniform Administrative Procedures Act — no filed rule observed this run (tn.gov SBE meetings page returned 404 to a plain client; not confirmed either way). Task force report due 2026-12-31.

    Implications.

    • program — A Department-approved registered apprenticeship program is the entry condition for the new clinical-site pool. If Relay Tennessee wants birth-to-K clinical placements in private child care settings, the apprenticeship is the prerequisite to build, not an optional add-on.

    • partnership — Private child care providers and licensed child care agencies become a viable placement network for the first time, which is a different partner set from the LEA and charter relationships Relay already holds in Tennessee.

    • advocacy — The State Board rules are unwritten. What counts as a qualifying registered apprenticeship, and what clinical-experience standards a child care site must meet, are both open.

    • funding — The task force must report by 2026-12-31 on gaps in early-educator training and credentialing, naming Workforce Pell and Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act dollars among the resources to be better leveraged. Gap findings in that report are where the next Tennessee early-educator funding is most likely to attach.

    CO SB26-126 — out-of-state teacher licensure opened: 7-year recency limit repealed, 30-day Compact licensing with no added coursework, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 67)

    Jev: ACT 73 · Claude: ACT 71 · CO · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 67 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act amends C.R.S. 22-60.5-201 to widen two routes into a Colorado teacher license for people licensed elsewhere. First, it removes the requirement that the three years of successful, evaluated out-of-state teaching experience supporting a professional teacher license have occurred within the previous seven years, so older experience now counts. Second, it adds a new subsection (6) requiring the Department of Education to issue an INITIAL teacher license within thirty days of receiving a complete application from a person licensed by a state participating in the Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact, where the applicant holds an unencumbered eligible license equivalent to a Colorado eligible license, is not subject to current disciplinary action, suspension, investigation or restriction, and has cleared a Colorado criminal history record check. Critically, subsection (6)(b) bars the department from requiring any additional coursework, examinations or program completions beyond those three conditions as a condition of INITIAL license issuance, while expressly preserving its authority to require them for license RENEWAL. The department must determine which Colorado endorsement areas most closely correspond to the applicant's out-of-state license, and must publish an annual table mapping licenses from each reciprocal-agreement state to Colorado endorsement areas. Subsection (6) self-repeals once the department begins issuing licenses under the Compact itself.

    Relay angle. This cuts both ways for Relay and the honest read holds both. Subsection (6)(b) forbids Colorado from requiring additional program completions of Compact-state licensees at initial issuance, which is a straightforward reduction in demand for Colorado-specific preparation among already-licensed teachers. At the same time, a national, multi-state, primarily-online provider benefits more than an in-state one from a regime where a license earned in one state travels cleanly: Relay completers licensed elsewhere gain a fast, thirty-day path into Colorado classrooms, and the removal of the seven-year recency limit helps career-changers and returners, a population Relay's model already serves. The annual endorsement-crosswalk table is a concrete artifact worth obtaining as soon as CDE first publishes it — it will state, officially, how licenses Relay's completers hold map onto Colorado endorsements.

    Implications.

    • risk — Subsection (6)(b) prohibits Colorado from requiring additional coursework, examinations or program completions of Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact licensees at initial issuance. For already-licensed teachers moving into Colorado, that removes a route by which preparation providers pick up incremental enrollment.

    • program — Relay completers licensed in a Compact state now have a statutory thirty-day path to a Colorado initial license. A multi-state footprint becomes a recruiting argument in Colorado in a way it was not before.

    • program — Repeal of the seven-year recency limit on the three-years-experience route reopens the professional-license path for career-changers and re-entrants whose classroom experience is older — a population that maps onto Relay's candidate profile.

    • compliance — The department may still require additional coursework, examinations or program completions as a condition of license RENEWAL. Advising should distinguish the initial-issuance bar from renewal requirements rather than treating Compact entry as a permanent exemption.

    • advocacy — CDE must publish an annual table mapping each reciprocal state's licenses to Colorado endorsement areas. Obtaining the first published table establishes how Relay completers' credentials are officially classified, and the table's construction is a reasonable point of engagement.

    IL HB5321 — only accredited graduate credit with an instructor of record may count for teacher salary advancement (Public Act 104-0795)

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 87 · IL · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Adds a new Section 24-8.2 to the Employment of Teachers Article of the Illinois School Code, signed 2026-08-07 as Public Act 104-0795 and effective the same day. For continuing education coursework completed on or after July 1, 2026, a school district, special education cooperative, or other public educational employer may recognize that coursework for salary advancement ONLY IF it (1) is graduate-level, degree-eligible credit offered through a regionally accredited institution of higher education and documented on an official academic transcript, and (2) includes an instructor of record. The Act defines 'graduate-level, degree-eligible credit' as transcripted credit applicable toward a master's, education specialist, or doctoral degree, and defines 'instructor of record' as a credentialed educator holding at least a master's degree, academically qualified in the content area, who provides substantive instructional support throughout the course and returns individualized written feedback aligned to course objectives. It applies only to licensed classroom teachers holding a Professional Educator License under Section 21B-20 who are covered by a collective bargaining agreement, and expressly excludes administrators. Carve-outs: nothing requires an employer to create a salary schedule or advancement pathway that does not already exist, nothing precludes bargaining over other compensation-related advancement, and implementation — documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, compliance monitoring — is left to each employer rather than to State Board rulemaking. Passed unanimously at every recorded vote: House 105-0-0 (2026-04-16), Senate 57-0-0 (2026-05-21), House concurrence 112-0-0 (2026-05-28).

    Relay angle. This regulates the market for Relay's Illinois products directly, and it cuts both ways. Relay is a Middle States-accredited, master's-degree-granting institution, so its MAT and advanced-certificate coursework is exactly the transcripted graduate credit the Act preserves as salary-bearing — competitors selling ungraded, self-paced, non-transcripted seat-hour PD are now barred from Illinois salary lanes. The same clause is a risk to Relay's other Illinois line: Teacher Professional Education, the job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD product, does not carry transcripted graduate credit and so cannot support a lane change under the new Section unless it is delivered through the degree-granting side with an instructor of record.

    Implications.

    • risk — Relay's Teacher Professional Education line (job-embedded coaching and microcredential PD) is not graduate-level, degree-eligible transcripted credit. Where Illinois district contracts were sold partly on teachers earning salary-lane movement, that value proposition no longer holds for coursework completed on or after 2026-07-01. Audit the Illinois PD contracts and any marketing language that implies lane credit.

    • program — The clean response is a credit-bearing delivery path: route Illinois PD sequences through the degree-granting side so participants receive transcripted graduate credit with a named instructor of record who grades and gives written feedback. The Act's instructor-of-record definition (master's degree, content-qualified, substantive support throughout, individualized written feedback) is a design spec, not a formality.

    • partnership — Section 24-8.2(f) leaves documentation, transcript verification, accreditation checks, and compliance monitoring to each district and special education cooperative individually. Illinois partners now need a per-district answer on what evidence they will accept — an opening to supply that documentation package rather than wait to be asked for it.

    • funding — For the MAT and advanced-certificate lines this is favorable demand policy: Illinois teachers seeking lane movement are pushed toward accredited graduate credit, which is what Relay sells. Worth testing in Illinois enrollment messaging for the coming cycles.

    • compliance — The Act imposes no direct obligation on Relay as an institution — the duty runs to the employer recognizing the credit. Relay's exposure is entirely commercial and reputational: being able to evidence regional accreditation, transcripting, and instructor of record on demand.

    Source. Illinois General Assembly (ilga.gov bill status + enrolled full text)

    IN Public Law 150 (SB204) — a STEM bachelor's plus nine credits now earns a grades 5-12 initial teaching license, treated by statute as equal to finishing a preparation program

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 82 · IN · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Senate Bill 204, enacted as Public Law 150, amends Indiana Code 20-28-5-16.5 effective July 1, 2026. As amended, the Department of Education SHALL grant an initial practitioner license to an individual who: holds a bachelor's degree with a grade point average of at least 2.5 on a 4.0 scale from an accredited postsecondary institution with a major in any combination of science, technology, engineering or mathematics; completes at least nine academic credits covering high-impact practices in lesson planning, instructional design, instructional activities, learning modalities and (where applicable) laboratory experiments, use of digital media, learning management software and technology, teaching inductive and deductive reasoning, metacognition, problem framing, interpreting results and data-based decision making, diagnostic, direct, indirect, formative and summative assessment, feedback loops, engagement and peer-to-peer and small-group strategies, constructive feedback and preventing disruptive behavior, early intervention strategies and professional standards, and teaching students with disabilities; demonstrates subject-matter proficiency by written examination under IC 20-28-5-12(b)(2); completes the training in IC 20-28-5-12.3; and participates in one or more of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives, or full-term student teaching, as determined by the Department. A licensee under this section may teach only in grades 5 through 12 as determined by the Department, may not be granted the license to teach special education, and — by express statutory command — 'shall be treated in the same manner as an individual who receives an initial practitioner license after completing a traditional teacher preparation program,' including during the transition from an initial practitioner to a practitioner license. The section was originally added by P.L.194-2025; this act amends it.

    Relay angle. Indiana is an authorized Relay jurisdiction, and this is a nine-credit statutory substitute for the thing Relay sells. A candidate with a STEM bachelor's and a 2.5 GPA can reach a grades 5-12 Indiana license without enrolling in a preparation program at all, and the statute forbids treating that licensee differently from a program completer. That is a direct competitive threat to a graduate teacher-preparation pathway in exactly the shortage fields where alternative certification demand concentrates. It is also an opening: the nine credits have to be taught by someone, the coursework list reads like a syllabus Relay already teaches, and Indiana law does not say who may offer it. One caveat on our own side of the ledger — Relay's Indiana operating footprint is an open verification item in the org profile, so the size of the exposure is not yet established.

    Stage. Enacted and in force. Signed into law as Public Law 150 on 2026-03-12; the amended IC 20-28-5-16.5 is effective July 1, 2026, so the route is live now. Next expected event is Department of Education implementation — the statute leaves the Department to determine the grade range and which of the four experience options applies, and no Indiana rulemaking notice was located this run.

    Implications.

    • risk — A nine-credit, no-program route to a grades 5-12 Indiana license, statutorily equal to a preparation-program completion, undercuts the value proposition of a graduate teacher-prep pathway for STEM candidates in Indiana.

    • program — The nine required credits map closely onto content Relay already delivers. Indiana law does not name an approved provider for them, which makes a for-credit nine-hour sequence for STEM degree holders a concrete product question rather than a speculative one.

    • compliance — The license may not be issued for special education and is capped at grades 5-12, so Relay's special-education advanced certificate line and any K-4 pathway are outside the substitution.

    • advocacy — The Department of Education decides which of job shadowing, field experiences, teaching cooperatives or full-term student teaching satisfies the clinical requirement. That determination is where preparation quality is either preserved or hollowed out, and it is made administratively, not legislatively.

    Source. legiscan_in

    CO HB26-1090 — teacher, EPP-student and charter-hire criminal-disclosure certifications rewritten into four categories, effective Aug 12 (Ch. 68)

    Jev: ACT 72 · Claude: ACT 77 · CO · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Signed by the Governor on 2026-04-20 as Session Laws Chapter 68 and effective at 12:01 a.m. on 2026-08-12, this act rewrites the criminal-conviction certification that three different populations must sign under penalty of perjury, and it makes the same change in all three places: teacher-license applicants (C.R.S. 22-60.5-103(2)(a)), students in educator preparation programs (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3(2)(a)), and applicants offered employment by a charter school (C.R.S. 22-30.5-110.7(2)). The prior form required disclosure of every misdemeanor regardless of date, excluding only traffic offenses. The act replaces that with four categories: (A) any felony, regardless of date; (B) any misdemeanor for which an element of the offense was that the victim was an at-risk person as defined in section 18-6.5-102 or a child under eighteen, regardless of date; (C) any other misdemeanor where the application is submitted within seven years after the disposition of the conviction, still excluding traffic offenses and infractions; and (D) any misdemeanor enumerated as grounds for denial, annulment, suspension, or revocation of a license, certificate, endorsement, or authorization under 22-60.5-107(2)(b), regardless of date. New language requires that each conviction in these four categories be listed individually, with the offense, the date of conviction, and the court entering judgment. Each of the three statutes also gains a savings clause stating the change does not alter the department's obligation to evaluate criminal convictions under C.R.S. 24-5-101. A provision in the introduced bill that would have required the department to waive the program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for applicants with two or more years of Colorado private school teaching experience does NOT appear in the final act — it was removed before enactment.

    Relay angle. Section 2 amends the record check that Relay's own Colorado educator-preparation students execute, so this is a Relay compliance surface rather than an ecosystem observation: the certification language and the itemized-listing requirement changed, and the act has been in force since yesterday. Section 3 does the same for charter-school hiring, which is the placement channel for much of Relay's network. The stripped private-school waiver is the quieter finding: had it survived, Colorado would have let two years of private-school experience substitute for completing a preparation program, a direct substitution for what Relay sells. It did not survive, and that is worth recording as a live legislative appetite rather than a settled question.

    Implications.

    • compliance — Relay's Colorado educator-preparation record-check certification (C.R.S. 22-2-119.3) must match the new four-category language and the requirement that each conviction be listed individually with offense, date and court. The act is already in force, so any form still using the old 'all misdemeanors regardless of date' text is out of date now, not at some future compliance date.

    • program — Candidates previously deterred by having to disclose decades-old minor misdemeanors now disclose non-traffic misdemeanors only within a seven-year window, which modestly widens the admissible Colorado applicant pool. Offenses against at-risk persons or children, and licensure-disqualifying misdemeanors, remain lifetime-disclosable.

    • risk — The introduced version would have waived program-of-preparation, alternative-teacher-program and induction requirements for two years of Colorado private-school experience. It was removed before enactment, but the proposal establishes that an experience-for-preparation substitution has sponsors in Colorado and may return in a later session.

    • partnership — Section 3 changes the same certification for charter-school employment offers, so Relay's Colorado charter partners are updating the identical form on the identical timeline — a low-cost, concrete reason to compare notes with placement partners.

    Source. Colorado General Assembly (leg.colorado.gov bill page HB26-1090; Final Act text, bill_files/114467; Session Laws Ch. 68)

    CT Public Act 26-149 — aspiring educators scholarship redefined and opened statewide (up to $10k/yr), teacher-shortage areas now include underrepresented subgroups

    Jev: ACT 70 · Claude: TRACK 69 · DISAGREE · CT · LEGISLATION

    What it does. Substitute Senate Bill 220, signed 2026-06-04 as Public Act 26-149. Section 2 rewrites C.R.S.-equivalent Conn. Gen. Stat. 10-156ii, renaming the 'aspiring educators diversity scholarship' the 'aspiring educators scholarship' and changing who qualifies: the geographic restriction to graduates of alliance-district high schools is replaced with graduation from any public high school in the state, while the beneficiary definition narrows from 'diverse students' to 'aspiring educators', meaning individuals in a population subgroup that is underrepresented in the teaching profession AND identified as a teacher shortage area by the Commissioner of Education under section 10-8b. The award remains up to $10,000 per year while the recipient is enrolled and in good standing in a teacher preparation program at any FOUR-YEAR institution of higher education. The department must develop an administration policy by 2027-01-01 and award annually from the fiscal year ending 2027-06-30 onward; the Commissioner must develop repayment criteria for recipients who do not go on to teach as certified teachers in Connecticut. Section 3 rewrites section 10-8b so the Commissioner must annually by December 1 identify teacher shortage areas in three categories — subject, geographic, and population subgroups underrepresented in the profession — certify them to the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, and by March 1 distribute shortage-area information covering at least the prior five years to the president of every institution of higher education in the state offering a teacher preparatory program. Section 4 (effective 2027-01-01) establishes an American Sign Language education working group charged with recommending curriculum guidance, ASL teacher certification standards including a proficiency benchmark, an alternative certification pathway for native ASL users and interpreters, and reciprocity with other states' ASL certifications, plus guidance to educator preparation programs on expanding ASL programs, creating incentives such as tuition support and credit enhancement, and establishing bridge, endorsement or alternative programs. Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in a public school rather than only those employed by a local or regional board of education, reaching charter school paraeducators, with up to $300,000 of unexpended FY2026 funds transferred by 2026-07-15.

    Relay angle. Two Relay-relevant asymmetries. The scholarship — the money in this act — is restricted to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education, which excludes a graduate school of education, so Relay's Connecticut candidates cannot reach these dollars. But Section 3's distribution duty runs to every institution offering a teacher preparatory program, which does include Relay Connecticut, and the newly required identification of underrepresented population subgroups as formal shortage areas is a designation Relay's recruitment work is well positioned to speak to. Section 4's charge to advise educator preparation programs on alternative-route and bridge programs for native ASL users is the clearest programme-design opening in the act, though it does not begin until January 2027.

    Implications.

    • risk — The up-to-$10,000 aspiring educators scholarship is limited to teacher preparation programs at four-year institutions of higher education. Relay's Connecticut candidates are structurally outside it, and the same exclusion appears in Delaware's new Teacher Academy scholarship — a pattern worth naming rather than treating as two coincidences.

    • advocacy — From December 1 each year the Commissioner must formally identify population subgroups underrepresented in teaching as shortage areas. That designation drives scholarship eligibility, and it is a decision Relay's recruitment and completer data speak to directly.

    • program — Section 4's working group must advise educator preparation programs on bridge, endorsement and alternative-route programs for native ASL users and certified interpreters seeking teacher certification — an alternative-certification design space matching what Relay already operates. It convenes from 2027-01-01.

    • compliance — By March 1 annually the department must send five years of shortage-area data to every Connecticut institution offering a teacher preparatory program. Relay Connecticut should be on that distribution list and should confirm it is.

    • partnership — Section 6 extends the paraeducator health-benefit subsidy to paraeducators employed in public schools including charter schools, strengthening a paraeducator-to-teacher pipeline population that alternative-route providers recruit from.

    Source. Connecticut General Assembly (cga.ct.gov, Public Act 26-149 full text)

    ED proposes full rewrite of accreditor-recognition rules (34 CFR 602) — comment window closed Sept 21, now at drafting

    Jev: ACT 63 · Claude: ACT 87 · US · REGULATION

    What it does. Notice of proposed rulemaking rewriting the Secretary's accrediting-agency recognition regulations at 34 CFR part 602 (conforming changes to parts 600 and 668) to implement Executive Order 14279. Verified from the Federal Register text this run, the NPRM: requires accreditors to hold member institutions to program-level student-outcome expectations — completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns — assessed "without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex"; requires accreditation decisions to be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology (proposed 602.18, with a religious-mission exception); adds academic-freedom and intellectual-diversity review, cost-benefit analysis, and program-length review to 602.17; REMOVES the 602.15(a)(4) requirement that programmatic accreditors seat educators, practitioners, and employers on evaluation and decision-making bodies; lowers barriers to recognizing new accreditors and to institutions switching accreditors (new 602.12(e): qualifying experience may be national, State, or programmatic); and makes it a recognition-review factor whether an agency joined a "concerted effort to unnecessarily restrict the qualifications necessary for a student to sit for a licensure or certification examination" or inflated entry requirements through "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" (proposed 602.31(g)(1)). Docket ED-2025-OPE-1042, RIN 1840-AD82. Comments close 2026-09-21 (~21 business days), via regulations.gov only — no fax or email.

    Update 2026-09-23: the FTC's Office of Policy Planning and Bureau of Competition filed a comment on Monday September 21 — the last day of the window — strongly endorsing the proposal, and the Commission issued a press release on September 22 (read raw this run). The comment argues that accreditation monopolies drive up tuition, limit choice and stifle innovation because incumbent accreditors have an incentive to impose rigid requirements and oppose flexible standards, citing that 21 of 27 commissioners on the Middle States Commission on Higher Education are university administrators or faculty. The comment states that the situation for PROGRAMMATIC accreditors — the category that covers educator preparation — is 'often worse,' because they are guided by incumbent members of the profession with incentives to raise educational costs and create barriers to lower-cost alternatives.

    Relay angle. Relay's operating licenses run through this rule twice: MSCHE (institutional accreditor and Title IV gatekeeper) and CAEP (educator-prep accreditor) are both Secretary-recognized under Part 602, so the proposed outcome metrics and the credential-inflation review factor would reshape the standards both apply to Relay.

    Stage. Proposed rule; comment window closed 2026-09-21. The FTC's competition staff filed a supporting comment on the closing day and publicized it September 22. Next expected event: the final rule; ED has not published a date. NACIQI, which applies the current recognition criteria, is in session today and tomorrow on six renewals — the two tracks are running in parallel.

    Response window. Closed 2026-09-21. No remaining input route before the final rule. (0 business days out.)

    Implications.

    • compliance — MSCHE and CAEP would be re-reviewed against rewritten recognition criteria; whatever standards survive flow down into Relay's next reaffirmation cycles, with program-level completion, licensure pass-rate, and earnings data as the evidence currency.

    • program — Program-level economic-returns metrics put graduate-EPP tuition-to-earnings ratios under accreditor scrutiny — Relay's employment and certification outcomes become either an accreditation asset or an exposure, program by program.

    • risk — Proposed 602.31(g)(1) treats "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" for entering a profession as a mark against an accreditor's recognition — a federal thumb on the scale against graduate-level entry expectations for teaching, rhyming with the state-level deregulation the board is already tracking (IN Pub. L. 150, CO SB26-126).

    • advocacy — Comment window open to 2026-09-21. Relay can speak as a graduate EPP with strong licensure outcomes; coordination with AACTE and with MSCHE/CAEP comment strategies is the near-term decision.

    • advocacy — A sitting federal competition authority has now argued on the record that programmatic accreditors — the category that includes educator-preparation accreditation — create barriers to lower-cost alternatives. That framing, if it survives into the final rule's preamble, is favorable to alternative-route providers and worth tracking as the rationale, not just the rule.

    The short version

    New York City banned classroom AI for two-thirds of its students three weeks ago and this board never saw it. On September 2 the Mayor and Chancellor imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI in grades 2-K through 8 — close to 600,000 students — with graded screen-time caps beneath it, five named approved pilots as the only permitted high-school use, and a mandatory two-module AI-literacy requirement for every high-school student. Both the announcement and the standing policy page were read in full this run. It reached the board only because an opinion column linked the policy page; no NYCPS source is wired, in the district that employs more of Relay's graduates than any other. That is the run's most consequential finding and its most consequential gap. The mandatory AI-literacy modules are teaching work that nobody was prepared to do, in Relay's home market, with a one-year clock on the district's own decision.

    A federal court threw out the rule that would have made Head Start check every family's papers. On September 21 Judge Mary S. McElroy in Rhode Island granted summary judgment to twenty states and the District of Columbia, declaring the July 2025 PRWORA notices unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act, vacating them, and enjoining HHS, ED and DOL from enforcing them against the plaintiffs. The full twenty-five-page order was located through the New York Attorney General's decisions archive and read here rather than taken from coverage — the same plaintiff-state-AG route that produced last run's Teacher Quality Partnership order, now used twice. The Department of Education is a named defendant. The caveat is the whole story for planning purposes: the court ruled the agencies skipped notice-and-comment, not that the policy is forbidden, and expressly left them free to re-promulgate through proper rulemaking. Read it as a threat deferred and a future comment window, not a threat removed.

    The federal government is putting the loan-forgiveness loyalty oath back in the drawer, and the window is open. A Federal Register notice published this morning removes the employer attestation — sworn under penalty of perjury that the employer engaged in no activity with a substantial illegal purpose — from the PSLF certification form, because a judge vacated the rule behind it on June 30, one day before it would have taken effect. Comments run to October 22. The executive order that produced the attestation has not been rescinded, so this is the current state, not a settled one.

    Three federal windows are at the edge. EDGAR closes tomorrow. The New York science-of-reading rule for teacher preparation programs has three business days (its September 27 deadline falls on a Sunday; Friday the 25th is the last business day). New York's accountability rewrite has five.

    Texas still will not say what it did. Four checks on, TEA has published no Chapter 229 adoption outcome; its own "Adopted Rules — Not Yet Effective" page states there are none, and this run tea.texas.gov did not answer a plain client at all. The agenda confirms Item 6 was the adoption motion. The 80 percent Accredited bar should not be treated as adopted.

    A rubric gap worth the operator's attention, now precisely diagnosed. COURT is not a defined signal class in config/impact.yaml, and the liveness gate has no COURT clause — it names LEGISLATION, REGULATION, AGENCY and COMMENTARY only. The consequence showed up immediately: the PRWORA order, entered yesterday with continuing legal effect, scored a liveness gate of 0.36 and drew ARCHIVE(liveness) advice. The board's three court rulings currently carry three different classes — COURT, AGENCY and COMMENTARY — because there is no class for them to take, and the gate treats each differently in consequence. This is the same shape as the AGENCY gap the operator closed on 2026-09-20, and the same fix would close it. Related and softer: 28 of the 30 archive-advised rows on the first scoring pass were carried rows whose text had not changed, since the per-run status and movement markers reset on every carried row by design and the gate reads that as staleness. One caveat on that observation, stated because the first version of this digest overstated it: re-scoring the same unchanged row twice in one morning produced liveness 0.49 with archive advice and then 0.51 without it, so single-row readings wobble around the threshold. The aggregate and the missing COURT class are the solid findings; the single controlled case is suggestive, not decisive.

    Business-day counts exclude federal holidays (Columbus Day 10-12, Veterans Day 11-11, Thanksgiving 11-26, Christmas 12-25).

    Leadership brief — ED proposes EDGAR rewrite — termination 'for convenience,' continuation-award discretion, merit certification for grantees; comments close Sept 23

    Update September 21: two business days remain — comments close Wednesday, September 23, confirmed this morning against the Federal Register's own record. This is the rule that would let the Department cancel grants 'for convenience' and exercise more discretion over continuation awards. A federal court ruled on September 17 against a related mechanism the administration had been using to attach conditions to education money without a rule, which makes this rulemaking the administration's remaining route to the same discretion. The U.S. Department of Education proposed rewriting its general grant rules (called EDGAR) — the terms that govern every discretionary grant the Department makes, including the kinds Relay holds. The headline changes: the Department would write into regulation its power to end any grant early 'for convenience' (that is, without the grantee doing anything wrong), and to reduce or deny each year's continuation funding at the Secretary's discretion. Grantees would also have to certify that hiring and admissions under the grant are strictly merit-based and that employees are not required to make statements of belief. Public comments are due September 23; final rules are expected late this year.

    Federal grant revenue becomes less predictable: a multi-year award could be ended or reduced at any annual renewal, with limited appeal rights. Grant-funded hiring and admissions language would need legal review against the new merit certification. And applications proposing lower overhead (indirect) rates could earn preference points — a real tradeoff between competitiveness and cost recovery.

    • We have two days. Do we comment, and do we cite the September 17 apportionment ruling?

    • Should Relay file a comment (directly or via AACTE) by September 23, and on which provisions — the continuation-award discretion, the merit certification, or both?

    • Do budget scenarios for current federal awards assume continuation funding that this rule would make discretionary?

    Coverage:

    • FutureEd (early warning, pre-publication)
