    Federal — Federal court vacates the July 2025 PRWORA notices that would have forced Head Start, adult education and other federally funded programs to verify immigration status — HHS, ED and DOL enjoined as to twenty states and DC · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in SCAN

    Jev: SCAN 57 · Claude: ACT 70 · DISAGREE · NEW

    Title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 bars some categories of noncitizens from receiving defined federal, state and local public benefits. Quoting the order read this run: shortly after PRWORA's enactment the relevant federal agencies issued guidance interpreting that prohibition as excluding various programs, including those constituting 'widely available services' (61 Fed. Reg. 45,985, Aug. 30, 1996), but 'beginning in July 2025, these agencies took an about-face by issuing new notices that purport to reinterpret PRWORA as applying to a swath of federal programs that had previously been excluded.' Twenty states and the District of Columbia sued. The court had already granted a preliminary injunction, holding that the PRWORA Notices of the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Education and the Department of Labor were final agency action reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, that they implemented legislative rules and were therefore subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking, and that they posed irreparable harm to the plaintiffs given the impracticality and cost of compliance. The parties then agreed to proceed directly to summary judgment. The disposition, quoted from the order's final page: 'The PRWORA Notices are declared unlawful under the APA and are ordered set aside and vacated. Defendants are enjoined from implementing or enforcing the PRWORA Notices or the interpretations contained therein against Plaintiffs by any other means.' One express limit, also quoted: 'this injunction does not prohibit HHS, ED, DOL, HUD, and their respective heads from promulgating new rules related to PRWORA after a period of notice-and-comment rulemaking as required under the APA.' Per the New York Attorney General's release of the same date — attributed, not drawn from the order — the vacated rules threatened Head Start, Title X family planning clinics, food banks, domestic violence shelters, adult education and community health centers, and would have required those programs to check the immigration status of everyone they serve, turning away not only undocumented immigrants but some people with legal status including student visa holders, temporary workers and exchange visitors.

    Relay angle: The Department of Education is a named defendant and its PRWORA notice is among those vacated, which is what puts this on an educator-preparation board rather than a social-services one. Two threads matter to Relay. First, Head Start and adult education are early-childhood and adult-workforce employers whose staffing this verification regime would have disrupted directly; a program that must check the status of everyone it serves is a program with less capacity for everything else, including hosting and supervising candidates. Second, and more durable: the court did not bar the agencies from trying again. It held the notices were legislative rules that skipped notice and comment, and expressly left HHS, ED, DOL and HUD free to promulgate new PRWORA rules through proper rulemaking. That converts an adverse policy into a probable future comment window, which is the form in which this board can actually act on it. Nothing is required of Relay now.

    Stage / latest action: Decided 2026-09-21 by Judge Mary S. McElroy, District of Rhode Island. Plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment granted. The order was located through the New York Attorney General's decisions archive — the same plaintiff-state-AG route that produced the Teacher Quality Partnership order on 2026-09-21 — and read in full via pdftotext this run.

    Implications:

    • risk — The order rests on procedure, not substance: the agencies were told they skipped notice-and-comment, and are expressly free to re-promulgate through proper rulemaking. Treat this as a threat deferred, not removed.

    • advocacy — A re-promulgated PRWORA rule from the Department of Education would arrive with a comment window; that is the point at which a preparation institution with placements in Head Start and adult-education settings has standing to say what verification would cost.

    • partnership — Head Start and adult-education providers in the twenty plaintiff states and DC are relieved of a verification burden that would have consumed administrative capacity — capacity that clinical placement and mentoring draw on.

    Leadership brief — A federal court has struck down the rule that would have made Head Start check every family's immigration status

    In July 2025 four federal agencies, including the Department of Education, reinterpreted a 1996 welfare law to cover a wide range of programs that had always been exempt from it. The practical effect would have been that programs like Head Start, adult education, food banks and community health centers had to verify the immigration status of everyone they served and turn away anyone who could not prove it — which, the states argued, would have caught citizens and lawful residents who simply lack government identification. Twenty states and the District of Columbia sued. On September 21 a federal judge in Rhode Island ruled for them, declared the agencies' notices unlawful, and threw them out. We located and read the full twenty-five-page order rather than relying on coverage. One caveat matters: the judge ruled the agencies broke the rules for how policy must be made, not that the policy itself is forbidden, and explicitly said they may try again if they go through the proper public comment process.

    Nothing is required of us today. Head Start and adult education programs employ early-childhood and adult educators and host candidates, and they have just been relieved of an administrative burden that would have consumed a great deal of their capacity. The part to watch is the opening the judge left: if the Department of Education comes back through formal rulemaking, there will be a public comment period, and that is the moment we could say something useful about what verification would cost the programs our people work in.

    • Do we want to be positioned to comment if the Department of Education re-issues this through formal rulemaking, and who would own that?

    • Do we have visibility into how many of our placements and alumni sit in Head Start or adult-education settings, which is what would tell us how much this actually matters to us?

    Notice of proposed rulemaking rewriting the Secretary's accrediting-agency recognition regulations at 34 CFR part 602 (conforming changes to parts 600 and 668) to implement Executive Order 14279. Verified from the Federal Register text this run, the NPRM: requires accreditors to hold member institutions to program-level student-outcome expectations — completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns — assessed "without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex"; requires accreditation decisions to be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology (proposed 602.18, with a religious-mission exception); adds academic-freedom and intellectual-diversity review, cost-benefit analysis, and program-length review to 602.17; REMOVES the 602.15(a)(4) requirement that programmatic accreditors seat educators, practitioners, and employers on evaluation and decision-making bodies; lowers barriers to recognizing new accreditors and to institutions switching accreditors (new 602.12(e): qualifying experience may be national, State, or programmatic); and makes it a recognition-review factor whether an agency joined a "concerted effort to unnecessarily restrict the qualifications necessary for a student to sit for a licensure or certification examination" or inflated entry requirements through "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" (proposed 602.31(g)(1)).     Leadership brief — Federal proposal rewrites the rules for college accreditors

    Update September 21: TODAY IS THE LAST DAY to file a comment. The Education Department's rewrite of the rules governing how it recognizes accreditors closes its public comment period at the end of today, September 21, confirmed this morning against the Federal Register's own record. After today the only remaining influence on this rule is through our accreditors and through sector associations. The U.S. Department of Education proposed new rules for how it recognizes accreditors — the organizations that certify colleges and control access to federal student aid. The proposal would push accreditors to judge institutions on measurable results for each program: how many students finish, how many pass licensure exams, and what graduates earn. It would also make it easier for new accreditors to enter the market and for institutions to switch accreditors, and it directs the Department to weigh, when reviewing an accreditor, whether that accreditor helped raise the education requirements needed to enter a profession. Public comments are open until September 21, 2026.

    Both of Relay's accreditors — Middle States (institutional) and CAEP (educator preparation) — are recognized under the rules being rewritten, so the standards Relay is held to in future reviews would change. Program-level results reporting would become the currency of accreditation, and the provision against raising professional entry requirements could add federal pressure against graduate-degree expectations for teachers.

    • This closes today. Is anyone filing on Relay's behalf, and if not, is that a deliberate choice or an oversight?

    • Are our program-level completion, certification pass-rate, and graduate-earnings data ready to stand as accreditation evidence?

    • If switching accreditors becomes cheap and new accreditors enter, does our own accreditation strategy change?

    Federal — Education Department moves to strip the 'substantial illegal purpose' employer attestation back out of the PSLF certification form after a federal judge vacated the rule — 30-day OMB comment window closes Oct 22 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in SCAN

    Jev: SCAN 46 · Claude: ACT 82 · DISAGREE · 21 business days · NEW

    Federal Student Aid is asking OMB to approve a revision to the Public Service Loan Forgiveness and Temporary Expanded PSLF Certification and Application form (OMB 1845-0110), and the revision is a removal. Quoting the notice read this run: 'The Department is now removing the attestation from the PSLF form in order to comply with the court order. No other changes have been made at this time.' The attestation in question required a borrower's employer to swear, under penalty of perjury, that it had not engaged in any activity with a substantial illegal purpose on or after July 1, 2026. It was added to implement Executive Order 14325 ('Restoring Public Service Loan Forgiveness,' signed March 7, 2025), which made individuals employed by organizations whose activities have a substantial illegal purpose ineligible for PSLF; the requirement was written into 34 CFR 685.219(i) by final regulations published October 31, 2025 (90 FR 48966). On Tuesday, June 30, 2026 — one day before the rule was to take effect — a federal judge vacated it. The Department has requested emergency processing for the revision. The collection covers an estimated 913,713 annual responses and 456,857 annual burden hours. Borrowers use the form to have qualifying public-service employment certified and progress toward forgiveness recorded; they are encouraged to file annually and required to file at 120 qualifying monthly payments. This notice is the 30-day OMB stage of the collection this board already tracks at the 60-day ED stage (fedreg:2026-14053, comments closed 2026-09-11). Caveat on the notice's own text: it dates the NPRM to 'August 18, 2026' while citing 90 FR 40154 and a comment close of 'September 17, 2025' — the year on the NPRM date appears to be an error in the notice, and this board does not restate it as fact.

    Relay angle: Relay is a nonprofit whose graduates go to work in public schools, which is the population PSLF exists for, and Relay is itself a PSLF-qualifying employer that certifies employment for its own staff. The vacated attestation would have put every one of those employers — districts, charter networks, Relay itself — in the position of swearing under penalty of perjury about the legality of their own activities before a borrower's payments could count. Its removal restores the prior form and the prior certification burden. The comment window is real and open for 21 business days; the substantive question a commenter can still raise is whether the Department's removal is complete, since the notice says no other changes were made and the underlying executive order has not been rescinded.

    Stage / latest action: Published in the Federal Register 2026-09-22 (Vol. 91, No. 182, p. 60119); filed 2026-09-21. Full notice text fetched raw and read this run. Comments to OMB via reginfo.gov on or before 2026-10-22. Federal Student Aid contact: Linnea Hengst, 202-453-6737.

    Leadership brief — The loan-forgiveness form our graduates depend on is losing the employer loyalty-oath question, and the public can comment until October 22

    Public Service Loan Forgiveness cancels the remaining federal student debt of people who work ten years in public service, including public-school teaching. A 2025 executive order directed the Education Department to disqualify people employed by organizations engaged in activities with a 'substantial illegal purpose,' and the Department put that into effect by adding a line to the forgiveness form requiring the employer to swear, under penalty of perjury, that it had done no such thing. On June 30 of this year — one day before that rule would have started — a federal judge struck it down. The Department has now formally asked the White House budget office to approve taking the line back off the form, and says it has made no other change. The public may comment through October 22. About 914,000 people file this form each year.

    This is a direct financial matter for the teachers we prepare and for Relay as an employer that certifies its own staff's service. Had the rule stood, every district, charter network, and nonprofit employing our graduates would have had to make a sworn legal statement about itself before those graduates' payments counted. That burden is being lifted. It is worth noting the executive order behind it has not been withdrawn, so a redrafted version could return.

    • Is it worth filing a short comment before October 22 describing what the certification process actually costs our alumni and our staff, given how rarely a preparation institution's voice appears in these records?

    • Do we need to notify alumni that the form is changing, and if so, when — the Department has asked for emergency processing, so the timing is not fully predictable?

    • How much weight does loan forgiveness carry in our recruiting case, and what is our position if the Department returns with a redrafted eligibility restriction?

    New York — NY proposes science-of-reading requirements for teacher preparation programs (8 NYCRR 52.21, 80-3.7) — literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, 15 of 100 field-experience hours and the full student-teaching placement spent on evidence-based literacy instruction, SWD literacy credits 6 → 9; comments close Sept 27, adoption expected October

    Jev: ACT 80 · Claude: ACT 86 · 3 business days · UPDATED

    Proposed rulemaking EDU-30-26-00007-P, published in the July 29, 2026 State Register (no hearing; 60-day comment period, so comments are due September 27, 2026; the Register text and the NYSED full-text index both list the rule and neither prints a calendar deadline, so the date is computed from publication). Amends §52.21 program-registration requirements for teacher preparation programs in bilingual education, early childhood (birth-grade 2), childhood (grades 1-6), ESOL, literacy, and special education (blind/visually impaired, deaf/hard-of-hearing, speech and language disabilities, students with disabilities at every level). Requires the study of literacy skills or methods of teaching reading in those programs to align with the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including theories of literacy development, evidence-based instruction, assessment and intervention through a multi-tier framework, and dyslexia, dysgraphia and other language-based learning disabilities (definitions, detection, screener administration, evidence-based instruction, accommodations for ELLs); removes the 'methods of reading enrichment and remediation' language. Clinical requirements for candidates first enrolling Fall 2028 or later: at least 15 of the 100 field-experience clock hours must include evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with one or more students with reading difficulties, and candidates must teach reading and writing throughout the student teaching or residency experience (70 days or longer), assessing learning in whole-group and small-group settings; literacy programs must spend at least 25 of 50 practicum hours the same way. Programs must comply by September 1, 2028 or at new-program registration, whichever is first. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs must add three semester hours in language acquisition and literacy development (six to nine total) for candidates first enrolling Fall 2029 or later; §80-3.7 makes the same 6 → 9 change for the individual-evaluation certification pathway from September 1, 2033. The notice states SWD programs in childhood and adolescence will no longer be registered on or after September 1, 2029. Cost statement names $1,335 CUNY tuition per three-credit course and $7,100 per adjunct literacy course as illustrative private-party costs. Permanent adoption anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Grounded in the Hunt Institute Path Forward initiative (NY joined Fall 2023) and the December 2024 NYS Dyslexia and Dysgraphia Task Force report.

    Relay angle: This is a direct rewrite of what Relay's registered New York programs in childhood education, students with disabilities and any ESOL/bilingual-extension offerings must teach and how their clinical placements must be structured, with a September 1, 2028 compliance date and a residency-specific clause: the entire student teaching or residency experience must include teaching and assessing reading and writing. The comment window is the first and only formal input point before the Regents adopt in October. Never on the board: the rule was published July 29 while the NYSED newsroom source was down and the State Register is not a wired source; found by the cross-engine sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 29 issue.

    Leadership brief — New York wants every teacher preparation program that touches reading to teach the science of reading, and the comment period closes September 27

    Update September 21: four business days remain. Comments are formally due Sunday, September 27, which in practice means filing by Friday, September 25. The New York State Education Department has proposed a rule that would rewrite the literacy requirements for teacher preparation programs in childhood education, early childhood, special education, English as a second language, bilingual education and literacy. Coursework on teaching reading would have to follow the state's Science of Reading Framework, including specific content on dyslexia and related disabilities. Starting with students who enroll in fall 2028, a set share of pre-service field hours would have to be spent teaching a struggling reader, and the student-teaching or residency year would have to include teaching and assessing reading and writing throughout. Special-education programs would add a three-credit literacy course for students who enroll in fall 2029. Programs would have until September 1, 2028 to comply. The Board of Regents is expected to adopt the rule in October; public comments are being accepted until September 27.

    Relay's New York programs in childhood education and special education fall squarely within the rule, and any ESOL or bilingual offering does too. The residency clause matters most: Relay's residency model would need to guarantee that every affected resident teaches and assesses reading and writing across the year, which is straightforward for elementary placements and harder for some secondary and special-education placements. Curriculum revisions and literacy-qualified instructors would be needed before the 2028 deadline, and the comment window is the only formal chance to shape the phase-in and the residency language.

    New York — New York City Public Schools bars student-facing generative AI in grades 2-K through 8 for 2026-27 and caps daily one-to-one screen time, with five approved high-school pilots and a required AI-literacy module · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 62 · Claude: ACT 84 · DISAGREE · NEW

    New York City Public Schools has imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence for grades 2-K through 8, effective for the 2026-27 school year, and layered graduated screen-time limits on top of it. Read from the NYCPS policy page this run, the grid is: grades 2-K through 2, student-facing AI banned and no one-to-one screen time at all; grades 3 through 5, banned, with no more than 30 minutes of daily one-to-one screen time recommended; grades 6 through 8, banned, with no more than 45 minutes recommended; grades 9 through 12, AI limited to approved, vetted programs, with screen time left to the school and course. The district's announcement puts the reach at nearly 600,000 students, about two-thirds of total enrollment. High schools get a required floor and a narrow ceiling: every high-school student must complete two 45-minute AI-literacy modules covering how AI works, data privacy and bias, and appropriate school use, while actual student use of generative AI is confined to five centrally approved pilots (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools), each with a published expected weekly dosage from 15 minutes to one class period, and to career-readiness pathways such as Career and Technical Education and FutureReadyNYC where the tools are used under teacher supervision. Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots; applications are reviewed case by case and a student may participate in only one pilot. Carve-outs: the policy does not reach assistive technology provided through a student's Individualized Education Program or 504 Plan, and it exempts assessments, out-of-school learning, and centrally approved instruction such as e-books, robotics, coding, and simulations from the screen-time caps. Teacher-led whole-group and small-group use of devices remains allowable throughout. Tool selection for the pilots ran through the district's Enterprise Request Management Application data-privacy and security review; NYCPS says it is developing a limited evaluation plan for the pilots.

    Relay angle: This is the single largest employer of Relay's graduates setting the terms of instructional practice they will be evaluated on, and it landed three weeks ago without reaching this board — no NYCPS source is wired. Two things follow directly. First, any Relay coursework, clinical assignment, or edTPA-style performance task that has candidates put students in front of a generative-AI tool is now out of bounds in every 2-K-through-8 placement in the city, and in high school is confined to five named products. Second, the high-school AI-literacy requirement is a teaching task with no established preparation behind it: every NYC high school must deliver two 45-minute modules on how AI works, data privacy, and bias, and the teachers delivering them were not prepared to. That is a preparation gap in Relay's home market that Relay is positioned to fill, and the one-year framing means the district will revisit this before the 2027-28 year with evidence it is actively collecting.

    Stage / latest action: Announced 2026-09-02 by Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels; announcement page updated 2026-09-11. Both the announcement and the standing policy page were fetched raw and read this run. In effect for the 2026-27 school year; the moratorium is stated as a one-year measure.

    Implications:

    • program — Relay's NYC clinical placements in grades 2-K through 8 cannot include student-facing generative-AI activities; any course assignment that assumes students will use such a tool needs to be re-specified before candidates hit those classrooms.

    • program — The mandatory two-module high-school AI-literacy requirement creates immediate in-service demand: NYC high-school teachers must teach how AI works, data privacy, and bias without existing preparation for it.

    • compliance — Only five tools (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, Intel AI-Ready Schools) are approved for student use in grades 9-12, each through a case-by-case school application, with one pilot per student — a constraint Relay's NYC faculty need to know before recommending any tool to a candidate's host school.

    • partnership — NYCPS says it is building a limited evaluation plan for the pilots and frames the moratorium as one year; the evaluation and the renewal decision are both openings for a preparation partner with data on what candidates and mentors actually need.

    • risk — Relay's own AI-in-instruction positioning now runs against its largest district partner's stated posture for two-thirds of that district's students; messaging that presumes classroom AI use will read badly in NYC through at least the 2026-27 year.

    Leadership brief — New York City has banned classroom AI for younger students for this school year — and created teaching work nobody is trained for

    On September 2 the Mayor and the Schools Chancellor announced that for the 2026-27 school year, students in pre-K through eighth grade in New York City public schools may not use generative artificial intelligence — the kind that writes text or makes images on request. The district puts the reach at close to 600,000 students, about two-thirds of its enrollment. The district also set daily limits on how long younger students may work alone on a screen: none at all in pre-K through second grade, thirty minutes in grades three to five, forty-five minutes in grades six to eight. High schools are treated differently: students there may use AI only inside five specific approved products, or in career-and-technical coursework under a teacher's supervision, and every high-school student must complete two forty-five-minute lessons on how AI works, what it does with their data, and where it goes wrong. Students who need technology for a disability or as an English learner keep it — the policy explicitly does not touch those tools. The ban is written as a one-year measure.

    Our largest placement market has just drawn a line through a set of classroom practices, and we did not see it coming — no New York City schools source feeds this tracker. Anything we teach or assign that puts a K-8 student in front of an AI tool has to come out of the New York City version of our program for this year. At the same time the district has created a teaching job it has no trained teachers for: every high school now has to deliver AI-literacy instruction. That is squarely our work, and the one-year clock means the district will be deciding what comes next while it is still collecting evidence.

    • Do we treat New York City's line as a constraint to comply with, or as the opening position in a conversation where we bring evidence about what teachers actually need?

    • Should we build and offer AI-literacy preparation for New York City high-school teachers now, while the requirement is new and unmet, or wait to see whether the district builds it internally?

    • How much of our current public positioning on AI in instruction assumes classroom student use, and what does it cost us in New York City if we leave it unchanged this year?

    Texas — TX SBEC proposes rewriting educator-preparation accountability: Accredited bar drops to 80%, a warning year is inserted before probation, and a $4,500 continuing review becomes mandatory — comments closed Sept 14; adoption vote Sept 18 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 79 · Claude: ACT 90 · DISAGREE · UPDATED

    The State Board for Educator Certification proposes amendments to all six operative sections of 19 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 229, the rules that assign every Texas educator preparation program (EPP) its annual accreditation status under the Accountability System for Educator Preparation (ASEP). Four changes carry real consequence. (1) The Accredited threshold drops: §229.4(b)(1) would require 80% of possible ASEP Index points, replacing the current 85% — the bracketed deletion '[85%]' appears in the proposed rule text. (2) The status ladder is restructured. Today a program between 80% and 85% is Accredited-Warned and anything under 80% is Accredited-Probation; under the proposal the first year below 80% is Accredited-Warned and only the second and later consecutive years below 80% are Accredited-Probation (§229.4(b)(3)(A), (b)(4)(A)) — one additional year before probation attaches. (3) New §229.5(b) makes a continuing EPP review under §228.13 MANDATORY whenever a program is assigned Accredited-Warned or Accredited-Probation, satisfied by an in-process review if one is already under way. The fiscal note prices that review at $4,500 per program, paid by the EPP: of nine programs that scored below 80% on the 2024-2025 ASEP Index, five had been Accredited the prior year and one was already due its five-year review, so TEA models four discretionary reviews, $18,000 in new EPP cost and $18,000 in new state revenue. (4) New reporting: Figure 19 TAC §229.3(f)(1) adds 'EPP contact information' — names, email addresses and phone numbers of the EPP's legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair, due by August 1 each year through the Educator Certification Online System, and the figure states these 'must be three separate people.' New §229.2(19) and (23) define 'governing body' (including at minimum its chairperson) and 'legal authority' (the person with final decision-making authority — dean, director, owner, executive director, superintendent or program director). §229.7(b)(4) and (c) then route accreditation-status notices to all three roles and let the legal authority request an informal review. Also proposed: the first year a redesigned principal or teacher survey replaces a prior survey is report-only and not used for accreditation (§229.4(a)(2), (a)(5)), because both surveys are being revised to track the updated T-TESS observation rubric; and beginning in 2026-2027, candidates are evaluated against the Chapter 228 Subchapter F field-supervision frequency and duration requirements effective September 1, 2026 (§229.4(a)(4)(A)(ii)). New definitions align 'host teacher' and 'intern mentor teacher' with §228.2. The comment period runs August 14 through September 14, 2026; SBEC will also take registered oral and written comment at its September 2026 meeting. DETAIL ADDED 2026-09-21 from the Item 6 agenda PDF (september18agendaitem6.pdf, 1.45 MB, read raw with pdftotext this run): the item is styled DISCUSSION AND ACTION and gives SBEC 'an opportunity to adopt, SUBJECT TO STATE BOARD OF EDUCATION (SBOE) REVIEW,' amendments to 19 TAC Chapter 229 Subchapters A, B, C and E. Stated scope: adjustments to the Accountability System for Educator Preparation (ASEP) Manual; clarified processes and timelines for new certification tests, surveys and observation requirements; updated sources for population identification; increased ASEP communications; and time and supports for EPPs with a lowered ASEP status. EFFECTIVE DATE, quoting the packet: 'The proposed effective date would be December 27, 2026 (20 days after filing as adopted with the Texas Register). The proposed effective date is based on the SBEC and SBOE meeting schedules' — so the December date is contingent on BOTH SBEC adoption and SBOE review, not on the 09-18 vote alone. FISCAL DETAIL not previously on this row: the packet prices a discretionary review at $4,500 per program and estimates that of the nine programs scoring below 80% on the ASEP Index in 2024-2025, four would receive a discretionary review under the proposed rules, amounting to $18,000 in new state revenue and $18,000 in new costs to EPPs. The packet repeats that 'no changes are recommended since published as proposed, but additional changes may be recommended at the time of the meeting based on public comment.' The VOTE OUTCOME REMAINS UNVERIFIED — see the action note.

    Relay angle: This is the rule that decides whether Relay's Texas EPP may recommend candidates for certification at all — 19 TAC §229.1(a) bars any program not accredited under Chapter 229 from recommending a candidate. Texas is named in the rubric as a deep-partnership jurisdiction, the window is open, and the changes cut in both directions. The threshold drop and the inserted warning year are relief: more headroom at the Accredited line and one more year to recover before probation, which matters because §229.4(b)(5)(A) revokes approval after three consecutive probation years. The mandatory $4,500 continuing review is new downside attached to the very first sub-80% year, converting what is today a status label into an immediate review obligation and a bill. The three-separate-people governance requirement is the sleeper: it is a structural condition on the EPP, not a data request, and Relay should confirm it can name three distinct individuals as legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair for its Texas program before the August 1 reporting date arrives.

Update September 18: still nothing published from the September 10 meeting on the July certification package; the posted minutes file does not open. Georgia's teacher-certification agency votes on September 10 on the rule package it proposed in July: a new Artificial Intelligence for Educators endorsement (a formal credential teachers can add) with a lighter micro-endorsement tier, and a route that lets already-certified teachers add elementary grades by passing a test instead of completing an elementary preparation program. The public comment period closed August 29. The agency's preparation committee agenda for September 9 already lists two Regional Educational Service Agencies as approved providers of the AI endorsement programs, so providers are being approved ahead of the vote. Changes take effect October 15. Update, September 10: the vote is today; the Commission's preparation committee met September 9 and recommended approving the first two providers of the new endorsement, both regional education service agencies, before the rule itself is adopted. Update, September 11: the Commission met as scheduled on September 10, but as of the morning of September 11 it has not posted a report, minutes, or any notice of the outcome, and its proposed-rules page still shows the package as pending with the October 15 effective date; we will confirm the result on Monday, September 14. Update, September 14: still no published result from the September 10 vote after a fourth check; the rules are still listed as proposed with an October 15 effective date. Update, September 15: the agency has still not posted the September 10 result (fifth check); its August minutes, posted September 14, confirm that a new literacy-coaching credential and a rewrite of the school-leader certification rules are on track to be proposed in October. As of September 16 the Commission still has not posted the result of its September 10 vote. Update, September 17: seventh check, still no posted result from the September 10 vote.

    The AI endorsement is a program opportunity in a state where we already operate, and the market is forming now rather than after the vote; the first approved providers are the state's regional service agencies, which serve the same districts we would. The elementary test-in route cuts the other way: it creates a path into elementary teaching that bypasses programs like ours. Two more rewrites, a literacy coaching endorsement and an overhaul of school-leader certification, are queued for October.

    Delaware — DE Professional Standards Board proposes Elementary Teacher certificate amendments (14 DE Admin. Code 1521: current ETS test codes plus sunset dates for the old tests) and a new Elementary Montessori Teacher certificate (1528) — comments close Oct 1

    Jev: ACT 66 · Claude: TRACK 66 · DISAGREE · 7 business days · UPDATED

    Two Professional Standards Board proposals published in the September 1, 2026 Delaware Register of Regulations (Vol. 30, Issue 3), both under 14 Del.C. sections 1203, 1204(a), 1205(b) and 1220, both taking written comment at the Department of Education's Office of the Secretary (Attn: Regulation Review, 401 Federal Street, Suite 2, Dover) or through the online form at de.gov/doeregs until 4:30 p.m. on October 1, 2026. (1) 1521 Elementary Teacher, the standard certificate for Delaware elementary teachers: strikes unnecessary definitions in Section 2.0; in Section 4.0 replaces the prior ETS test codes with the current codes and adds a subsection stating the dates after which the outdated tests will no longer be accepted; clarifies the application requirements in Section 5.0; simplifies Section 10.0; the Board states no cost to the state or local boards. The full proposed 1521 text is not printed in the Register and the separately posted copy is a JavaScript-only page that could not be read this run, so the synopsis is the verified scope. (2) 1528 Elementary Montessori Teacher, a NEW standard certificate required to teach grades K-6 in a Delaware public Montessori school, with two acceptance carve-outs written into Section 1.2: the Early Childhood Montessori certificate for grades K-2, and the 1521 Elementary Teacher Standard Certificate, which 'may be accepted instead' for grades K-6. Requires a bachelor's degree from a regionally accredited institution plus a Montessori teacher-education program accredited by the Montessori Accreditation Council for Teacher Education, and 6 college credits (each equating to 15 hours) in evidence-based reading instruction; it is not a content-area certificate and is not accepted in non-Montessori schools. Both are Board proposals; adoption follows the comment period and Secretary and State Board action.

    Relay angle: Delaware is an authorized Relay jurisdiction and the Elementary Teacher certificate is the credential Relay's Delaware elementary candidates hold. The 1521 rewrite is the item to read closely: candidate test plans key to the ETS codes, and the new subsection fixing dates after which the old tests stop being accepted is a compliance clock for any candidate still relying on an older passing score. The Montessori rule cuts the other way: it lets the 1521 certificate stand in for the new Montessori certificate in K-6 public Montessori schools, which keeps Relay completers placeable there without a MACTE credential. Seventeen business days remain to comment; the proposed 1521 text itself was not read this run, and the sunset dates are the fact to pin down before commenting. Found by the cross-engine sweep, not by a wired source: the Delaware Register is not yet in config/sources.yaml.

    Stage / latest action: Proposed in the Delaware Register of Regulations Vol. 30, Issue 3, 2026-09-01; written comments due 4:30 p.m. 2026-10-01 (17 business days). Verified this run from the Register PDF (pages 118-119 synopses and the printed 1528 text).

    Movement this run: comment window: 7 business days left

    Implications:

    • compliance — The 1521 amendments replace the ETS test codes and set dates after which the outdated tests will no longer be accepted. Any Delaware candidate holding a passing score on a superseded test needs to know that date; Relay's Delaware advising should confirm the sunset dates from the posted text before the comment window closes.

    • program — The new Montessori certificate explicitly accepts the 1521 Elementary Teacher certificate in its place for grades K-6 in public Montessori schools, so Relay's Delaware elementary completers stay eligible for those placements without a separate MACTE-accredited credential.

    • advocacy — A 17-business-day comment window on a certification rule in an authorized state is a direct opportunity: the question worth raising is whether the sunset dates give in-progress candidates enough runway to retest under the current codes.

    Leadership brief — Delaware is updating the elementary teacher certificate's required tests and creating a Montessori certificate; comments are open until October 1

    Delaware's Professional Standards Board, the body that writes teacher-certification rules, has published two proposals. The first updates the Elementary Teacher certificate rule so it names the current versions of the required ETS tests and, for the first time, sets dates after which the older versions of those tests will no longer count. The second creates a new certificate for teachers in public Montessori elementary schools, which requires a Montessori-accredited training program and coursework in evidence-based reading instruction, but it states that the ordinary Elementary Teacher certificate can be accepted instead. Written comments on both are due by 4:30 p.m. on October 1, 2026.

    Delaware is a state where Relay is authorized to prepare teachers, and the Elementary Teacher certificate is what Relay's Delaware elementary candidates earn. The test-code change is mostly housekeeping, but the new cut-off dates could catch a candidate who passed an older version of a test and has not yet been certified. The Montessori rule is good news in a small way: Relay graduates holding the standard certificate remain eligible to teach in public Montessori schools. The full text of the elementary-certificate proposal has not yet been read, so the exact cut-off dates are still to be confirmed.

    • Do any current Delaware candidates hold passing scores on older test versions, and would the proposed cut-off dates affect them before they are certified?

    • Is it worth submitting a short comment by October 1 asking for adequate runway for candidates already in the pipeline?

    • Should Relay's Delaware advising materials be updated to the new test codes now, ahead of adoption?

    The short version

    We can now read the court order, and it says more than the coverage did. On 2026-09-17 Judge Angel Kelley vacated the Education Department's February 2025 DEI grant-termination directive in its entirety and declared it unlawful under the APA. The order — 70 pages, retrieved this run as a PDF from the California Attorney General's press-documents archive and read in full — records that the Department terminated 104 of 109 Teacher Quality Partnership and SEED awards under it. Those are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for. The court expressly reasoned that vacatur restores the ordinary priorities governing the forthcoming FY2026 awards, which the Department said on 2026-09-09 it was preparing to make. Two corrections to what this board carried last week: the court's figure is 104 of 109, not the 31/72 split Education Week drew from its own database; and the effect on pending awards comes from vacatur, not from an injunction — the court denied injunctive relief as unnecessary.

    Two federal comment windows are at the edge. The accreditor-recognition rewrite closes today. The EDGAR rewrite — the Department's discretion to terminate grants "for convenience" — closes Wednesday. The apportionment ruling issued the same day as the grant ruling cuts directly against EDGAR's premise, which makes it citable material for a comment that has two days left in it.

    Texas opened a redesign of how EPPs keep their approval, and there is no comment period. SBEC's Item 8 on 2026-09-18 was a discussion-only item on 19 TAC Chapter 228: contingent renewals, differentiated cure periods, risk-based monitoring, and revised new-entity approval. Staff will bring proposed text back at an unannounced future meeting. This is the pre-rulemaking stage, when input is cheapest to give — and it is the one item this run that the wired sources missed entirely.

    Texas voted on Chapter 229 Friday and nobody can tell what happened. Three days on, TEA has published no minutes, no adopted rule (the expected PDF 404s), and the Texas Register's rule viewer has moved. The 80% Accredited bar and the December 27 effective date should not be treated as adopted. The cross-engine sweep labelled this item "adopts" and marked it verified; its own internal note concedes it read the agenda, not the outcome. The agenda is not the vote.

    Federal — ED proposes full rewrite of accreditor-recognition rules (34 CFR 602) — comments close Sept 21 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 54 · Claude: ACT 83 · DISAGREE · 0 business days · UPDATED

    Notice of proposed rulemaking rewriting the Secretary's accrediting-agency recognition regulations at 34 CFR part 602 (conforming changes to parts 600 and 668) to implement Executive Order 14279. Verified from the Federal Register text this run, the NPRM: requires accreditors to hold member institutions to program-level student-outcome expectations — completion, licensure pass rates, and economic returns — assessed "without reference to race, ethnicity, or sex"; requires accreditation decisions to be neutral with respect to viewpoint and ideology (proposed 602.18, with a religious-mission exception); adds academic-freedom and intellectual-diversity review, cost-benefit analysis, and program-length review to 602.17; REMOVES the 602.15(a)(4) requirement that programmatic accreditors seat educators, practitioners, and employers on evaluation and decision-making bodies; lowers barriers to recognizing new accreditors and to institutions switching accreditors (new 602.12(e): qualifying experience may be national, State, or programmatic); and makes it a recognition-review factor whether an agency joined a "concerted effort to unnecessarily restrict the qualifications necessary for a student to sit for a licensure or certification examination" or inflated entry requirements through "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" (proposed 602.31(g)(1)). Docket ED-2025-OPE-1042, RIN 1840-AD82. Comments close 2026-09-21 (~21 business days), via regulations.gov only — no fax or email.

    Relay angle: Relay's operating licenses run through this rule twice: MSCHE (institutional accreditor and Title IV gatekeeper) and CAEP (educator-prep accreditor) are both Secretary-recognized under Part 602, so the proposed outcome metrics and the credential-inflation review factor would reshape the standards both apply to Relay.

    Stage / latest action: Update 2026-09-21: THE COMMENT WINDOW CLOSES TODAY. Federal Register API comments_close_on re-read raw this run: 2026-09-21 (0 business days remaining). Type: Proposed Rule; action: Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM); published 2026-08-20. (2 earlier updates on the dashboard row.)

    Response window: closes 2026-09-21 (0 business days out)

    Implications:

    • compliance — MSCHE and CAEP would be re-reviewed against rewritten recognition criteria; whatever standards survive flow down into Relay's next reaffirmation cycles, with program-level completion, licensure pass-rate, and earnings data as the evidence currency.

    • program — Program-level economic-returns metrics put graduate-EPP tuition-to-earnings ratios under accreditor scrutiny — Relay's employment and certification outcomes become either an accreditation asset or an exposure, program by program.

    • risk — Proposed 602.31(g)(1) treats "unjustified increases in education or training requirements" for entering a profession as a mark against an accreditor's recognition — a federal thumb on the scale against graduate-level entry expectations for teaching, rhyming with the state-level deregulation the board is already tracking (IN Pub. L. 150, CO SB26-126).

    • advocacy — Comment window open to 2026-09-21. Relay can speak as a graduate EPP with strong licensure outcomes; coordination with AACTE and with MSCHE/CAEP comment strategies is the near-term decision.

    Federal — ED proposes EDGAR rewrite — termination 'for convenience,' continuation-award discretion, merit certification for grantees; comments close Sept 23 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 63 · Claude: ACT 82 · DISAGREE · 2 business days · UPDATED

    Notice of proposed rulemaking amending the Education Department General Administrative Regulations (34 CFR parts 75, 76, 77, 79; 2 CFR parts 3474, 3485), docket ED-2026-OPEPD-2542, RIN 1875-AA14. Verified from the Federal Register text this run: revised 75.901 gives "clear notice to all recipients of the Department's ability to terminate discretionary awards for convenience," citing the 2025 per curiam opinions in Department of Education v. California and NIH v. American Public Health Association and reasoning that grant agreements are "ultimately contractual in nature," and adds FAR-modeled temporary-suspension provisions. Revised 75.253 removes subsection (c) and codifies the Secretary's discretion to reduce or deny continuation awards using any relevant information, with the General Education Provisions Act declared inapplicable to those decisions; revised 75.230 states that approving an application does not obligate future funding; new 75.251(d) lets ED adjust awards based on unspent balances. New 75.228 authorizes competitive preference for applicants proposing indirect-cost rates below their negotiated rate. New 75.500(f) requires grantees to certify that hiring, admissions, promotion, and compensation under the grant are merit-based "without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or proxies thereof" and that employment practices do not compel statements of belief. Revised 77.1 realigns the evidence-tier definitions (strong/moderate/promising) to ESEA statute, removes What Works Clearinghouse references, and adds an "evidence framework" definition allowing third-party-funded evidence reviews. 75.562(c)(2) keeps the 8% MTDC cap for training grants without a negotiated rate and bars the de minimis rate on training programs. Styled an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action; ED intends to finalize in late 2026. Comments close 2026-09-23, via regulations.gov.

    Relay angle: Every ED discretionary grant Relay holds or pursues (SEED, TQP-structure partnerships) would sit under codified termination-for-convenience and continuation-at-discretion terms — the regulatory codification of the 2025 grant-termination fights — while the 75.500(f) merit certification reaches into grantee hiring and admissions practice and 75.228 puts competitive pressure on indirect-cost recovery. The 77.1 evidence-framework change also alters how applicants prove moderate/strong evidence in competitions.

    Stage / latest action: Update 2026-09-21: comments close Wednesday 2026-09-23 — 2 business days left. Federal Register API re-read raw this run: comments_close_on 2026-09-23, published 2026-08-24, Proposed Rule / NPRM. The abstract states the Department 'intends to finalize these regulations in late 2026.' (2 earlier updates on the dashboard row.)

    Response window: closes 2026-09-23 (2 business days out)

    Implications:

    • risk — Termination-for-convenience plus discretionary continuation determinations (GEPA inapplicable) would let ED end or shrink any Relay federal award mid-project for alignment-with-priorities reasons, with reduced procedural recourse.

    • compliance — The 75.500(f) certification obligates grantees to attest merit-based hiring/admissions/promotion practices 'without regard to race, color, religion, sex, national origin, or proxies thereof' and to avoid compelled belief statements — Relay's hiring and admissions language for grant-funded work would need review against it.

    • funding — Competitive preference for below-negotiated-rate indirect costs (new 75.228) pressures Relay to discount indirect recovery to stay competitive; unspent-balance adjustments (75.251(d)) tighten multi-year budget management.

    • advocacy — Comment window open through 2026-09-23 — Relay (directly or through AACTE) can seek clarity on continuation-award criteria, the scope of "proxies thereof," and evidence-framework governance.

    NY — NY proposes science-of-reading requirements for teacher preparation programs (8 NYCRR 52.21, 80-3.7) — literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, 15 of 100 field-experience hours and the full student-teaching placement spent on evidence-based literacy instruction, SWD literacy credits 6 → 9; comments close Sept 27, adoption expected October

    Jev: ACT 82 · Claude: ACT 86 · 4 business days · UPDATED

    Proposed rulemaking EDU-30-26-00007-P, published in the July 29, 2026 State Register (no hearing; 60-day comment period, so comments are due September 27, 2026; the Register text and the NYSED full-text index both list the rule and neither prints a calendar deadline, so the date is computed from publication). Amends §52.21 program-registration requirements for teacher preparation programs in bilingual education, early childhood (birth-grade 2), childhood (grades 1-6), ESOL, literacy, and special education (blind/visually impaired, deaf/hard-of-hearing, speech and language disabilities, students with disabilities at every level). Requires the study of literacy skills or methods of teaching reading in those programs to align with the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including theories of literacy development, evidence-based instruction, assessment and intervention through a multi-tier framework, and dyslexia, dysgraphia and other language-based learning disabilities (definitions, detection, screener administration, evidence-based instruction, accommodations for ELLs); removes the 'methods of reading enrichment and remediation' language. Clinical requirements for candidates first enrolling Fall 2028 or later: at least 15 of the 100 field-experience clock hours must include evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with one or more students with reading difficulties, and candidates must teach reading and writing throughout the student teaching or residency experience (70 days or longer), assessing learning in whole-group and small-group settings; literacy programs must spend at least 25 of 50 practicum hours the same way. Programs must comply by September 1, 2028 or at new-program registration, whichever is first. SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs must add three semester hours in language acquisition and literacy development (six to nine total) for candidates first enrolling Fall 2029 or later; §80-3.7 makes the same 6 → 9 change for the individual-evaluation certification pathway from September 1, 2033. The notice states SWD programs in childhood and adolescence will no longer be registered on or after September 1, 2029. Cost statement names $1,335 CUNY tuition per three-credit course and $7,100 per adjunct literacy course as illustrative private-party costs. Permanent adoption anticipated at the October 2026 Regents meeting, effective October 21, 2026. Grounded in the Hunt Institute Path Forward initiative (NY joined Fall 2023) and the December 2024 NYS Dyslexia and Dysgraphia Task Force report.

    Relay angle: This is a direct rewrite of what Relay's registered New York programs in childhood education, students with disabilities and any ESOL/bilingual-extension offerings must teach and how their clinical placements must be structured, with a September 1, 2028 compliance date and a residency-specific clause: the entire student teaching or residency experience must include teaching and assessing reading and writing. The comment window is the first and only formal input point before the Regents adopt in October. Never on the board: the rule was published July 29 while the NYSED newsroom source was down and the State Register is not a wired source; found by the cross-engine sweep through the September 9 pending-actions index and verified from the July 29 issue.

    Stage / latest action: Link note 2026-09-21: the 2026-07-29 State Register PDF at dos.ny.gov is behind a Cloudflare challenge today and returns HTTP 403 to curl AND to the browser pane, so it is not a deliverable citation this run. Substituted the Board of Regents Higher Education Committee item of 2026-07-13, 'Proposed Amendments Relating to Registration Requirements for Certain Teacher Preparation Programs that Focus on Literacy Instruction and Corresponding Certification Requirements' (regents.nysed.gov, HTTP 200, 1,125,025-byte PDF, opened and read this run). It confirms the proposal's substance and origin in the NYS Path Forward initiative and the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework. The 2026-09-27 comment deadline continues to rest on the State Register publication read in prior runs, not on this document. (3 earlier updates on the dashboard row.)

    Response window: closes 2026-09-27 (4 business days out)

    Implications:

    • compliance — Every affected Relay New York program (childhood, students with disabilities, and ESOL or bilingual extension if registered) must show literacy coursework aligned to the NYS EPP Science of Reading Framework, including dyslexia and dysgraphia content, by September 1, 2028 or at the next new-program registration, whichever comes first.

    • program — For candidates enrolling Fall 2028 or later, 15 of the 100 pre-student-teaching field hours must involve evidence-based literacy instruction and assessment with a struggling reader, and the residency itself must include teaching and assessing reading and writing throughout, in whole-group and small-group settings; Relay's residency design and partner-school placements will need to guarantee that exposure for secondary-leaning placements too.

    • program — SWD (Birth-Grade 2) and SWD (All Grades) programs gain a three-credit language-acquisition-and-literacy course for Fall 2029 entrants (six to nine credits total); the notice also says SWD childhood and adolescence programs stop being registered after September 1, 2029, which bears on how Relay's special-education offerings are structured in New York.

    • advocacy — Comments are open through September 27 to the Office of Higher Education; a program-level comment from Relay could address the residency-wide literacy clause for adolescence and secondary placements, the clock-hour accounting, and the 2028/2029 phase-in.

    • funding — The cost statement anticipates new coursework and literacy-expert instructors for registered programs; Relay would bear curriculum-development and faculty cost for the affected New York programs.

    GA — GaPSC initiates July certification-rules package: Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement created, Elementary P-5 test-in route added — comment closes Aug 29 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 67 · Claude: ACT 72 · DISAGREE · 17 business days · UPDATED

    Alongside the Math Matters Act program rules, the Georgia Professional Standards Commission initiated a certification-rules package at its July 9, 2026 meeting, all on the same comment clock (open through 2026-08-29, adoption vote 2026-09-10, effective 2026-10-15). The pieces that matter here: (1) new Rule 505-2-.198 creates an Artificial Intelligence for Educators ENDORSEMENT and 505-2-.199 a companion micro-endorsement — a new credential field educator-preparation providers can build programs for (the paired program rule 505-3-.114 is already posted); (2) Rule 505-2-.34 (Add a Field) is amended to allow a TEST-IN option for Elementary Grades P-5, letting already-certified educators add the elementary field by assessment rather than program completion; (3) Rules 505-2-.08, .26 and .106 are amended to bar obtaining the Special Education Reading academic content concentration solely by passing an assessment — closing an assessment-only route; (4) Rule 505-3-.64 (Instructional Technology Program) is repealed and replaced on the 2024 ISTE standards. The Executive Secretary's report also fixed the fall pipeline: a Georgia Literacy Coaching Endorsement rule drafted for October initiation (public comment ~November, adoption December, released to EPPs January 2027), and an Educational Leadership Task Force recommending 'significant changes' to leadership preparation and certification rules, also due for October initiation. Update 2026-08-31: the proposed 505-2-.199 PDF (revised copy fetched this run) structures the AI credential as a MICRO-endorsement available to holders of a level-4+ renewable Professional or Five-Year Induction certificate who complete only standards 1 and 4 of the full 505-3-.114 Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement program — a lighter-weight tier below the full endorsement, both riding the same GaPSC-approved-program requirement. Update 2026-09-04: the September 9 EPCC agenda lists Middle Georgia RESA and Northwest Georgia RESA as administratively approved providers of the Artificial Intelligence for Educators Endorsement and the Foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Education Micro-Endorsement (the micro-endorsement's public name, confirming the 505-2-.199 tier). The September 10 Commission agenda confirms the adoption item. The EPCC's next meeting is 2026-10-07, the expected venue for the October initiations (literacy coaching endorsement, leadership rules).

    Relay angle: Three separate levers on Relay's Georgia surface: a brand-new AI endorsement field Relay could build a program for — and the provider market is forming now, with two RESAs approved before the rule is even adopted; a test-in route into elementary certification that bypasses preparation programs (demand-side risk, mirror of the assessment-only closures elsewhere in the package); and an October pipeline (literacy coaching endorsement, leadership rules rewrite) with the EPCC's 2026-10-07 meeting as the likely first sighting.

    Federal — Court VACATES the Education Department's February 2025 DEI grant-termination directive in its entirety — the order that killed 104 of 109 Teacher Quality Partnership and SEED awards is set aside as arbitrary and capricious, and the ordinary framework now governs the forthcoming FY2026 awards · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 66 · Claude: ACT 91 · DISAGREE · UPDATED

    VERIFIED FROM THE PRIMARY ORDER this run: California v. U.S. Department of Education, No. 1:25-cv-10548-AK (D. Mass.), Document 176, filed 2026-09-17, 70 pages, Hon. Angel Kelley — retrieved as a PDF from the California Attorney General's press-documents archive and read in full with pdftotext. This SUPERSEDES the wire-attributed account this row previously carried. Holding: Plaintiff States' Motion for Summary Judgment is GRANTED, Defendants' Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment is DENIED, and the Motion to Strike is DENIED AS MOOT. Relief, quoting the order: pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 706 and 28 U.S.C. 2202 the Court 'VACATES and SETS ASIDE, in its entirety, the Department's February 5, 2025, Directive, titled "Eliminating Discrimination and Fraud in Department Grant Awards," as arbitrary and capricious and not in accordance with law'; and pursuant to 28 U.S.C. 2201 it is DECLARED that the Directive is unlawful because it violates the APA. The Court DECLINED to enter the permanent injunction plaintiffs also sought, reasoning that the declaratory judgment and principles of preclusion make injunctive relief unnecessary against a hypothetical future policy document. Facts as found in the order: the plaintiffs are eight States (California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Colorado, Illinois, Maryland, New York and Wisconsin); defendants are the Department, Denise Carter in her official capacity as former Acting Secretary, and Secretary Linda McMahon; the February 5, 2025 Directive implemented Executive Order 14173 (2025-01-21) and Executive Order 14190, 'Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling,' 90 Fed. Reg. 8,853 (2025-02-03); and 'as of March 12, 2025, Defendants terminated 104 out of 109 total grants pursuant to the February 2025 Directive, including forty from Plaintiff States.' The order also records that 'since June 5, 2025, the Department has not relied on the February 2025 Directive in issuing any termination or non-continuation decisions for TQP and SEED grants.' On the reach of the remedy, the court reasoned that vacatur 'would leave in place the statutory and regulatory framework for TQP and SEED grants, as well as the most recently promulgated agency priorities, which ordinarily govern the Department's grant award process, including the forthcoming FY2026 grant awards.' TWO CORRECTIONS to the previously reported account: (1) the court's own figure is 104 of 109 TQP and SEED awards, not the 31 SEED / 72 TQP split Education Week drew from its own database of canceled grants; (2) the effect on the pending FY2026 awards comes from the VACATUR of the Directive, not from a separate injunction barring use of the executive order — the order denies injunctive relief. The order does not itself restore terminated funds; the court had previously held that recovery of the money lies with the Court of Federal Claims.

    Relay angle: Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for as a graduate institution and educator-preparation provider, which makes this the run's most consequential item. The directive that suppressed those competitions is now vacated and declared unlawful, and the court expressly framed vacatur as restoring the ordinary priorities that govern the FORTHCOMING FY2026 awards — the same awards the Department said on 2026-09-09 it was preparing to make (16 SEED and 12 TQP). That converts a watch item into a live eligibility question with a short fuse: the competitions are imminent and the legal cloud over DEI-adjacent program design has lifted, at least as to this directive. What the ruling does NOT do is return terminated money, and it does not enjoin the Department from adopting a new, properly reasoned policy. Relay's decision is about posture on the next competition, not recovery of the last one.

    Stage / latest action: Update 2026-09-21 (PROMOTED TRACK 72 -> ACT 91 on primary verification): the court order was located and read in full this run, resolving the verification gap this row had carried since 2026-09-18. Document 176 in No. 1:25-cv-10548-AK (D. Mass.), filed 2026-09-17, served as a PDF by the California Attorney General's press-documents archive and read with pdftotext. NOTE ON METHOD: prior runs recorded that court orders were unreachable because CourtListener's docket API requires authentication and the Massachusetts Attorney General's newsroom refuses plain clients. In a multistate action, any plaintiff State's attorney general may post the order; the California AG's press-docs path served it to an ordinary client. Worth trying first in future multistate matters.

    Implications:

    • funding — The FY2026 TQP and SEED competitions are the near-term opportunity. With the February 2025 Directive vacated, the ordinary statutory framework and most recent agency priorities govern the award process — the court said so explicitly.

    • risk — The court denied a permanent injunction. A new directive, issued with adequate reasoning and process, could reimpose similar conditions. This is a reprieve on one instrument, not a durable rule.

    • compliance — Program descriptions written defensively during the directive's life may now understate what Relay actually does; conversely, nothing here immunizes a proposal from a future policy. Design to the statute, not to either directive.

    • advocacy — The reasoning — that mass termination on DEI grounds was arbitrary and capricious and contrary to the TQP, SEED and GEPA statutes — is directly citable in Relay's EDGAR comment, which closes 2026-09-23 and concerns the Department's discretion to terminate grants for convenience.

Mass., 2026-09-17)

    TX — TX SBEC proposes rewriting educator-preparation accountability: Accredited bar drops to 80%, a warning year is inserted before probation, and a $4,500 continuing review becomes mandatory — comments closed Sept 14; adoption vote Sept 18 · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 79 · Claude: ACT 90 · DISAGREE · UPDATED

    The State Board for Educator Certification proposes amendments to all six operative sections of 19 Texas Administrative Code Chapter 229, the rules that assign every Texas educator preparation program (EPP) its annual accreditation status under the Accountability System for Educator Preparation (ASEP). Four changes carry real consequence. (1) The Accredited threshold drops: §229.4(b)(1) would require 80% of possible ASEP Index points, replacing the current 85% — the bracketed deletion '[85%]' appears in the proposed rule text. (2) The status ladder is restructured. Today a program between 80% and 85% is Accredited-Warned and anything under 80% is Accredited-Probation; under the proposal the first year below 80% is Accredited-Warned and only the second and later consecutive years below 80% are Accredited-Probation (§229.4(b)(3)(A), (b)(4)(A)) — one additional year before probation attaches. (3) New §229.5(b) makes a continuing EPP review under §228.13 MANDATORY whenever a program is assigned Accredited-Warned or Accredited-Probation, satisfied by an in-process review if one is already under way. The fiscal note prices that review at $4,500 per program, paid by the EPP: of nine programs that scored below 80% on the 2024-2025 ASEP Index, five had been Accredited the prior year and one was already due its five-year review, so TEA models four discretionary reviews, $18,000 in new EPP cost and $18,000 in new state revenue. (4) New reporting: Figure 19 TAC §229.3(f)(1) adds 'EPP contact information' — names, email addresses and phone numbers of the EPP's legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair, due by August 1 each year through the Educator Certification Online System, and the figure states these 'must be three separate people.' New §229.2(19) and (23) define 'governing body' (including at minimum its chairperson) and 'legal authority' (the person with final decision-making authority — dean, director, owner, executive director, superintendent or program director). §229.7(b)(4) and (c) then route accreditation-status notices to all three roles and let the legal authority request an informal review. Also proposed: the first year a redesigned principal or teacher survey replaces a prior survey is report-only and not used for accreditation (§229.4(a)(2), (a)(5)), because both surveys are being revised to track the updated T-TESS observation rubric; and beginning in 2026-2027, candidates are evaluated against the Chapter 228 Subchapter F field-supervision frequency and duration requirements effective September 1, 2026 (§229.4(a)(4)(A)(ii)). New definitions align 'host teacher' and 'intern mentor teacher' with §228.2. The comment period runs August 14 through September 14, 2026; SBEC will also take registered oral and written comment at its September 2026 meeting. DETAIL ADDED 2026-09-21 from the Item 6 agenda PDF (september18agendaitem6.pdf, 1.45 MB, read raw with pdftotext this run): the item is styled DISCUSSION AND ACTION and gives SBEC 'an opportunity to adopt, SUBJECT TO STATE BOARD OF EDUCATION (SBOE) REVIEW,' amendments to 19 TAC Chapter 229 Subchapters A, B, C and E. …

    Relay angle: This is the rule that decides whether Relay's Texas EPP may recommend candidates for certification at all — 19 TAC §229.1(a) bars any program not accredited under Chapter 229 from recommending a candidate. Texas is named in the rubric as a deep-partnership jurisdiction, the window is open, and the changes cut in both directions. The threshold drop and the inserted warning year are relief: more headroom at the Accredited line and one more year to recover before probation, which matters because §229.4(b)(5)(A) revokes approval after three consecutive probation years. The mandatory $4,500 continuing review is new downside attached to the very first sub-80% year, converting what is today a status label into an immediate review obligation and a bill. The three-separate-people governance requirement is the sleeper: it is a structural condition on the EPP, not a data request, and Relay should confirm it can name three distinct individuals as legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair for its Texas program before the August 1 reporting date arrives.

    Stage / latest action: Update 2026-09-21 (MOVEMENT, outcome UNVERIFIED): the adoption vote was taken at the 2026-09-18 SBEC meeting and the RESULT IS NOT YET PUBLISHED. Checked raw this run: (1) the TEA meeting page for 2026-09-18, retrieved through a real browser, still serves only the AGENDA — it confirms Item 6 was 'Adoption of Proposed Amendments to 19 TAC Chapter 229 ... Subchapters A, B, C and E' but carries no vote, minutes or disposition; (2) no adopted-rule PDF exists yet at the TEA sbec-adopted path (0926-229.pdf returns HTTP 404); (3) the Texas Secretary of State Texas Register TAC viewer has relocated to a new site and did not resolve to Chapter 229 text this run. Therefore: DO NOT treat the 80% Accredited bar, the warning year, the mandatory paid continuing review, or the proposed 2026-12-27 effective date as adopted. The staff packet recommended adoption without changes, and adoption remains subject to State Board of Education review, but the board's actual action on 09-18 is unknown here. Re-check next run. (3 earlier updates on the dashboard row.)

    Response window: closes 2026-09-18

    Implications:

    • compliance — New annual submission by August 1: names, emails and phone numbers of the EPP's legal authority, chief operating officer and governing body chair, filed through the Educator Certification Online System — and the figure requires three separate people. Confirm Relay's Texas EPP can satisfy the three-distinct-persons condition and decide who is named to each role.

    • risk — A single ASEP Index year below 80% would trigger a mandatory continuing EPP review under §228.13 at $4,500, paid by the EPP. Under current rules a first sub-80% year produces probation status but no automatic review; the proposal adds cost and an oversight cycle at the first miss.

    • compliance — Accreditation-status notices would go by email to all three named roles, and the legal authority gains standing to request an informal review — so the internal routing for a 14-day informal-review deadline under §229.7(b)(3) needs to be settled in advance, not when a notice lands.

    • program — Field-supervision frequency and duration for candidates in clinical teaching, residency or internship shift to the Chapter 228 Subchapter F requirements effective September 1, 2026 for the 2026-2027 evaluation year. The 95% compliance standard in §229.4(a)(4)(A) is unchanged and the small-group exception does not apply to it.

    • advocacy — Nineteen business days to file written comment, plus registered oral comment at the September SBEC meeting. The most useful comment is narrow: the preamble describes the §229.4(b)(3)(A) restructuring but does not separately itemize the §229.4(b)(1) drop from 85% to 80% that the rule text marks, and asking SBEC to confirm the Accredited threshold on the record protects every program's planning assumption.
