    Federal — H.R. 7890 'Science of Reading Act of 2026' passed the House Sept 16 by voice vote — writes a statutory definition of the science of reading into federal education law, bars the three-cueing model from 'comprehensive literacy instruction,' and requires state literacy-grant plans and subgrant priorities to align to the science of reading · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 60 · Claude: ACT 76 · DISAGREE · UPDATED

    The House passed H.R. 7890 on 2026-09-16 under suspension of the rules, as amended, by voice vote; the engrossed text was read in full this run. The bill amends the Elementary and Secondary Education Act's comprehensive literacy provisions (20 U.S.C. 6641-6644, the Comprehensive Literacy State Development program) in four ways. First, it adds a new subparagraph (M) to the definition of comprehensive literacy instruction providing that the term 'does not include the use of a three-cueing model.' Second, it defines 'science of reading' in statute as an interdisciplinary body of evidence-based research that identifies phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and writing as essential components of skilled reading, that establishes the importance of background knowledge, oral language and the reading-writing connection, that explains why some students struggle, and that does not use three-cueing; and it defines 'three-cueing model' as an approach using meaning, structure/syntax or visual cues as the primary basis for teaching word recognition, or teaching visual memory as the primary basis for word recognition. Third, it requires a state applying for a Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant to describe the extent to which its state literacy plan is aligned to the science of reading, and conditions the grant priority on that alignment. Fourth, it applies the same alignment condition to both subgrant priorities, birth-through-kindergarten-entry and kindergarten-through-grade-12. The Act appropriates no money and creates no new program; it changes what existing literacy dollars may support and adds a rule of construction preserving IDEA, Section 504 and ADA rights and barring federal officials from directing curriculum or instruction. The changes apply to funds awarded on or after enactment. The bill now goes to the Senate, where no action is scheduled. UPDATE 2026-09-21: per the GPO bill-status record read raw this run, the House action of 2026-09-16 (passed by voice vote under suspension, as amended, after forty minutes of debate on a motion by Mr. Walberg; motion to reconsider laid on the table) was followed on 2026-09-17 by receipt in the Senate, two readings, and referral to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

    Relay angle: A federal statutory definition of the science of reading, with three-cueing written out of it, becomes the reference point state literacy and educator-preparation rules converge on — including the New York teacher-preparation literacy rules Relay's New York programs must meet, which are up for adoption in October. It also sets the content bar for Relay's literacy coursework and its Teacher Professional Education literacy offerings in every state.

    Stage / latest action: Update 2026-09-21 (MOVEMENT, verified): H.R. 7890 was RECEIVED IN THE SENATE on 2026-09-17, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Read raw this run from the GPO bill-status record (BILLSTATUS-119hr7890.xml). This supersedes the prior note that nothing was scheduled in the Senate: the bill now has a committee of jurisdiction. No hearing, markup or companion measure appears in the status record. Passed the House 2026-09-16 by voice vote under suspension of the rules, as amended (GPO bill-status record BILLSTATUS-119hr7890, read raw this run). Earlier actions in that record: introduced 2026-03-12 by Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN-9) with 3 cosponsors and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce; ordered reported as amended by the Yeas and Nays 33-0 on 2026-03-17; reported as amended 2026-06-29 (H. Rept. 119-717) and placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 623. Next expected event: Senate referral, no Senate companion identified and no action scheduled. Note: secondary coverage dates the passage September 17; the GPO record and the engrossed text both say September 16, and the primary date is used here.

    Implications:

    • compliance — If enacted, a federal statutory definition of the science of reading would sit underneath state educator-preparation literacy rules, including New York's proposed 8 NYCRR 52.21 and 80-3.7 requirements, giving Relay's literacy coursework a single national reference standard to align to.

    • program — The explicit exclusion of three-cueing from comprehensive literacy instruction sets a content floor for Relay's literacy methods courses and for the literacy modules in its Teacher Professional Education coaching line.

    • funding — Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant priorities would turn on science-of-reading alignment, so state literacy plans that fund district coaching and professional development become a more selective market for providers that can document that alignment.

    • advocacy — The bill is in the Senate with no action scheduled, which is the open window for comment from educator-preparation providers on how the statutory definition interacts with preparation-program requirements.

    Source · Education Week, 'Federal Science of Reading Legislation Passes the House' (2026-09, cross-engine sweep) · WBIW, 'Rep. Houchin bill to improve literacy education practices passes House' (2026-09-17, cross-engine sweep) · The 74, 'Ohio Reading Scores Rise. Is the Science of Reading Working?'     TX — TX SBEC opens a redesign of how educator preparation programs keep their approval — continuing-approval review, risk-based monitoring and contingent renewals discussed Sept 18, with rule text to follow · ⚠︎ Jev placed this in TRACK

    Jev: TRACK 64 · Claude: ACT 76 · DISAGREE · NEW

    Item 8 of the 2026-09-18 State Board for Educator Certification meeting, styled DISCUSSION ONLY, opened a redesign of 19 TAC Chapter 228 — the rules under which an approved Texas educator preparation program keeps its approval. Read raw from the agenda packet this run. The packet frames it as supporting 'development of a redesigned approach to continuing approval review, monitoring, and program support,' and lists the specific policy questions staff put to the board: (1) Continuing approval definitions, processes and renewal decisions — proposed updates to the Continuing Approval Review process 'including how to operationalize the quality review'; options for CONTINGENT RENEWAL decisions and DIFFERENTIATED CURE PERIODS graded to the nature and severity of noncompliance; and treatment of programs initially approved to offer PREP-funded preparation routes. (2) Use of risk factors — the role of risk factors in continuing-approval reviews, monitoring and compliance oversight, and updates to the risk factors in 19 TAC 228.13(c)(1)-(3) and how they prioritize agency review and intervention. (3) Technical assistance — the role of technical assistance following review outcomes, and 'approaches for developing a technical assistance service.' (4) Related updates such as revisions to EPP NEW ENTITY APPROVAL requirements to align with the continuing-approval changes. Statutory basis cited includes Texas Education Code 21.0443, which requires SBEC to set standards for approval and renewal of EPPs and to review each EPP at least once every five years. Staff named as responsible: Melissa Yoder, Director of Quality Preparation; Josh Jones, Director of EPP Field Support and Operations; William Sea, Director of EPP Continuous Improvement. NO RULE TEXT EXISTS YET and none of these are decisions — this is the direction-setting stage.

    Relay angle: This is the most directly Relay-facing item the run surfaced, and the wired sources missed it entirely — it came from the cross-engine sweep and was then confirmed against the agency's own packet. Chapter 228 continuing approval is the mechanism by which Relay's Texas program remains an approved EPP; Chapter 229, which the board already tracks, is the accountability rating that feeds it. Two of the questions on the table would change Relay's exposure directly: contingent renewal with differentiated cure periods replaces a blunt approve/sanction decision with a graded one, and risk-based monitoring under 228.13(c) determines how often and how hard a program is examined. The timing is the point. There is no rule text and no comment period, which means this is the pre-rulemaking window when an agency is still deciding what to propose — the stage at which a provider's input is cheapest to give and most likely to land. Once this reaches the Texas Register as proposed text, the room narrows to a formal comment.

    Stage / latest action: Discussion-only item at the 2026-09-18 SBEC meeting. Agenda packet (september18agendaitem8.pdf, 131 KB) read raw with pdftotext this run. The packet states: 'TEA staff anticipate presenting proposed revisions related to EPP continuing approval, review, monitoring, and support to the SBEC at a future meeting for approval to be published in the Texas Register.' No date is given for that future meeting.

    Implications:

    • compliance — Contingent renewal and differentiated cure periods would change what a finding against Relay's Texas EPP actually costs — potentially a graded remedy rather than a cliff, but also more frequent intermediate determinations.

    • risk — Updated risk factors in 19 TAC 228.13(c)(1)-(3) set how often and how intensively TEA reviews a program. Where Relay's Texas program lands against revised factors is worth knowing before the factors are written, not after.

    • program — Continuing approval of programs offering PREP-funded routes is explicitly on the table, which bears on any Relay pathway that uses or might use PREP funding.

    • advocacy — No comment period exists yet. Direct engagement with the named TEA staff during the drafting stage is the available route, and it closes when proposed text is published.

Diagnosed this run: www.nysed.gov serves an incomplete certificate chain. curl repairs it by fetching the missing intermediate through the certificate's Authority Information Access extension; Python's urllib does not, and fails even with certifi. This is a fetcher bug, not an empty feed, and it is fixable by routing that source through curl or bundling the intermediate. No code was changed in this unattended run. Severity is lower than the zero-streak implies: fetched manually this run, the NYSED newsroom's most recent release is 2026-09-15, and the only policy-relevant item in the month-long blackout — the NY Inspires diploma-sunset announcement of 2026-09-14 — was already on the board, captured by the cross-engine sweep.     The House passed the Science of Reading Act on September 16, putting a statutory definition of the science of reading into federal education law and writing three-cueing out of "comprehensive literacy instruction" — the first federal item this year that reaches directly into what teacher-preparation literacy coursework has to teach. A federal judge ruled the 2025 cancellation of roughly $600 million in teacher-training grants unlawful, though no money comes back and the order itself is not yet readable. Texas SBEC votes today on the Chapter 229 accountability rewrite and opens two further certification rule actions. Georgia is at eight checks with no posted result. The accreditor comment window closes Monday.

    Business-day counts below exclude federal holidays (Columbus Day 10-12, Veterans Day 11-11, Thanksgiving 11-26).

    ACT

    US — H.R. 7890, Science of Reading Act of 2026 — ACT 76, NEW. The House passed H.R. 7890 on Wednesday 2026-09-16 by voice vote under suspension of the rules, as amended. The engrossed text was read in full this run. It amends the Elementary and Secondary Education Act's comprehensive-literacy provisions (20 U.S.C. 6641–6644) in four ways: it provides that "comprehensive literacy instruction" does not include the use of a three-cueing model; it defines "science of reading" in statute (phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and writing as essential components, plus background knowledge, oral language and the reading-writing connection) and defines "three-cueing model" as teaching word recognition primarily from meaning, syntax or visual cues, or from visual memory; it requires a state applying for a Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant to describe how its literacy plan aligns to the science of reading, and conditions the grant priority on that alignment; and it applies the same condition to both subgrant priorities. It appropriates nothing, applies only to funds awarded on or after enactment, and carries rules of construction preserving IDEA, Section 504 and ADA rights and barring federal officials from directing curriculum or instruction. Stage: engrossed. Per the GPO bill-status record, introduced 2026-03-12 by Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN-9) with 3 cosponsors, ordered reported 33-0 on 03-17, reported as amended 06-29 (H. Rept. 119-717), Union Calendar No. 623. Relay angle: a federal statutory definition of the science of reading, with three-cueing excluded, becomes the reference point state literacy and educator-preparation rules converge on — including the New York teacher-preparation literacy rules up for adoption in October that Relay's New York programs must meet. Response window: none formal; the Senate has no companion identified and nothing scheduled, which is the open period for comment from preparation providers. Next step: decide whether Relay states a position while the bill sits in the Senate, and confirm our literacy coursework is documentably free of three-cueing practice. verified 2026-09-18 (full text and bill-status record read raw). Note: Education Week and WBIW date the passage September 17; the primary record says September 16 and that is what is recorded. Evidence coverage: The 74 on Ohio's first year under a science-of-reading mandate (Ohio is outside Relay's jurisdictions; attached as evidence, not as a tracked item).

    Teacher-training grant cancellations ruled unlawful — TRACK 72 (scored 72, held at TRACK by the unverified-primary cap), NEW. Per the Associated Press via WBUR, read raw this run: U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley in Massachusetts ruled Thursday 2026-09-17 that the Education Department's February 2025 directive cancelling about $600 million in teacher-training grants violated federal law and was arbitrary and capricious. AP reports the judge found the Department skipped the law's notice-and-comment requirements and failed to weigh reliance interests, quoting the order that "the reliance interests are many, substantial, and deep-rooted." The ruling does not restore the money — AP reports the judge wrote that recovery must be pursued in the Court of Federal Claims. AP states the directive stripped the majority of funding from the Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development programs, affecting more than 100 programs, and that eight Democratic-led states sued. Also carried by the Boston Globe. What is not verified: the order itself was not read. The CourtListener docket and search APIs returned "Authentication credentials were not provided," its public docket pages for the two matching case records returned server errors, and mass.gov returns HTTP 403 to plain clients. The case caption and docket number are therefore not recorded. Relay angle: TQP and SEED are the two federal programs Relay is structurally eligible for, and the same two whose new award slate the Department said on September 9 it would announce shortly. Next step: read the order when a public copy is reachable. attributed 2026-09-18 (AP); primary court record not read.

Both attached as coverage to the existing row.

    • AEI's Michael Horn argues the binding constraint on ed-tech tutoring is the learning model, not the technology (09-17) — attached as coverage to the AI-tutoring trials row, consistent with its engagement finding.

    New Jersey

    • A3056 would establish a New Jersey Student Teacher Scholarship Program — SCAN 49, NEW. Introduced 2026-01-13 and referred to the Assembly Education Committee, with a single history entry and no action since. It surfaced today only because the bill's detail record was refreshed — not because anything happened. Tracked as the New Jersey entry in the student-teaching-stipend family alongside Pennsylvania's operating program and Georgia's failed HB310.

    • A2534 'Jersey Strong Public Service Scholarship Program' — SCAN 49, NEW. Reported from the Assembly Higher Education Committee 09-17 and re-referred. The bill text was read this run: up to $25,000 toward two academic years after one year of full-time work in a shortage public-service sector, up to $50,000 after two years — applicable only at a public institution of higher education in New Jersey, so Relay students could not use it even if public schools land on the Commissioner of Labor's shortage list (the bill says the list "may include employment in hospitals or public schools"). Applicants must be recent New Jersey high-school graduates. Ecosystem interest only, as a possible paraprofessional-to-credential pipeline. The sweep reported the committee vote as 6-0; the LegiScan history records the report and referral but not the tally, so the count is attributed and not confirmed.

    • A1646 (timelines for the Commissioner's review of annual certified audits from approved private schools for students with disabilities) was reported out of committee with amendments to second reading 09-17 — verified from the LegiScan history, noted on the existing New Jersey fiscal-oversight row.

    • Literacy continuation grants (COACH, FOCUS K-3) — applications due 09-22, 2 business days.

    Indiana

    • Voucher enrollment tops 80,000 and tilts upmarket — SCAN 34, NEW. Per Chalkbeat Indiana (09-17, read raw) on new state data: growth slowed for a second year, adding about 4,000 students to reach roughly 80,000; for the first time more Choice Scholarships went to households above $100,000 than below, with about 7,000 going to families earning more than $200,000. Income limits were removed entirely effective July 2026, so universal eligibility will not show in the data until next year.

    Tennessee

    • Sixty percent of Tennessee assistant principals want the principalship — SCAN 46, NEW. Per an Annenberg EdWorkingPaper (Moyer and Goldring, September 2026, abstract read raw) using the 2024 Tennessee Educator Survey: encouragement from their own principal and early-career status are the strongest predictors of aspiring to the principalship; Black assistant principals are more likely to aspire than white ones, concentrated among Black men; high-school assistant principals less likely than elementary and middle. Relevant to the National Principal Academy Fellowship and principal-supervisor partnerships, and a companion to the board's earlier Tennessee finding on licensed leaders who are not actually available to lead. Working paper, not peer-reviewed; held at SCAN by the commentary ceiling.

    TRACK

    Federal

    • H.R. 8747 'K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act of 2026' — TRACK 53, NEW (board gap). Introduced 2026-05-12 by Rep. Randy Fine (R-FL); the House Education and Workforce Committee's July 21 release (read raw) lists it among ten bills advanced at that markup. The introduced text (read in full this run; one operative section) amends four allowable-use provisions of ESEA Title IV, Part A — state and local, student instruction and educator activities — to add instruction in, and giving teachers, paraprofessionals, librarians, specialized instructional support personnel and administrators the knowledge and skills to use and teach, artificial intelligence "safely, effectively, and responsibly, including through professional development." No new money; it widens what existing Title IV-A dollars may buy. No reported (RH) text is on govinfo, so the committee release is the only record of the vote; no floor scheduling, no Senate companion found. Relay angle: educator AI professional development would become an explicit allowable federal use, a purchasable category for Relay's Teacher Professional Education line; it is also the only federal AI-in-schools bill past committee, unlike H.R. 10315 (introduced only). Surfaced by the sweep (Opus); the July action predates the tracker's federal-bill wiring. Leader brief written. verified 2026-09-17.

    Federal

    • AEI, 'Pedagogy of the Progressives' — SCAN 39, NEW. Per AEI (Daniel Buck, published 09-09; web page and PDF read raw): a review of over 400 readings from 75 courses at eight graduate schools of education finds the programs "deeply partisan"; the author states the sample is neither representative nor comprehensive. The recommendations to states: eliminate financial incentives for graduate degrees of limited demonstrated value, tie ed-school funding and accreditation to measurable outcomes, expand alternative certification pathways, and push intellectual diversity within graduate schools of education. Relay is in the sector the report targets; two of the four recommendations match levers already moving in ED's accreditor-recognition and Title II report-card proposals.

    • NACIQI fall meeting — SCAN 44, window day: the written-statement and oral-comment request deadline (09-16) has passed; meeting 09-23/24 (4 bd), six accreditor renewals on the agenda.

    • Per The 74, Instruction Partners' "AI in Action Learning Tour" initial findings — 20 student-facing AI products observed in 16 school systems across seven states; general-purpose chatbots judged the biggest threat to student thinking, targeted tools such as Khanmigo and Quill the strongest learning experiences — attached as coverage to the AI-evidence row (now 15 items).

    New York

    • Federal scholarship tax credit opt-in — SCAN 46, NEW. Per Chalkbeat New York (read raw), a coalition of union officials and civil-rights leaders urged Governor Hochul on 09-16 to reverse her plan to opt New York into the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit (Internal Revenue Code section 25F; from January 2027, a dollar-for-dollar credit for donations up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations funding private tuition, tutoring and other costs). Her office says it is waiting for Treasury regulations, expected later this month, to check for "poison pills." The NYSUT release (read raw; surfaced by the sweep, Opus and Codex) names the speakers: NYSUT's Melinda Person, AFT's Randi Weingarten, the NAACP New York State Conference's L. Joy Williams. Primary check: the IRS participating-state list ("as of September 14, 2026", page updated 09-16) shows 30 states that have made an advance election for 2027 — Colorado, Georgia, Indiana, Tennessee and Texas among Relay's states — and New York is not on it; nor are CT, DE, IL, NJ, PA, RI or DC. The second live opt-in fight in a Democratic-governor Relay state after Illinois; the Treasury regulations are the trigger for both.

    Connecticut

    • Blue-Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Accountability — SCAN 44, NEW. Per the Governor's commission page (read raw; sweep lead: Codex): Executive Order 26-3 (04-16) tasked the commission with "a top-to-bottom overhaul of how the state funds its public schools," with a final report of recommendations due 2027-01-15. The full Commission meets today at 10:00 am in the Legislative Office Building with the Education Cost Sharing working session held in-person (agenda "coming soon" at run time); parallel working sessions run on accountability (09-22, 10-13), the choice system (09-16, 10-01, 10-08) and special education (09-24). Public listening sessions and a survey are open. The formula that funds every district Relay's Connecticut partners operate in; the January report sets the 2027 session's education-finance agenda.
